The real magic of this forest is the trail system and being able to link up trails together, such as the Longleaf Greenway trail with Eastern Lake trail, making it an ideal trail system more suited toward distance runners or cyclists who can cover big mileage, than hikers.  In fact, a majority of the trail system is on fire road/double track, which unfortunately takes away some of the immersion, not having enough singletrack.  That said, the trails here are amply marked (albeit there are no reliable mile marker signage indicating how far you've gone between points).  It's terrific having such a large protected area right here on the Emerald Coast, where future growth and overpopulation in a nature sensitive area is often overlooked.

When we tried hiking here a year ago (maybe slightly more) the bridge was out on the singletrack hiking trail.  Guess they never rebuilt it and the map was never updated.  From what I understand the main 'trail' is the gravel double track starting from the frisbee golf area and goes to an adjacent trailhead (off Roscoe Road).  It is halfway paved, with some feeder fireroad trails.  Park also has a canoe launch, which is a short paddle into Wolf Bay (be warned the water is quite swampy and stinky, though.  You will want to wash your boat off after).  The park also has a huge field which was nice play area for kids and dogs, but since they added the archery, I'm not sure if you're allowed into it since it's inline with the targets...
likes: Huge field for kids and dogs

reviews_attraction.text: While the spring is absolutely beautiful, and almost always clear, this place can be a human zoo at times...uncontrollable kids, jammed pack with people, and loud music.  It was also setup as self-service honesty pay station when we went, and I'm pretty sure we were the only ones who actually paid.  The two hiking trails can be scenic, but are short.  There is a larger plot of state land on the southern side of Interstate 10 still considered part of Ponce de Leon State Recreation Area, which includes a second spring called Jackson Spring, but it is completely inaccessible as far as I am aware.  It's too bad there is no trail system connecting Ponce de Leon Springs with Jackson Spring.

Despite having never lived anywhere near Tallahassee, we first started coming to Tom Brown annually almost 20 years ago for mountain bike races.  Then I eventually left the sport and years passed.  Several years ago I made the first return to Tom Brown for model RC racing and it brought back many memories.  This past week I made another return to Tom Brown while in Tallahassee and it brought back even more memories.  The most amazing thing of the last 17 years is just how little the park has changed, while still making many improvements.  I'd love to return with a bike and ride the Greenway addition which previously did not exist years ago.

While this museum is no comparison to the Naval Air Museum in Pensacola in size, it is still definitely worth checking out if you're in the area.  This museum operates off donations, meaning it's free entry to all ages!  Most of the aircraft exhibits are outdoors, but there are some great indoor stuff to see.  There is also a gift shop on-site.  We came here when I found out there was an SR-71 on display. The only thing thing negative I can say is most of the outdoor displays were in desperate need of repainting, which the Blackbird was currently undergoing repaint while we visited.  Definitely worth the visit if you are in the area.

This is a unique little park.  We stopped and walked here while exploring takeout options for kayaking on Turkey Creek (we're from out of town).  This park is what I'd call more "commercialized", with a boardwalk throughout the entire length, ramps for swimming, and even staffed personnel, trying to increase accessibility for everyone.  It's quite easy to walk the entire length.  I can only imagine how packed this place is during the hotter summer months.  On-site bathrooms with running water is a nice convenience, and there is a giant sheltered pavilion at the entrance.

This is a very nice seasonal park run by Jackson County.  It is clean and we'll maintained.  Be aware of a couple things before your visit that may help make up your mind: This is a seasonal park and only runs Memorial Day to Labor Day.  The swimming areas are  monitored by lifeguards, so you must follow by their rules.  It can be *very* crowded here during peak days and times.  The springs part is very select - there is one major fissure, while most of the swimming area is sandy bottom, so you may or may not be impressed if you wanted to snorkel.

A quaint little park.  Roadside parking is minimal.  I would say there is probably a quarter mile of trails in total, with thick shaded canopy over most of it.  Trails are not marked, but it's near impossible to get lost.  There are plenty of benches throughout.  Lack of signage along the trails can make interpretation hard, as visually there is not much to see unless you know what you're looking at.  While we wouldn't go out our way to come here again, this is a good way to kill some time, particularly if you're waiting for the next ferry.

This is a fun stop if you happen to be in the area, but having now seen it, I would probably not bother coming back unless it was to show someone else.  This is mostly a glorified photo op.  The stones are made from fiberglass and there is nothing else to really see or do here, aside from the occasional dinosaur on your drive in.  If you were planning on continuing your trip down to the marina to see Lady in the Lake, you might reconsider...there is no real public viewing area to easily see her.  This would be a fun trip for children.

Cons: Packed, packed, packed!!!  The beach here is busy and overcrowded, but a lot of that has to do with the fact the main beach is very small.  And we came in October, not summer! This park is also one of the most expensive Florida State Parks at $8/vehicle.
Pros: Absolutely gorgeous emerald clear water.  The jetty also provides excellent snorkel opportunities.
This would be 5/5 if it weren't so packed.  I come to state parks because I want to be with nature, not a beach party with cigarette smokers and loud radios.

This is a terrific state park nestled within the much larger Blackwater State Forest recreation area.  While this park is primarily for swimming and paddlers, you can use the parking area for the nearby Florida Trail hiking.  If you visit in the summer months you'll find loads of children swimming, but if you visit in the cooler winter months, you'll find an empty and truly picturesque look at what Florida's vast pine forests once looked like.  The showers and bathrooms here are very clean and well maintained.

Beautiful park that is almost reminiscent of a stereotypical park from a movie or novel.  You'll see people walking dogs and children out playing.  A sidewalk meanders around the entire perimeter of the lake (which I believe was technically formed from an old sinkhole year ago).  Paths lead right to historic downtown Defuniak Springs, while picturesque houses line adjacent to the water's edge.  There is a visitor center in the old train Depot, as well as a self-guided tour along the area.

Beautiful Gulf beaches, sand dunes, intracoastal, Pensacola pass, Fort, picnic areas, etc.  Whether you plan on swimming or just walking around, there's a lot to see here.

Only criticism I have is the general store near the campground was closed in the middle of July, despite NPS website mentioning it!  To leave the park from the far end, find a place to get a snack (closest is Tom Thumb gas station), and come back in to the far end of the park is about a 45-minute round trip drive.

It's what you make of it!  This can either be a 10 minute walk-through or a two-hour adventure.  This is a self-guided tour through one man's personal collection, with everything from historic cars, to random sports memorabilia, to old typewriters.  While it's certainly not the largest collection nor most immaculately cared for, it was worth the visit and experience.  It was a great way to spend a couple hours just perusing the museum when in town.

This is a nice little park to stop off at and have a look at the intracoastal.  The barrier island directly to the West of this park is Air Force property, which offers a unique view of what the undeveloped barrier island looks like in its natural setting.  The biggest negative for this park is definitely the bathrooms...they were filthy and in desperate need of repairs.

Worth the walk for some great views and cool ocean breeze during the heat.  A one-time entrance is only $1.25, which is a great value.  Rules against fishermen here are pretty strict, which make it more pleasant to those who have no interest in fishing.  Located right next to the Casino Beach Bar and Grill (although you'll find better dining options out nearby).

This is mostly an "events" type park, where special events get held. There isn't much to do of you come here on a regular day, except​ have a picnic or walk-around (although the park sits adjacent to busy Highway 98/59 intersection and is filled with noise of cars).  Bathrooms are clean.  Checkout the adjacent museum for cool things to see.

One of my favorite places in the entire state.  Blackwater WMA is miles of pine scrub forest with some of purest sandy bottom rivers in the country flowing right through it.  There are hiking trails, equestrian center/trails, mountain bike trails, multiple recreation areas, kayaking/canoeing, camping, among other activities.

One of the nicest little parks in Baldwin County.  Good for picnicking, small children to play, and taking walks alongside the small creek that flows adjacent to it.  A sidewalk connects this park with downtown Silverhill.

There are a surprising amount of aircraft nestled in this hangar, and many of the aircraft are in much better condition than some static displays at other museums.  This hangar is a nice compliment to the Battleship.
Very nice Pier - clean and well maintained, not overcrowded with inconsiderate fishermen. You are given a hand stamp for same day re-entry.  Open 24 hours.  Refreshing sea breeze.
A very small park with limited access to the water.  Not much here to do except have a picnic or enjoy the view.  Almost no shade in afternoons.

I wanted to visit this place just because of the building! The museum is housed in the old city and it looks like a castle! The museum doesn’t have tons of hands on displays, but there is still enough hands on that my 7 year old gave it five stars. All three kids loved the old type writer set up so they could use it. There was videos here and there throughout the museum and so much information! The very rare (1 of 8 left) Jones Six automobile was my favorite. There was information about the city over the years, old toys, exquisite silver plated items, old furniture, aviation, and more. We spent three hours and barely saw everything, but were getting too hungry to keep learning. The lady working in the gift shop was super friendly and helped us with other places to see in the area. The only bummer was that they didn’t have a souvenir magnet of the museum in the shop (that’s our thing).

Playground is great. Camping was bad. The free camp is only 1 night bow and then $20 a night. No fire ring, picnic table, water hook up, electrical fuse (they have electricity but it's always hot), and it's right next to train tracks and an industrial complex. I wouldn't pay to be kept up all night by machinery and trains. They told us they are trying to earn money to make improvements, which is backwards. You can't charge people a bunch of money so you can make improvements, that's not how business works. Make the improvements, then raise you rates. With the trains and industry right there I don't see it ever being worth what they want to charge. If you want to take your kids to the playground or just have to stop, then this place will work.

This is an immersive historic experience with period actors! The buildings are old historic buildings that have been moved onto the site. They even have the first house built in Wichita by Europeans. The actors were friendly and informative. My big regret is that we went on a super hot Friday, when we should have went on the weekend. They have more going on during the weekend. Still a great way for the kids to learn about pioneer times. Some of the buildings have ac, luckily because it was 105 when we visited. The actors were wearing full cotton suits and still smiling! That is professionalism at its finest.

For a free museum, this place is amazing. We parked for free in the park and walked over. Not a single hands on activity for kids to do. Nice collection of art to view though. Kids enjoyed the arms and armor display. Staff wasn't very friendly and I got different instructions about my backpack at different entrances. Sculpture garden is weak. They start closing the place before closing time, so don't save the third floor for last. Surreal section of art is lacking. Nice antiquities section. Good variety in the museum.

Interesting place to learn about the Federal Reserve. Some hands on activities for kids. It was free and everyone could take a bag of shredded cash. It's a working reserve bank, so adults need IDs to get in and you have to go through a security check point. Free parking next to the bank. I thought it was ironic that the gift shop couldn't break my $100 bill. It was neat watching the workers handle huge amounts of cash near the vaults. We learned something's and enjoyed our visit.

$12 for water and electric camping. They have a dump station. Camp host was friendly enough. We met some nice locals and another full time family, so it was an enjoyable experience. We walked across the historic bridge and up the road. Saw turtles and frogs on the walk. My son caught a brown anole in camp. Lots of mosquitoes, but it is next to a swamp. We would stay here again. My only complaint is you have to reserve, we prefer to just get a site on arrival.

Great campground. I little tight for our 30 foot trailer, I wouldn't recommended this place for large trailers or class A's. We managed to fit though and this place was amazing. Super quite at night, with almost no one around. Lots of wild animals including deer and bobcats. Security drives through, a little too fast for a campground. They have a dump station , though it is the kind where you have to block the road to use it.

So the good- nice sites, descent prices, we saw deer in the camp, close to the city yet still quiet, nice bath house and some of the staff are friendly.
The bad- over priced wood, guy with leaf blower making noise for 8 hours a day (on a windy day which was silly), steep grade to get to the camp. Avoid Oak Park road like the plague. No junior Ranger program.

So some good and some bad, hence the 3 stars.
dislikes: Lack of activities (no junior Ranger program)

reviews_attraction.text: The campground is nice. Has power and water with a dump station to hit up on the way out. There was trash all around, we cleaned some up but there was still more. Not sure what the volunteers did, we never saw them in action. The lake was nice, though it was high so the fishing pier was underwater. Peaceful camp just outside the city. Verizon phone signal was good.

Great place to learn about Lincoln. Staff was friendly and informative. They had two videos, one was good and the other just mediocre. Our kids did Junior Ranger and earned a badge (just a standard one with the park name), a sticker and a temporary tattoo. We enjoyed the tour of Lincoln's House and the two small museums they have on site.

This place is amazing! It has free parking and all the rides are included in the general admission price. There is a lot to see and we spent an entire day and didn't quite see everything. Don't spend all your time inside, the rocket garden and military vehicles scattered around the ground are interesting too.

Very cool look out tower. Two playgrounds for the kids. It would have gotten five stars, except garbage was all over the place and there were no drinking fountains near the playground. Castle look out tower is neat though and you can go up to the top. No explanation sign saying why it was built or when.

Although the Rangers are just walking around so you have to hunt them up, they are friendly and helpful. Our kids did the Junior Ranger program and earned a cool badge. The museum costs money, but the memorial is free (parking nearby is $2 per hour for up to 2 hours or $5 at a lot).

It's a busy National Park Visitor Center, but the Rangers and Volunteers are awesome. There is a short walk with signs about the native plants of the area, a short film about the native people with a unique ending, and a gift shop with more magnet options than we have ever seen!

$20 a night to camp and we got the only full hook up site! You have to pay at the courthouse. There is a small amount of noise at night from the distillery, but it isn't too load. The play ground was a hit with our kids.

A great place to spend the afternoon. We caught a show about parrots and the kids were allowed to pet and hold the birds! We thoroughly enjoyed our visit even though it was winter and two of the exhibits were closed.

They have facilities for changing. It's surrounded by industrial complexes. You can see Chicago way off in the distance if it's clear outside, but not close enough for pictures. Not the best beach by far though.

It was packed. They don't honor out of state museums for all. ASTC only covered 4 people and this place is pricey at $17 a person. The gift shop was expensive too. Kids had fun though and that's what counts.

So the bad part is lots of broken displays. Good part is the hands on learning and they had experiments setup for the kids to do. It has a good layout and is very large. Parking costs $8 or $6 for members.

Excellent beach. Watched seals swim all day. Not very many seashells, but tons of cool rocks. Nice sand and National Seashore facilities. (As a cautionary note don't swim with the seals, ask a ranger why)

We had a great time trying to find diamonds.
Didn't find any, but got to keep some cool rocks. Kids had a blast and we're happy with what we found. Staff was helpful and we could bring a picnic lunch.
It has a splash pad, which was fun for the kids. There was a lot of trash around. I wish the locals took better care of the park, but still a nice place to visit.
The lighthouse is a great historic site, but it is expensive to get into. The state park is a better place to get pictures of it.
Some of it was being worked on, but it was nice still. Junior Ranger badge is cool and volunteers were super friendly.
Great place to see. View of the bay and skyline. Hard to get good photos from here though because of the crowds.

Going in on a cold Monday morning, I started out pretty disappointed that after 15-20 minutes into the one-way loop around the park, I hadn't seen any animals! Between Covid and the cold, several exhibits were closed or empty. But eventually, I got to the good stuff - the seals and bears, big cats, and elephants. It takes about 2 hours to go around the whole loop, and I decided to do a quicker walk-through again to see if any extra animals had shown up and was able to see the fun penguins and see the tiger better. It was less crowded the second time around as well.

Keep in mind, the dining options are very limited right now, when I was there, only one snack counter at the front and the African Outpost over halfway through were open, and the Outpost only had grab and go sandwiches and some hot soups available. The carousel is open but not the train or the tram.

In all, I was able to see 36ish different animals and only 13 animals/sections (like the whole Herpaquarium) that weren't available. Here's what was closed when I went: the whole Asian section with the Tapir, Babirusa, Sumatran Tiger, Siamang, and Orangutan; a corner with the Island Pavilion (I'm not sure what's in there) and the Komodo Dragon; the HerpAquarium, the Metazoo was closed, not sure what that is either (I'm not local) and no stage show there; the lorikeet landing and walkabout; the Sea Eagle Aviary was closed but you could kinda see them from the outside; no shows for the seals; no pigmy hippos, naked mole rats, or lemurs.

But I DID get to see: tons of tiny, noisy blue-black penguins (but only on my second go-round), black swans (not even sure they're a real exhibit!) plus ducks and turtles in the lake; a lynx I want to take home, two bald eagles, a cougar, a very cool maned wolf, a sloth in a bucket, a leopard, a flock/flamboyance of flamingos (at a distance - I think there may have been other birds in there too), there was a blue macaw but he stayed hidden, a llama-type guy (I couldn't see the sign), some type of sea birds? I spotted two, 2 harbour seals and a grey seal (or the other way around? - they are SUPER fun to watch and put on a show themselves), a HUGE brown bear, a polar bear, a snow leopard, a tiger, a silverback gorilla and some other apes (I'm not sure if they were all silverbacks, I guess so - they were all kept inside), 3 fat meerkats, 3 sleepy colobus monkeys (inside enclosure, not out and about), 3 zebras, 2 camels (no rides), 3 elephants including baby Fitz (all of which were getting training at the time, which was cool to see), 3 lions (1 male, 2 female), 4 types of exotic cattle (sorry, I forgot the names), 2 giraffe, 2 white vultures (plus a lot of Canada Geese) a sleepy rhinoceros, and 2 inquisitive warthogs.

One of the greatest things about this zoo is how close you can get to the animals and feel how big they are! They often come right up to the glass or fence though they have big enclosures and can stay far away if they like. Also the styling of the place is great - it's very successful on theming, like a theme park would do, especially around the Glacier Run area with the seals and bears.

I'll have to come back to see it in full force post covid and maybe in warmer weather. I'd love to see the pygmy hippos and ride the train! But my ticket, even with parking was only around $15 so I ended up more than happy with what I got out of it. Highly recommended!

OK, off the top, this is a really fantastic, interesting, emotional, important, informational facility. The presentations are top-notch with engaged, friendly people. You definitely should visit, especially if you have kids, it's really fun. I particularly like the presentation for the Atlantis space shuttle.

I'm docking it a star because I don't know that it functions super well as a whole. Instead of one building, or even a main entrance from where you'd branch out, it's a collection of buildings, sort of a hodge-podge. I think my complaint really is what Disney would call "wayfinding" - I never really knew where I was going or what I was about to see. I stayed confused the majority of the day, I'd walk into things not realizing what they were at all.

I managed my way through the day mainly by following the times guide and just going to what was next. And that way, I'm pretty sure I saw everything from the back to the front. I was there from 8:30 am (for a launch) to 3 pm. Had the bus tours been running, and maybe a few other things that were shut down, I'm not sure I could have done it all in a day, especially at their current hours of 10-4. (I'm not sure if that's seasonal, covid-related, or normal.)

And speaking of the launch - I got there a little before 8:30, they let the short line in at 8:30, then the launch was scheduled for 9:13. Unfortunately, they aborted the launch at 18 seconds to go...so even if one is scheduled, it may not happen. Folks weren't super great about wearing their masks or keeping their distance, either. But on the whole, during the day, there were so few people that keeping distance was usually easy.

So here are a few things that felt weird to me: First of all, I had been security screened for the launch but went back to my car to put stuff away and had to get re-screened to get back in. This time, they objected to a hard plastic "my kitty" keychain I have and made me leave it in my car. It is a self-defense item (I guess I can poke someone's eyes with it) but I wouldn't call it a weapon and I was annoyed at having to go back to the car a second time to put it away and be screened three times that morning. Once inside, my first stop was a guided tour of the rocket garden, but the presenter was so hard to hear that I didn't get much from it. Later, I looked on the time guide and saw a "walking tour" of the Atlantis shuttle at a certain time. I went there at that time, saw the fantastic presentation, then when inside with the shuttle, there was an employee there talking about the shuttle and I assumed that was the tour, but eventually I (and several others) realized it was a VIP guided tour and we got kicked off. Walking into the Mars presentation, and the launch simulation, I literally had no idea what was going on until it happened. I guess this isn't too unusual but usually you get a map or there's a sign out front that sort of indicates what to expect. And maybe there used to be maps handed out - I found the app to be less than helpful. And the wifi in the park seemed to either keep disconnecting or it was on a time limit. I kept being asked to sign back in.

I love house tours and this place was great! It has an interesting history, characters, and location and it's beautifully preserved and presented. I think a Christmas tour would be super fun here.

You start at the red brick store/old post office to buy your ticket then go out back to start the guided tour. They give you an overview of the three owners and walk you down a preserved section of the original Unicoi Turnpike to the grand house and through each room of the house. We got there when it opened at 10 and it was just the two of us until another family joined before we entered the house.

The house itself is pretty awesome! Lots of little tidbits that they'll tell you about on the tour, I don't want to spoil it. The whole thing may have taken maybe an hour? Then you are free to roam the rest of the grounds, which aren't huge, but there are several outbuildings to check out--the spring house, the massive dairy barn, the two-level horse and animal barn, etc.

Across the modern turnpike is an Indian mound that pre-dates the Cherokees, which one of the owners leveled off and built a gazebo on. You can't walk over to it (it's in the middle of a cow pasture) but you can take pictures from the farm side, or there's a  pull off of the road. Our guide told us that it's the 2nd most-photographed site in Georgia but I have my doubt. Nevertheless, I took many pictures of it!

The store has a great selection of local artisan goods, books, shirts and so forth, and there's a nice bathroom in here. Parking is adjacent up a set of stairs or a ramp, or you can walk in from Helen from the Hardman Heritage Trail which has more informational signs. There's even a scavenger hunt on the map of the farm that has to do with the trail. If you complete it, I think you get a little prize.

It's a great park but don't be swayed if you hear it's "the grand canyon of Texas." It's much, much smaller than that. And you can drive right down into it and drive around the bottom! Before that, there's a great visitor's center with a small museum, bathrooms, and lots of art and books to buy and a very nice employee/volunteer. Down in the canyon, there are loads of trails and areas for camping and a canteen for sandwiches and ice cream. (Both are pretty good - and good pickles on the fixings bar.)

On my visit, there were TONS of people out and Texans aren't masking anymore so I didn't hit the popular lighthouse trail, plus I wasn't prepared enough with water. In fact, there are a multitude of ways to die out here! It's dry and hot and hikes might be longer than you think. I ended up parking in the TEXAS musical lot and walking up half a mile of the CCC trail to the Goodnight Peak overlook. The views are great up here but be careful of the edge and the wind! I think you can also take a relatively more level path from a point halfway up the canyon drive to the same place. And it seemed that folks who want to hike the CCC do it from the top down - park a car at the bottom, then take another car to the top by the visitor center and hike it down instead of up. (That's what I'd do anyway.) The side trail off to Goodnight Peak isn't marked but it's clearly a trail with steps so it's not too hard to find.

What a great park! I had no idea what to expect when I came and mainly planned to see the giants (not really even knowing what they are.) There is a $10 donation and they'll direct you to the visitor center to start the walk. There are giant yellow footprints to help you get started. The giants themselves are three wooden troll-like figures - HUGE - that pre-covid you could walk up and touch and play with (though not climb on.) On the walk, you'll come across the first, and smallest, one peering at his reflection in the lake, then across the field there is Mama with lots of playthings around her (all roped off now, sadly) then keep going to find big sister playing in a field of rocks (you can still climb on the rocks.)

I continued on around the lake loop and sort of wandered back to the visitor center - you aren't supposed to go back the way you came - the path through the field is one way, so I more or less walked along the road and was able to see most of the rest of the areas of interest.

Afterwards, I drove out to the tree canopy walk - it's an elevated platform overlooking the valley and the forest, and it's a great photo spot during the fall.

The Forest Giants trail/walk and the tree canopy walk are both easy but in the end I did do a lot of walking (mainly to get back to my car) so make sure to bring water and/or snacks.

This is a review of the Mingo Trail and as a visitor, not a local - it's rated as hard on the map but I wouldn't call it more than moderate. It has some elevation change so there are plenty of ups and downs. If you start the loop at the north end near the Mingo Lodge, I went right on the loop and I think that was the best way to go. Then all your ups are on wider, gentler slopes, and all your downs are on the steeper paths coming back. Trail markers are EXCELLENT, I doubted one once and ended up on a Seiberling Nature Realm trail that wasn't indicated on the trail map at all. It's a 3ish mile loop, taking about an hour and a half to walk.

There is a parking lot right at the head of the trail by the lodge, but when I was there today, the road to it was closed. There *were* cars in the lot and people in the field though, so I don't know if they were there for some official purpose or just drove around the gate in the road (or undid the lock - I noticed a padlock in the gate but it wasn't locked....) I ended up parking around the corner at the Shadowfield parking and taking the jogging trail to the Mingo trailhead.

I suspect this is more of an Airbnb as opposed to a museum--and it looks like it would be cool to stay here. I was trying to visit the museum, I knew it closed at 3, I showed up at 2:30 and found a note on the door saying you have to call a phone number if you want to visit. I called the number but no one answered. There were people inside, I could tell, but they didn't answer the phone or my knocks. I fiddled around for a bit, put some books in the nearby little free library and plotted the next steps in my afternoon when an employee came out at about 2:50. I asked her if the museum was open, she said they really stopped admitting folks at 2:30 and I said I called but no one picked up and she told me to stick around for the manager to come out and I should tell her. I waited for another 10 minutes but got tired of waiting and left.

Overall, my impression is that this is mainly an Airbnb with a small museum downstairs you might be able to see for $10. I could be wrong, but I was definitely put off by the experience.

This is a really excellent museum, and ties together all the civil rights movements around the country in well-done displays. It includes the rooms and balcony where MLK was shot and killed but there is so much more to this museum. It's a fantastically well-laid out timeline from African slavery to celebrations of black joy and art.

I will say, I was there on a Thursday morning in March, soon after it had reopened, and it was really crowded. After months of not seeing people, I remembered how annoying they can be... The path through the museum is smaller rooms and down hallways - it's pretty impossible to stay 6 feet away from others, though they've roped off seating areas and other markers, it's just a hard place to distance in.

DON'T skip the gift shop! It's an amazing store in its own right with beautiful items for your home. I ended up with a pretty pair of gloves that I never thought I'd find in a civil rights museum.

Well worth the time and cost.

This was a really lovely experience! Due to Covid, I pretty much had the place to myself on a Wednesday around noon. The collections are well organized and there is a lot of variety. If you don't like what's in one room, just move to the next. It's all worth considering. Three floors situated around a beautiful atrium.

During Covid, they are taking your temp at the entrance and the two people I saw were wearing masks. I had to pay admission in the gallery gift shop. Afterwards, I chatted with the security/temp-taking guard and the information desk/admissions lady and they were super friendly and suggested nearby Bake My Day for lunch which didn't let me down!

All in all, a very nice time in a beautiful location.

This is a great experience! Especially as an add-on to the Civil Rights Museum. The museum isn't currently open, so I'm visiting what I can and the sculpture is well done and powerful in its own right.

I did get a little hustled though by a homeless man - he told me "those signs won't tell you anything, let me tell you everything" and launched into a barely understandable spiel that lasted for a few minutes. I didn't mind (and didn't feel threatened) but unless you want to part with some cash, you might want to tell him you don't have any up front.

I love this area! Tons of paths to walk around and look at the water or sculptures, loads of open areas, benches, picnic tables, grills, bathrooms, a playground, and I love most the swings. There's a whole area that just swings and there are even lights strung up, so I guess those can come on at night. All with a great view of the river and the bridges. And sculptural quality of the hills in some areas can sort of divide up groups so you can feel like you have a section to yourself without seeing other families.

A really incredible house tour, especially for the price. One of my favorite house tours that I've ever done! The woodworking skill, especially the staircase and the first floor area is just astonishing. Our tour guide was really knowledgeable and did a really good job of trying to keep all parties socially distanced from each other. The house is currently decorated for Halloween - lots of candles and black fabric over the mirrors - for an evening candlelight tour they do, which sounds like loads of fun!

For a $4 zoo, it's a nice way to get outside and see some cute animals. The big guys - the lions, tiger, and bear (oh my) sleep most of the time. It's the smaller animals that are worth watching. The monkeys, the donkey, the turkeys, the porcupines, the bobcats and foxes. The badger is really cute during feeding time - or when anyone else is being fed. Only took me about an hour to walk around, and that's because I lingered to watch some animals get fed, which was worth the extra minutes.

It's definitely fun and a must-do experience at least once. But your enjoyment of it greatly depends on your guide. I heard much more fun and interesting facts from passing boats than I heard on my paid ride... Since you can't really pick you guide, I guess it's just hit or miss if you get a good one! They're doing reasonably well during Covid, spacing people out and wearing masks but still, some of the boats were packed pretty tight.

The museum isn't large but it's free and neat to look at. The shop is one of the best I'd been in, and I'd been all over Canyon Road, downtown Santa Fe and Taos. And the guy who owns it is super friendly! It's a little hard to get to right now - there are several streets blocked off nearby due to its proximity to the Capitol building. But it's worth seeking out, if just for the shopping!

You can't walk up to it or around it, since it's in the middle of a huge cow pasture, but there is a pull off with an informational sign and take pictures. During the Hardman Farm tour across the street, they told us it was the 2nd most photographed site in Georgia, after stone mountain. I'm not sure that's true but I did take several pictures!

I mean, it's not much but it's a nice little park and very comprehensive for all the conflicts. I like most the bells that ring every hour (?). I was there around 3:00 and they abruptly cut off at 10 after... but nice music while it lasts and you can even hear it over the traffic. I didn't go inside the building to see if there was more there.

Very well done! Moved me to tears. The only exhibit right now is in the alley where the attacks started, the story told in a very clear timeline with fantastic pictures. Read every word! There may be more to come inside the old bus station, but so far, it's empty. Anniston itself also has some really beautiful architecture as well.

What an amazing free museum! It's on the small side, you can see it in an hour or two unless you really stop to look. I was really taken with one piece made on handmade cotton paper painted black and a photo-realistic image made by poking holes from the back--it is phenomenal! Make sure to look at it close up and from a distance.

This is a great park for walking around and the large-scale sculptures are really amazing. I use this park to take a walk at lunch and have my favorites.

There are no real facilities, though, just a port-a-potty. It can also be pretty muddy after it rains and even dry, good walking shoes are best on the coarse gravel.

I just drove around a little and then got out and walked some of the short trails - beware biting flies!! My main experience came in the gift shop with a very nice chat with the gentleman there and really excellent and interesting local stuff for sale. I'd go back just to go shopping! And armed with bug spray.

This is a great little slice of well-preserved 1930's small southern town court life, with the recreated law offices and the beautiful oval courtroom. The displays are well done and the gift shop is amazing! Just step in there if nothing else. Well worth a trip, especially if you're a reader.

I don't think this place is in operation any more. I drove by to check it out and it just looked like a mostly overgrown field with 3-4 lily ponds and a hidden boardwalk behind it all. I don't know what it used to be but it's hardly anything to look at now.

Cute little park! Maybe not the best sculpture you've ever seen but a great place to be outside. I saw a few families doing a geocaching thing and there were signs for some Holiday-themed scavenger hunt.
A lovely walking path even when it's colder out. I assume it stretches farther but I think you can connect to a much large path system.

The park is located at the steep entrance to a small canyon. There are 2 main trails and many shortcuts created by regular users of the park. The trails are not well maintained and besides a few signs not blazed, which might be a bit confusing but rest assured you cannot get lost. The climb in and out of the canyon is a bit of a workout and not stroller or wheelchair accessible. The trails are adventurous including passing through small waterfalls (wait for some good rain the day before your visit), over riggedy bridges, sharp switchbacks with a 30 feet drop off, end on bluffs and are as much fun as you can find on a trail. A fieldstone dam creates a nice swimming hole that you can reach using a shortcut that starts under the porch of the entrance building. A great variety of wildflowers is located alongside the creek and climbing the opposite side of the canyon, the trail will lead you through Mountain Laurel thickets sprinkled with high blueberry bushes while box elders and big leaf magnolias are abundant throughout the park.  The twilight tunnel is a highpoint of every visit but I realized that I like it better when climbing up than down. Several bluffs in the 40' - 80' height range provide anchor points for repelling.
Best time to go is during wildflower bloom, when blueberries are ripe, rain enhanced waterfalls and creeks, or you want a short hike with densely packed highlights.
likes: Diverse flora (wildflowers, Mountain Laurel, blueberry bushes, box elders, magnolias)

reviews_attraction.text:
The trailhead of the rail-to-trails greenway is formed by a ballpark, dog park, and an interesting looking playground. The parks and trailhead are right at the inviting looking creek with small shoals running over shale.
An old railbed is a perfect location for a trail but since those rails were engineered to avoid curves and slopes, they make for boring hiking trails. Bring your bike and be happy or put on your running shoes for a fast run on a flat, well maintained surface, but bring a podcast when you are hiking or walking.
Starting at the ballpark you quickly reach the intersection of Leora Ave and Stouts Rd where the dog park is. Walking for about 1 mile on the wide and immaculate trail, but way above the creek, you see the first "Creek Trail"  sign. The narrow footpath, something I call a trail, leads you down to the creek where you Tee into a service (dirt) road that is used by ATV enthusiasts (I saw 4  ATVs today). Even though a road, I like this trail better since it is next to the creek, offers several ford crossings that can be a bit daunting after a rain, but don't worry, you don't have to walk through the creek and find your own trail alongside the creek to the next ford. Bring your kids, explore and play.
All in all an afternoon well spent.

Went last March weekend, stayed in a cabin, took tour, paddled, and used the boardwalk extensively.
Cabins are roomy, clean, air-conditioned, and provide all necessities from full-sized kitchen appliances to towels and porch rocking chairs. Plan ahead the next grocery  store is probably 1 h away. I didn't turn on the TV but there is no Wifi or cell reception. If needed there is a phone at the ranger station.
The guided tour in a slowly motoring boat with a very knowledgeable and accommodating ranger was extremely educational and enjoyable.  Highly recommended to get a feel for the swamp and basic information about nature, history, and the big fire.
The boardwalk allows you to visit the swamps and observe and identify wildlife flora and fauna.  I went several times and saw dozens of snakes, gators, frogs, lizards as well as owls, egrets , and plenty of unidentified birds.
Renting a canoe gives you a chance to get even more personal with the local wildlife. Paddling to Billy's Island felt a little adventurous, just enough to make it fun,  and presented plenty of opportunities to photograph wildflowers and gators, gators, gators.
In late March I did not have to use bug spray but sunscreen.

The trail starts out on a gravel road through a clear cut with no shade and not much to look at. The service road has no ruts or elevation but still feels like an obstacle to overcome before you get to the old woods in the canyon. After reaching the creek there is a pretty narrow trail along the rim that can feel a bit challenging and becomes challenging when you are descending to the bottom of the waterfall. The overhang behind the falls is huge and although the fall itself was not very impressive the backdrop made it quite spectacular. If you follow the creek downstream for about a 100 yards you will come to another small creek on the left and a path that follows that side creek to an enchanted  looking, smaller waterfall. We followed the main creek for quite a distance through an old camp side and enjoyed the scenery. A worthwhile trip to not so well known waterfalls.
The gravel road through a clear cut passing an oil derrick led to a one star deduction.

Park at the entrance (under construction in 2019). They do offer kennels for dogs as pets are not allowed in park. You can opt to drive to the upper parking lot and walk a short but informative self guided loop. I highly recommend paying for the grand tour ($16/ per person over 15 years), jump on a shuttle for the last 2.5 miles, and get a guided tour. We ended up with one of the best guided tours that I can remember. Our guide was extremely knowledgeable, well-educated, rooted in science,  and he peppered the tour with thought provoking questions while encouraging questions. During the tour you are "climbing" up a narrow rim trail with no other safety than your own common sense and steadfast walking. Watch your steps and watch your children. Our guide took regular breaks to explain geology, archeology, history, botany, and to let us catch our breath.

Red Mountain, a few miles south of Birmingham, was the premier iron ore source for the hungry furnaces of the Magic City. Today nature and overgrown mine ruins are the beautiful backdrop for this park planned and built for easy access and entertainment. The park features about 12 miles of well maintained trails, zip lines, tree top adventures, picnic areas, tree houses, mining ruins, outlooks, goats, and a big, fenced-in dog park separated into 3 areas for dogs with an issue, small dogs, and big dogs > 40 lb.  You find plenty of destinations to define a turning point and to keep children motivated. The wide trails allow peaceful coexistence of hikers, runners, dog walkers, and bicyclists.
likes: Variety of activities (zip lines, tree top adventures)
Family-friendly (picnic areas, tree houses, destinations for children)
Pet-friendly (dog park, wide trails for dog walkers)

reviews_attraction.text:
If possible try and visit outside peak hours.  I like to see a painting from a few steps away, close up, and from different angles but the popularity of this museum makes it quite difficult to step away without having another visitor getting in between you and the painting.
The exhibit provides sufficient reading material to follow the artist's evolution and the short movie is a  nice reminder of some highpoints.
I liked the frame exhibition that documents her attention to detail. 98 years is a long time and much of her life is not presented or mentioned in the museum. Read a bit more before you go to get your imagination and speculations going.

The trails are well worn, relatively smooth underfoot, clearly marked, and  even under a load of fall leaves you can't miss them. I am fascinated by the rock outcrops and small bluffs, enjoy the small changes in altitude, the meandering creek beds, and am interested in its historical places and features. The park can be accessed from different public roads which allows you to pick a favorite trail or destination and select a starting point that fits your schedule or fitness. There is no dog park but it is a park in an urban setting and you will meet almost as many dogs (on leashes) as hikers.

Nice little park  with dense wildflower populations. ~1 mile loop on a bluff alongside Shades Creek. Park is squeezed into a residential area and from most of the trail houses or yards are visible. Trailhead is blocked by a guard rail on Elder Street but neighbors installed helpful steps to get over the rail. I was very pleasantly surprised by the abundance of wildflowers (early April). Lots of trilium (I saw only cuneatum), rue anemone, woodland phlox, red buckeye, some blue-eyed grass, violets, jack in the pulpits, yellow, white, nd pink wood sorrel , little brown jugs, ..
likes: Abundance of specific flowers (e.g., trilium, rue anemone)

reviews_attraction.text: This is the best Vista point on Oak Mountain. A well marked trail from the Northern Trailhead is the quickest way to it. It's quite a bit of elevation but nothing even a couch potato couldn't do with a few catch-your-breath-breaks. For a bit of a challenge take the detour over Eagel's Nest. After having soaked in the view, I highly recommend continuing on a very scenic and almost level Blue Trail to the South Red-Blue Connector to loop back over Red Trail, Red-Yellow Connector, and Yellow trail. About a 2 h loop that includes some of my favorite stretches.

Don't give up, the petroglyphs are coming. We wanted to beat the heat and got on the trail before we got primed at the visitor center. We started getting disappointed when we were hiking for 1/4 mile, a sign told us that there was a petroglyph half way up the slope and we couldn't find it. A small group that was hiking in front of us decided to turn back not shortly after and we decided to take an interest in flora and fauna and continue on with a hike. After about 1 mile we hit the mother load of petroglyphs. Very nice, and an interesting hike.

The most Floridian attraction in the State. The mermaids are friendly, the underwater show very unique and quite entertaining.
I've been several times usually when they were about to close down. Environmentalists,  politicians, poor management, dominance of the Mouse,, there are many reasons for this place to be tethering on the brink of bankruptcy. But you can't beat this underwater spectacle. Very affordable when you look at the value of the ticket. Several underwater shows, a boat ride are included.

I guess everybody is exhausted after the Tabasco tour or wanting to go somewhere else. This 170-acre botanical garden was much nicer than expected. We probably got here at the wrong time because the bird density was rather low but we saw lots of gators and turtles, lots of flowers, Spanish moss and live oaks, and a well designed network of walkways. I recommend  taking  time to contemplate life in front of a sizable Buddha and a visit of bird city.
Bring water, binoculars, and a tele lens.

This is a wonderful place for observation, education, and contemplation. A boardwalk leads  you safely and on dry foot into the heart this 60 acres large ecological preserve. The forested swamp is dominated by Tupelo gums and sprinkled with a great variety of herbaceous plants. You can easily spot herons, that are fishing and a variety of snakes on the prowl. So stay on the boardwalk and be aware that all venomous snakes indigenous to Alabama are living here.

Good views of the windmill, some waterfowl, wildflower, native trees, and invasive plants alongside the Macatawa river. River Park offers lush (hip high) wildlower meadowes and a nice wooden and slightly crooked bridge that allows a better view of swan's nests. The smell of a nearby reclaimed water plant becomes more notable west of the bridge. This review is a review of the walk way Lincoln Ave and the trail end of the Window  stretching to W 1st Street.

Nothing to get out of your way to visit  but if in or coming through Alexandria  a neat little museum worthwhile a 30-60 min spin.
1st floor had a well documented temporary exhibition (6/3 - 8/20/2016) "Purchased Lives" about the American slave trade. I would have liked more artifacts or contemporary paintings, photographs.
The 3rd floor, only accessible by elevator, had an interesting exhibition of recent paintings and sculptures from local artists.

Wheelchair accessible "trailhead" to the Mississippi River Levee Path and Levee Loop (1.5 miles). Water fountain, power outlets, wheelchair ramp, few chairs, stunning view.   Walking on top of the levee offers great views and provides a perspective when the Mississippi is at flood stage and higher than downtown Baton Rouge. Anglers, joggers, walkers, photo shoots, I even saw two young women practicing pole dancing moves on the plentiful lanterns.

A good flow through time from the big bang to today's threat of climate change. Engaging exhibits with alternating displays that creat the illusion of open spaces and being deep inside the Earth's mantel. We were lucky enough to meet some  "junior volunteers" that were stationed throughout the exhibits teaching us specific angles to look at our surroundings. I was surprised how little I know about fluorescent minerals. Highly recommended.

Chill neighborhood park with a small spring, a short creek, and a pond that attracts waterfowl and anglers. A baseball field, an amphitheater, a playground and a walking trail around the pond with plenty of benches and dry-stacked walls for resting and relaxing.
All in all pretty clean and maintained but as always, you can find signs of sociopaths that dump a spoiled crawfish boil into the pond or litter.

Located on the Crest of Shades Crest Road in Bluff Park is a set of limestone boulders and outcrops. One prominent site called Lover's Leap  juts out over shades valley and allows for a quick thrill when walking up to its edge. The view into the valley is limited due to the large trees surrounding the rock but it is a nice and easy to reach spot for some contemplation.

The beach is narrow and it is quite a hike from the parking lot to the beach. I enjoy walking but I am sympathetic with the dad that carries water toys, chairs, and a cooler through the dunes.Too crowded, to narrow, and to many stones to make it top rated but it is nice to walk through the forest and dunes.

Very enjoyable in and out hike, cool tree house 50 yards away from the overview platform. View has a bit much industry in the foreground but on a clear day you can catch a great view over Birmingham. I am still debating if you can really see Vulcan in the distance.
Small, innovative "museum" focusing on the human experience. I would not call it a museum more an exhibition with us on display. More selfreflection than education more humanity than numbers.

Dense downtown park. Dog parks, tennis courts, ball fields, frisbee golf, pavilion, grills, benches, lot's of parking, and some short trails for walking.

Since it is rural it is very super busy so that is nice also.  If you are in this area, it is a great place to visit

I have been here a couple of times when visiting Tallahassee and I really enjoyed it both times.  It is not what you think of as a traditional MUSEUM.  It is very much an outdoor kind of place.  You Can learn a lot about Florida history and nature and see pretty plants and animals.

This is a nice little park.  I enjoyed the trails and pretty nature.  We went on the pier for a while and saw fish and crabs.  The beach area was clean and nice.  We saw turtles and an alligator along the trail.  I would definitely go here in again when visiting that area

This is a nice little park.  We saw many different turtles here in the little lake, soft shell, red ear sliders and snapping turtles.  We also saw alligator and birds and butterflies.  We saw many people fishing here.  The fountain in the lake is pretty too

This is a great zoo.  Even though many animals are behind high fences many come close to visitors.  We fed giraffes and budgie birds and that was so fun.  I would suggest this zoo for people that enjoy animals.  The staff is nice and it is clean and safe.

This was an AMAZING Safari!   We went here the morning of Thanksgiving Day and had such a great time.  I've never seen so many wild animals up so close.  We loved feeding everyone that came up to the car.  We drove through several times and just loved it.

This is an awesome museum if you like the art of Salavdor Dali.  They have SO much art and you can learn so much about he artists history and  his art.  They also have a great building with view of the harbor, a pretty little garden and a great gift shop

This is a nice nature park.  It is rather rustic and out of the way so not very busy so it was quite and nice.  The trails are a bit rough so you need to be a good hiker and wear good hiking shoes.  The staff their were knowledgable, nice and helpful.

This is a nice park along the riverfront/riverwalk area.  The true water park is very fun for kids.  We also saw a movie at night there and that was fun also.  If you check what they have going on you may find fun events you want to go to

This is a very nice place to talk a walk, ride bikes trails and go fishing.  I really like going for walks here and watching the wildlife and birds in the area.  It is pretty and quiet and never overly busy

This is a lovely nature park.  I saw deer and birds and loved the walk along the river and by the mini waterfalls.  They have very nice hiking trails and it is not busy so you can really enjoy nature here.
Wow, this park is gorgeous during the day and so special during Christmas season.  We loved all the lights and music.  If you are in the area you need to visit this park during Christmas season.
Nice park to walk your dog, have your kids play sports or use the playground.  They have bathrooms and water fountains so that is good and makes it a better park than some others in the area.
This is a very pretty park.  We enjoyed walking the trails and enjoying the pretty view of the bay.  I also liked the fact that it was not super busy so you could enjoy nature and quiet time.
Nice little boardwalk along the mangroves, watched birds, Fiddler crabs and fish, crabs and a stingray in the water.  After the walk, spend some time on the little but very quiet beach
This is a wonderful park if you want to take a nice walk and do some serious bird watching.  Local Audubon groups like to go here because there are so many pretty birds
This is a very pretty park on the Bay.  We enjoyed walking and seeing pretty flowers and wildlife.  The trails and beach were so nice.  I would love to go hete again
We went to visit this science center because my granddaughter loves marine life.  We all enjoyed the visit here, learned a lot about sea life and had a great time.
This was a nice park with good trails.  I saw lots of people dog walking and biking here and some folks going kayaking.  Trails were nice but not much wildlife
Make sure you get here early because the park can fill up and get busy.  It has lovely trails for hiking and paddling and lots of great nature to view.
This was a nice place to go for a hike and have my granddaughter play on the playground.  I liked the tree lined trails and seeing birds and wildlife.

There is a park and there is a library with a fountain. Once a year you can take your life into your own hands as you race up the side of a mountain trail to a waterfall with crazy mo'fos speeding by you. Is that a guy with a bone exposed in his ankle because he should have zigged instead of zagged? Yep. I don't need to eat a whole bowl of soup to know the whole bowl is bad. So, uh, yeah.

A newer modern art museum. Notable works are too many to list but there are Basquiat and Warhol pieces here. The infinity room has a wait. But worth it. Be sure to check-in to visit the room. Tickets are free. You can reserve in advance or you can show up the day of to wait for a possible opening to get in. But just reserve.

This place is great. Just off the highway. Your soak might include other people so be forewarned. The springs are lovely. Very relaxing and would come back.

You may want to change in the car before getting into the springs, I didn't see that there was a place to change clothes.

You can easily access great views of the city. Also you can get to the top of the Baxter steps! You do know about the secret stairs of Los Angeles don't you? Pff. Look, go down them stairs and keep going down baxyerbto find the two most San Francisco hills in Los Angeles.

A neat little garden. Fun place to come, sit, enjoy a coffee with a friend. There are tables and chairs hidden throughout. It's not huge or anything, so no getting lost. Just a random well-cared for park in Pasadena.

It's a cute park; a number of homeless folk do take residence here although they don't appear to disturb anyone. There's a tennis court, two actually. Only one court is open to the public during the week.

Lovely gem of a park. Ample space to relax. A good place to bring your family and kids to feed the ducks and geese. The park resides on either side of the 10fwy btw. There's a bridge connecting each side.
A fun hike that is moderate to mild in terms of difficulty. You get sweeping views of the canyon, Pacific Palisades and the Pacific Ocean. Get there early to score parking {before 9am}.
Nice and wide-open park for hiking, picnicking with family, or just a solitary walk with a loved one (or by yourself). Lots of sweeping views of the Willamette Valley to be had here.
Fun place to go with the family. It's a small amusement park. Lots of of games, rides, and things to do. They also have an awesome picnic area, most are first come first serve.
I mean, it's a good place to take your family and to do the touristy shopping thing. DTD is great for that. What's missing is a solid venue to see music now that HOB is gone.
Bag Girl State Beach. Interesting choice of name. It's a good beach. Parking is a challenge later in the day. But it's a great place to bring the family to take in the surf.
Super popular place where locals come. You'll get a great view of the city at the very top. There are stairs that will take you to the top quickly and painfully.
Great venue to see a show, Ive seen the last Phil there a few times now. The architecture is iconic. The grounds are interesting to walk around too.
Nice big park in old Pasadena. Great for sitting down reading or eating. There tend to be a lot of homeless here. Take caution but you'll be fine.
Lots of great Victorian houses. Closes at 4p. They offer tours. Close to the lummis house. THIS PLACE ISN'T AN IDEAL WALK FROM THE GOLD LINE.
It's a thing to see if you're over here on the westside. Part of the secret walks of los angeles, too. Nice houses that I cannot afford. =)
A site to see while at the Huntington. You'll definitely want to stroll through it. The Foundation is adding another section to this area
Spacious park. You can catch some decent baseball games here. Lots of areas to walk, it's adjacent to Elephant Hill, and Debs Regional.
Solid park with benches and space to relax and play. The Pasadena Pacers meet here on occasion. Lots of parking around the park.
Neat little park, scenic, and hidden away. A great place to come and catch your breath in the middle of this busy metropolis.
What's not to like about the bowl. Not a bad seat in the house and you can buy a bottle of rosè and sit in the lawn. Love it.
It's beautiful. You can still hear the hum of traffic nearby. But it's great for a hike or a jog, you'll get a good workout.
Lovely little park across from Eisenhower. You get a nice view of the city. Come near sunset. Also a good place for a run.
Hey fella humans, human fellas! Solid place to have your southern Baptist weddin'. Staff is superb and catering was great

In 1941 Alcoa aluminum made the government a gift of its Fontana property—a prime site for a TVA dam—in return for various considerations from TVA. A bill authorizing the construction of Fontana Dam was signed 10 days before Pearl Harbor. The dam construction began in 1942 and was completed in 1944 by a team of 5000 workers working in 3 shifts for 24 hours a day.

Located in Graham county in North Carolina, the Fontana dam is 480 feet high and stretches 2,365 feet across the Little Tennessee River. It is a gravity dam and contain 2,815,300 cubic yards of concrete. It is the tallest dam east of the Mississippi and forms 29 mile long Fontana lake.

There is a nice informative center with a pictorial history of the dam and the TVA. Good place to bring children.

There's a beautiful picnic spot with a beautiful view of the dam when you drive across the dam and veer left. It is handicapped accessible.
likes: Facilities & Services: Informative center, Pictorial history

reviews_attraction.text: Beautiful little city with incredible photo opportunities. Easy to walk the entire city on a cool morning and take the free trolley. Established as an army outpost in 1849, Fort Worth, Texas, is known as “Cowtown" for its cattle drive history. Located along the Trinity River where millions of cattle were herded on the Chisholm Trail, Fort Worth calls itself the "place where the West begins." During the wild era of cattle drives that passed through Fort Worth, gambling parlors, saloons, and bakeries sprang up around town and became known as “Hell’s Half Acre." When oil was discovered in Texas, such refinery and pipeline companies as Sinclair Refining Company, Texaco, and Humble Oil and Refining Company (later Exxon Company, U.S.A.) established operations there, it led to the establishment of oil stock exchanges in Fort Worth.

If you are into Nascar and its history, this is the place to visit!!!!  Showroom floor has an excellent selection of winning cars through the decades, an area dedicated to the drivers with their driving winning histories and images. Everything pertaining to Nascar is on display. Warning: if you suffer from asthma, use your inhaler prior to going into the building as the mold and mildew content is very high!!!!!!

Beautiful spot for a picnic! Most of the tables are huge slabs of rock with old logs split it half, guaranteed to drive a splinter up your arse. There are some newer tables tho. The whole area is a shady glen with ferns. Very cool in the summer due to the altitude. Beware the frequent summer thunderstorms if you decide to drive down the one way 28 mile narrow gravel portion.... there's no turning around!!!!!!!

Roaring Fork Falls is a 1.4 mile moderately trafficked out and back trail located near Burnsville, North Carolina that features a waterfall and is good for all skill levels. The trail offers a number of activity options and is accessible year-round. Dogs are also able to use this trail but must be kept on leash. It is particularly beautiful after rains with some great photo opportunity.

The walkway so close to the stacks up was an amazing experience. I thought about all the people who worked in that inferno, their deaths, their injuries and how they were exploited by the owners who totally disregarded their miserable plight. Very educational and a good place to bring older children so that they have knowledge of how horrible it was once upon a time.

Fall in Ouachita National Forest can rival the splendor of the northeast. Brilliant leaf color dazzles the eyes as the sunlight filters down through the reds, golds, and yellows. Stopping on the numerous overlooks looking out over the valleys is spectacular. There are no crowds, no car lines miles long, so pack a picnic and find a stream to stop at and enjoy.

The restaurants along the river offer a plethora of choices. Night time along the river is beautiful with the lights dancing on the waters. There are several paths to take that follow the river allowing you to get away from the restaurant din. There are also river cruises to while away the time, floating past beautiful landscaping and flowers.

What a beautiful botanical garden! It was a warm day, but I hardly noticed as I walked the paths leading to various plants. There was a very shaded area for the parrots with benches to sit on and enjoy the cool shade. The plumeria garden is fantastic. I loved the parrot houses. Very nice experience and will return the next time I am here.

Great visitor center with a very nice gift store. Interesting outbuildings depicting life on a farm in the 1800s. Great place to bring kids. Very crowded during the summer and the women’s restroom can get quite foul. Early morning visitors might see upwards to 30 elk in the area!!!!

Beautifully restored old school converted into a visitor's center featuring a gallery of crafted items for sale, an auditorium for seasonal concerts featuring local music of Appalachia. Nice grounds and a large gazebo for picnics. Grest place to bring children.

Beautiful location to start walking the canal. There's an old lockhouse where you can pick up some brochures and speak with a park ranger. This lock has an elevation change and a diverter for the water while the lock is in use.

Beautifully maintained park with many amenities available. Grills at picnic tables, open grassy areas for children and dogs to run... basketball, volleyball, fishing, etc.etc. Clean restrooms. Very nice.
What exceptional views from the tower! A shuttle took us up to the observation tower. Clean and well maintained structure. Bathrooms are clean too. A family friendly place. Handicapped access.
Beautiful gardens with nice paths meandering under trees with a variety of plants blooming throughout the summer. Best time to go is Sunday morning while it is still pleasant and not crowded.
Beautiful park out in the middle of nowhere. Nice views of surrounding hills, nice paths along river and not too crowded!!!!! Great place to get away from it all and have a nice picnic.
Large beautiful park with many trails and lots of room There's a dog park, picnic area and large grounds that's mowed periodically. Perfect park to bring the family!
A very popular pullout with some outstanding views. This pullout gets very crowded, it has a small parking area. Best go during the weekday or early in the morning.
Beautiful area for morning walks, enjoying watching the fishing boats come and go, the gulls flying by, the breeze in your face. Nice place to bring family.
What an incredible collection of bikes! The accompanying stories and displays was very interesting. Plan on taking your time browsing this fantastic place!
What a beautiful place to kayak/canoe! Doesn't appear to be a crowded spot. Fishing is great. Some nice picnic tables. Great place to bring kids fishing.
Moderately steep trail that can be slippery when the leaves have dropped from the trees. Several rock outcroppings offer fantastic views. Great trail!!
Beautiful old park. Very peaceful. Great for families, picnics, or just sitting around. Especially beautiful in the fall when the leaves turn.
Could be really nice if all the trash was picked up that has been tossed into the brush. Posting signs might cut down on this.
Absolutely beautiful spot to visit. Very nice picnic shelters, a nice trek up to beautiful views and some nice trails.

You do not have to be a Country Music fan to enjoy this really well thought-out designed museum! It is filled with knowledge and can entertain you easily for over 3 hours. Lots of interactive exhibits and music of course! Videos, seating for short films, and lots of connections to outside country music. Well worth the visit. Of you buy basic ticket, for $2 more can get audio stick that gives you access to 41 spots of information, well worth it!

You will certainly learn things you never knew! One of the tour guides seems very bent on making out white people to be evil. I get it but wasn't the owner of the house a German abolutionist, white? Didn't he save countless lives? Tone it down please, we all know slavery is hideous and an abomination to mankind, and yes racisim exsists still but being mad about it only freaks people out and then they stop listening.

Interesting! Go early morning in Summer to beat heat, but about 30 minutes after opening, we went near when they opened and they were just starting to unlock exhibits. Did not spend much time inside as was turned off by film which had 99% white people in it and only 2 people of color - 1 slave and one student. Come on they can do better!

Excellent information and displays. Afternoons are quieter. Top VIP tour great, ezpensive but worth it if you have funds. You get so much more out of touring and get to touch Elvis stuff. Meal included! But try as a snack the Meditterian pizza at Glady's you will not be disappointed!

Definetly worth time and effort and cost! Wear good grippy shoes and bring a jacket if you get cold easily. There are some steep areas coming back so make sure you can handle it physically - small kids had no problem but some seniors with hip or leg problems struggled.

Took guided tour. Was just 2 of us and guide so, very nice. Had lockers to put stuff. Lots of collections with focus on Napoleon, platters, pewter, paintings, shaving jars, self playing musical instruments, hat pins, wedgewood, and so much more.

Good if you are into Baton Rouge and LA political scene. Bit expensive but balances out if you go to Old Capitol Building. Can do audio tour with your iPhone as we did or catch a volunteer/docent tour.
Out of the way treasure! Very interesting dry canyon. Tours both short and long. About 60 degrees at all times. April to Oct is high season. Small tour in January! Loved the story of sloth bear!
Excellent agree with others - go early for smaller groups. It can get really tight at times and if you are at all claustraphobic it will help tremendously! Good for solo travelers!
Loved It! Learned all about area. Just a tip info office not open until 10, but if you want to go early you can and just pay $5 after. Well worth trail, not hard and kid friendly.
Really well done! We went on a Saturday and it must have been an anomaly as there was hardly anyone there. Really enjoyed Louis Armstrong and cultural upstairs exhibits.
Beautiful setting. Mixed emotions on him as a man and president so information is well presented for you to make own decisions. Explore all parts of place on foot.
Excellent information and guides! Super interesting architecture! Live that they split time described enslaved lives as well as slave owners life. Well done!
Extremely well done, gift shop has a good variety, exhibit currently thought provoking and well laid out  Liked fact they involved community as well.
Not huge but we saw juvenile armidillos, owl,   and center had snakes, and turtles and we got to pet baby gator. Nice walk and great nature  sounds.
Loved that they built museum over site.  Don't miss video. Lots to learn about. Good for kids and adults. Even has outdoor part. Price reasonable.
Tiny bit well laid out! Loved plant guide! Not big but had shady parts. Nice place to walk about. Right across from kids water and play area.
Big nice paddlewheel boat. Lunch very streamlined! Boat very smooth and has 2 indoor areas! Has railing all around each level. Staff nice!
Lots of places for kids and adults. Civil Rights Museum, Coca Cola Museum and Georgia Aquarium. All within walking distance of downtown.
Good aquarium, but no real staff to ask questions - only in 2 locations and only in Ocean section. Catamaran extra was a nice edition!
Awesome experience! Loved all the tech in the displays and exhibits. Gift store had range of items in got and was really well done!
Not huge but many genres represented. Could get some of videos to work. Car taken with vehicles! Can do in under 30 min.
Excellent place for adults and kids. Jim Henson exhibit Rocks! Recommend getting guide as you will get more out of it!
Probably once a great overlook, but plants need trimming to see it. Good place to take animals out for brief stretch.
Great fields, no trees, bring your own shade, park in lot when possible, street is crazy to try and get out of.

I had a great time at the zoo. Phoenix has a great Zoo. It is a lot of walking but worth it. I would totally recommend paying the 10 extra dollars and getting their total Zoo experience instead of just the general admission pass period for 10 extra dollars you get to ride a camel which was a blast, pet stingrays, and watch a 4D movie, and take a  ride around the zoo if you don't want to walk it. I've been to Zoos all across the country and many have a lot more animals than the Phoenix Zoo had but the interactive experience made up for that. The staff was super friendly and helpful. I also loved the walk-in monkey area where you walk in and monkeys literally come within  5 feet of you with no cage in between. Also, the Jaguar and cheetahs were spectacular as well.

I stopped here on my 1600 mile hike down the East Coast which started in Portland Maine. I thought the New Haven green was very interesting. There was a lot to take in. I could not believe how busy it was. It was awesome to experience it and Yale. The only thing that kept me from giving it 5 stars is there were transients and druggies everywhere and I mean everywhere. You can tell it's definitely a rough area and so you have to pay attention a little bit. Still a must see if you're ever in the area.

This was one of my favorite stops on my 1200 mile hike down the East Coast. I actually stayed in Ocean City 3 days just so I could enjoy the boardwalk and all the great treats that are on it. It was a blast watching all the different people ride bikes and walk on the boardwalk with the amazing ocean so close. I also love all the wonderful places to eat an awesome little shops along the boardwalk. I had a great time there and hopefully I can make it back someday

This place was awesome. So much interesting history and information. The Lorraine Hotel in room where Martin Luther King jr. Was shot is spectacular. They have done a wonderful job of preserving it. You can see right across the street where the shot was fired from. Very interesting to see firsthand. I would say that if you don't want to pay the admission to the museum, it's still worth going to see the memorial and hotel which is located on the same grounds.

Awesome museum detailing pieces and facts from every age of the history of the u.s. Coast Guard. The campus was awesome also. The museum is not overly large but it is very impressive and informative. Admission is free but they do have a donation box that you can donate to on the way out which is a great idea. Just keep in mind because it's on the campus you have to have a valid driver's license or u.s. ID to enter since it's a military base.

Awesome campground!! That was beautiful and for the most part much more quiet than most campgrounds I have been to. The staff was very friendly and helpful. I love walking around the reservoir on the trails. I definitely I would recommend staying here and Hiking a couple of the trails if you get a chance just don't forget the mosquito repellent.

A great paved trail crossing over several streets but giving you miles of trail with no cars. It is very hilly but also great for walking your dogs. You can access it from many different streets including Farmington, Division, Scholls, Hart, Nora, Barrows and many more. It is much less scenic than other trails in the area though.

Nice little park. Very easy beach access. There is a nice gazebo or you can look across and see the harbor seals at the opening of the Bay. The access to the beach is literally only 40 feet from where you park your car so very easy. It can be a little loud since it is right off the highway but when you're on the beach hits great.

Nice park and close to a lot of things to do. A few drawbacks though. They lock the gates on the roads at 9 p.m. and don't open them till 7 a.m. so you can't get your vehicle into the park if you have plans at night. Also only one mile from Durham Airport and you have to hear 737 Landing right over your tent all night long.

Most enjoyable State Park I have stayed at on my trip so far. I started in Maine and if not walked over 900 miles down the coast staying in state campgrounds. I really loved it here.
