One of them that is a great place to play or  camp is along the East Verde River.  Just minutes out of Payson on AZ87, take Flowing Springs Road to the right for up to 14 days camping. We went just for picnic and found two tree swings someone left set up.  That made our trip out to this part of the woods enchanting.  We found lots of crawdads and spiders.  Yes my daughter was freaking a bit about that once she spied them.  She spent the rest of the time hunting wild flowers away from the water edge.
In May the water was still chilly.

Another section of the East Verde River is not much further,  just before the bridge turn left onto East Verde Estates Rd to find another picnic spot down a steep bank immediately to your right to play by the river.

My review of: Loma Colorado Park

This park has no signage on the street.  There is a lot of parking but no bathroom that I could see.  The park is up a steep hill right next to the solar panel farm and has a great view of the big mountain to the East. There is a grassy field at the bottom of the hill for soccer.  There is a sign saying "No Dogs".  At the top there is a covered picnic ramada.

At the top the playground is surround by a fence that has shade screen over it.  It maybe to shield flying sand or act as a privacy screen. I'm not really sure.  The playground is covered in wood chips and has a second inner chain link fence in between the benches shaded by trees and the play ground.

The spinning equipment is fun, there is something that looks to be like an outdoor exercise bike.  This was a fun little park.

No easy access from Mesa Dr.  This long narrow park is only assailable using the roads S. Pima or S. Pasadena.  Each road dead ends in a parking lot on opposite ends of the sandy play area that do not connect with each other. There is a basketball court.  There is a volleyball court but the net is missing.  There is a water fountain but no bathroom.  There is a covered picnic area. Watch out for the large prickly pear batches on the hill above the play area.  I had a difficult time keeping my children out of it.  In mid march the prickly pear was getting ready to bloom.  The constant swoosh of cars rushing by on the freeway on the other side of the wall is soothing. Like listening to the sounds of water.  I did see some neighborhood children playing there unsupervised.

Go on a cloudy day.  Worth the $7 to park at the trail head.  Use hiking sticks especially if you are not a hiker like me. Water, bring 2 bottles of water. One for up and one down, maybe more.  It's a pet friendly trail.  Lots of wild flowers in the spring to look at.  Birds and ground squirrels at the trails end at the caves. A crack in the back of the largest cave has water seeping out of a crack, moss grows from it and bees come for a drink.  An old bee hive hangs from the cliff high over head. It's a great view of the city.  I never knew that the white stripe on Gold Mountain Pass had this trail that goes up to it an had Wind caves on its right side. So worth going...on a cloudy day.

My review of: Pima Park
This L shaped park has lots of covered picnic tables along Thomas Rd.  Along the side street is the playground, in full sun - no shared, and a splash pad, shaped like a giant walrus that circles the area with sprayers misting into the center.  Plenty of opportunity for cool down here.  There is restrooms.  The play ground is sand filled and it has a spinning bucket to sit and spin in.  The spring car makes noises as you rock back and forth in it.  The tall play structure has bells, drums and horns to experiment with.  There is a sand volleyball court that is currently being repaired and 2 full basketball courts that crisscross each other.

I love the purple blooming trees this park has in April/May.  Playground is wood chipped. Play equipment is new and looks exciting.  Bathrooms have doors. All people water fountains work but the dog bowl fountain does not. I couldn't get it to work.  There is basketball, he is volleyball and tennis courts. There is a parking glor. It has a beautiful walking path down and across the water basin.  There is no easy walking path down to the dog park from the central playground and bathrooms.  The dog park is cute with 2 separate areas for small and large dogs. That really makes it fun is the fire hydrants put out in each yard for ...you know what.
dislikes: Lack of easy access to dog park

reviews_attraction.text:
Review of: Escobedo Park
There is a connect entry to this park from 6th Street and 5th Place.  There are 2 covered picnic areas with grills, basketball courts, softball field, bathrooms, water fountains and a large grassy area for running in. The play area is filled with sand.  The new Escobedo at Verde vista housing is under construction near by.  Salvation Army in next door as well. Children can play while food boxes are picked up.  Many people walk their dogs here.  Please remember to pick up after your dog.  There are plenty of trash bins in the park.

Loved my visit here. Grills to cook on, and picnic benches. Many vendors to buy suvinors from.  Watch out for giant ants out on the Utah side of the grill area. $5 entry, closing time can vary but it is posted at the front gate. Fry bread was amazing. I loved that the plants had name labels.  It was very windy in May.  There are bathrooms on the Newmexico side. Sadly the brand new stone restroom is sliding down the clay hill and is in the process of being moved. But dont worry, they still have the original restroom and port a potties.

Although you must pay for parking on the week days, did you know that there is a public park just with in the gates of this museum?  It's enchanting.   A music garden, water fountain, dragons, a unicorn you can ride on, climbing equipment.  It's wonderful.  Despite the number of homeless that gather in the park across the street, they don't venture inside these gates and I felt safe with my children.  No public bathroom outside though.

Checkout the amazing architecture and stain glass of this beautiful building.

My review of Pioneer Park: Located right next to this church.  The park has no signage to indicate it's name.  There is parking. There are covered picnic ramadas with tall established trees shading them and an amphitheater facing them.  Restrooms are on the other side of the amphitheater where the sand filled play ground is.  There is racquetball and basketball courts.  Currently there is a Splash Pad being built on the north end of this park.  I love the field of horses across the north road of this park.

Huge park. South half is desert scaped. Sand filled playground is right between the desert and grass zone in the middle of the park. Bathrooms are at the far north end of the park by the softball fields. There is an exercise trail with work out stations.  Has a few covered picnic ramadas. Tennis, soccer,volleyball...all the traditional sport stuff. Loved that a park watch sign was posted.  The locals love their park.

It's a wonderfully huge and exciting place.  Parking was a bit crazy. Prepare to wear good walking shoes. Escelators are one way.  Up at the begining of the event and down at the events end. Prepare to go through metal detectors before you get in line to wait.  Do not park in the lot off of 91st Ave. That is for the employees. The best place to park is the North side by gate 2. That off of Maryland Ave.

My review of: Cesar Chaves Park

I came here one evening and was impressed by it's cleanliness and it's huge lake.  There are bathrooms on both sides.  The play area is sand filled.  There is small roofs on top of the play equipment in an attempt to provide shade but falls short of actually keeping anything cool in the summer.  I loved the small rope merry go round.

Review of: Ensenada Park
Tall mature trees make great shade for relaxing in.  No parking lot, street parking only.  No bathrooms.  There are water fountains and shade covered picnic benches.  But there is no shade for the large sand filled play area.  There is 4-square and hopscotch painted on the cement.
dislikes: Lack of shade in play area

reviews_attraction.text: You have to come here.  Air conditioned dino fun.  Robotic dinosaurs that move and roar, tunnels, haunted jail, elevators, special exhibit rooms a theater that plays non stop dinosaur adventures. This place is great! You can find several bathrooms on each level of this 3 story adventure land.

Review of: Whitman Park
This is a large park with grassy fields.  The play area is an equally large sandy area but all the play equipment is in full sun.  It has a full basketball and volleyball court.  There are shaded picnic areas with grills but there are no bathrooms.

This park has 2 separate parking lots, exercise stations are spaced out around the top rim of the grassy basin.  Covered picnic ramadas but no shade covers on the wood chipped covered play area.  There are water fountains but no restrooms.  This park does not have a pond.

Review of: Park of the Canals
This park offers a lot.  Hiking trails, a desert botanical garden, bathrooms, waterfountain, picnic area and a playground that is bridge accessed over an ancient Hohokam canal.  The play area is covered in wood chips.
I love the dragon statues on the roof.  This heavily gated, dog guarded gem is worth the stop to see.

(Translated by Google) Contrary to what one might think, saguaros cacti are by no means everywhere in the western US but only in the Sonoran desert.

The Saguaro National Park is divided into two parts located to the west and east of the city of Tucson. The western part is more accessible and close to the Sonoran Desert Museum, so it is more crowded. The eastern part is more mountainous.

But on both sides, one has the opportunity to observe multiple specimens of these impressive cacti that can reach more than ten meters high.

Beware, the heat in the Tucson area in the summer is overwhelming and you have to plan a lot of water, even if you do not make any effort!

(Original)
Contrairement à ce que l'on pourrait croire, les cactus saguaros ne sont de loin pas présents partout dans l'ouest américain mais uniquement dans le désert de Sonora.

Le Saguaro National Park est divisé en deux parties situées à l'ouest et à l'est de la ville de Tucson. La partie ouest est plus accessible et proche du Sonoran Desert Museum, ce qui fait qu'elle est plus fréquentée. La partie est est plus montagneuse.

Mais des deux côtés, on a l'occasions d'observer de multiples spécimens de ces cactus impressionnants qui peuvent atteindre plus de dix mètres de haut.

Attention, la chaleur dans la région de Tucson en été est écrasante et il faut prévoir beaucoup d'eau, même si l'on ne fait pas d'effort !

(Translated by Google) This hike provides access to the beautiful Kanarra Creek Falls, located in a beautiful canyon. Walking is not particularly complicated, but the ladders to "pass" the falls can be very slippery.

The most interesting parts are located at the entrance to the canyon. Two sections of "slot canyon" around the falls have nothing to envy the Zion Narrows for the reflected light they can offer if we come at the right time ... Once past the two waterfalls, the canyon widens and even if the ballad is nice, it is not so beautiful.

Small precision, the walk is done most of the time in the river.

(Original)
Cette randonnée permet d'accéder aux magnifiques Kanarra Creek Falls, situées dans un très beau canyon. La marche n'est pas particulièrement compliquée, par contre les échelles permettant de "passer" les chutes peuvent être très glissantes.

Les parties les plus intéressantes sont situées à l'entrée du canyon. Deux sections de "slot canyon" aux alentours des chutes n'ont rien à envier aux Narrows de Zion pour la lumière réfléchie qu'elles peuvent offrir si on y vient à la bonne heure... Une fois passé les deux cascades, le canyon s'élargit et même si la ballade est agréable, cela n'est plus aussi beau.

Petite précision, la marche s'effectue la plupart du temps dans la rivière.

(Translated by Google) The Canyon of Chelly National Monument deserves national park status.

There are 2 canyons (Chelly Canyon and Muerto Canyon) meeting near the Navajo town of Chinle.

The two canyons each have a panoramic road. De Chelly has more beautiful views and it is possible to go down to White House and Del Muerto has more beautiful ruins.

The canyon has the particularity of being still inhabited today by the Navajos. It is for this reason that access is forbidden except with guides.

(Original)
Le Canyon de Chelly National Monument mériterait d'obtenir le statut de parc national.

Il s'agît de 2 canyons (canyon de Chelly et canyon del Muerto) se rejoignant près de la ville navajo de Chinle.

Les deux canyons possèdent chacun une route panoramique. De Chelly a de plus beaux points de vue et il est possible d'y descendre à White House et Del Muerto possède de plus belles ruines.

Le canyon a la particularité d'être encore habité aujourd'hui par les Navajos. C'est pour cette raison que son accès est interdit hormis avec des guides.

(Translated by Google) Morning Glory Pool is one of the park's most famous pools. However, it is losing its beautiful colors because of objects (coins, pebbles, ...) thrown by tourists and who began to block it.

So do not expect to find it like some older photos with very bright colors.

On the other hand, the path that leads along the Fiehole River from Old Faithfull is worth it alone with many other pools and geysers very interesting.

(Original)
Morning Glory Pool est l'une des piscines les plus réputée du parc. Cependant, elle est en train de perdre ses magnifiques couleurs en raison des objets (pièces de monnaie, cailloux, ...) jetés par les touristes et qui ont commencé de la boucher.

Ne vous attendez donc pas à la trouver comme sur certaines photos plus ancienne avec des couleurs très vives.

Par contre, le chemin qui y mène en longeant la Fiehole River depuis Old Faithfull vaut à lui seul la peine avec bien d'autres piscines et geysers très intéressants.

(Translated by Google) Shafer Canyon Overlook is one of the most beautiful views of the American West.

It allows you to see the Shafer Canyon Rd meander into the canyon. At the end of this road is an intersection to either White Rim Rd to go around Island in the Sky (2 days drive) or the Potash Rd to Moab passing under Dead Horse SP and the ponds. If you have a car with good ground clearance, you must go back to Moab by this road.

(Original)
Shafer Canyon Overlook est l'un des plus beau point de vue de l'ouest américain.

Il permet de voir la Shafer Canyon Rd serpenter pour s'enfoncer dans le canyon. Au bout de cette route se trouve une intersection permettant d'emprunter soit la White Rim Rd pour faire le tour de Island in the Sky (2 jours de route) ou la Potash Rd menant à Moab en passant sous Dead Horse SP et les bassins de potasse... Si vous avez une voiture avec une bonne garde au sol, vous devez absolument rentrer à Moab par cette route.

(Translated by Google) Long House is located on Wetherill Mesa. It is only visited in the company of a ranger who also gives very interesting information. Note that all bookings for visits are at the Visitor Center on Chapin Mesa.

Long House is my favorite site in Mesa Verde. If it is visited at the right time of day (early afternoon), the alcove is lit by a very beautiful reflected light.

The site is large enough and is very well preserved.

(Original)
Long House est située sur Wetherill Mesa. Elle ne se visite qu'en compagnie d'un ranger qui donne d'ailleurs des informations très intéressantes. A noter que toutes les réservations pour les visites se font au Visitor Center sur Chapin Mesa.

Long House est mon site préféré à Mesa Verde. Si il est visité au bon moment de la journée (début d'après-midi), l'alcôve est éclairée par une très belle lumière réfléchie.

Le site est assez grand est très bien conservé.

(Translated by Google) This is one of my favorite museums in Las Vegas. It traces the whole history of organized crime in Sin City, but also in the United States. The understanding of English will be an advantage to better understand the place, but it is quite possible not to be bored without knowledge of the language ...

If you are staying in Downtown, it is definitely worth a visit. You can easily spend half a day there.

(Original)
Il s'agît de l'un des musées que j'ai préféré à Las Vegas. Il retrace toute l'histoire du crime organisé à Sin City, mais également aux Etats-Unis. Le fait de comprendre l'anglais sera un avantage pour mieux appréhender l'endroit, mais il est tout à fait possible de ne pas s'ennuyer sans connaissance de la langue...

Si vous séjournez à Downtown, il vaut vraiment la peine d'aller y faire un tour. On peut facilement y passer une demi-journée.

(Translated by Google) Dinosaur National Monument is one of the most beautiful park in the American West.

Its location away from conventional circuits makes it much less crowded.

However, he has a lot to offer. Aside from the Dinosaur Quarry, there are some great hikes, some of Utah's finest pictograms and some of the most impressive views of the American West.

(Original)
Dinosaur National Monument est l'un des plus beau parc de l'ouest américain.

Sa situation éloignée des circuits classique fait qu'il est beaucoup moins fréquenté.

Par contre, il a énormément à offrir. Hormis la Dinosaur Quarry, on peut y faire de très belles randonnées, voir certains des plus beaux pictogrammes de l'Utah et certains des points de vue les plus impressionnants de l'ouest américain.

(Translated by Google) Signal Hill leads to a small rocky hill where there are some pretty petroglyphs.

It overlooks the valley filled with saguaros with the mountains in the background and is very joy at sunset.

On the other hand, as in all the region, the heat can be stifling and it is better to carry water, even for a small walk.

(Original)
Signal Hill mène à une petite colline rocheuse où l'on trouve quelques jolis petroglyphes.

Elle surplombe la vallée remplie de saguaros avec les montagnes en arrière-plan et est très joie au coucher du soleil.

Par contre, comme dans toute la région, la chaleur peut être étouffante et il vaut mieux emporter de l'eau, même pour une petite marche.

(Translated by Google) Before the flash floods of 2008, the configuration of this place was totally different. Navajo Falls was further downstream and is now dry.

However, the place is still beautiful and the basin deep enough at the foot of the new Navajo Falls allows you to take a dip on the way between Supai and the campsite ...

(Original)
Avant les flash floods de 2008, la configuration de cet endroit était totalement différente. Navajo Falls était située plus en aval et est maintenant asséchée.

Cependant, l'endroit est tout de même magnifique et le bassin assez profond au pied de la nouvelle Navajo Falls permet de piquer une tête lors du trajet entre Supai et le camping...

(Translated by Google) Little Wild Horse Canyon is a beautiful canyon slot located not far from Gobelins SP.

In places, it is so thin that it is impossible to put the foot flat ...

There are beautiful multicolored walls, swiss cheese and a beautiful reflected light according to the time at which one goes there.

(Original)
Little Wild Horse Canyon est un très beau slot canyon situé non loin de Gobelins SP.

Par endroit, il est si fin qu'il est impossible d'y poser le pied à plat...

On y trouve de très belles parois multicolores, du swiss cheese et une magnifique lumière réfléchie selon l'heure à laquelle on s'y rend.

(Translated by Google) Toroweap is one of the most breathtaking views of the Grand Canyon.

It is a 1000 meters high above the Colorado. The view is beautiful at sunrise.

The way to get there is long, but not especially complicated except for the last miles which are a bit more technical.

(Original)
Toroweap est l'un des point de vue les plus vertigineux du Grand Canyon.

From the early 1800’s through the early-to-mid 1900’s, Bays Mountain provided for those families who settled on the mountain. The mountain provided settlers with land to farm, wood for building houses, a church and even a school. Obviously life was much different then, but relying on Bays Mountain to provide the resources, wildlife and harvest needed to survive and thrive was a given. It surely wasn’t easy, as there are challenges provided by any mountainous terrain, but those families who did make the mountain their home, proudly did so. Many of their stories are wonderfully told in our Farmstead Museum.In 1907, one of Kingsport’s founders, J. Fred Johnson, began buying up land on Bays Mountain to create a lake to be used as a water source for fledgling Kingsport. By 1914, Johnson had purchased the roughly 1,200 acres that surrounded the watershed and sold it to Kingsport Waterworks Corporation who promptly began work in 1915 preparing to build the now iconic dam seen as visitors enter the common area atop Bays Mountain Park.  Bays Mountain’s dam was built by approximately 35-40 men who worked 10 hour days to complete the project. Many of those who assisted were family members of those living on and around the mountain. For example, mountain landowner Jerome Pierce provided a wagon and team of mules to haul the rock and steel needed to build the dam. Much of the rock was quarried from the mountain itself.In 1916, water began flowing to the city and in 1917 the dam was raised six more feet creating a 44-acre lake, the same size the lake is today. Bays Mountain’s lake served the city until 1944, when the city had finally outgrown the lake’s capacity to provide. But in some ways, this is where the modern day Bays Mountain story begins.  From 1944 through 1964, Bays Mountain served locals in different ways: timber was selectively harvested, hikers enjoyed the early trails and views, while fisherman and hunters challenged their skills. As this usage grew, so too did the public’s interest in preserving the mountain for usage. Thus, in 1965, Mayor Hugh Rule appointed a committee to study ways to possibly develop the mountain into a park. Following the committee’s report, which included hiring a naturalist, the City of Kingsport hired the National Audubon Society to help design a park. Among those representing the Audubon Society was the park’s first director, Robert Holmes.  The National Audubon Society’s recommendations were to designate the area as a nature preserve to also allow hiking, naturalist-led activities, natural history studies, research and leisure activities such as photography, painting, wildlife observation and school day-use. They also recommended building a maintenance shed, a residence for a caretaker and an interpretive nature center. In short, the park was to be of great service to the public, including schools, while also serving to preserve the natural habitat it featured.  As development began in 1968, so did visitation on a very limited basis. Work was still being completed on the service/entrance road and the parking lot remained unfinished, meaning a strict 100 car limit was enforced. In 1969, the park’s first naturalists were hired, one part-time and one full-time, to accommodate visitors and park users.

The Tipton-Haynes State Historic Site tells the rich story of the history of Northeast Tennessee and of the several families that lived here. The site includes 45 acres, eleven historic buildings, the Tipton/Gifford/Simerly cemetery, a limestone cave, a natural spring, a buffalo trace, a nature trail, and a Visitor Center. The Visitor Center contains a permanent exhibit, museum store, educational spaces, a library, and archives.

Purchasing the site in 1784, Colonel John Tipton (1730-1813) moved from Shenandoah County, Virginia to settle in what was then Washington County, North Carolina. For the next four years, the formation and decline of the State of Franklin became an important issue for the area and the life of Colonel Tipton, who stayed loyal to North Carolina. In February of 1788, the Battle of the State of Franklin turned the peaceful home of Colonel Tipton’s into a battle ground for Franklin independence. Colonel Tipton would later help with the development of Tennessee becoming the 16th state of the Union before retiring from public life.

After his father’s death, John Tipton, Jr. (1767-1831) inherited the property. Before moving to Washington County, Tipton, Jr. was already a successful state legislator and wealthy land owner in Blountville, Tennessee. Tipton, Jr. expanded his father’s cabin in the 1820s, making it a Federal style farmhouse. While attending the 19th General Assembly, he died in Nashville.

The heirs of John Tipton, Jr. sold the property to David and Rhoda Haynes in 1837. For a wedding gift, David and Rhoda gave the property to Landon Carter Haynes (1816-1875), their oldest son, in 1839. That year, Landon had married Eleanor Powell. In the 1850s, he expanded the former Tipton home into how it appears today. Haynes is best known for being a Confederate senator, but was also a state legislator, politician, farmer, newspaper editor, Methodist minister, and attorney. Losing his home during the Civil War, Haynes moved to and lived the rest of his life in Memphis, Tennessee. The site would eventually return to the Haynes family when, on May 1, 1882, Sarah L. Gifford Simerly (1847-1935) purchased the property. Sarah was the niece of Landon Carter Haynes.

The site for Cove Fort was selected by Brigham Young because of its location about halfway between Fillmore, then the capital of the Utah Territory, and the nearest city, Beaver. It provided a way station for people traveling the Mormon Road. A town would have been constructed at the Cove Fort site, but the water supply was inadequate to support a sizable population.  Another key factor in the selection of the site was the prior existence of a wooden-palisade fort, Willden Fort. The fort is a square, 100 ft on each side. The walls are constructed of black volcanic rock and dark limestone, both quarried from the nearby mountains. The walls are 18 ft high and 4 ft thick at the base, tapering to 2 ft thick at the top. The fort has two sets of large wooden doors at the east and west ends, originally filled with sand to stop arrows and bullets, and contains 12 interior rooms. As a daily stop for two stagecoach lines, as well as many other travelers, Cove Fort was heavily used for many years, often housing and feeding up to 75 people at a time. In addition to providing a place to rest, a blacksmith & farrier resided at the fort, who shod horses and oxen, and also repaired wagon wheels. With its telegraph office and as a Pony Express stop, it also acted as a regional communications hub.

The site was closed when I stopped but I was able to walk around the outside and check it out.  Jeff Mullins Photography Adventures.  Get Your Hike On!

Dead Horse Point, 2,000 feet above a gooseneck in the Colorado River, an ever-changing landscape unfurls. Immense vertical cliffs meet with canyons carved by ice, water, and wind creating a visual masterpiece. Plants and animals surviving on the edge of existence face many challenges of extreme conditions within this high desert environment. Stories of ancient hunters, resting along the cliff tops while knapping chert in preparation for the next hunt, and cowboys of the late 1800s, chasing wild mustangs onto Dead Horse Point, using the narrow neck to block off the natural corral. Canyonlands National Park is an American national park located in southeastern Utah near the town of Moab. The park preserves a colorful landscape eroded into numerous canyons, mesas, and buttes by the Colorado River, the Green River, and their respective tributaries. Legislation creating the park was signed into law by President Lyndon Johnson on September 12, 1964.  The park is divided into four districts: the Island in the Sky, the Needles, the Maze, and the combined rivers—the Green and Colorado—which carved two large canyons into the Colorado Plateau. While these areas share a primitive desert atmosphere, each retains its own character.

Hike down into Walnut Canyon and walk in the footsteps of the people that lived here over 900 years ago. Under limestone overhangs, the Sinagua built their homes. These single story structures, cliff dwellings, were occupied from about 1100 to 1250. The people that lived here moved on to become the modern pueblo people of today. Walnut Canyon is one of their ancestral homes.

Nestled between the Painted Desert and ponderosa highlands of northern Arizona, Wupatki is a landscape of legacies. Ancient pueblos dot red-rock outcroppings across miles of prairie. Where food and water seem impossible to find, people built pueblos, raised families, farmed, traded, and thrived. Today, if you linger and listen, earth and artifacts whisper their stories to us still.

This is a difficult review because relative to the surrounding area this park deserves a 5 star for beauty, but when compared to Zion, Bryce, Yosemite or GC, it's a 3 star. If this area was in Utah it wouldn't be a park. That being said, we had a great time. The vistas were impressive and the road was in great condition. Not having ever visited the Texas panhandle I was amazed by the contrast with the surrounding area. The water level measure stations in the bottom of the canyon indicated that they can get some serious floods. As we drove deeper into the canyon the temperature warmed up and it was not as windy as up on the plateau. If visiting the area I would suggest stopping or if you live in the panhandle take advantage of the hiking opportunities. The gift shop had a lot of cool goodies, but they tended to be more expensive than we found at the national park visitor centers. Admission was $8 per person. Pricey for a 1 hour drive thru the park, but reasonable if you plan to spend more time in the park.
Highly recommend.
dislikes: High admission price for short visit

reviews_attraction.text: We could not believe how big this place was inside. The pathway into the cavern was very well designed. The elevation drops 750 feet in a very short distance. Take good walking shoes! The surface is gritty asphalt and provides good footing on the dark. We arrived early and had no problems getting tickets. Our national park pass covered the cost of the tickets. Inside the visitor center they have good exhibits to help understand the cave structure. Suggest hitting the restrooms before going in because it's a long trip before the next opportunity. Parking was setup for large crowds and I did see parking for large vehicles. Highly suggest visiting this park. We stayed in the town of Carlsbad. Its an easy drive to the park.

We visited San Diego in August during the pandemic and were looking for a nice bike trail that wasn't too crowded. We found this trail on trail link. We started at the eastern most point and rode west to the ocean approximately nine miles each way. The trail runs along the south side of the San Luis river. Parking at the east end is a small dirt parking lot with about 10 to 15 spots. The trail has plenty of places to pickup food and drinks along with parks with picnic tables and restrooms. Pavement was in great condition. No road crossings, all were underpasses at cross roads. As we approached oceanside and the beach it did get windy. You can access the mission San Luis Rey from the trail.
likes: Facilities & Services: Food, drinks, picnic tables, restrooms

reviews_attraction.text: White sands is very special. It's like no other place I've ever been. The experience is different depending on what time of day you visit. We saw that the hours were extended for the full moon so we arrived about 6:30 pm and hiked a short distance into the dunes. We did take gps and headlamps to avoid getting disoriented and lost after dark. We watched the most beautiful sunset  and then watched the corn moon rise over the mountains to the east. The quiet was unreal.  Also, jets were taking off in formation from Holloman air force base in the distance. I hope this place does not get ruined by crowds in the future. It is so wonderful.

This sculpture is really cool and at a very nice rest stop before entering Las Cruces east bound. The restrooms were clean and there was no garbage. The roadrunner is made of all sorts of recycled products. An employee of the facility told us it was made from surplus products from companies no longer in Las Cruces due to over regulation in the Rio grande valley. Not sure if that true but that's what we were told. Access when traveling westbound is tricky and you must go several miles further west then travel back eastbound to access the rest stop. Great views of Las Cruces and the mountains to the east.

If you are on I-8 it is really worth the 10 mile drive off the highway. The road is paved and in perfect condition. The concentration of petroglyphs is amazing. Some early visitors carved their initials and dates  into the rocks back in the 1920's along with the native people. Several covered picnic tables are available and there are restrooms at the parking area. The petroglyphs are easily accessible from the parking areas. Highly recommend.

Smathers beach was fantastic! We rode our bikes from our hotel and it worked out very well. We were at the far east end of the beach and it seemed less crowded than the west end. The water temperature was perfect with the baby blue color. The sand was clean and didn't have much seaweed in the water. I was able to walk far out to a sand bar it was so shallow, about three feet deep. Suggest wearing aqua socks. Highly recommend.

Really cool place. It felt like being in Spain right here in the US. The history or the Spanish in Florida was facinating. The national park service has done a good job of managing the fortress. Instead I had already visited the Grand Canyon West 10 years earlier, in 2009.
Inevitably it comes from comparing the three places.
It 'difficult to assign judgments goals and objective, so I limit myself to my perceptions and memories.
Each of the three places deserves to be seen, each one is worth the trip.

In Grand Canyon West Skywalk experience is special, very iconic sites are the Eagle Point, named for a mountain coastline in the shape of an eagle sacred to Native Hualapai and Guano Point, which takes its name from an ancient cave (located on the opposite bank of the Colorado) full of bat guano that some decades ago was exploited just for the extraction of this product.
A helicopter ride and boating on the river for a few kilometers was an unforgettable experience.

The South Rim is what we usually think of when referring to the Grand Canyon in a general sense, at least here in Italy.
I found beautiful observation points including one for all, Desert View Watchtower.
The heart of the park, but is popular with tourists and, in some respects, resembles a city fabric, thus limiting the wild and lonely aura (but not beauty) that should characterize a place like the Grand Canyon of the Colorado.

I have always perceived the North Rim as a "secondary" place and so I wanted to make a direct experience.
Not only I was very surprised by the beauty of its sites, but I also found out the places from which the views are truly breathtaking, including one for all, Angels Window.
Another peculiarity of the North Rim is his height that allows you to have a dominant view on the Grand Canyon.
Some viewpoints are located at almost 2700 meters high and this also means the experience of altitude characterized by crisp air and clear skies, which permeate particularly vivid and saturated colors.
Finally the journey, I have undertaken to Page to get here.
Roads that you walk easy, relaxed driving that leads you dall'Horseshoe Bend, making you cross the Navajo bridge and leads you along a slope of colorful Vermilion Cliffs.
A route that guides you through a barren piece of land, and that as salt making you share meet a very diverse vegetation, from the desert to grassy meadows and conifer forests.
Features that do not find in the other two places, but here in the North Rim.

About the North and South Rim want to emphasize competence, friendliness, professionalism, friendliness of staff, cleanliness of the rooms.
The quality standard of the National Park Visitor Center, understood as persons and available mass media, is very high and they are really a point of reference, a valuable guide for each visitor.

Parlando del Grand Canyon del Colorado, in questo viaggio del 2019 ho avuto modo di visitare il North ed il South Rim.
Invece avevo già visitato il Grand Canyon West 10 anni prima, nel 2009.
Inevitabilmente mi viene da paragonare i tre luoghi.
E’ difficile assegnare dei giudizi obiettivi ed oggettivi, quindi mi limito alle mie percezioni e ricordi.
Ciascuno dei 3 luoghi merita di esser visto, ciascuno vale il viaggio.

Nel Grand Canyon West l’esperienza dello Skywalk è particolare, molto iconici sono i siti Eagle Point, così chiamato per una costa di montagna con la forma di aquila sacra per i Nativi Hualapai e Guano Point, che prende il nome da un’antica grotta (situata sulla riva opposta del Colorado) piena di guano di pipistrello che alcuni decenni fa venne sfruttata proprio per l’estrazione di questo prodotto.
Una gita in elicottero e la navigazione sul fiume per alcuni chilometri fu un’esperienza indimenticabile.

Il South Rim è quello che di solito si pensa quando ci si riferisce al Grand Canyon in senso generale, almeno qui in Italia.
Ho constatato bellissimi punti di osservazione tra cui, uno per tutti, Desert View Watchtower.
Il cuore del parco, tuttavia è molto frequentato dai turisti e, per alcuni aspetti, assomiglia ad un tessuto cittadino, limitando così l’aura selvaggia e solitaria (ma non la bellezza) che dovrebbe caratterizzare un luogo come il Grand Canyon del Colorado.

Ho sempre percepito il North Rim come un luogo “secondario” e così ho voluto fare un’esperienza diretta.
Non solo sono rimasto molto sorpreso dalla bellezza dei suoi siti, ma ho anche scoperto dei luoghi dai quali i panorami sono veramente mozzafiato tra cui, uno per tutti, Angels Window.
Un’altra peculiarità del North Rim è la sua altezza che permette di avere una visuale dominante sul Grand Canyon.
Alcuni punti di osservazione si trovano a quasi 2700 metri di altezza e ciò implica anche l’esperienza di un’altitudine caratterizzata dall’aria frizzante e dal cielo terso, i quali permeano colori particolarmente vivi e saturi.
In ultimo il viaggio, che ho intrapreso da Page per arrivare fin qui.
Strade che percorri facilmente, una guida rilassante che ti conduce dall’Horseshoe Bend, che ti fa attraversare il ponte Navajo e ti conduce lungo un versante delle coloratissime Vermilion Cliffs.
Un tragitto che ti guida attraverso un territorio arido e che man mano sale di quota facendoti incontrare una vegetazione molto eterogenea, da quella desertica fino a prati erbosi e foreste di conifere.
Caratteristiche che non trovi negli altri due luoghi, ma solo qui, nel North Rim.

A proposito del North e South Rim voglio sottolineare la competenza, la cordialità, la professionalità, la cortesia del personale, la pulizia degli ambienti.
Lo standard qualitativo dei Visitor Center nei National Park, inteso come persone e mass media disponibili, è veramente alto e sono davvero un punto di riferimento, una preziosa guida per ciascun visitatore.
likes: Dominant view and altitude experience (North Rim)
Competent and friendly staff (North and South Rim)
High-quality visitor centers (North and South Rim)

Mission San Cayetano del Tumacacori was founded by Jesuit Father Eusebio Fransisco Kino in 1691. Originally built on the east side of the Santa Cruz River, it was located near a native Sobaicuri (O'odham) settlement. After the O'odham Uprising (also called the Pima Revolt/Rebellion) in 1751 against Spanish settlements, this mission was abandoned.

In 1753, Mission San Jose de Tumacacori was re-established but built on the west side of the Santa Cruz River, its current location. The first church on this site was finished in 1757.

In 1768, the Spanish King Carlos III ordered all Jesuit priests out of Mexico and the missions they controlled. He had become convinced that the Jesuits were faithful to the Pope and not to Spain. The Mexican missions were then placed under the control of the Franciscan order and Father Junipero Serra. Fr Serra, soon after (seeking new converts), traveled to Alta California and established its El Camino Real (the King's Road).

In 1880, the Franciscan order was determined to build a new church to rival the northern Mission Xavier del Bac (near Tucson). In the first year, a foundation was laid. Over the next few years, a wall of only 7 feet was built as there was little funding. By 1821, with the sale of cattle, the church walls were raised to 14 feet before work stopped again. Over the next few years work continued but Mission San Jose was never finished.

With the expulsion of all Spanish-born missionaries by the Mexican government in 1828, Franciscan Father Diaz (born in Mexico) became the last priest to serve at Mission San Jose. As one if the two last remaining Franciscan priests, they divided and then were forced to constantly travel between Pimeria Alta's (Sonoran desert) many missions. Father Diaz died in 1841.

By 1848, Mission San Jose was completely abandoned. Restoration began in 1908 when President Theodore Roosevelt declared it Tumacacori National Monument. As a NPS site, a visitor center was built in 1937, the Tumacacori Museum was finished in 1939. In 1990, it became the Tumacacori National Historic Park.

Mission San Jose de Tumacacori is in ruins. But that doesn't diminish this site or its history. The museum contains many exhibits, a video and small educational bookstore. Tours are offered or you can take a self-guided trip around the grounds. One highlight is the fantastic tortilla maker that displays her craft, serving fresh tortillas to visitors. If interested in southwestern history, Mission San Jose is definitely worth a visit.

Mission San Antonio de Padua de los Robles (Saint Anthony of Padua of the Oaks) was the 3rd mission founded by Father Junipero Serra in 1771, after Mission San Diego de Alcala (1st) and Mission San Carlos Borromeo del Carmelo (2nd).

Because the first site didn't have a stable water source, Mission San Antonio was moved in 1773 to the 'Valley of the Oaks' (now the Salinas Valley) near the San Miguel Creek. After building a dam, a three mile long brick aqueduct system and reservoir were built to provide a steady supply of water to the new Mission location.

The current church was completed in 1813. This became the first mission to use the distinctive red roof 'mission' tiles.

In 1821, Mexico gained independence from Spain and took possession of the lands of Alta California. It is estimated that the mission system controlled almost one sixth of this land. With the Mexican Secularization Act of 1933, most missions were sold in 1834. Because no town was located nearby, Mission San Antonio went unsold and eventually became neglected. In 1863, the mission ruins with 33 acres were returned to the Catholic Church by President Abraham Lincoln.

Restoration of Mission San Antonio began in 1903 but stopped after the destructive San Andreas earthquake of 1906. Further reconstruction occurred from 1948 to 1952.  Required earthquake retrofitting continues to this day. Donations are greatly needed to continue these state-mandated costs for required earthquake retrofitting. Given that Mission San Antonio is not located near a large population of supporters, it also receives fewer visitors which makes its need unique.

Because the Mission has been protected by Ft Hunter-Liggett and the William Randolf Hearst Estate, it has kept the Mission grounds more true to its original times. Unfortunately, this same isolation has created other issues-- most notably, its need for a financial support base in its restoration and preservation needs. Please support Mission San Antonio.

If one is on a journey through CA’s historic times by visiting its series of 21 missions, I found Mission San Antonio to be one, if not its best. Although its location from Hwy 101 may be perceived as the most difficult to reach due to distance (about 45 minutes), it is well worth this little extra time.

Mission San Antonio also has the added bonus of being a retreat (individual or group) with one being able to make overnight reservations for solitude or devotion, or single day events like weddings.

One could argue that the history of Point Defiance Park started with President John Quincy Adams who requested funding in 1828 for the United States Exploring Expedition. Eight years later, under President Andrew Jackson, Congress finally approved the funds for what would then be called the Wilkes Expedition of 1838-1842. It was a naval expedition that was to survey and explore the Pacific Ocean and its surrounding lands.

Like the Lewis and Clark Expedition, it was a major scientific endeavor, especially in the new field of oceanography. Many species and items were collected which were subsequently added to the newly created Smithsonian Institute (1846). Over 60,000 bird and animal specimens were collected. Of that, 254 live plants would become the United States Botanic Garden (1850). Coastlines were mapped and 280 islands were explored.

During coastline exploration in 1841, Navy Lieutenant Charles Wilkes surveyed the areas surrounding Fort Clatsop, Fort Vancouver, Fort Nisqually, Bainbridge Island, the Strait of Juan de Fuca and the Hood Canal. It was during his time surveying the Puget Sound that Wilkes declared that if a fort was built at the point of the narrows (now looking across to Gig Harbor), its position could "defy" the world. With this declaration, the lands of Point Defiance became a military reservation.

In 1888, President Grover Cleveland authorized the area to be used as a public park. It contains 700+ acres, much of it old growth forest. It also includes the Point Defiance Zoo and Aquarium, Fort Nisqually (moved from Dupont WA in 1933), Owen's Beach, a boardwalk and boat house, a WA State ferry terminal to Vashon Island, and miles of beautiful trails.

There are also formal gardens, including a Japanese Garden with a Pagoda (1914, originally built as a streetcar station), Dalhia gardens, and over a acre of roses. The first Rose Garden here was established in 1895.

This is a fantastic park. Its famous Five Mile Drive closes down on weekends so that walkers, joggers and bicycles can safely use the roads. On a sunny summer day, there is no better place than Point Defiance to walk along the beach or hike gorgeous trails, picnic, wander through gardens or play Frisbee across expansive lawns. Definitely worth checking out.

Warning: if using Google Maps for directions using AZ Hwy 179 from Sedona, the route takes you under Interstate 17 to a four mile dirt road. Although shorter in distance, one might prefer heading south onto the freeway (hang a right) and doubling back through the town of Rim Rock.

Located 11 miles away from Montezuma Castle NM, Montezuma Well NM is located outside the town of Rimrock. As an adjoining unit, Montezuma Well NM contains a large limestone sinkhole (386 ft in diameter) that produces 1,500,000 gallons of spring water a day. Even in periods of drought, it continues to reliably discharge water.

Both the Yavapai and the Tonto Apaches consider Montezuma Well as a sacred site of creation where they believe the first humans emerged into our world.

Located in the Verde Valley, ancient inhabitants have lived near the Well for centuries. Indigenous peoples have been known to reside in the area from 700 to 1425 CE. Most notable was the Southern Sinagua who used the constant flow of water from the Well for irrigation purposes. Ancient canals were built (one almost seven miles long) to supply water to many acres of farmland. Some portions of the canal system is still visible today.

Montezuma Well’s water is highly carbonated and contains a high level of arsenic. Because of this, five endemic species have been discovered living within the Well. Information about these species can be found at this Park's visitor center.

Amazing prehistoric cliff dwellings of the Sinagua people were built along the rim of Montezuma Well. Pit houses and other Sinagua house ruins, dating from 1050 CE, are nearby and accessable by trails.

Today, residents of Rimrock continue to access these waters, still using the 1,000 year old ditch built long ago. If visiting Montezuma Castle, this short side trip to Montezuma Well is a great addition to understanding the ancient Sinagua, their culture and traditions.
likes: Cultural Value: Sacred site, historical significance
Facilities & Services: Visitor center, information availability

reviews_attraction.text:
Canyonlands NP is an expansive desert park. It is divided into three major sections, neither of which are accessible to each other. Each is distinctive. And it takes hours to drive between their separate entrances.

The “Island in the Sky” district is the north entrance, located outside of Moab, Utah. This is the most visited section of Canyonlands. It is located very near Arches NP, so if you’re short on time, visiting both parks within a day is very doable. It is the most visitor-friendly district with paved roads, with short day hike options, great vistas, a visitor center/educational bookstore and a campground. In other wards, it’s the more typical national park experience.

The “Needles” district is more remote, located in the southeast corner of Canyonlands. It requires 4 wheel drive vehicles and long trails to visit an area of awesome sandstone spires. Approachable by either Moab or Monticello, take UT Hwy 211 for 35 miles where it dead ends into the park. This is the only paved road into the Needles district. The use of maps is highly recommended, the use of GPS is notably discouraged.

The “Maze” district is even more remote and it is the least visited section of Canyonlands for a reason. It requires high clearance 4 wheel drive vehicles into an area so remote that expertise in self survival is highly recommended. A visit here requires days.

Not to forget the rivers, one can have the experience of guided float trips via private concessionaires. Both the Colorado and the Green Rivers have carved the majestic canyons within Canyonlands and they converge here. The Colorado River is accessible at Moab and Potash; the Green River is accessible at the city of Green River, Ruby Ranch or Mineral Bottom. Although half day trips are available, many trips are weeklong. This is a amazing way to discover Canyonlands NP.

There are three compelling reasons to visit Great Basin NP:

First is the very noticeable Wheeler Peak, at 9,886 ft in elevation, it is Nevada's highest point. One can choose to climb its summit or hike into the fantastic Bristlecone  Forest on it's flanks. The summit hike is 8.2 miles RT, with an elevation gain of 2,900 ft. More moderate hikes include the Bristlecone Trail and the Alpine Lakes Loop, both less than 3 miles RT and a 600 ft elevation gain. There are plenty of amazing hiking options in this park. The Island Forest Trail is wheelchair accessible.

Second would be the limestone Lehman Caves. Most people come to Great Basin to take this ranger guided tour. There is the Lodge Room 60 minute tour or the Grand Palace 90 minute tour. For those unable to manage multiple stars, a First Room tour is available (check at desk). Just be aware that these tours are very popular and reservations are recommended. Also, only handheld cameras, cellphones and flashlights are allowed in the caves.

A third great reason to visit here is the night. In 2016, Great Basin NP was designated as an International Dark Sky Park. This designation is not easy to achieve. Now it must protect the "pristine nighttime environment for scientific, recreational and cultural values." This is a big deal. Having what are considered to be some of the darkest nighttime skies, gazing at the Milky Way here is astounding. Few places in the US are comparable. There are numerous activities for viewing from a Saturday night Astronomy Program to Moon Hikes to afternoon Solar Telescope Viewing. Also, an Astronomy Festival occurs in September. The night sky at Great Basin NP is well worth a visit.

Saguaro National Park sits in the middle of the Sonoran Desert. The park is divided into two distinct districts. East of Tucson is the Rincon Mountain District (RMD), also referred to as Saguaro East. To the west of Tucson is the Tucson Mountain District (TMD), also refered to as Saguaro West. The city of Tucson snugly fits between these two districts.

Saguaro West is probably the most visited district. It is known for its namesake, the giant saguaro cactus. There are so many here it is considered a be a Saguaro Forest. The Red Hills visitor center should be able to answer all questions concerning the area, including ancient petroglyphs, hiking trails and 4 wheel drive roads. February through April are considered the best months for visitation due to the gorgeous cactus blooms. Saguaro cacti typically bloom in April.

Saguaro East is different. It is called a "Sky Island," an area that protects such animals as the bear, cougar and the coati. It contains the Cactus Forest Loop Drive, as well as hiking trails to a historic homestead and cabin. There is a great visitor center located at the start of the loop drive.

There are six small walk-in campgrounds within Saguaro NP,  but only the largest (Manning  Camp with 6 sites) has water year-round. It is located 7.5 miles from its trailhead. All others (3 spots each) are dry camps, the closest being a 4.1 mile hike.

Be aware that the "monsoon season" happens at Saguaro from about June 15th through September. Thunderstorms occur most afternoons and dangerous flash flooding can occur. Also, Saguaro NP closes one day a year, on Christmas Day.

Coronado NM is a memorial, not a monument. The NPS website states that this park "was established to interpret the Coronado Expedition," further stating  that there is no evidence that Francisco Vasquez de Coronado entered these Park lands in 1540. All that is known about the route of this Spanish expedition is that they likely entered the southwest along the San Pedro River nearby. They were searching for the fabled seven cities of gold.

Located on the Mexico/US border in southern AZ, Coronado NM is not a busy park. It is out of the way from just about everything. As an out-of-stater, it took dedicated effort to visit here, situated between the towns of Nogales and Bisbee. Located in the Huachuca Mountains, the visitor center sits at 5,230 ft in elevation.

Coronado NM was established to memorialize the Spanish Expedition and the visitor center certainly has dedicated exhibits detailing the men and the influence they brought to the area. There is also a small educational book store. If you're not careful, you might think that this is all the park has to offer.

Also located here is the Coronado Cave (1/4 mile west of the visitor center) via a 1/2 mile trail with an elevation gain of 500 ft.  No permits are required. Don't forget headlamps (two light sources advised) and to protect the limestone, gloves are requested. Stop at the visitor center for cave visitation guidelines.

There is also the Monetzuma Pass Overlook (western entrance), at 6,575 ft in elevation, one can look across the US border into Mexico. It is certainly worth a view.
likes: On-site Activities: Cave exploration, Scenic overlook

reviews_attraction.text:
Olympic National Park is truly exceptional. For any outdoor enthusiast, there should be an adventure for everyone. The Olympic Mountains are surrounded by a fantastic rain forest (big clue that it's wet here a lot) so hiking any trail into the woods brings the added picturesque bonus of lush moss on giant old-growth trees. If mountain climbing is your thing, one can backpack high into its glacial peaks. The Pacific Northwest National Scenic Trail (PNNST) takes one on a  1,200 mile journey from the coastline of Olympic NP crossing through Idaho and Montana to the Continental Divide in Glacier NP.

Maybe wandering on miles upon miles of wild, often rugged beaches along the Pacific Ocean is what you're looking to do. Olympic NP protects 73 miles of truly awesome coastline. During low tide (check online or at ranger station for daily tide information), tide-pooling is listed as being especially popular at Mora's Hole in the Wall and Kalaloch's Beach 4.

Maybe fishing in one of the Park's many streams for wild salmon or trout is on your list. Or one may simply choose to have a pleasant day trip driving to Hurricane Ridge, just for the magnificent view.

It's all here. Camping or lodging, hiking or backpacking, beaches and tide pools, fishing or boating,  birding or wildlife watching, ranger stations and visitor centers-- this is Olympic National Park.

Klondike Gold Rush-Seattle is a smaller historical part of the bigger event that occurred in Alaska. The major portion of this duo-park is located in Skagway, AK at the Klondike Gold Rush NHS. Both National Park sites tell the story of the Gold Rush from start (Seattle) to finish (Skagway and the Chilkoot Trail).

Located in the famous Pioneer Square, the Seattle unit focuses on the beginning of the mad rush north and the preparations required to survive the Chilkoot, described as the "meanest 33 miles in history." From 1897-1898, the supplying of necessary provisions in its now-busy waterfront and overcrowded stores made many wealthy in Seattle.

The Klondike Gold Rush-Seattle unit is located in a small section of a historic Cadillac Hotel on 2nd Avenue. A visitor center is located in the building that offers 2 floors of exhibits, park-related films and an educational bookstore. Park rangers are on hand to answer any questions concerning the Gold Rush. A self-guided walking tour of the historic Pioneer Square, just outside the door, is locally available. It follows a 'Trail to Treasure' map that identifies 16 historic points of interest nearby.

The Klondike Gold Rush Seattle NHS tells a story, the beginning of a story, about a captivating piece of American history. If in Seattle, this National Historic Site is well worth a visit.

Located north of Flagstaff AZ, Wupatki NM can be accessed through Sunset Crater Volcano NM. Paying the entrance fee here covers both parks. A loop road from Sunset Crater to Wupatki takes one through both parks and exits further north, on AZ Hwy 89.

The ruins at Wupatki lay across a vast area of prairie desert. A visitor center is located near mile post 21 of the loop road. Here, one begins to discover the history of the Native American Indians that built these pueblos 900 years ago. The park trails are self-guiding and are open from sun-up to sunset. No back-country overnight hiking/camping is allowed. No pets are allowed on any trail.

The largest ruin, the Wupatki Pueblo, is estimated to have 100 rooms. There is a short 0.5 mile loop trail that begins at the visitor center. A ball court is located nearby.

Other trails along the loop road include the Lomaki and Box Canyon Pueblos (0.8 mile trail)  the Citadel and Nalakihu Pueblos  (0.4 mile trail) and the Wukoki Pueblo (0.4 mile trail). There is also a Doney Mountain Trail (0.8 miles) that takes one to the top of a cinder cone.

Wupatki NM protects dozens of ancient village communities that once thrived in this area. This park is outstanding in its effort to protect the past. A visit here is certainly worth an afternoon (or day).
likes: Facilities & Services: Visitor center, self-guided trails

reviews_attraction.text:
Fort Vancouver NHS is a duo-park. Nearby is a visitor center (not within the fort). And the historic Pearson Field and Museum is a short drive away, also run by the NPS.

Built by the Hudson's Bay Company in 1825, Fort Vancouver (named after Captain George Vancouver) sat the the north bank of the Columbia River.  Its  first manager was Dr John McLoughlin, a position he held for 22 years (1824-1845). He retired nearby in Oregon, his house now a McLaughlin House National Historic Site.

The first Fort Vancouver was built northeast of its current location. The present location was established in 1829. The fort served as the center of HBC's western operations, controlling fur trade from Alaska to Mexico.

The current Fort Vancouver is a replica. The fort had completely burned in 1866. From 1947-1952, the NPS began excavations of the present site. Reconstruction began in the 1960's. The present fort was based on historic written descriptions and excavation-based archeology.

If you are interested in the history of the Hudson's Bay Company and its impacts on the PNW, a visit here is worthwhile. If you're lucky, you'll catch the blacksmiths working their forges or woodworkers in their shop. There's lots to learn here, come visit.

Sunset Crater Volcano NM sits adjacent to Wupatki NM and share a 34 mile loop road that takes you through both parks. From the high Ponderosa forests surrounding the Sunset Crater, the road drops some 2,000 ft into a desert prairie that provided a home to dozens of ancient villages 900 years ago. The entrance fee here covers both parks. If only you drive the loop and visit the distinct visitor centers, there is much to see.

Sunset Crater VNM protects a fragile area, one that in its past had a violent, explosive history. Around the year 1085, a major eruption not only changed the landscape but also greatly impacted the Native Americans who lived nearby.

Several trails are in the park. The Lava Edge Trail takes one along the Bonita Lava Flow (3.4 miles RT). The Lenox Crater Trail (1.6 miles RT) brings you to the summit with views of Sunset Crater and the distant San Francisco Peaks. The Lava Flow Trail (1.6 miles RT) take you around the base of Sunset Crater. There is no access to the summit of the Sunset Crater.

If in the area of Flagstaff, this duo-park is an amazing way to spend a day. There are fantastic landscapes combined with truly beautiful ancient ruins.

Seven Magic Mountains are seven colorful, massive towers of brightly painted stones, reportly stacked up to 35 feet high. Sitting near a parrallel frontage road alongside Interstate 15 between Jean and Las Vegas, the bright neon colors definitely bring contrast to the surrounding muted Mojave desert landscape.

Created by the mixed media Swiss artist Ugo Rondinone, the artwork was built from Nevada-quarried limestone boulders. A total of 32 massive boulders were used to create the towering "seven mountains."

This is a temporary art installation which opened in May, 2016.  The towers were originally planned to remain at site for only two years but public interest and outcry has extended the length of this brilliant art display. Currently, the artwork is now scheduled to remain until the end of 2018. Many would like to see these seven structures remain permanently.

Whether traveling by car to or from the south along I-15, or visiting Las Vegas by any other means, the close proximity to the city (about 12-15 miles south of the strip) makes a visit here worthy of your time. It's an incredible work of art.

Pipe Spring NM is located near Fredonia, AZ about 45 miles east of Hurricane, UT. It showcases the conflict between the local Kaibab Piaute Indians and the arriving Mormon settlers (1850's) and their struggle for water. For centuries, Pipe Spring was a life-saving oasis for the native people of the northern Arizona strip (north of Grand Canyon). With Mormon settlers building a major settlement for massive cattle operations at Pipe Spring, the struggle for water intensified.

The museum on-site tells the story of the people who used Pipe Springs in order to survive: the Ancestral Puebloans, the Kaibab Piaute Indians and the LDS Mormon settlers.

Also located here is the historic Winsor Castle (inside tours available on the hour), built as a defensible fort for protection. Constructed in 1872, the fort was built to sit directly over Pipe Spring. Anson Winsor (the fort subsequently became known as Winsor Castle) was appointed by Brigham Young to operate the massive LDS cattle ranch along the northern Arizona strip.

Knowing that I am not great on exposure and would probably never climb straight up (the normal way) to the top of El Capitan -- I opted for the backcountry trail. I was not disappointed. This is a fantastic trek allowing any seasoned hiker simply awesome (but different) views of Yosemite Valley.

There are several routes, the quickest being the trail to the top of Yosemite Falls. From there you can connect onto a trail that will ultimately take you to the summit of El Capitan. Note though, that this would be a very strenuous, long hike in just one day. Be prepared with lots of water and a good flashlight.

I opted for a 3 day adventure taking me from North Dome, across Yosemite Falls and onward to El Cap. Although you stay along the rim, this route is by no means flat. It's constantly up and down. But it connects three iconic features, and sunset at night looking across at Half Dome (from North Dome) can be amazing.

When exiting Natural Bridges National Monument and heading southbound via UT Hwy 261, I was very surprised to discover the Moki Dugway. This road is not for the faint of heart. You literally come to the edge of the mesa and the road drops you down the face along a very steep, non-guard-railed, switchbacked, grated dirt road. It is some 3 miles in length that drops over 1,000 ft in elevation. It is a one lane road with wider spots on the curves (only place wide enough for passing). You seemingly crawl down the vertical face of the red sandstone mesa.

On my trip (obviously heading downward), there are warning signs of a 10% grade posted at each end of this steep cliff road. But it doesn’t necessarily prepare one (for the first time) for the sudden drop. Definitely eye opening. As scary as it was, it’s simply an amazing drive switchbacking down a step sandstone cliff face.

Five stars if you are 8 and younger, three stars if you are older--so four stars average. Simply, this museum was built for kids and caters to kids. There is little in way of adult-oriented exhibits or content, and labeling is sadly lacking.

That being said, this is a great place for families with small children. There is much for children to enjoy and leave a little more excited about our many  natural environments and those critters who share (or once lived long ago) our planet.

Given the amount of money that flows through Vegas on a daily basis, it is somewhat sad or frustrating that more funding isn't available to update and improve these exhibits. Children deserve a place like this (a better place actually), to get excited about science, to widen their curiosities that may become life-long passions. But it's a start, well deserving of a couple hours of time.

Although a visit to.the Eugene O'Neill National Historic Park site requires advanced reservations for guided tours, it is every bit worth this added challenge. A mini-bus picks up small groups in front of the railroad museum in downtown Danville.

The Eugene O'Neill house is closed on Monday and Tuesday. Also, there are no guided tours/reservations required on Saturday. Call the Park or go to their website for further visitor information.

My visit involved a bus driver, tour guide, and a cashier at the onsite bookstore, one very talented individual. He was very passionate and extremely knowledgeable about Eugene O'Neill and the history of the Tao House which made my visit beyond exceptional. A trip here is well worth the required couple hours of time.

The Four Corners Monument (by the way, it is not a National Park Service site) does not actually sit on the corners of these four Western States. Modern technology finally caught up with the real world and discovered a few years ago that someone goofed. With that said, I guess it is fun to take a picture of yourself standing on the monument's ground marker simply because nearby (now determined to be 1,807 ft away), this 4-state corner actually does exist. Operated as a Navajo Nation Tribal Park and as a fee area, it essentially provides one access to various booths, selling local native crafts.

On a side note, after states starting suing to extend their state lines, the Supreme Court gave this 4-corner spot legality, even though incorrect.

It's hard to give any National Monument one star but given that this specific monument is only a loosely dedicated site and name at this point in time, one star it is. It actually is much more in that the Big Dig did happen and countless fossils were unearthed at this site. Many more are probably still in the ground. Someday, hopefully sooner than later, a fence will be built to define the monument. A visitor center will follow, giving visitors an idea of the types of fossils discovered at the Big Dig. If we're lucky, some of the original fossils will return to their point of discovery. And maybe, continuing fossil digs will return on site under the direction of the NPS. One can hope. I can hardly wait to see what fossils are buried here.

Joshua Tree NP is a desert park and gets very hot in the summer when most people are vacationing. Make sure you come prepared for extreme heat conditions if visiting during the summer.

During other seasons, this park has a lot more to offer. If you have never seen a Joshua tree in bloom, a trip here in the spring is well worth the experience. The tips of their branches have a exceptionally large, beautifully bright white flower in awesome display. They’re gorgeous.

And there is much more to Joshua Tree NP than their namesake tree. There are fantastic outcrops of granite that provide experienced and novice rock climbers alike with varied routes. This park is very popular with rock climbers during winter months.

Five stars, if you are into aviation history. Pearson Air Field and its Museum are attached to the NPS with the neighboring Fort Vancouver National Historic Site. It is a small (free) museum concerning the aviation history of the adjacent Pearson Air Field involving the Pacific coast as well as the local Vancouver, WA/Portland, OR area. There is a variety of historical planes on display inside the museum. The history of flight is also displayed.

Pearson Air Field is well worth a visit if you are interested in early aviation history or that of the Pacific Northwest. A visit here is easily combinable with the nearby Fort Vancouver National Historic Site for an afternoon of additional discovery.

Although Shasta State Historic Park is seemingly small (approximately one block in length) of mostly brick building ruins, visiting here is certainly worth a trip. It is located about six miles west of Redding California (before Whiskeytown NRA) and easy to find along Hwy 299. The accompanying museums are fantastic, especially wandering about the historic store that was sold to the California State Park system. It is still intact with its original merchandise. The on-site Ranger certainly helps visitors discover products on the shelves of this old mercantile. The park is a great place to spend an afternoon, learning about one of California’s great historic places
likes: Cultural Value: Historic ruins, original merchandise
Facilities & Services: Accompanying museums, on-site Ranger

reviews_attraction.text:
The Rocket Garden is located along Utah Hwy 83, outside the headquarters of the Northrup Grumman building located in Corinne. Listed as a museum, the outside display contains numerous older NASA or military rockets and missles. Each piece has a sign that describes its history and military specifications.

If visiting Promontory to visit the Golden Spike National Historic Site, visiting here is a no-brainer if interested in rockets or military history. It is located just a couple miles north on Ut-83 from the turnoff to Golden Spike. So it's very easy to combine this outdoor "rocket museum" with a visit to the National Park.

Eight miles outside of Montrose is Hwy. 346, a spur road leading to the Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park. The park contains 12-miles of the 48-mile long Black Canyon of the Gunnison River.
The national park itself contains the deepest and most dramatic section of the canyon, but the canyon continues both upstream and downstream from here. The canyon's name owes itself to the fact that parts of the gorge only receive 33 minutes of sunlight a day.
We chose to drive along the South Rim Drive, which features several overlooks during its course of seven miles from Tomichi Point to High Point. It is possible to hike down into the canyon but this requires permits and a great deal of skill; more than we have. The South Rim Campground is open all year, but without water hookups or dump stations.
The first Viewpoint, Tomichi Point, at 8248 feet. This is the first glimpse of the Black Canyon for South Rim visitors. Most of the rim is above 8000 feet, so it is cooler. And the viewpoints all have ample parking. restrooms are at Tomichi Point and the Visitor Center.
Gunnison Point is the second viewpoint along the South Rim. Gunnison Point is the most popular in the park as it lies just behind the visitor center, linked to Tomichi Point and the campground by a one-mile trail along the rim.
There is a ranger led 1.5 hour, 7-mile boat tour of the Gunnison River by reservation only. The dock is 25 miles west of Montrose on Hwy. 50. It’s 232 steps down to the trail and then a ¾-mile walk to the dock. And then again in reverse. It costs $24.
Two miles further along the road, the next stop is Pulpit Rock Overlook, where even more of the river is in view, as it curves round a 90-degree bend. A 134-yard trail leads to the viewing area.
The park road rounds several tight bends before passing the parking area for Cross Fissures View, reached by a 357-yard path.
Chasm View is one of the most spectacular overlooks in the park. A very short path descends slightly to a sizeable, railing protected viewing area above perhaps the steepest part of the whole canyon, where the cliffs fall 1,840 feet over a horizontal distance of just 400 feet.
The next viewpoint, Painted Wall View, has a different panorama. Painted Wall is the highest cliff in Colorado, bordering the far side of the river; a 2,250-foot wall of rock about half a mile across. This marks the end of the most enclosed part of the Black Canyon. When you see it, you'll understand the name.
The road continues to High Point, which also has picnic tables but no views of note. Most people come here for the 1,373-yard trail to Warner Point, the furthest overlook on the South Rim. This trail steps down to a saddle giving views of green fields, 1,000 feet below to the south, with the city of Delta visible in the hazy distance beyond.

You'll find this almost unknown National Monument about 25-miles south of  Mountainair, NM. If you wish to stay in the area, the nearest town with hotels and services would be Moriarty, east of Albuquerque on I-40. Its roughly 40-miles.
Gran Quivira is one of three missions of the Salinas Pueblo Missions spread across roughly 40-miles, near Mountainair. It is the farthest away at 26-miles. The main Visitor Center is in Mountainair, but each pueblo has its own Ranger Contact Station, with adequate parking and restrooms. Some have picnic areas and even small play places.
Construction of the missions began in 1622 with the advent of the Franciscan priests and was completed in 1635 . Gran Quivira was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.
In these pueblos, the National Park Service has this pet policy: "Leashed pets are allowed on the trails, provided the owners will clean up any messes the pets might make".
We visited Gran Quivira. It is the largest of the three, with 7 kivas and well over 200 rooms, and is only partly reconstructed, including two church ruins. The Franciscans came on order of the Spanish king, who in turn had orders from the Pope to 'christianize' the natives of the New World. None of the three pueblos had a full-time priest, so when the nearest priest travelled to visit on rare occasions, they were known as ‘visitias’.
Efforts began in good order on the building of Gran Quivira. The pueblo started out with a good reserve of stored food and became so busy, learning the new language, taking Christian-Catholic classes to learn the new faith, building the second and much larger church, and quarters for the priest to stay in, that they had no time to work in the fields to raise the crops. Since there were three years of food reserves, this was not a problem and they ate into those reserves. Then there was a severe drought which resulted in a famine. By 1670, 70% of the population was dead, (450 at Gran Quivira alone) having starved to death. This ended the construction effort and destroyed the pueblo.
Today, the ruins are left for us to see and contemplate this life lifestyle. They are remarkably well -preserved due to the arid climate. There is a paved .05 trail running through the ruins. where one is free to explore at will. Be advised that the sun is very bright and strong and sunburn happens quickly. It is hot and dry and there is no shade. We found the Ranger very helpful and interesting. He obviously loved his work and this isolated place.

If you arrive at Yellowstone Park from Cooke City, MT through the NE park entrance, this will be the first major feature you will see. Watch for the Buffalo herds in Lamar Valley right before you get here. From the road junctions at Tower, you can choose to go south over Dunraven Pass, at almost 8900 feet, or you can continue mostly west to Mammoth Hot Springs, where the North Entrance is.
Tower Fall is upstream from where Tower Creek joins the Yellowstone River and is named for the rock pinnacles at the top of the Fall. We heard it before we saw it as it drops 132-feet straight down. There is a nice pull out there to stop and rest a bit, take photos, and if there is time, to even take a hike down to Tower Creek. It's steep, so know this in advance. Good hiking footwear would be needed for this.

During the winter of 1807-08, John Colter traveled through this area after he broke away from the Lewis and Clarke Expedition. He was one of the first to describe what became Yellowstone Park as a place of 'fire and brimstone', and people thought he was delusional. Many more testimonies and 40 years would go by before anyone actually thought he could be correct.

Due to time constraints, we just stopped at the overlook. But the view of the Fall and Tower Creek was very impressive. A taste of things to come.

Tower-Roosevelt is a full service stop. There are cabins, camping, two general stores, and a Gift Shop, plus restaurants.

We have appreciated Terry Redlin's work for a long time. Mr. Redlin was a local Watertown artist. 150 of his original works are housed in this museum, which was designed by his son. It sits on several acres of parkland, ideal for outdoor weddings, photos, or other events. Some of the buildings are available to rent for this. Mr. Redlin had the museum built to house his works as a gift to the people of Watertown. Therefore, there is no admission fee.
Guests are free to wander among his works without an escort, and read the descriptions that explain his inspiration for the piece. Guided tours are also available. He has done several series and my favorite is the 'America the Beautiful' series.
