Take into account that this area get crowed usually after 9 am, so plan accordingly and try to arrive before that. Also, there is no shade, so be careful on sunny days and wear clothes that cover your arms/shoulders and also a hat/cap to protect your head. Finally, during spring it is the best time to come, but also it is usually wet and muddy so wear water proof boots, long pants and an extra pair of socks in case you step on a puddle.

Nice place to have a walk, enjoy the birds or simply have a picnic on the grass. In some areas it looks a bit dirty, and it feels a bit small too, but the views of the river and the oldtown across the street was worth it. There are also some interesting informative panels about the history and the animals in the area. I do recommend, however, to go the other side. To me, much better than this other side! The have restrooms and bike and board renting if you want.

Nice and pleasant hike trails. You can choose what to follow here but I recommend taking the loop from/to the parking lot. You can have views of the coast, the beach and the trees. The hike is short, around 30 minutes have is mostly flat and shady. If you have time the beach is very nice to walk and pet friendly too. The parking lot area is pretty big and not too much crowded.

Nice park and the arches made up with horns is very original and impressive. At night they are also illuminated with changing colors. There is one arch on each of the four corner entrances to the park. Even during the covid pandemic in October 2020 it was a very lively place. There are plenty of restaurants, stores and activities to do nearby. What a great place!

One of my favourite places of Lake Tahoe. Awesome views of the lake and Emerald bay. Especially beautiful at sunset or sunrise and even better in winter with the snow. There are even better lookout points (more centered) a bit down the road, but there are no "oficial" parking spots to stop and take picture.

A bit hidden, but perfect to enjoy the sunset while watching at the ocean, listening to the birds, the waves and enjoying the views of the golden gate bridge. The trail is a bit steep but short from the main path. The beach itself is not too big but usually not too many people are present.

This an unconventional national park: small and it is all about hiking. It was a pleasant surprise, the wilderness, massive boulders, caves, trails, overlooks, flowers...really worth visiting to have an unique experience. If you are lucky enough you can even watch condors.

I actually liked this one better than the grand prismatic, at least from this walk (Grand prismatic views from observation point are unbeatable, mind you). Still, pretty nice colors, steam and formations in this one. Cannot miss it as it is on the way o grand prismatic.

Awesome. First part of the half dome trail among others. Beautiful but tough. All the way uphill, slippery, wet, but rewarding. I recommend going in late spring when there is more water to see it at full and choose different ways to go up and down to see both.

I love the main squad and this church is just as impressive. I haven been inside but just staying outside looking at the decoration and taking picture is worth a visit. I recommend going on a weekend to enjoy the place better without the student crowds.

Absolutely a must-see!!! A bit hidden and with a very narrow open time, but it is one of the best things to do if you like route 66 stuff. Admission is free. History, souvenirs, information and an outstandingly kind clerk will help you out.

I was interested in coming in to have a look, and I would have even bought something, but when I found out they charge you $5 just to let you in...I passed. No way for a store/tiny place...otherwise the place looked nice and full of history

Aweome place. Several pathways to trek by the river with great views of waterwalls across the river. One can go all the way down but the beat views are actually feom above. There is a small parking lot with a map in a sign.

The central place of redwood national park. Plenty of hikes, spots, stops, trees and mind blowing scenery. There is also the visitor center and many many pullover spot to enjoy the view and take pictures as well

Beautiful bridge on the scenic CA-1 road. Nice views of the ocean, coastline and the bridge. There are few parking spots on both sides of the road but be careful as this is usually a congested and crowded area.

Nice easy walk seeing pinnacles on the way. The place is a bit secluded from the lake. It is worth the visit but if you don't have enough time I would choose other points or hikes to do instead of this one.
Small but nice park to have a seat, enjoy a picnic or just relax in the shade of the trees or the grass. There are some restaurants where you can have something to eat/drink while being here.
We loved the small hut that serves as a gift shop and snack bar. Perfect place to enjoy a hot drink while resting by the fire and resuming your trip or heading back with the shuttle.
The best place in Yosemite! Astonishing breathtaking scenic views of the valley. It takes time to reach there and it is closed for the cold season but definitely worth going!
Beautiful place. Nice views of the dam and Mt Shasta in he background. It is worth taking the CA-151 to the vista point, it is few minutes away and you won't regret it.
Quite small compared to other visitor centers but rangers are nice as usual. They still have a store and some food\drink options
Beautiful place with nice views of the rock formations and hoodoos. Together with bryce point the best place in bryce canyon
One of my favourite places in San Francisco! On a clear fair day you can have amazing views and enjoy the flowers
Nice views of the valley with palm springs, mt jacinto and other places from above. Worth going for some pics
Great place that can be reach after a short and easy hike. As the name says, especially good for sunset.

A nice little state park. The day use fee is $7 which I feel is a little much for what the park offers. There is only about 3-4 miles of trails. One trail is about a mile long and loops in the canyon region and goes up to an old school house. The other trail goes further up the hillside and about a mile into the woods/park but is primarily an old degraded fire road, I turned around at the larger bridge since there was no exciting scenery. The cove is nice and is just a short walk from the parking area. The final trail is a coastal cliff side trail that you need to leave the parking area and park on the side of Hwy 1 to access, which does not require a day use fee. Overall the park is nice and you can easily spend and hour or two here. The campground looks nice as well, I wish the day use fee was only $5 or even less for what the park offers.

One of the best day trips for hiking I have had in the entire Bay Area. The best time to go is in the summer months when the weather is clear to experience the best views the park offers. You can get to Angel Island via ferry boat from Tiburon or San Francisco the ferry ticket covers the park entrance fee. There ia a perimeter road about 5 miles around the edge of the island and hiking trials on Mt. Livermore in the center of the island. If you take the first ferry to Angel Island and leave on the last you should be able to see everything in one day trip if you have a good pace. The views from various location on the island are great but there are 360° views of the entire Bay Area from the top of Mt. Livermore.
likes: Cultural Value (implied through historical significance, though not explicitly stated)

reviews_attraction.text: Palo Corona Regional Park is a great park to go hiking or simply walk. The first part of the park is an old abandoned golf course which has slowly been reclaimed by nature with the Carmel River flowing by, and old cart/walking paths and nice scenery. The other half of the park is mostly preserve/ranch land with dirt trails over a large area of rolling hills, and a fire road type trail which clumps up a hill to Inspiration Point which offers incredible views of the Carmel region on a clear day. Well worth a visit to go hiking and explore for families to experts.

Poly Canyon is a collection of unique and interesting structures/projects that were designed over the years by Cal Poly Architectural students on the outskirts of the Cal Poly campus in the Cal Poly Canyon. The hike to the structures is about a half mile or so and they are all located in a general area. Each project was designed over a year or two and has a different architectural aspect in the design. Well worth a visit if in San Luis Obispo or Cal Poly.

Tomales Point is a great place to hike to. The trail to the point is about 4.7 miles one way and is moderate. You do hike up two hills and there is about a half mile of sand to hike near the end. However, the views from the point on a clear day are spectacular. Due to its distance from the parking area the point is hiked by fewer people willing to make the almost 5 mile hike one way. Well worth the hike for the tremendous views and scenery.
dislikes: Fewer people (implied as a positive, so not listed under dislikes)

reviews_attraction.text: A great county park with a multitude of trials that gradually ascend the hillside. As you continue on the trails the ecosystem of the forest changes and the trees increase in height and change form eucalyptus to redwoods the high in elevation you go. Trails vary from wide multi use such as hikers, bikers, and horse riders to only hiking trails which are much narrower. Peaceful setting within the forest which gives you a sense of solitude.

A great little State Park to check out. There a few miles of trails which lead to some historic mine sites at the Park and also provide some great forest scenery. The visitor center also has a ton of historic facts about the mining operations that took place here. They have multiple artifacts, gems, minerals, gold, and even an entire miniature scale model of the mining tunnels which are underground across the park and region.

A great hiking destination. The trails are relatively flat with some sloping up and down. The Zinfandel Trail is mostly flat and the best trail to hike in my opinion since it is also the longest. Towards the beginning of the trail if you start at the winery there are a few short trails that branch off and the Vista Trail brings you to the too of a small hill with some amazing views of the surrounding scenery.

This historic bridge and dam are a very interesting site to see. The bridge is quiet long and a narrow two lane road crosses it. The historic dam is very cool and has a unique arch design for it's strength. It is partially demolished in one part and a small lake or pond has formed there. This appears to be a popular fishing spot for some. A great place for a pit stop if passing through or if on a road trip.

Sugarloaf Ridge State Park is a great state park to spend a day at to go hiking. The hike up to Bald Mountain isn't to long or to difficult, but well worth the extra effort for the views at the summit. The park is vibrant with colors and blossoming flowers in the spring with flowing water in the creeks. Best to visit on a clear day to enjoy the best scenery and views.

A great park with two loop trails which can be combined to form a larger hiking loop. There are multiple lookout viewpoints from the trail and a few small bridge crossings. The trail climbs up the hillside or canyon to the top and follows the rim of the hill before descending again. Overall a great trail that is about 1.5 miles in length for the larger combined loop.

Laguna wetlands preserve is a very small preserve. There is one loop trail about a quarter mile long with views of a cow pasture, a small wetland pond and a river. There are blackberry bushes along most of the trail as well. The preserve is not that exciting and is in poor condition. I would not recommend going here.

A great hiking destination with some parking on either end of the trailhead. The northern trailhead is nicer with a designated parking lot. The trail from one end to the other is about 1.6 miles long. The battety sites are very cool and worn out but share a time in history.

A very isolated area of Arizona but with some amazing desert scenery. This wildlife refuge is only visited by few due to its isolated location. If you are looking to experience the desert wilderness all by yourself or with only a few people I would recommend this place.

A great coastal park with a small peninsula that allows you to get a full perspective of the Monterey shoreline. There are tons of ground squirrels and even some crabs visible in the rocks near the water. A great park with some great views and a small beach.

A great place to get an amazing view of the Golden Gate Bridge. Best to go on a clear sunny day to get the best views and visibility. There is a large parking lot and plenty of trails from this overlook that connect to Sutro Baths and Lands End.

Awesome state park, not to crowded, some amazing red rock and geographic feature to see. Great hiking trails, scenery and landscape, feels like another world. Less than an hour drive from Las Vegas, well worth the drive to escape Sin City.

A great unique scenic area with beach access. There is plenty of parking and access to two beaches on either side of the Goat Rock parking area. There is even an arched rock formation off the coast that is visible from the parking area.

A great loop trail with an easier, gradually ascending side (right), or a steeper side (left). The loop is about 3 miles or so total and offers some great views and scenery of the Palm Springs area and nearby mountain ranges.
A cool sight to see hidden among a neighborhood. It is a short five minute hike up to Pumpkin Rock and there are a few other trails also. The views from the top are also a great bonus.
A cool roadside attraction to stop at and see. A large railroad trestle with some unique history and a interesting location near the ocean and over a river.
A nice hiking area that allows dogs and has some good views of the Bay. Not to many trails and only a small hill so trails are relatively flat and easy.
A great short trail to Arch Rock and some great rock formations. The unique rock formations are a great sight and are fun to hike around and climb on.
A very unique rock formation to see. Arch Rock is just a short hike from the parking area and the surrounding rock formations are also a great sight.
A very cool and large battery to see. One of the largest in Marin Headlands and one of the furthest west batteries.

What a nice place to visit for the whole family. Lots of walking trails, some wheelchair accessible. Plenty of plants and animals to see. Stop by a few of the ponds for ducks and other birds. We saw few different kinds of fish too. And if you're lucky you can see coyote too. Visit the visitor center and spend little time learning about the history, why are these wetlands here and different kinds of fauna and flora. There are interactive activities for kids to keep them interested and also learn something.  Best part is it's free so consider donating. Enjoy!

Beautiful views as everywhere in Canyonlands. We visited in April, weather wasn't the best, overcast, cold, windy with few sprinkles of rain and in spite of all that we weren't able to find parking at the Grand View Point Overlook parking area. Orange cliffs is just a short walk from that parking area so I highly recommend you park here if you're planning on taking the Grand View Point Overlook hike, because there are no views from the road there, you have to walk.

Great walk, about 7,5 miles all the way to Hoover Dam and back. Very easy. Take plenty of water. Best to visit November - March. Tunnel 3 is closed right now for repairs, which is about half way, so you can either start at Railroad trail trailhead or start at Hoover Dam to tunnel 3. Free parking at the bridge not at Hoover Dam. Beautiful views, take the whole family, including dogs, always on leash,  in winter months to avoid overheating.

You will most likely miss this turnout on your way to the Grand View Point Overlook, because it's kinda hidden behind you but for sure stop here on the way back. At the time of my visit it was the only turnout that wasn't clearly marked, maybe the sign was missing at that time. Just watch for it on your way back. It will be on your left hand side.

Honestly, I enjoyed Canyonlands way more than Arches, I just wish I had more time to spend here, I'll be coming back for sure. If you stop by the Visitor center for souvenirs or information, just walk across the road and you'll be able to see into Shafer Canyon and Road, but there's a better overlook just down the road from the visitor center.

There's a nice shaded playground for the kids. I go to the equestrian part. They have couple of turn out pens, one big arena, only barrels there. Must bring your own jumps and a dressage arena. Footing is great, probably the best I've seen at a public equestrian park. No shade, no lights, only usable in cold/cool months.

Amazing views from this overlook. Don't just stay at the parking area, take a short walk to this "island in the sky" overlook, watch cars and bikes scaling the Shafer Road. From the information posters you'll also learn that the road is wider than it looks. It was made to accommodate big, mining trucks.

Beautiful, beautiful views from here, a must stop, you'll be also able to learn a little about the history of mining and farming in the area not so long ago. If you come earlier in the year, when there's still snow on the La Sal Mountains in the distance, the contrast of all the colors is amazing.

It's great to be able to walk on and by where the lava has flown and see the massive size of it. And this is what's left of it about 1000 years after the actual event. It was cool 60 degrees outside but you could feel the heat from the lava flow in the areas where trail leads directly through it.

If you only have time for one short hike in Canyonlands, this is it! Must do hike, it's fairly short and easy. You will recognize this iconic shot of Canyonlands. Any time of the day, it's beautiful. And watch for the snowy mountains in the distance through the arch.

If you're in the area passing by, of course stop here, be prepared to pay $5 per person to enter and then you'll spend some money on the souvenirs. You'll probably spend about 15 minutes here, take couple of pictures and that's it, not much else to do or see here.

If you're running out of time or you're not in a good physical condition, you can still take great pictures of this iconic arch from the lower viewpoint. I believe a staff member at the visitor center said that this is THE founding arch of the national park.

There's good signage notifying you it's coming up, you just park at the turnout, it's right by the road so you don't even have to get out of the car and you'll have nice pictures. But if you feel like stretching your legs you can climb all the way up to it.

I attended a dog show at this park. There's nice grassy area with trees and few benches with tables. There's a skateboard park there too and indoor area for events. Parking is pretty easy, plenty on the street or in front of the recreation center.

If you're in Moab area, visiting Arches and Canyonlands,  stop by here. It's a lot of fun for kids and adults who like to learn about dinosaurs. There are also play areas for kids and you can take pictures with some of the dinosaurs.

Great place to visit year round. Beautiful hiking trails in the summer. Skiing in the winter. All within an hour of Las Vegas. Be prepared for lots of traffic and crowds during holidays. Any other time is quite peaceful.

Nice, quick hike, if you go early in the spring there's a waterfall off to the left coming up the trail, you'll hear it and see a trail to the side, just follow it, it's right there. Views from the top are great.

Must see for anyone who prefers to see animals in their natural environment. I especially enjoyed the drive through portion. Plan on spending about 3 hours here to see everything without feeling rushed.
Depending on how much time you have, you can walk all the way to the arches or just about half way and still get great pictures. It was pretty crowded there already in April.
I was in a rush, since it was pretty late in the day already, and I missed this arch completely. Don't make the same mistake, it's right next to the North Window Arch.
Must see, worth all the fees. Had the best guide. I recommend stay in the front of the tour to hear all the fun facts and see the best spots and angles for pictures.
Lot of people will miss this turnout, pay attention to your map you receive when you pay the entrance fee, it's worth a short stop and a quick walk.
I'm not into roller coasters, this ride is fast, quite outside of my comfort zone, but I still rode it 4 time. You have to try it.
Quick stop at this viewpoint is enough but if you like exploring I believe you need a permit to hike here.
You can see this arch from the road but it's an easy hike to it so take it, it's worth it.

An absolutely massive collection of fire apparatus and.... some other stuff.  First, the big deal, this is the largest collection of fire apparatus in the world with pieces dating from the 1700s to the 2000s.  Most is from the US, with a smattering from other places.  There are also other items such as tools, uniforms, helmets, and models.  On the other hand, they have made some curatorial decisions that I disagree with.  The exhibits are nearly all static and very few items can be touched or interacted with.  Information on the exhibits can be accessed through an app or by borrowing a binder from the front desk, but there are few signs actually with the exhibits that explain them.  I feel like this is a missed opportunity to not only show the equipment, but also explain how it is used and give a better understanding of what it is to be a firefighter.

Something for everyone!   The big attraction is of course the locks themselves, which allow vessel movement between the saltwater of Shilshole bay and Lake Union.  Unlike most attractions, and especially technological ones, you can get right up to them and even walk across the lock doors. Attached to the locks on the Ballard side are the magnificent botanical gardens and on the other side is the fish ladder with underwater viewing windows.  Just downstream of the locks, and easily visible, is one of the largest moving bridges in the Seattle area, which opens frequently for vessel traffic.

A very cool experience,  but with some quirks.  The first is that large bags, including purses are not allowed,  so leave them in the car.  You come in and will be given a time for the next tour, which can be a while depending on how busy they are.  First thing on the tour is a 20 minute video, then they take you into the silo.  55 steps each way.  There is an elevator,  but you need to ask for it.   After a launch demonstration in the control room and a quick look at the missile it is back up 55 stairs to the surface.  Overall worth it,  but not the friendliest experience.

This is a really awesome little park with a lot of history.  The centerpiece are the two Endicott Era gun batteries which defended the entrance to Bremerton until 1920.  The more impressive battery is not well marked and cam be found by parking at the boat launch at the north end of the park and following the trail that leads uphill near the bathrooms.  After you go around the corner, look for a spur trail to the right that will take you to the upper battery.  The shell rooms go down two levels, so bring a flashlight!

I was pretty disappointed with this one.  I was expecting a park up in the Crags with lots of hiking opportunities,  and instead it's basically one view point a couple of miles away and some campsites.  Speaking of the viewpoint, there is a marked trail to the left of the parking lot that is wheelchair accessible,  but an unmarked one to the right that is much shorter and not difficult at all.  I want my $8.00 admission back.

So, this is kind of a bait and switch, but a tolerable one.  That big, giant, beautiful rock you see? The one you want to hike to? Yeah, it's actually on federal land.  The state just put in the parking lot and a trail up to the fence so they collect the revenue despite the attraction being on the other side.  That said, it's a nice place and convenient, and the trails do connect through the fence, so, whatever.

This place is absolutely incredible! They have one of nearly everything and I didn't manage to see all of it in 2.5 hours.  Much of the collection is outside, so wear good shoes and sunscreen.   Plan to be here all day as well!  An additional bonus is the military aircraft flying out of Davis Mohan AFB next door.  We saw A-10s, C-130s, and a Blackhawk flying around while we were there.

Calling this place a ghost town is about like calling Disneyland an antique castle.  The only thing really original are a few of the foundations and one wall.  That said, they have done a nice job restoring it into an authentic feeling, family oriented, tourist trap.  There are lots of actual artifacts and you can have quite a number of old west experiences.  Just bring your wallet.

Really neat urban park with something for everyone.   There are walking paths and picnic areas and play areas for the rugrats, and a 14 and under fishing pond.  A recent addition are mountain bike courses for both adults and also a small one for the training wheels set.  There are four fairly impressive waterfalls within the park, and just a lot of cool stuff.

We only had breakfast, so I can't comment on the casino experience.   The food was good and very inexpensive, though a bit basic.   The building itself is dark and windowless, and while the HTC system does a good job,  you can still smell the cigarette smoke.  Overall it seemed distinctly down scale and even more depressing than most casinos.

It's kind of a small park just outside a not-kindof-small town.  There are some cool artifacts from the mining days including a stamp mill, a drill and orecart tracks, as well as an old blacksmith shop.  Also a small lake that attracts a fair number of birds.  Historically interesting,  but not really a destination.

Pretty nice park with great play equipment (which is actually open!), picnic tables, a water park (Not open), river access and a boat launch (also not open).  Unisex bathrooms and decent parking.  Also serves as an access point to the Centennial Trail, which crosses the river here on a historic bridge.

This is one of the nicest, if not largest, museums on the west coast.  One of the definite attractions is that most oft the aircraft and tanks are in operating condition, so what you see is very much like how they were in service.   The exhibits are constantly changing and so it's always something new.

It's a nice, if basic, park.  One bathroom, a little bit of grass, and beach access.  The beach is pebbles and rocks and disappears at high tide, but still yields interesting things.  That said, if you're already on Libby Rd and have a Discover Pass, the beaches at Fort Every are much more interesting.

This is the farm area of the old Northern State Hospital.   The park has a number of the old barns to explore, but also the former creamery, bakery, and slaughterhouse.  Some of the buildings are partially or totally collapsed, so it becomes a pick your own adventure sort if experience.

Neat site for a number of reasons.  We were there to see the ruins of the sawmill? Which is an excellent UrbEx location with some awesome graffiti.  The lake is Also nice and has ducks and the like.  Parking fee is $5, which is kind of expensive for what the park has to offer IMHO.

Kind of small and out of the way, but with a nice beach and some gold amenities.  there are picnic tables and vault toilets.  The Lighthouse is a fairly small one but the keepers quarters, or half of it anyway, is available as a vacation rental.  Mind the speedbumos on the way in.

It's a small community museum with a fair number of artifacts, but doesn't do the best job of putting them in context.  They do have a locomotive and caboose that visitors can go inside of (and blow the whistle), which is a big draw for the kids, and the bane of neighbors.

Awesome views, somewhat impeded by the trees that have grown up.  It was pretty crowded on a Sunday afternoon with people flying drones and driving R/C trucks on the rocks.  Also, watch the potholes where you turn off the main road, they can eat small cars

Awesome park with a ton of historical interest.  There are forts from the Endicott era, as well as WW2 installations.  There are vacation rentals available as well as camping and conference facilities.  Lots to see and do for all ages.  Highly recommended!

Beautiful park in a wonderful location, but kind of limited on amenities.   There is parking for maybe 6 cars and just a single porta-potty.  Still, a really nice beach and an awesome, fairly secluded spot to hang out.  Also a good place to launch a kayak

This is one of the most beautiful spots on Highway 2 and very worth a stop
When it rains the fog forms over the river and the effect is just stunning.  Expect a moderate scramble down the hill from the highway to the falls and be careful not to fall in!
This is a small - ish sculpture garden located in a hilltop park.  There are some cool things to see, but not more than an hour's worth to do.  Bathroom are nice, though.
Really nice park with a boat launch, swimming area, lawns, and I believe cabins.  Looking forward to coming back and exploring the waters around it.
Really nice urban park with play equipment for kids of all ages, walking trails, a boat dock, public tennis courts, and outdoor performance spaces.

(Translated by Google) The only curiosity of this city is in fact an amazing round barn, the Round Barn, which dominates the Route 66 and which one can not miss because located at the edge of Route 66. So do not enter the city if you want to see it.
It is an oak barn, round in shape, more than 18 meters in diameter and bright red, bordering Route 66 at 107 OK-66. It was built in 1898. Its roof collapsed in 1988 and a team of volunteers led by Luke Robinson worked to rebuild the structure, and the restoration work was completed in 1992 and fully restored in 2000. This round shape protect it from tornadoes. It was originally used as a barn for cattle but it also hosted the village festivals.
According to the legend, its acoustics are so good that we can hear a pin falling at the other end of the room. Today, it hosts an exhibition of Route 66, a souvenir shop owned by its owner.

(Original)
La seule curiosité de cette ville est en fait une étonnante grange ronde, la Round barn, qui domine la Route 66 et que l'on ne peut pas manquer car située au bord de la Route 66. Donc ne rentrez pas dans la ville si vous souhaitez la voir.
C'est une grange en chêne, de forme ronde, de plus de 18 mètres de diamètre et de couleur rouge vif, en bordure de la Route 66 au 107 OK-66. Elle a été bâtie en 1898. Son toit s'est effondré en 1988 et une équipe de bénévoles dirigée par Luke Robinson a travaillé pour reconstruire la structure, et le travail de restauration a été achevé en 1992 et restauré entièrement en 2000. Cette forme ronde la protégerait des tornades. Elle servait à l'origine de grange pour bétails mais elle accueillait aussi les fêtes du village.
Selon la légende, son acoustique est si bonne que l'on peut entendre une épingle tomber à l'autre bout de la salle. Aujourd'hui, elle héberge une exposition de la Route 66, une boutique de souvenirs tenue par son propriétaire.

(Translated by Google) From the Governor's Square (Plaza of Gorvenors), you can walk in two streets starting from this square, the first one you meet is E Palace Avenue. It will bring you to the museums, to the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi and several very ornate shops some of which are lost in flowered and planted patios. The second street that you will come down from the Basilica of St. Francis of Assisi is E San Francisco Avenue that will take you to La Fonda, a small shopping center and some Indian art shops.
The Governor's Palace was built in 1610, entirely on the Plaza of the Governors. Around this square, framed by small adobe buildings in Spanish pueblos style, every day from 8:00 am is held an Indian handicraft market.

(Original)
De la Place des Gouverneurs (Plaza of Gorvenors), vous pouvez vous promener dans deux rues partant de cette place, la première que vous remontrez est la rue E Palace Avenue. Elle vous amènera aux musées, à la basilique de Saint François d'Assise et plusieurs magasin très décorés dont certains sont perdus dans des patios arborés et fleuris. La seconde rue que vous descendrez depuis la basilique Saint François d'Assise est la rue  E San Francisco Avenue qui vous amènera sur l'hôtel La Fonda, un petit centre commercial et quelques boutiques d'art indien.
Le Palais des Gouverneurs a été construit en 1610, entièrement de plein pied sur la Plaza of the Governors. Autour de cette place, encadrée de petits bâtiments en adobes dans le style pueblos espagnols, tous les jours dès 8h00 se tient un marché d'artisanat indien.

(Translated by Google) The official start of Route 66: Starting in the footsteps of historic Route 66 in the heart of Chicago is the obstacle course. Very rarely reported, the few road signs alluding to it are regularly stolen by nostalgic indelicates.
The starting point of Route 66 is marked by the famous "Begin" sign with the round commemorative plaque on the ground at its feet. Here we are at the beginning of Route 66, which you will find just before the Russian Tea Time restaurant at 77 E Adams St. Route 66 begins on this street on South Adams Avenue, a few meters from the Adams / Wabash metro station called the Loop or the L Metro.
NB: E (East for East) and St (Street for Street)

(Original)

For some reason, I had low expectations for the River Walk. "It's something to see, but don't spend too much time here". I went one evening with a friend and ended up spending 4 hours here! We drank frozen margaritas, took the boat tour and went to a few more bars. It was so beautiful!!! I cannot recommend the River Walk enough and can't wait to come back although I don't think it would have the same charm during the day.

Everyone says the Alamo is smaller in person than they expected it to be, but having seen many frontier forts, it seems reasonably sized if you include the Alamo plaza area that once was part of the mission. The $15 guided tour was an excellent way to learn the history of the site and you get to skip the line. I expected to spend about an hour here, but there is easily enough to do here to spend 2 hours.

Wow what a cool museum! Because of its clandestine nature, the mob is not a group that readily shares its information. The Mob Museum does a great job at explaining the history of the mob from its roots in Prohibition up to the present day. I spend 2 hours here and loved every second of it. Also, they have a pretty good student and locals discount.

Home of the world's largest cave! Make sure to reserve a tour or arrive early because tours fill up fast!

There are nearly 15 different cave tours offered throughout the year. They are all good.

One thing to note: this cave does not have very many formations- it's mostly long passageways.

A hidden gem in remote Chanute, Kansas, the Safari Museum chronicles the travels of Martin and Osa Johnson, the pioneers in adventure film making 80 years before the Discovery Channel existed. Their African and Polynesian mask collection is bar none the greatest I've seen.
likes: Cultural Value (African and Polynesian mask collection)

reviews_attraction.text: One of the oldest churches in the United States, San Fernando Cathedral has played a major role in the history of San Antonio including the Battle of the Alamo. The remains of the heroes from that battle are now stored on the left side of the main entrance of the church.

One of the weirdest city parks I've ever seen. The interior of the chapel is very beautiful, but the rest of the park doesn't flow well and isn't well-connected with the rest of the street. I also think it's more austere than pretty.

The quietest of the mission grounds today, San Juan Capistrano is only worth visiting as part of the whole mission trail. It doesn't offer anything that you cannot find in one of the other missions. Still, it is very pretty.

This neat little museum carefully preserves the house of a former Spanish captain. It did not belong to a governor and it was not a palace. Make sure to check out the hidden courtyard in the back. Admission is $5.

This is where the organizers of the Boston Tea Party met. $6 is admittedly a lot to see the small museum, however there are also plenty of historic exhibits on the Boston Tea Party to make it worth your while.

I have been to more than half of the state capitols and the Pennsylvania Capitol is one of the top 3 most beautiful I have seen! The murals are so ornate and the green square in the back is beautiful.
Home of the Kentucky Derby, Churchill Downs is perhaps the world's most famous horse racing track.The buildings seem a little run-down, but on Derby Day, the atmosphere here cannot be beat.
This symbol of Freedom can be viewed in the beautiful Liberty Bell Visitor Center. After 15 minutes of exhibitions, you finally get to see the famed bell up close. Well worth the crowds.
A great spot to go wine tasting in the Santa Rita Hills. They have two tasting flights- go with a friend, order them both and you get to try 9 wines instead of 5 (there is an overlap).
Every American should visit this place to remember the atrocities committed by the US Government during World War II. Fabulously preserved. The museum and park film are must-sees.
The second largest canyon in the country, Palo Duro Canyon is a great place to soak in the natural beauty of Texas and the Llano Estacado. Worth a visit if in the Amarillo area.
The Falls are honestly okay, but the hike getting here through the canyon is beautiful! Do not expect peace and quiet on this hike. Takes about 90 minutes roundtrip.
This engineering marvel was the first bridge constructed across the Mississippi River. Today, it carries cars, pedestrians and the Metrolink. Worth a gander.
Incredible rock formations unlike anything you've ever seen! Worth the drive. The best way to experience Chiricahua is to go for a hike in the rocks.
Eerie/beautiful family mausoleum deep in the woods. I can only imagine the number of fraternity and masonic rituals that have happened here.
A really nice museum that explores an overlooked era in American history. Exhibits are well done and the views from the tower are stunning.
The Augusta winery had my favorite wines in the region, albeit in a smaller and simpler tasting room. Try the icewine.
This pier is very narrow. The only reason to visit is to fish at the end. Not tourist friendly unlike the Naples Pier.
Come here to play disc golf in the summer! Due to the altitude, your frisbee will go a lot further than you think.
I went on a Tuesday evening and didn't wait. The zip line was really fun and reasonably priced for what it is.

Plenty of parking here and it's a central location, so it's nice to park here and walk around the rim to sunrise and inspiration points. This canyon is really beautiful and was a nice susprise. The shadows created the all of the peaks in the canyon are great and the orange colors are different from any other place. If we were here for longer, I would deifntly take the trial down into the canyon.

A lot of parking on both sides. great in the warmer months for a bike ride, run, or walk. Great in the fall to see the leafs change. Great at night for star gazing when they're open. Its key to the longer bike rides I like to do from hopewell to new paltz, and now the river to ridge trail. A great reuse of aging infrastructure. Hope to see more of these projects going forward.

Recommend the Lady Bird Johnson hike (1.4 easy miles) in the national park and driving on Drury Scenic Parkway in the state park to pull over and walk through "big tree" and "corkscrew tree." The prairie creek visitor center also has a lot of helpful information and there are sometimes elk there. Thomas kuchel visitor center is very helpful for the national park.

One of our favorite parks because of its diversity. Really could spend over a week here hiking all the trails, but we spent a day at hurricane ridge, lake crescent, sol duc falls, rialto beach, and the hall of mosses at hoh rain forest. If we had more time, it would be nice to see ruby beach and quinault rain forest. Will defintely be back.

Our favorite local ski area. They have stuff for everyone. I really like the black diamonds, and my wife learned how to ski here last winter. Great helpful staff all around from instructors, to the ski patrol, to the lodge staff. Very affordable prices for the variety of trails and snow making capabilities.

Pretty surreal, reminds me of avatar. Quick easy loop at the visitor center to see some mossy trees. About an 8mi access road to get there. But there's plenty of parking.. There was an elk in the road on our way back to the highway, so be aware.

Defintely worth the visit to see period items of how paul revere lived. Nice square with restaurants and shops to relax also. The freedom trail is the best way to see all of these historical sites in boston. They really did a great job.

Visitor center has some good mas nd make sure you take the Drury Pkwy instead of the 101 to drive through the redwoods. There are nice stops. Long the way with quick trails through the redwoods like Big Tree and Corkscrew Tree.

The arch is pretty far away, but with only one day in the park and not enough time to hike all the way up, the lower viewpoint was a nice quick stop. It's still a little bit of a hike to the viewing point, so bring some water.

Pleasenty surprised with all the huge trees and seating areas. was just expecting a simple trail, but nice to see some mature trees have been saved and incorporated in a great trail. The bridge over the river is cool also.

Really nice park to see glaciers, mountains, and the power of hydro. We were in the area for the morning so we drove along highway 20 to see Gorge lake, Diablo lake, Ross lake, and Washington pass observation site.

Easy half mile hike from the visitor center on a paved trail to a great waterfall right in front of rhe mountain. Recommend getting there early or late since the visitor center parking fills up quick.
Plenty of parking and nice views to see the usual sunset, sunrise, and inspiration points. Would be nice to see in the winter with snow on the peaks, but we went in september and it wasn't too hot.
This is the best zoo on the east coast. Humane treatment of animals. Friendly and helpful staff. Great exhibits. Wednesdays are free, but it is really crowded, almost better to go on the weekends.
Cool to see this bridge we learned about it school. Not sure how redding got a Calatrava bridge, but defitnly a cool thing to see when in the area. Viewed from 800 sundial bridge drive.
Had no idea about the history between Thailand and the city of boston. This is a nice memorial to the King and to learn about the historical relationships between Boston and Thailand.
Best place to come to take te boat to the statue and ellis island. The new 911 memorial is also really nice. Nice views and of city also. Plenty of parking also.
We just did the first half mile of the 6 mile loop to myrtle falls and it was great!! Easy trail with not much grade change and great views of the mountain.
A lot of parking, but it fills up fast since alot of trails start here. Nice gift shop and facilities also. Good trail and park closure info as well.
Glad we stopped here on the way up to hurricane ridge. Great park and trail info, as well as maps to take with us. Thanks for the great service.
Long access road, but fairly easy hike. A little steep in some spots, but its well maintained.gets crowded so recommend getting there early.
one of the best places to go in the summer. a ton of walking, hiking, and bike trails. nice swimming areas. and fantastic views all over.
Very nicely maintained and quiet trails! Not nearly as crowded and bear mountain, storm king, or minnewaska. Nice views at the top.
Great local stop if you are in the area. Only paid guided tours are available, but the grounds are free and a nice visit
Nice and fairly easy hike with an unbeatable view at the top. Less steep than the others in the area.

The Old State House (US$10 per adult) is one of the important stops on the Freedom Trail in Boston. Here you will find a very good American Revolutionary Museum which spells on in good detail the events leaving up to the American Revolution, including the infamous Boston Massacre which happened just outside this building. Opening Hours are 9-5pm daily.

The Old State House was built in 1713, making it one of the oldest standing and functioning buildings in the United States. This was original seat of power colony of New England's, a national landmark and another nice example of Georgian period architecture that you can see in this area of Boston.

Within the Old State House, you will find a gift shop with a large collection of Freedom Trail souvenirs, similar to what you will see at the Faneuil Market. You then visit the rooms which house the American Revolutionary Museum collection.

The museum collection is a comprehensive set of displays which detail events as they occurred and led to the American Revolution from the British Crown. There are historical items, paintings and furniture on show as well, helping bring the information to life. You can browse the displays that are of interest and see all in 20-30 minutes or give more attention to them and easily find yourself here for an hour or more.

We found the upstairs rooms, decorated with period furnishings to be particularly interesting. There are a couple of rooms with interactive and hands-on experiences which children will enjoy more than the traditional museum inclusions at the Old State House.

Note: There are free tours of this historic building every 30 minutes starting on the ground floor. Attending one of these might be a good way to experience the Old State House if you don't fancy an independent visit as much.

In the end, we felt the $10 entry fee was steep for this attraction but having saved a bit by purchasing the Freedom Trail combo ticket (see below), we didn't mind. The museum collection helps visitors build up an understanding of New England during the American Revolutionary period, something that is important when it comes to getting the most of your visit to the Freedom Trail attractions.

Note: At the Old State House, you can buy a combo ticket ($16 per adult) that includes entrance into the Old South Meeting Hall and the Paul Revere House, giving you a $3 savings compared to buying each ticket individually.

One of the interesting geological areas to visit and hike in Death Valley is the Ubehebe Crater 8 miles northwest of Scotty's Castle at the end of Scotty's Castle Road.

Note that the castle is currently closed for renovations but as of April 2019 you can still drive up to the crater to hike there.

There is a carpark with enough space for probably 15-20 vehicles. No public toilets at the trailhead. However, you will find them back 8 miles or so at the Ranger Station.

Views into the crater are ok from right in front of the carpark. As such, theoretically, if it is too hot outside, you can still see much of the crater without having to take the hike around the rim.

There is a 1.5 mile loop trail around the rim of the crater. It is generally easy. There are only a few small ascends to make and mostly smooth flat surface near the rim to hike. You'll find many views into the 600 foot deep crater. You will also pass by two smaller sister craters on the south and west side of Ubehebe Crater.

We visited on an early morning in April. At this time of year, it is hot by late morning but only 57 degrees first thing in the morning at the crater. It was very windy as well, making the cool air feel very chilly. We were wearing layers which was very helpful early on.

Unfortunately, visiting early in the morning means you won't be able to see the richer colours of the crater as most of its walls will still be in the shadows during your hike. However, by starting your day at Ubehebe, you can finish here early and spend the rest of your day further south where there is a higher concentration of hikes and viewpoints.

Bryce Point is one of he Scenic Drive viewpoints and is situated on the south side of the Bryce Amphitheatre facing north. We really enjoyed this particular viewpoint, even if it was the busiest found along the Scenic Drive.

To reach Bryce Point, you turnoff the main Scenic Drive east for two miles. You will first pass a quick turn to Inspiration Point, which is also very much worth visiting.

Note: There is a Shuttle bus stop at Bryce Point for those who are not planning to drive their own vehicle. Further, the Rim trail start/stops at Bryce Point if you are interested in walking the Rim back to the Lodge area

At Bryce Point, you will find an extended concrete platform, providing nearly 270 degree views into the Amphitheatre and lower canyon area to the south. You will spot endless hoodoos and other delightful land formations, trees, hiking trails. The colours are wonderful. We were lucky to have visited while their remained a decent amount of snow in places. This made for great photographs.

In the end, of all the viewpoints, this may have been the one we enjoyed the most. We stopped here on both days we spent in Bryce Canyon National Park, enjoying our early visit as well as being here late afternoon.

Note: The viewpoints along the Scenic Drive are best visited from south to north. As such, start with Rainbow and Yavimpa Points at the end of the road first. Then start making your way back north, pulling over to the right hand side when you approach a viewpoint which strikes your interest. If you are like us - they all will!

The Isabella Stewart Gardner museum is an impressive private collection, well worth seeing if you are an art lover visiting Boston. Opening Hours 11am to 5pm with extended hours until 9pm on Thursdays, the museum is closed on Tuesdays.

The permanent collection at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum features some very impressive works. Sadly, highlight Vehmeer and Rembrandt masterpieces were stolen from here in 1990 and have yet to be recovered. However, there remain numerous fine works, which you can view within the museum exhibition rooms.

In many ways the Isabella Stewart Gardner museum has a Sir John Sloane (English antiquity collector) quality to it. She amassed an wide collection of antiquity, artefacts and paintings, which allowed her to compose a museum of various themes reaching several important historical periods.

Beyond art, centred in the museum is one of the most lovely atrium gardens you may ever see. Visitors will be happy to know that you can take photos of the museum garden. This is a real highlight of the Isabella Stewart Gardner museum that you wont want to miss.

In the end, the Isabella Steward Gardner is wonderful art museum and well worth your time and effort if you are a fan of art. As far as private art collections go, very few will top what is available to be seen here.

One of the light and easy hikes in Zion National Park is the Temple of Sinawava Trail, which follows the Virgin River from the Temple of Sinawava Stop at end of the Scenic Drive Route in Zion NP to the Narrows, a famous hike which starts at the end of this trail.

The trail is paved and scenic. Less exciting and interesting compared to Zion's more famous hikes, this is a nice option for those with families and less mobile members who can't take on more difficult trails. The scenery is nice throughout, just be prepared to share the trail with many others making use of this trail.

At the end of the trail, the Virgin River extends into the distance, through the Narrows. At the time of our visit, this trail was closed due to water levels being too high. However, you could peer down the river and take a few pictures before circling back and returning down the Temple of Sinawava Trail.

In the end, best to plan at least 1 hour for this trek, depending on your walking speed. Note that you can take the Zion free shuttle to Stop (9) - Temple of Sinawava. This is the last stop along the route leaving from the NP Visitor Centre and takes 40 minutes journey time from original departure. Shuttles drop off and pick up passengers every few minutes.

The Desert View Watchtower (free entry) is a 70 foot tower constructed in the style of the Colorado Puebloan people. This National Historic Landmark was built in 1932 by architect Mary Jane Colter and can be visited by way of the 25 mile drive along the Desert View Road out of the Grand Canyon Village.

The tower is a lovely building architecturally. Constructed of boulder stones, it includes several floors which are adorned with Native American paintings and artwork. These are just as interesting to see as the stunning views of the Grand Canyon and Painted Desert seen through the watchtower windows.

There is a platform outside the watchtower, providing excellent views of the remarkable terrain available to see at this location. At this attraction, you'l also find a cafe, toilet facilities, gift shop at the Watchtower as well as a General Store.

Note: Plan on at least a 2-3 hour roundtrip from the Grand Canyon village if you are wanting to drive the 50 mile round trip to the Desert View Watchtower and back. You want to allow some time for additional stops at the various viewpoints into the Grand Canyon as well as the Tusayan Museum and Ruins which you can see along the way.

The Hopi House is one of the National Historic Landmark buildings in the Grand Canyon Village that makes for an interesting place to visit.

This building was designed by Mary Jane Colter (1905) in the fashion of the Hopi Indian abode pueblo. The exterior of the Hopi House greatly contrasts to other landmark buildings in the area and makes for nice photographs.

Colter built the Hopi House as a gift shop and it has continued to serve this purpose to this day. Inside, you can find two floors of Native American crafts, artworks, gifts and other souvenirs. Notice the interesting interior architecture as well, including the thatch roof being branches, many of which still have dried leaves.

Note: If interested in other Native American inspired building constructions by Mary Jane Colter, you can drive out to the Dessert View Watchtower building along Desert View Drive.

Note: There are other interesting landmark buildings nearby that are also interesting places to visit. These include the Railway Depot, Verkamp's Visitor Centre and Museum and historic El Tovar Hotel. Collectively, these make a good way to spend an hour of your time at the Grand Canyon Village.

The Furnace Creek Visitor Centre is located along Highway 190 in the middle of Death Valley National Park. Opening hours are 8am to 5pm daily.

There is a fair amount of parking some of which is shaded. You'll find toilet facilities as well. Park entry fees can be paid here and you'll find a small gift and souvenir shop section as well.

Importantly, this is where you find park rangers and staff able to provide information regarding trail and road conditions. There are park maps you can pick up. Rangers lead walks and talks around the centre between November and May. See schedule near the ranger desk.

There is a 20 minute film you can watch about the history of Death Valley. You will also find a small area in the centre setup for displays related to mining history, wildlife and the geography of the area. These are both informative and provide something for visitors to do when the weather is too hot outside.

In the end, we found the Furnace Creek Visitor Centre to be a good resource top to make in Death Valley and a good representation of the National Park Services visitor centres which are found in all of the national parks around the country.

One of the interesting memorials at the Tidal Basin is the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial. This is a nicely designed monument constructed by Chinese sculptor, Lei Yixin in 2011.

Here you will find what appears to be a large granite boulder, with a clean middle section cut and shifted forward towards the basin. On the front of the centre piece is a carving of Martin Luther King Jr. standing with arms crossed. It is a nice composition and depiction of Dr. King.

Flanking the sculpture are two curved walls with engravings of important quotes made by Dr. King along with dates and locations where they were delivered. These statements help provide context behind the Martin Luther King Jr.'s civil rights activism and ambitions for the nation to achieve greater racial equality.

Note: You can visit the monument as part of a walk around the Tidal Basin, which includes stops at the Jefferson, George Mason and Franklin D. Roosevelt Memorials. Alternatively, you can walk here in 8-10 minutes from monuments along The Mall if you are near the Korean, WWII or D.C. War Memorials.

We always enjoy seeing the Hans Christian Anderson bronze statue at the Conservatory Water in Central Park. It was particularly nice seeing it this past week (first week of May) while the spring blooms were starting to appear in the Park. This provided a nice backdrop for taking pictures of the statue at this time of the year.

The statue is bronze figure of an elderly H.C. Anderson, the Danish author noted for his children's stories and fairytales. Here you see an elderly Anderson, seated on a park bench with an open book. The page is filled with the story of the Ugly Duckling. On the ground is a small bronze of a duck looking up at Anderson. It is a neat sculpture in Central Park

Note: Like the nearby Alice in Wonderland Statue, just a couple minutes walk from here, it is fine for children to touch, climb on and around the Hans Christian Anderson statue. There are always fewer visitors here than at the Alice in Wonderland statue so it is much easier to take unobstructed photos here.

One of the important stops on the Freedom Trail in Boston is the site of the Boston Massacre that took place just outside the Old State House on 5 March 1770. Many consider this event to be a catalyst for the eventual American Revolution that saw the colonies formally part ties with the British Crown.

The site is marked by a seal upon the location where British soldiers, being harassed by a mob, fired upon a crowd, killing 5 colonists. There are plenty of opportunities to learn about this monumental event in American history as you make your thought the Freedom Trail attractions in Boston. However, at this location, you simply see the seal marking the location of the event.

You can conveniently take in a viewing of the seal and location in a couple minutes before going onward into the Old State House or over to Faneuil Hall depending on which directly you are going as part of your Freedom Trail visits go. As such, it is an easy sight to take in if you are sightseeing in the area.

We recently transected an area of the Glen Canyon Recreation Area along Scenic Route 95 and very much enjoyed the scenery in this area of southern Utah.

Along Utah Route 95 south of Hanksville, you eventually enter the Glen Canyon Recreation Area near Lake Powell and the Colorado River. There is a lake overview point and areas where you can see the Colorado flowing amidst outstanding scenery. The drive is particularly picturesque throughout.

We particularly enjoyed seeing the Hite Crossing Bridge in the Glen Canyon Recreation Area. This is the only vehicle crossing of the Colorado for nearly 300 miles between Moab (upstream) and the Glen Canyon Dam (downstream). The steel arch bridge is simple, yet looks attractive against the backdrop of the Recreation Area.

Overall, we were impressed with the beauty of the Glen Canyon Recreation Area in southern Utah. It was a place we would have liked to have had more time to explore, perhaps something we can do during future visits.

There is a monument to early 19th century politician Daniel Webster located along the 72nd Street Transverse Road in Central Park, just southwest of Wagner Cove at The Lake.

This monument is the works of American sculptor Thomas Ball and was erected in 1876. It is of an middle-aged Daniel Webster, a highly regarded statesman and oratory. He is standing in stately attire with his right hand tucked inside his vest upon his heart, as if amidst an important speech to audience before him.

The statue stands upon a granite pedestal with modest ornamentation. Near the base of the monument are the words 'Liberty and Union, Now and Forever, One and Inseparable' given by Webster during a famous speech to the U.S. Senate in 1830.

This is one of many interesting monuments and statues that can be viewed within Central Park and is very much worth having a quick look if you plan to spend time around The Lake or Strawberry Fields in Central Park.

Along the Waterfront is a city park known as the Christopher Columbus Waterfront Park. Interesting things to see here include a statue figure of Christopher Columbus situated amidst two trellis covered walkways. There is also plenty of open green space and good view of the harbour.

You can conveniently visit the Christopher Columbus Waterfront Park if staying in the Waterfront area hotels or if visiting the Faneuil Hall Markets nearby, where you can pick-up a lunch and bring it here to enjoy outside.

Crowds were not much of an issue when we visited here during the mid-autumn period but I can image this park would be quite busy during the summer.

In the end, during the autumn period, at least, I wouldn't make this a priority stop but simply enjoy the park if you are in the area and seeking green space instead. For better park experiences, make your way to Boston Common and the Boston Public Garden instead.

The Father Crowley Vista is located 7.5 miles west of Panamint Springs along Highway 190 near the western boundary of Death Valley National Park. From here you are enjoy nice views into Rainbow Canyon, a location noted for its impressive and interesting rock layers.

There is a carpark for probably 20-25 vehicles. You'll find public toilets as well as a plaque with information relating to Father John Crowley, a Catholic priest who served the area during the 1920-30s.

We visited early in the morning on our way out of Death Valley. The geography is attractive but no doubt this seems like a place better seen later in the morning when the sun strikes the sides of the canyon, highlighting the rich wall colours of the canyon.

In the end, this is a good viewpoint, worth a few minutes of your time if entering or exiting Death Valley National Park from the west along H-190.

The 'Group of Bears' bronze sculpture just south of the MET at 79th Street and 5th Ave. in the Ruth and Arthur Smadbeck-Heckscher East Playground area is interesting to see before or after visiting the museum.

The sculpture is cast of the Paul Manship original bronze from 1932 and was erected here in 1989. It is similar to but more playful than the Manship 1963 bronze cast situated within the MET.

The Group of Bears is a child-friendly monument, similar to the nearby Hans Christian Anderson and Alice and Wonderland sculptures. Thus children are welcome to touch and climb upon.

There are park benches surrounding the Group of Bears so this can be a good place to take a quick rest of feet while your little ones enjoy the playground and the sculpture. Then move on with other intended sightseeing around Central Park and Museum Mile.

One of the interesting attractions in Kingman is the historical Bonelli House ($2 suggested donation) which was built in 1915, representing an example of Anglo Territorial Architecture. Opening Hours 11am to 3pm (Monday-Friday).

This century old homestead was built out of local tufa stone by George Bonelli and was used by the Bonelli family until 1973 when it was purchased by the city of Kingman.

The exterior of the house is very interesting to see if you enjoy architecture. You can also tour the inside of the Bonelli House, being led by a local volunteer who will take you through various rooms of the house, explaining the period furniture available to be seen.

Overall, this is a neat building to see both on the inside and out and is worth 30-45 minutes of your time if sightseeing in the Kingman area.

One of the most interesting overlooks in the Island in the Sky section of Canyonlands National Park is that of the Shafer Canyon which is found half a mile past the Visitor Centre after entering the park.

Here you can look down into the canyon floor and admire the narrow off-road which winds up the side of the wall to the Island in the Sky plateau. Look for the 4 wheel drive vehicles and bikers slowly making their way up and down the road. This is one of those 'Wow' roads to see.

In addition to seeing the Shafer Trail Road, the vista views here are very impressive. You can look eastward into the distance. The scenery is beautiful.

Overall, we very much enjoyed this particular overview. This is one of the places within Canyonlands that we would consider a must-see stop when visiting the National Park.

Near the intersection of 7th Ave and H Street you can find a traditional Chinese Archway, known as the Friendship Archway.

This structure was designed and built by Alfred H. Liu in 1986 to foster the growing relationship between the District of Columbia and Beijing Municipality (China) at that time.

The archway is larger than traditional archways you will find in China or in Chinatowns in other cities around the world, crossing the entire four lane road. It is quite colourful, vibrant with includes classic Chinese images and design features.

Overall, the Friendship Archway is nice to see if you are in the area but we'd not go out of our way for this one.

For those familiar with the beautiful black and white images of Yosemite National Park by early 20th century Ansel Adams, one of interesting places to visit in the valley is his studio. Opening hours 9am to 5pm daily.

Today, the Ansel Adams studio is an art gallery where visitors can find photo reprints of Ansel Adams as well as numerous other art related gifts. It is a nice shop to see even if you don't intend to buy anything.

Note - within the gallery you'll find a wall with history and images of Ansel Adams as well as information related to the establishment and running of his studio here in Yosemite Valley during the early days.

Balanced Rock is a famous landmark in Arches National Park that you can see along the Arches Scenic Drive, just before the intersection with Window's Road.

Here you will see a 128 foot standing single rock structure that resembles a large rock balancing on a thiner pedestal. There is also a short and easy trail that circles the Balanced Rock that you can complete in 10-20 minutes.

In the end, the Balanced Rock is a quick and easy attraction to see and is quite interesting if you enjoy geological land formations. Give it a quick stop for a few pictures even if you're not interested in the short hike here.

One of the interesting things near the White House is the First Division Monument situated at 17th and E Street, just south of the Eisenhower Building.

Constructed in 1924, here you will see a single standing column that is topped by a gilded figure of the Lady of Victory. It is a simple, touching and respectable tribute to the valiant soldiers who participated and those to perished during World War I.

You can conveniently see this monument if visiting the area attractions or when making your way between the White House and the National Mall.

The Balanced Rock trail is a short an easy hike, no more than 15-20 minutes, when walking slowly and taking time for occasional photographs of this interesting land formation.

We visited rather early in the morning and found the carpark completely empty, making it easy to stop here. Passing by in the early afternoon on another day, the carpark was full up. Be patient if this self-driving and trying to stop here for a short hike. Visitors will likely be making a short stop so you should be able to find a parking spot soon enough.

Larb Hollow Overlook is one of the viewpoints along Scenic Bypass Route 12 in southern Utah. We enjoyed stopping here for a few minutes during our drive between Bryce Canyon and Capital Reef National Park.

The pullover is 10 miles south of Grover and is worth a quick stop if you want to see the Waterpocket Fold of Capital Reef National Park to the east. This unique land formation is the centrepiece for the national park so its nice to see if you are making your way that direction.

This is a late 19th-century monument by Augustus Saint Gaudens. It honours the first African American volunteer unit in the Civil War. Here you see a detailed bas relief that is quite impressive and worth spending a few minutes to enjoy if you find yourself in the area.

The Hidden Valley Trail is one of the more popular areas in the park, providing easy access to a rock garden perfect for scrambling and a shallow basin that narrows into a canyon.

For the casual visitor, the well defined trails provide a quick overview of the environment in the park.  Those with an adventurous streak can continue into the canyon and follow the dry stream bed (not recommended when there has been rain in the area due to flashflooding) to its end at one of the parks dirt road.  Parts of the trek may require short scrambles across rocks that the 'stream' cascades over when flowing.  From the end of the canyon, a single-track trail leads to the south around the west side of the rock formations defining Hidden Valley.  If you decide to take this option, be sure you have map and compass and are familiar with land navigation.  While the trail is fairly well defined, it is still possible to get lost and the desert is unforgiving in hot weather.

The trailhead has plenty of parking and two vault toilets but no running water.  There are also a handful of picnic areas with charcoal grills.  There is little or no shade in the picnic area so bear that in mind when planning a picnic.

If hiking, keep in mind this is desert and bring plenty of water, especially if you are considering hiking all the way through the canyon.  In hot weather, a hat and sunscreen are highly recommended.

This museum is located literally in the middle of nowhere off of the 10 freeway in the middle of the Mojave Desert.  The location, however, has significance.  This area was where the troops in World War II trained for desert combat in North Africa.

This museum documents the training camps that were built in the area to support the training operations.  There is also a huge relief map of the Mojave Desert that was used during planning for the California Aqueduct project.  The highlight of the museum is found outside where armored vehicles and tanks from around the world are displayed including one that appears to be a tank converted into a fire fighting vehicle.

The museum can be gone through quickly in less than an hour so it might make an ideal stop if you or your kids want to get out and stretch your legs in the long desert segment between Phoenix and Los Angeles.  If you have more time, you can easily spend 2-3 hours going through in depth.  Be sure to talk to the people working there as they love to share the info they have on the museum.

A 1.6 mile (2.5 km) round-trip single-track trail leads to a mostly intact stamp mill from the mining glory days of Joshua Tree.  The mill itself is fenced in so you will not be able to get into it but you can get a good view of it from outside the fence.  An interpretive sign provides more details about the mill and mining in the area.  The trail is mostly level and is formed of packed earth. The last hundred or so feet cross a dry stream bed of loose sand so the going is a little tougher if your footing is unsure.

The trailhead is reached via a compacted dirt road that is accessible to almost all vehicles when it is dry.  If you are driving a lowered vehicle, have fancy airdams and trim, or low profile tires, you might have to park at the Parker Dam paved lot and cut across to the Wall Street access road, adding another 1/2 mile (0.8 km) to your hike.

There is a vault toilet at the trailhead but no water so plan accordingly.  Take water on your hike and drink liberally.  Wear a hat and sunscreen, especially in warm weather.

JPL rolls out the red carpet once a year and it is worth braving the crowds to get a look at the cutting edge of technology and space exploration.  Many of the labs and workshops are open and the people who actually build and work on the space probes and satellites are on hand to talk about their missions and how the spacecraft are built.  Be sure to get there early as the event is always packed to the gills.

If they offer it, be sure to take the shuttle bus up to the deep space simulator building where you can see the giant vacuum chamber where spacecraft are stress tested before heading off into space.  If you really want to make someone's day, have your kids bring a space science book and ask the engineers and scientists for autographs.  My daughter did that one year and I can't tell you how happy they were that someone thought so highly of them.  I can't think of a better way to say thank you to them for all they do that goes unrecognized.

This is an atypical nature center in that it is also a historical site.  The area has been used in the past as a Rancho in the early days of California, a gun battery between World Wars I and II, and as a missile defense site during the Cold War.  There are several options for trails that include a flat loop and several ways up the hill.  You can choose to keep to a natural hike or can make your way up to the former gun emplacement to see what it California's coastal defenses used to look like.  The staff in the Visitor's Center is cheerful and more than happy to provide you with insight into the historical and natural history of the site and the Palos Verde Pennisula as a whole.  Kids will enjoy the Nature Center as well with easy, flat hikes and lots of looking and touching items in the visitor center.

The Pioneer Register is a section of rock wall where early European visitors and settlers carved their names into the rock wall dating back to the mid 1800s.  The map marker is is the location of the trailhead with the actual register being about 1/2 mile up the wash.  The hike is mostly level and, if done in the early morning or late afternoon, provides shade.  Avoid the hike mid-day during the summer as it gets very warm in the canyon. The parking area can hold 20-30 cars.  The road to the parking area is is a narrow dirt road that had some bumps but is accessible to most cars. A number of RVs had made the trip when I wad there.  The only vehicles that might not make it would be lowered cars as they would hit rocks and scrape through some of the dips.

Keys View is the highest road point in Joshua Tree NP.  From here, there are views of a good chunk of the Coachella Valley and the Salton Sea in the distance.  In the foreground of the view, a keen eye can discern the line of ridges and water features that mark the path of the world famous San Andreas Fault.  A short paved trail leads up to the best views.  There is a less steep path that should allow persons requiring accessible paths to the vista point.

A single-track trail leads west from the parking area across the higher ridges if you are looking for more spectacular views.

There is a vault toilet but no running water so plan accordingly.  The area can get very windy so beware of loose items such as hats and papers blowing away.

The Pueblo is the ruins of a Native village from the long before the railroad passed through the area.  A paved trail loops through the ruins past the foundations of several buildings and a small collection of petroglyphs.  The trail is 1/4 mile (0.4 km) long and is gently sloped at places and has a smooth surface.  There is a short paved extension from the main loop to view the petroglyphs.

There is a restroom at the parking lot but no water.  The parking lot is a pull-through with several bus and RV spaces.  Rangers provide walk and talks to provide more insight to the ancient and more recent history of the site.  Check with the visitor centers for times.

The Agate Bridge is a petrified log that had the earth washed out from underneath it.  The log began to break down so a concrete support has been placed underneath, taking away some of the majesty of the original site.  If coming in from the north entrance, this will be the first close-up view of the petrified wood that is found all across the southern end of the park.  A paved 150' (45 m) walkway leads to the overlook for the bridge.

There is a restroom at this site but no water.  An interpretive sign provides more information about the Agate Bridge.  The parking lot has spaces for buses and RVs.

The Ray Miller Trailhead is one of two entry points into the Mugu backcountry (the other being the Chumash Trailhead).  Of the two, this one has a more gently climb with the drawback of being longer.  It slowly crawls out of the campground and into the southeast corner of the La Jolla Valley.  From here, you can either continue climbing up to Mugu Peak for views of the Pacific Ocean and Oxnard Plain or continue around the relatively flat La Jolla Valley loop of trails.  Beware hiking into the Valley after rain as the mosquitoes come out in cloud and they can bite through your clothes.

The arboretum has a short circle hike that goes through a few different environments and offers some nice views onto the high desert in Apple Valley. There are flush toilets on the site.  One of the docents that was there was very friendly and knowledgeable but just know if you start talking with him, it may take a while to break away because he has so much information about the Arrowhead/Big Bear region that he wants to share.  Parking here requires a Forest Service day pass which can be purchased at the information kiosk.

Jasper Forest is a vista point overlooking a small collection of petrified logs that have washed down the hillside.  The logs themselves are inaccessible from this point.  A level, paved 130' (39 m) walkway leads to the vista point.  This collection of logs is not very impressive but, if coming from the north entrance, wets the appetite for the upcoming areas.

There are no facilities at this site.  An interpretive sign provides information about this area.  The pull-through parking area has space for buses and RVs.

A little known monument to the history of the Pacific Missile Test range and all of the missiles that were developed and tested here at the Mugu NAS.  It is free and is outside the fences of the military base so access is no problem.  For those who are interested in military history, it will be difficult to find such a complete collection of U.S. military missiles outside of the Smithsonian.  There is also a small picnic shelter for a quick lunch before hitting the road again.
