A small natural preserve that protects one of the only 2 habitats for thr Torrey Pine. There are a few miles of trails that lead out onto the bluffs with nice views of the San Diego coast.  The elevation change isn't too bad although some parts of the trail can be slippery with loose sand over rock.  There is little shade on the trail so dress appropriately for the sun if you are prone to burning.  Also check the small historic lodge building that acts as a visitor center.

There is a short 2/10 mile (0.3 km) round-trip hike to get to one of the few arches found in this park.  The arch is not huge so don't expect it to be like the ones found in Utah.  The arch has a couple of boulders laying against it you may not get any fantastic natural frame pictures.  Still, an interesting site for a small effort.  As with all hikes in Joshua Tree, bring water, wear sunblock and a hat as there is little or no shade depending on the time of day.

This is a wild lava tube that is reached via well signed and maintained dirt roads.  There is a small side tube that you can crawl in addition to the main tube. The main tube is covered by a fence but has a small gate that is opened seasonally. You have to crawl through the gate to get in and there is no light so bring at least 2 flashlights per person. There is also a  vault toilet and picnic tables at the parking area.

This natural bridge is a small cousin to the ones found further east in arches and the view is not as spectacular as you are looking down from above. It is also inaccessible so you won't get a close look other than from the overlook. Still, if you aren't going to be trekking to any of the other Utah National Parks, you can get a first-hand look at the unique formation of a rock bridge. It's worth pulling over to see.

This is a clean, well maintained park with an excellent running track that has a low-impact surface.  The playground is fun for kids with accessible ramps and equipment.  The one downside is that there is no shade for parents to sit in while children are at the playground.  All the seating is in hot, blazing sun during the warm months.  The park also has a disc golf course, a relative rarity in city parks.

The museum is undergoing a renovation (January 2018) so large sections are closed. For a small city museum, this one is very well laid out and organized with exhibits that are informative and attractive. The museum also has a small planetarium that puts on a variety of shows for all ages several times a day. During renovation,  admission is discounted to reflect the reduced offerings.

A really fun park with a Colonial America themed playground on an island.  The island received a remodel several years ago to replace all the "dangerous" playground equipment with safe equipment, not quite as fun in my opinion, but the kids still love it.  This is also a popular location for wedding, prom, and quinceañera pictures.

The schoolhouse is a restored structure that was used a school until the 1940s. If there is a ranger available, the building will be opened for a closet look inside. Most of the furniture inside is a replica but there is the remains of one original desk. The Ranger can answer questions about the schoolhouse and history of the area.

This is a small park along busy Del Amo Blvd.  This is deceiving as the entrance to the park is actually in the neighborhood north of that street.  There is very little parking so visitors may have to park in the neighborhood.  The facilities are adequate but don't hold your parties here due to the parking issue.
Cute house with some fun elements hut nothing to go out of the way for. May be a good place to take young children while older siblings ride Gadget's Go Coaster next door.
Decent sized event room. Lots of activities but only if you are a resident of Cerritos and they screen for residency more strictly than TSA screens air passengers.
A nice quiet walk along the riverbed. It can be warm and dry during the summer as there are few mature trees.

Sorry I can't put in more than 5 stars. There are plenty of pictures and posts so here is a fresh one. from new Covid life:
1- Plan ahead via the internet to get a time slot to get into the Caverns. When they say they don't have any slots TRY going there anyway! We could not get a time slot BUT we went to the visitor center early (about 8:15 am) and they had a 9:30 slot available.
2- with the Visitor Center and outside trails open there is still HOURS of things to do. Plan on a driving / hiking trip anyway.
3- While the current website says the DOG KENNEL in closed. When we went they were able to take in dogs. You CANNOT leave a dog in the car, van or small rv. You may get a nasty fine. But as of April 2 2021 the kennels were available.
4- If you get in plan on the WHOLE self guided tour. You can skip parts with short cuts but take the 2.9 mile full route. It is worth it.
5- At a 5.00 per person cost OR we had the senior Park Pass for free admission this was a great experience.

With live people giving tours of the museum and the outlining homes of Frogtown (Morgan our guide was excellent) the museum was very focused on the people and places in Savannah. All the wars as well as the development of the Girl Scout chapters in America show the real people story of history in Savannah. Frogtown shows the diversity of the working class looking to help each other as well as themselves to survive and build a better life. Minorities based on color and country came to try and find a job and a home around the train repair yards. We got to walk to 2 examples of the he's of the real workers seldom left over from "progress". The homes of the wealthy are nice to see but the worker class homes need to be preserved as they tell the Savannah story too.

Just a beautiful example of PRE statehood architecture of a home build by a free black carpenter as a wedding gift for a white owner. Florida was awarded statehood after this house was built and the Knott family kept the original furnishings and wall paper (in the main hall only) when they gave the entire house to the government.
Picture a home as a time capsule from 1928 to 1941! The outdoor kitchen and bath from the original 1843 home has been moved inside then left alone. Mrs. Knott did a great job decorating the house and even wrote poetry for many pieces of furniture. She was very active in prohibition and sufferage.Mr. Knott was in the government accounting. FREE admission but bring a good donation. It is worth the 2 plus hour guided tour.

FANTASTIC 4 hour walking tour. Small but very nice Florida Animal representations. As you walk up high in a wooden walk you are looking down into the areas. BUT be sure to look in the trees for Fox and Black Bears!
Very special examples of a real working plantation main house, school house, train caboose and church have been moved to the Museum and you can walk through everything. The real buildings also include a complete farm with all outbuildings, live animals to show what life was like in the 1800's.
If you are more adventurous ? Try the ziplines and treetop walking action. A little extra from the regular Admission but there is plenty for.the cost. Admission was very fair and worth the effort. Special prices for young kids and seniors.

This was just beautiful. The ride out to the reservation was eye opening as you saw some conditions on the reservation that pointed to the way we treat our Native family. But the glass overlook constructed to step out in the canyon was impressive to see nature's wonders. We spent the day stopping off at the western town, having a GREAT lunch of BBQ chicken with the fixings, and seeing the display of the different types of traditional housing and talking to the tribe members helped to understand the culture lost to the European invasion. A great day to try and understand nature and the history of a great civilization.

If I could give more stars I would. The Kwahadi (pronounced "Kwadi")are a subtribe of the Cherokee. The museum is really dedicated to ALL Western /Plains and even the Mexican tribes. FANTASTIC art and artifacts are available to see. The people are very knowledgeable and friendly and the private collection of art and books from Mr. Thomas Mails was breathtaking to see the original art used in his books. This is a MUST SEE when you are in the area. Hours are limited to 1pm-4:30pm Sat and Sunday. You will need several hours to really see all the items in this dedicated muse

WOW! What a great time on this self guided tour of the complicated Vadalia Onion. The museum allows a free tour to see the history of the Largest cash export of the State of Georgia. Yes while the state is known for peaches and pecans the Real revenue is from the name protected onion. Stand back "Champaign" from France, and "Tequila" from Jalasco, Mexico. "Vadalia" onions are only available from Georgia USA! The town is great. The museum is a great place to learn about the official state vegetable!

Alexander Springs is part of the Ocala National Forest and even though there is a small fee (6.00 per person) to get is as a day user it has great picnic areas and easy access to the spring for swimming. Unfortunately the walking trail is CLOSED so you can relax by the spring and play in the open area but you cannot get to the overlook areas or walk the trail. I hope they get the path back open. We didn't know to ask at the guard gate about the trail so we had a short stay.

Great way to spend some time and get some exercise. A real water wheel mill that commercialized the area with work sawing, cotton gin, and grits / grain milling. All needed in the area during the 1880 to 1972. Walk through the mill. Enjoy an easy walk in several nature paths. Book your campsite early as they fill up really fast so they didn't allow for drive ups. The day trail is free with a 5.00 parking fee per car.

WOW what a great place to see nature and walk around. $4.00 per car with free parking is a real deal! We walked the Gulf beach and saw sand crabs, jelly fish, lots of sea shells, horseshoe crab shells, all kinds of birds. We had a great time. LOOK for small signs to get around. Plenty if areas to walk but it is hard to use the park map so just relax and walk around.

My 18 month old Pointer loves to run at full speed. The park is so large he can really get going to burn off excess energy. Water buckets are always full. Gravel and grass is well kept up and all the people are really friendly. Sheltered benches for the humans and places to put waste.. We will be here often during the winter season.

6 star Fantastic. Areas dedicated to each of the different climates in the state. Due to excellent planning you can really get close to the animals with minimal barriers. Even the squirrel were friendly.With Covid restrictions everything was still open to see. Some storm damage but all pathways were open. What a great day.

When was the last time you were over 10,000 feet above sea-level without an airplane? Come to the top of the mountain and look down on a great city. We drove the road and looked from the top. Due to Covid all was closed so traffic was very quiet. Social distancing? Well 10,000 feet above Albuquerque was pretty distant!

WOW! Every trail held so much to see and experience.  Bring a lunch and enjoy the constructed eating areas. Remember the CCC program during the depression as several sites have structures built at that time. A great day in a National Treasure. Restrooms are open even if the park welcome center is not.

A really beautiful place of historical signicance. As you walk the grounds you can see the influence of the Spaniards blending with the local First Nation people. The outbuildings like the food storage and kitchen add real life perspective. The Church was the gathering place for a public community.

As one of the first main religious areas in Savannah and close to the first Jewish synagogue and Protestant church St John the Baptist is very impressive. There were services going on in the Cathedral on sat and of course Sunday but other time it is open to the public for inside viewing.

One of many "Green Square" areas in Savannah and the largest. We were there on Saturday and they had a merithon going as well as a farmer market and soccer matches. Lots of space with lots of people enjoying 60 degree February weather. It is free and a lot of fun.

Every 2nd Tuesday of the month is free admission but you must get pretickets on line for a specific time frame.  Everything is just beautiful and very organized and informative. Walked about 4 miles over 3 hours to see it all.

Lots to see and you can even get into the locomotives and cars. Follow the tour guides to get some real history of the work yards and the people behind the maintenance shop. Right next to the battlefield in downtown Savannah.

Great gunfight at high noon and every hour on the hour. Lots of shops and really good prices. Lots to see just walking around as well as the paid history tours, train ride and off road tours. All is open but wear a mask.

What a beautiful National Treasure. Due to limited hours the tour center was closed on Tuesday but it is open on Thursday. But the information and park is open. Limited trials for my dog to walk but unlimited views.

Very somber but really very well documented. All you can ask is WHY? 2 floor museum is worth the several hours to tour and the rows of chairs really let you feel the impact of the senseless act against mankind.
They are closed due to Covid BUT I needed to go anyway just to look outside. The building is very well designed and the two memorials I did see were very impressive. I will make sure to come back.
Really beautiful but closed right now due to severe ice strom damage. A lot of trees are down here as well as around OK City. But you can see this is a beautiful green space in downtown OK City.
Very nice Park area. Excellent dog park (Wiggley Field). Great walking paths. Play ground equipment. Skate board area. Fishing pond / creek fed. Frisby Golf course.  Plenty to do and all free.

Trails that leave from the parking lot go north, west and south.  To the west and north, there are many choices that connect to other trail complexes and you can build a hike of whatever distance you like.  Although there are a few steep sections, they are generally easy to moderate.  The trails to the south go up Thumb Butte and are quite steep, although the main trail is actually paved.  You will either need a pass or have to pay $5 to park in the lot.  Be sure to display your pass or receipt.

As most every review says - this is an awesome place for a walk to just enjoy the plants.  It seems camellia bloom season is January - March although there are still plenty of flowers on the plants in mid-April (the camellias actually grow as trees here).  The Cherry Blossoms are also in bloom now.   Try straying off the paved walkways and get up close and personal with these flowers - they are wonderful.  As of April 2018, it is $9 for an adult and $6 for a senior - I missed the kids discount.

I have mixed feelings about these kinds of places. I hate to see wild animals penned up, however Out of Africa seems to have done a reasonable job of giving them enough room to roam. And most of these animals are rescued or born in captivity so it seems like a humane way to treat them.  The folks there seem very dedicated to keeping them healthy and as happy as can be and it was a very enjoyable visit from that point of view.  The MOG ride around the park was fun and very interesting.

Museum doesn't really describe KidsQuest.  It's more of an indoor play area where kids can learn while having fun.  It is very well designed for kids in the 5 to 10 year old range.  Our 2.5 year old granddaughter had lots of fun, but it's not clear how she might have learned.  The biggest pain is parking - don't park in the library garage.  Try the Hilton - they will valet park you and after the museum stamps your ticket, will only be  $5.50.

A beautiful hike through canyons with lots of water, vegetation and native American history.  It's about 6 miles round-trip and can be hot - in any case, start early or you will not find a parking place and you will be walking in a long line of people all the way to the falls.  The falls are beautiful - notice the water seeping from the walls, which form small streams that join the main creek.

This is an awesome loop trail.  The trail heading north from the parking lot is about 3 miles to the summit and lookout on Spruce Mt.  Continue south along the ridge to the intersection with the Isabella trail and turn west to head down and back to the trailhead.  The loop total is about 9.5 miles.  Although you might meet hikers or mountain bikers along the way, it is usually not busy.

This is a small zoo with a small number of animals and very little space.  They have done the best they can with the space - you can get close to the animals without endangering either you or them.  I know the animals are mostly rescue or born in captivity, but the incredibly small areas they live in can't be healthy so I am really conflicted about the value of these types of zoos.

Unfortunately, with the 2017/2018 winter being so dry, the falls are dry (May 2018).  The location is less than a 1/4 mile from the Sycamore Falls trailhead off of Forest Road 109, just north of Whitehorse Lake campground.  Based on the number of rock climbers on the Monday we visited, the rock climbing must be great.  There are some photos on-line so you can see what you missed.

We hiked the piece of the AZ Trail that heads south from FR303 to the Walnut Canyon Overlook.   It's flat for the first third, then drops down into a side canyon of Walnut Canyon,  then climbs back up to the overlook.  The overlook is great, although there are alot of trees blocking the view.  We only went 3 miles out, but it is a wonderful walk with lots of elk sign.

The monument has a short walk where you can see the "castle" and various other rooms built into the cliff walls.  You cannot get very close to the buildings, which doesn't matter much - the ruins have been substantially looted over the years.  It's relatively expensive to get in, but probably worth the cost to support the work to maintain the ruins.

An absolutely fabulous learning and play experience for kids of all ages.  My 3 year old grandson and his 60+ year old grandpa had a wonderful time.  There are more exhibits than you can understand and play with in 1 day.  Get a family membership and go back.  Parking was horrible even though the museum was not particularly crowded.

This parking lot is the start of several trails and requires a Red Rock Pass, which can be purchased by credit card only at the lot.  We took the Brin's Mesa trail up to the top of the Mesa and climbed a rock outcropping at 1.5 miles.  Great views!  The trail is rocky and relatively steep, but worth the effort.

This park has nice equipment, lots of shade,  grassy play areas and a large shaded picnic area.  Unfortunately, the picnic area has been taken over by a group of homeless people.  Although there weren't any problems, I felt like I had to watch the kids carefully.   It was a less than pleasant experience.

Evergreen is a fairly large, very nice park.  There are tennis courts, a challenging disc golf course, lots of grassy areas to run in, quite a bit of forested area and a mediocre kids play equipment area.  There are porta-potties scattered around the park, sometimes clean and sometimes, not so much...

Many of the animal enclosures are reasonably sized, although they have a way to go.  There are lots of activities that kids will enjoy and many of the animals are close enough for kids to see.  Most of the plants are labeled - a great way to learn the names of the plants you see every day!

We hiked Upper and Lower Calf Creek Falls, Peek-a-boo and Spooky slot canyons and a couple other short trails.  We drove route 12 over the mountain into Dixie National Forest (9600'  ! ).  Outfitters and Circle D were great meals.  I'm sure we missed some things but it was a great visit.

This Arizona State Park is incredibly we'll run.  Sheila is the wonderful enthusiastic ranger - she shared guns from the safe with us.  She knows everything about the buildings and the fort history.  The buildings are very well maintained and worth the short walk.

This is a nice, small beach with limited parking.  We visited in early March and had large waves, very broken, so there were only a few surfers out and no swimmers.  The waves breaking at the end of Devil's Teeth Trail we're spectacular.

One of the few parks in California without an entrance fee.  As of March 1, 2017, the beach sand is gone but the play equipment is great for toddlers.  Plenty of room to run and safe places to explore.
Very friendly folks at the Visitors Center.  If you're a hiker, ask for a trail list!  The walk is paved but steep.  Some good views of the lake on the way up.  Friendly ranger at the dwellings also.
The train ride was a bit boring - bring some activities for the kids.  The museum was great, with RR toys for the kids, a nice selection of RR cars and the tour leader was awesome!  Very interesting!
dislikes: Train ride无聊的火车旅程 - 请为孩子们准备一些活动。博物馆非常棒，有给孩子们玩的铁路玩具，各种各样的铁路车厢模型，导游也非常棒！非常有趣！

reviews_attraction.text: We went for a very short walk to the Willis Palms Oasis.  Being early March in a heavy rain year, the wildflowers were spectacular.  The trail is quite Sandy with loose rocks - watch your footing.
A very nice trailhead with restrooms,  covered picnic tables, grills and many very pleasant trails.  Take your pick of short and flat to long and hilly.
A fairly big parking lot at the trailhead - maybe 40 cars.  There is an outhouse, but no place to buy the forest pass.  Get it before you arrive here!
dislikes: Lack of forest pass purchase option

reviews_attraction.text: Great kids outdoor play equipment.  Ducks to feed across the street.  Lots of grass to play on.  Only negative is lots of traffic.

Something fishy going on here..  Visited in early June 2017 and found that the cost of entry for a Senior {$39.95} was less than the {$7.00} discount for Veterans and others.

Lots of fish, displays, and one can spend the entire day here reading the placards and other descriptions.  This was a Cannery at one time and thus has limitations to what they could do with the building and the displays.  They did a good job, but I have been to much more interesting and complex aquariums in Camden, New Jersey and Myrtle Beach, South Carolina that did not cost as much.

Most of the visitors did NOT spend the time to actually see and read about the Old Cannery {a separate section of the aquarium} and that is a shame as it is one of the reasons to go there.

There is a FREE Trolley from the downtown parking garage, and using it is almost a must as parking near the site is nearly nonexistent.

There is a restaurant internal to the site not far from the restrooms, but trying to get a sip of WATER is near impossible {Gee and right next to the ocean at that}.   {Corporate greed forces you to purchase drinks like water}.

The main tank show was disappointing in that it is NOT closed off during the feeding show and people kept going from room to room in front of much of the audience {Once the show starts, that area should have been blocked off- people with baby carriages, people in wheelchairs, people with luggage, and such did not want to see the show, only move through it}

Be prepared for lots of people and children pushing and shoving when the feeding of the otters and penguins is happening.  Children do have a 'hands-on' touch me, pet me {says the fishy} area.

It was the first week in June 2017 and the weather was not brutal, but was on the chilly side, so wear suitable clothing.

All in all a good way to spend four to six hours.  Lunch at their restaurant was reasonable, but nothing to write home about.

First of all the location shown by Google is WRONG, the park entry is actually several hundreds of feet north of the location shown on the Google Map..

GPS Tumacácori National Historical Park
1891 Interstate 19 Frontage Rd, Tumacacori-Carmen, AZ 85640
31.568517, -111.050911

Most people do not see all that there is to see, for they do not follow all the trails to the rear areas and the Kiln, farms, trails, and river areas.  Additionally, many people do NOT take the time to actually view and read the many historic signs and building details, which is a shame as this is a Historic Site and there is much to learn about our history, why the park exist, and its relationship to the White Dove near Tucson.

When leaving the park, one should head north on the frontage road to Tubac, and the State Park there, this park completes the local story of the mission and the people of yesteryear.

As a reporter for SeniorCitizenLocalWeb who has documented all three locations I have to recommend that you start at Tumacácori, then go to Tubac, and finish your day at the White Dove, it is an adventure and well worth the time. Share the experience with a friend or family member.

The park is part of the NPS, and the NPS passes will work, to those without the NPS pass, you can purchase it there, and if not then the modest $3.00 2014 entry is well worth the price.  You can purchase a guide booklet, or 'borrow' one for the few hours you will be there, just remember to return it.  There is a small book and gift store when you enter the massive front door and ticket counter.  Ask questions, the National Park people there are well informed and helpful. Rest rooms are to the right when exiting to the park grounds, and on many days you can join guided, but privately run, tours.  Don't miss the graves and the history of the little child.

Kitt Peak tours are mostly by foot, therefore wear comfortable walking shoes, be prepared to do some mild hillside climbing, and note that it can become chilly and windy as you are on the top of a mountain range.  The best purchase for most is the three one hour tours that start about 10 AM in the morning and last until about 4 PM, with two breaks in-between tours. Bring a camera and lots of film or batteries as you will be taking pictures, our last trip used 600 shots between two of us.

On the way up the mountain there are several 'turn-outs' that allow for nerves to settle, vehicles to cool down, and tremendous pictures of the Native American Reservation in the valley below.  Kitt Peak is on Native American Land, so respect it; many of the Native Americans work at the guest center and other areas of the complex.

There is a small gift shop and bathrooms and drinking fountains, but little to no food as the only restaurant is for astronomers and workers of the complex.  Astronomers frequently book time on the telescopes and stay in one of the guest rooms provided.
The guides are knowledgeable and friendly, do not be afraid to ask questions as there are no stupid questions, and the guides welcome the interaction, it shows interest.
From the ground level in the valley one can see only one or two telescopes, but once you get to the complex, you will find over 20, of which you will visit one to three depending on the tour selected.  As you leave the complex and proceed down the mountain, take the side trip to the picnic ground area, there you will see a very large uncovered antenna dish which is part of the National Radio Astronomy Observatory Array a world wide system of tracking items in space.  You can find out gps directions and much more on SeniorCitizenLocalWeb a southwest tourism resource.
likes: Cultural respect for Native American land

reviews_attraction.text:
I would give the State of California a negative 50 stars for this State Park.

The park guide at Mono Lake was recommending that foreigner {from Japan with a small rental vehicle} take the ride to Bodie, a bad move!

Before going to the area we contacted the State and found the road CA-270 to be closed, then a day before leaving home it was found to be open.

I have wanted to see this park for 40+ years, and thus the day before arriving in the area consulted the California park service that told me that the June winter storm had the last three miles of the road muddy and thus "travel was at one's own risk".  The day and hour we got to CA-270 the road was clear and dry, and no where in the area could we find any more info.  Thus we decided to take the 13 mile {one way} drive to the site.  The first 10 miles is paved and the last 3 are dirt, which I have driven upon millions of times in my life; what I have not driven upon is a 'WashBoard' that shakes the living .... out of the vehicle {2005 Hyundai} and the passengers.

This Washboard road has NO guard rails and cliffs on the left that go up, and cliffs on the right that drop hundreds of feet.  The car shook so violently that we only made it 300 yards before doing a dangerous 3-point U-turn.

Perhaps a large RV or a large SUV with big tires and an insane driver can make the 6-mile round trip on this 'pavement?", but if you are in a small vehicle it is not recommended and may be very dangerous.  The road was dry when we tried it; I cannot imagine going on it when the road is wet with rain or snow and slippery as grease.  The State of California is highly neglect and should be ashamed of this.

I will not ever be back until the last three miles are paved and guard rails are installed.

About 12 miles north of Benson, Arizona is a place missed by most tourist, and that is a shame as it is delightful, and the proprietor is an interesting character that not only believes in the 'Old West', but relishes in describing it to all that venture out to the property.

I met Mr. Gammon, as you may, if you take the short trip into the desert mountains to visit the town; and yes, it is a town, be it a Ghost Town, or a Movie Set Town, or be it both, which it is.  There are a complex mixture of old, new, reproductions, originals, that span the mid-1880's to the 1930's and then some within this working movie production complex.  Gammon has put together a place on earth where those wanting to film a Western Movie may, or where those that want to become 'hitched' (married) can do so in the comforts of the 1880's saloon, complete with banjo and piano music, tasteful 'R' rated old west picture, and checkered tablecloths, all while being surrounded by history and movie greats like 'Dean Martin', and 'Rex Allen'.

Had birthday party there, and it was fun and different for those that have never seen the place.  SeniorCitizenLocalWeb has a great write-up with GPS turn by turn instruction, including the area's speed traps.

Give the place a try, spend two to three hours, and note that the cost of the personal, and very delightful and historic tour is less than the cost of a hamburger.

Turkey Creek Canyon near Pearce, Arizona
John Ringo at Turkey Creek Canyon

This dirt road and canyon is near AZ-181 and US-191.    The road goes up into the mountains and is known for its one historical marker, the grave site of John Ringo a gunman and outlaw that is said to have sat in the fork of the oak tree and shot himself in the head; the story is controversial as many think he was shot by others and placed there as a warning to those that would do bad.

The canyon is one of the few in the area that seems to have year-round water flowing in its creek.  This brings on bear, deer, and other wild animals, and if you drive up the canyon toward the waterfall (about 8 miles) you may see Black Tail or Mule deer along you trip.

The marker states

"John Ringo.. The remains of this noted gunman and outlaw lie here. A
Teamster traveling from West Turkey Creek found the body sitting in the fork of a nearby oak tree with a bullet hole in the right temple. A coroner's jury reported the death to be a suicide, and Ringo was buried on the spot. There were others who viewed the body and maintained that the July 13, 1882 death of Ringo was Murder"

Pearce, Arizona
Make a stop at this Ghost Town, it is still occupied, is near a newly opened Gold Mine, has several buildings from the past, a jail, and a graveyard worth seeing.

This was to be a highlight of our CA-1 to Crater Lake adventure, and it was in some aspects.  Unfortunately there was a Pacific storm coming in {June 2017} and the combination of cold Pacific water and storm drizzle made for nasty weather.

The path to the Lighthouse was clear as the water level was low, but the long walk, wind, and coldness won out and we only took pictures from the edge of the parking lot.

Not to sure if persons with physical handicaps can do this short tour as the path toward the ocean part appears to be rocky and rough, and WILL get covered with several inches to feet of water when the high-tide rolls into the bay.

There are 'squirrels' all around the grounds and it seems that people have been feeding each as several came up to my leg looking for food.  One should NOT feed these 'wild' animals as one has no idea when one will turn mean or carry a disease.

Crescent City boast that this Lighthouse as one of its most attractive tourist sites, but has done nothing to improve the access or the signage from US-101.  One would hope that in the future it will build 'handicap' ramps that are above the high-water line so that those with physical disabilities, children, and seniors can enjoy the site.

Think of June 2017 as being a time of very warm to hot temperatures, and then arrive in a snow storm blizzard with an inch of wet slush on the entry road and the paths.  Well that tended to limit the 'cave' explorations from three or more hours to about 45 minutes at Mushpot Cave the only cave that one could walk to in freezing weather.

Mushpot cave has a steep metal staircase leading down into it, and it was slippery but navigational so we did descend into the bowels of the earth for a few pictures and a 'yes we have been there' event.

The visitor center is fair and the National Park Employees were understanding and tried to make the visit 'ok'.

Leaving the park going south from the visitor's center was easier as there was far less snow and slush on the road.

If you get there during good weather, then visit the many caves and lava fields that are in the area.  Plan on spending from one to three hours.  Note that you are in the wilderness, thus be prepared for all events, and bring lots of water as it can and did get hot the day after the spring blizzard storm.

As a reporter for SeniorCitizenLocalWeb I visited the Monastery in November of 2014 and enjoyed a few hours of peace and reflection in a natural environment that has something for most to enjoy.

This Catholic retreat has facilities for RV's, retreat rentals, and group gathering activities.  Most who visit miss the walk to the Stations of the Cross, the walk to and around the two ponds, the small museum, the well-stocked library, and the Meditation area, will you?

The book store and gift shop is well-stocked with religious items and contains the Angel Room featuring children's books and a restroom.

The main church, Our Lady of Guadalupe Chapel, is one of the more unique in the country, look at the architecture and the pecan wood use.

Plan on a stay of about two hours and plan on shooting from a dozen to a hundred pictures, yes there are that many things to see and enjoy.

On the way Back to Benson, Arizona from Saint David make a stop at the Gallery of Dreams, it is a consignment gallery featuring local artist.
likes: Variety of facilities (RV, retreat rentals, group gatherings)

reviews_attraction.text:
I love my Mummy, I do.. You will too when you go to this museum which I believe has the second largest collection of ancient Egyptian artifacts, mummies, and information.  {Largest I believe is in Germany}

Plan on spending three to four hours in this multi-level building and the Planetarium next door. {They have movies there that are always interesting}.   Plan your visit so you have plenty of time to see the exhibits, the movie, and then return to the exhibits and gift shop.

The site has a gift shop, a parking lot out back, a flower and Koi pool garden, and much more.

The entry fee is low and the value is tremendous.  If you are in the San Jose area for one day, then I recommend going to the Winchester House in the AM, then to the Rose Garden and a restaurant for lunch, and then to this Egyptian Museum in the afternoon .   It is a full day, but well worth it.

Ten stars if possible.  Great museum with paintings and sculptures from the Great Masters.  This museum houses some of the greatest artworks of mankind and is a pleasure to visit.

There are also outside sculpture gardens and a pond that make the experience even more great.

Do not miss the ancient Asian exhibit or the special exhibits on the lower level.

Plenty of on site parking, low entry cost, and ease of freeway access makes this a perfect stop for the art enthusiast and traveler.

Special thanks to the staff member that found my camera case that had dropped out of my pocket and then searched for me to return it.

Super clean bathrooms, helpful people at each exhibit, and security that rivals Fort Knox make this museum a good visit.

Be sure to allow two to four hours or more, and be sure to bring your camera {NON-Flash photography is allowed}.

Interesting part of the history of the U.S.A. -- Good tour and great tour guide that was not just knowledgeable, but fun and interesting; and would actually answer questions with factual info.

The June 2017 trip to San Simeon was to continue up the coast on CA-1, but due to the massive landslide a week earlier and the detour that cut our stay by hours we did not have sufficient time to 'self-tour' the grounds.

Basic tour is $25 per person and worth the fee.  Parking is at the bottom of the mountain and you will be bused to the mansion at the pinnacle, which after you see the road is probably best.

Be prepared to spend from two to four hours at this historic site.
likes: Facilities & Services: Knowledgeable, engaging tour guide
Facilities & Services: Bus service to mansion

reviews_attraction.text:
Caution.. Do not count on getting gasoline or food at this town, everything was boarded up when we visited in June 2017.  Nearest gasoline is about 17 miles north up US-101

Now, the drive thru tree, yes it is there, and yes if you have a small or mid-size vehicle you can drive through this giant living Redwood.  You should be able to get pictures of your vehicle in the 'tunnel' and many people then park and get pictures of themselves standing in the tree's tunnel.

There are a gift shop and bathrooms as well as a picnic area by the lake so you can enjoy an hour or two with nature in the wild.

RVs can use the road and the bypass around the giant tree.

Neat place.  Fern Canyon is 8 miles from US-101 by the ocean, and this is Elk Meadow.   The Elk were at first not seen from the Davison road and thus, we left and drove up toward the Elk Meadow resort, and there they were.  Dozens of Elk grazing in the open field just posing for us as we took pictures.   There is also a {Steel} Elk at the corner by the resort, and a sign that allows you to document where you are.

Fern Canyon is a State run facility with $8.00 per day entry, and I believe $35 for overnight camping.  We did not get there as we were under time constraints, but the pictures on Google show it as a pretty nice place to spend an hour or so.

Open - NOT!

We got there early this past week {June 2017} and found that the Gift shop is open, but the Museum was not, and in fact it is closed due to being moved to another building that per the person running the gift shop will not be for a year or more.

You can though go out back and see dozens of mining machines that were used in the area during the Borax and Gold rush era.

There is an eatery across the street, and there is the Furnace Creek Museum nearby, which is a great place to visit.

They have various musical shows, check for dates and times.  The place has a lot of history, but if you do not meet the bald-headed gentleman that appears to reside there during the touring season, you may not every find out about the history (He spent nearly 30-minutes providing some great stories).

When open, there are various facilities that you can partake of, but otherwise the place is closed.  Plan on 15 to 30 minutes when it is closed, and hour to four when a show is in progress.
dislikes: History information dependent on specific staff

reviews_attraction.text:
Everyone has to make a buck these days and this place is no different.  They charge $1.00 per person to enter the museum, but if you order an ice cream for $1.50 you can come in free.  Hey, what a bargain.

There are banana everything to look at, or purchase, and smell or feel.  Yes, the museum is to get you in the door and to purchase something, but  hey it is unique and now you will forever be able to say that you visited the International Banana Museum..

Good stop for some Native American history.  The caves are closed to the public, but are good for a photo shoot.  This is private land and therefore you are a guest, so please respect the property and do not add trash to the site.

The Shoshone museum is near as is a small restaurant, but do not depend on either being open as their advertising states.  Both were closed mid-week for various questionable reasons when we visited the site.

This is a place on the way from the Winchester House to the Rosicrucian Egyptian Museum that you should not miss.  The vastness and variety of the rose bush plants is amazing.

But be warned, that when the local schools are having their grad ceremonies this is the spot many chose for their day in the sun.  {Yep, got there that day and could not find a parking spot nor any way to stop and smell the roses.}

Liked the reviews of others and thus took the long way to Las Vegas across Death Valley from Lone Pine, California.  Guess what, the entire place was closed on with sign that they had a Power Outage.  Restaurant next door also closed for 5 days of 'Cleaning' ..  Total bust.

Dublin Gulch across the street was worth seeing, but in all the extra hour's drive was not worth it.

Here is a situation that can frost a person.  The opening hours are posted and we were there during those hours only to find the doors locked tight.

We did get to take some pictures of the logging equipment and of the Redwood Sawmill down the street.  But, since we took the time to detour and see this museum, it really would have been great to see inside the building.

Your tax dollars at work and being well spent.  The NPS {National Park Service} runs this museum and it is clean, informative, and the personnel are well informed.

This is a good stop when in Death Valley, California.  Also, nearby are gas stations, restaurants, and the Borax Museum {under construction in June 2017}.

I see a Camera spot on Google maps, it is on the right side of CA-1 as you go north, and in the woods.  This is NOT the fort, the fort is on the left side of the road between the road and the beach, near the Conservatory.  You will see it to your left as you travel north up CA-1 before the left turn entry.

The museum is upstairs in a sizable used book shop.  It does feature some of Mr. Anderson's items and a few tools used to make wooden shoes, but not too much more.  Worth a 10-minute visit if you are in town.
