The visitor center is manned outside with a table for maps and a ranger. The book store was closed today due to Manning issues not covid.

A lot of people are wearing masks out on the trail to the cliff dwellings with out being near anyone ...which is actually quite dangerous because of lower oxygen levels with recycling air,  elevation and heat here.

Every park employee we encountered was super friendly and helpful.

Great place to bring kids to teach them stuff they wont be taught much about in school these days.

Junior Ranger Program available without a lot of time needed to complete, which is great if you are on the road and compressed for time.

Staff was friendly. Was clean and lots of history to read about in the visitors center.

4 passport stamps available here:  Saratoga, Erie, Hudson and Champlain

Went here for a birthday party for a 6 year old.  Staff was very friendly and helpful.

Clean and well lit.   Not a lot of egress points and the one to the outside is alarmed. When it's pushed by a kid multiple staff members hurry to the open door to prevent anyone from running off with your kids.

Only one toilet though. Which is not so great when a lot of people are there.

This is a nice park nearer nicer neighborhoods than a few other County Parks. Well maintained. The boardwalk is nice but can lead  you into different directions if you're not careful of your navigation. The tower is nice for views of sunset right before park closes.

I've seen racer snakes in the pines trees above the boardwalk before but never any on the walkway itself.

First time visit, family of 6 on February 1, 2020.   We parked by the observation tower where there is no fee to park then walked across the metal bridge.

The color scheme of the park is a bit unappealing. There is a rest room in the far back of the park.

Overall not a bad park.  Just $5 fee if you park in the parking lot is a little silly to me.

Family of 6 visited here in July 2019.
Make sure you have a jacket at the top of the pass.  While it might be warmer at lower elevations, there was still snow here in mid July and the kids had a snowball fight in the back of the visitor center.

The visitor center itself was kind of a let down- not much but a bathroom and small gift shop.

Nothing nearby, but it is a really neat place. Even when 100 degrees, there are shorter paths that are spectacular, near the visitor center.   If going to carlsbad caverns, take the extra couple hours and come here.

There are no food, gas or services anywhere nearby, so bring food and water and a full gas tank,

The biggest downfall is it closes early...  430pm
Visitor Center is in a trailer.

They have a Junior Ranger Program which is not too time consuming
The boat ride tickets are not available in the visitor trailer, you must go down the street for them

Staff was friendly and interacted with the kids nicely

Family of 6, visited in July 2019.  It is a ways off the beaten path but worth the drive.  The big loop is one way only so if you go the other direction, you cannot do the full loop.

Lots of photo opportunities here.  Not packed with an abundance of other vehicles.  Definite recommend.

I never happen to arrive here when the visitor center is actually open, but there is a nice little Canoe access (Halfway Creek
Paddling Trail Access) at the end of the road behind the visitor center.  It also has public restroom (open when visitor center closed)  if you are driving 41.

This park is not being taken care of as much as it was before.  Lots of leaves on the ground everywhere.   Solar compactor trash cans are from Delray Beach.  And they cleared a lot of the forest inside of the park.

While not terrible, it's also clearly not a top notch park either.

There is about a million different paths to get to this point. I highly suggest you take a GPS plot of your vehicle so you can find it when you get off the Queens Garden Trail. Look at the map, there are so many paths that lead here but only one will be right for you to leave,

They have the ink stamps here for your stamp books (National Park, etc)
They are not part of the national park service and there is yet more official visitor center around the corner east on US 89 just past Wendy's.  More stamps there for  your collection.

A ride more geared towards younger kids...

The hydraulic actuator to go up and down really lags and takes a long time to respond.

The ride had a wait time of 25 minutes and the ride itself seemed pretty short in duration, in my opinion.

Nice clean park.  The area with the play ground however makes me feel a little uneasy because there is a back entrance to it where your kids could disappear quickly in the scrub palms if you take your eyes off then more than seconds.

Parking over flow is on the grass. watch for fire ants.  Fun play ground outside of community center.  The Community center looks like it is in an apartment complex, so don't think you're going down the wrong road when you go there.

A nice state park away from the waterfront area.  Great history and friendly park employees here.  Kids enjoyed it too.

Its a bit winding of a drive to get to so watch your signs closely and use a GPS to go there.

Friendly place.  My 4 year old needed water and this place let me buy a bottle of Desani water for $1.89 using a debit card with no minimum limit like another cigar store, Cuban. Paraduse nearby does.
Very neat place.  We had a lot of fun on the dunes.  It gets toasty on them so bring some cold water with  you.  If you have a sled, bring it, its fun like sledding on snow!

Jamestown Settlement is an indoor and outdoor museum. Indoor is a very large building with displays telling the story of Jamestown (founded 1607) and notable inhabitants (including John Smith and Pocahontas who married John Rolfe not Smith). We saw a special exhibit on the women who came to Jamestown as well. The outdoor museum included a reproduction of the Jamestown fort (with working docents), reproductions of the three ships which brought the colonists and a reproduction of a Powhatan indigenous peoples village. Everything was done in wonderful detail and our visit was very educational - enlightening. I would highly recommend this museum. If you have a bit of time, you can drive down to the archaeological digs as well and get a good feeling for the locale.

Beautiful park with a large lake. We stayed in stone cabins with a great view of the lake. The cabin we had comprised a bedroom with two large beds, a full kitchen (no microwave) and a living room with a working fireplace and a small dining table. Wood is available at the camp office. Bring everything you need except the cabins had a small coffee pot, bed linens and shampoo.  Also outside was a grill, a picnic table, a fire ring and wooden chairs (for 3). We had a friendly sheep for a couple of days and lots of birds (for December). There also are some nice hiking trails and lake access. Come to enjoy yourself. We did!

We love Gatorland and visit every time we are staying in Orlando. It is an alligator and crocodile study facility and fun park. There are alligators of all ages from the very young and cute to the very old and large and scary. There are several shows during the day. In addition there are plenty of wAlking trails with exhibits. This might as well be a bird sanctuary as well as so many birds are present. It is fun go see birds and alligators compete for treats. The birds are fearless. There is a small water park for kids and Ziplines for adults. Don't forget the train ride! Fun!

Wonderful park! Mostly a botanical garden of Sonora Desert plants (including the rare and exotic) but also a zoo with an aquarium, bird sanctuary, butterfly garden, etc. Touch a meteorite older than the sun! See a moon rock! Good for half a day or all day. This is the only place I have seen golden barrel cactus and golden saguaros. If I lived in Arizona, I would become a permanent member. It is nice now in January but different flowers will come out in various seasons. Lots to do for nature lovers of all ages!

This should be five plus stars! Met at the shop for breakfast. They bussed us to the cog train station and we met again at the top of Pike's Peak. They had everything: bikes, helmets, jackets, gloves, filled water bottles. The ride down was fun. Magnificent views. Plenty of stops for pictures. Our guides were freindly and helpful.  There were a few uphill believe it it not but you could walk your bike if needed. This was all followed up with a great lunch.  We want to go again with this company!

Mesa Verde is a wonderful national park. Driving through the park you are presented with stunning views of the main canyon. It is a desert environment, quite dry. Bring lots of water. There are several loops with multiple turn-outs. There are also several ancient cliff dwelling "towns." Each has it's own tour and difficulty. Read up before you decide which to take. There are also interpretive sites, museums and a great ranger station. I highly recommend a visit!

We visited the west side of Saguaro National Park. The Red Hills Visitor Center offers a lot of interpretive information, nestled in the most sense Saguaro cactus "forest". A naturalist gave us a tour of a garden with all the types of plants we would see later. We hiked several trails while driving a loop road. The scenery is other-wordly. You will not find this beauty elsewhere! This is a must-see national park.

We enjoyed our visit to this state park. We walked the Summit Trail and found a fantastic view. We also hiked the South Ridge Trail and a bit of the Bounday Trail. Adults are $6 but seniors are only $2. That being said, mostly we found obstructed views. Trails were overgrown with roots and there were lots of rocks. It had rained so everything was slick. We had to really watch your step basically all the way.

The Cliff Palace tour was a high-light for me on the visit to Mesa Verde. There are a lot if steps and a few ladders but I always felt safe. The ranger gave an excellent tour and pointed out many new findings. I found the diversity of peoples as witnessed by the diversity of kivas to be quite interesting. Don't pass up a chance to take this tour!

A decent park (I walk there all the time). On the Louetta side, it is mostly paths around soccer fields. Across Cypresswood, it is a similar situation but with a very nice playground and duck pond. A path leads away to Cypress Creek and a dishing pond/lake. The path continues on under Stuebner Airline and into Collins Park.

I enjoyed the architecture and memorabilia of a truly remarkable man. You can get some understanding of Jefferson during the tours. Some parts of Jefferson are not so easy to understand. The slave quarters and description of their lives for one. Well worth seeing and discussing.

If you have any interest in air planes, air warfare, air travel, air rescue, you will enjoy this open and covered air museum! The trolley wasn't working today due to recent storms but walking was no problem. Excellent docents in site. Good lunch spot as well. Enjoy!

Take the long walk down from the surface or you will miss so much! Once on the bottom, many wonders await. This cave has the best of everything: stalagmites, stakagtites' soda straws, draperies, etc, plus formations found nowhere else. My favorite cave!

I have played disc golf here at Agness Moffitt Park and both times have been enjoyable. The whole course is 1.5 - 2 miles with some really nice long layouts. The occasional tree in the way makes it more challenging and fun.

The park itself is very nice.  Rugged with lots of hills/small mountains. Good trails. There is a skyline drive that we took often in the morning or at sunset. Good bird blind for viewing. Contains the Indian Lodge.
We played disc golf on a great course at T. C. Jester Park. There are 21 holes, well spread out with long fairways and some good obstacles. Be prepared to walk --- we did a couple of miles that day.
This is a good stopping point on the roads within Garden of the Gods. Climb the formations and take photos. Parking is limited so grab a space nearby and hike over. Warning: no restrooms.
The inside show was great but the outdoor viewing is at the whim of nature. We had nearly a full moon which wiped out a lot of stars. We were able to view the moon and the planet Saturn.
This is a wonderfully curated extinct cinder cone volcano.  Lots of wildlife. Many trail. We especially enjoyed the trail around the top of the volcano and to the bottom of the crater.
There are hiking and biking trails leading from this park. Plenty of space for family and/or friends. You can rent a kayak up until 4 pm.  It looks like you can even rent a jet ski.
Trails to and around the beach were quite nice.  Plants were unusual and unique.  Provided maps were pretty useless.  The fort was small but interesting (see pictures attached).
Mom and pop museum of nut crackers and nut picks through the ages. This is a carefully curated collection and quite extensive. We had a lot of fun there; it's a visual treat.
Located in the old Flagstaff train station (still servicing Amtrak!), The FVC has lots of good info on Flagstaff and northern AZ. The staff are very friendly and helpful.
likes: Facilities & Services: Friendly staff, helpful service

reviews_attraction.text: Well maintained trail around the circumference of the island. Several auxiliary trails provide beach access. Forest scenes and water views aplenty.
Played the disk golf course and had a great time. Good mix of long and short fairways. Not many big trees. The one water hazard was not too bad.

I always wanted to visit Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles and finally made it here. I had about 3 hours to see it and it should be more than enough. I honestly expected the museum to be bigger - if you have been to Chicago or LA Auto show those are 3 times larger and have a lot more cars to see every year. However, the value of Petersen Automotive Museum is in its movie cars and crazy concepts. Even non-car people would appreciate the museum as we all watch movies and know celebrities.

There are many cool cars on 3 floors but I definitely recommend to start with the Vault Tour. You can book it online in advance or try your luck onsite. The vault has some of the most unique and most valuable vehicles of all times. From movie cars, to crazy unique concepts, to celebrity haulers (Elvis Presely, Steve McQueen, Jack Nicholson) - all of them are here. Too bad you can't take photos and 45 mins aren't nearly enough to check out all of the cars on a guided tour. But the tour guides are fantastic!

The main floors have some cars from movies like Star Wars, Mad Max, Fast and Furious, Blade Runner, Batman, I Robot... Lots to see. And you can take photos! You can also find some prototypes of the US makers from 80's, 90's, and modern times. There is a small exhibit by Ganassi racing, too, that includes the Indy500 car driven by Scott Dixon.

Lastly, even the museum building itself is an architectural masterpiece and don't forget to check out some artifacts in the parking garage!

Pricing: it doesn’t look expensive at first but it gets expensive. $16 general admission, $28 vault tour, $17 parking... That’s $61 for a visit. If it was in the $40 range it would be great value but as of now I’m not sure. But I do really love cars.

This resort is probably as good as downhill skiing/snowboarding gets near Indianapolis. Obviously, it’s not Colorado, Alaska, or Pacific Northwest.

It’s not overly expensive if you buy tickets online / for a group / once a week pass / season pass. Slopes and equipment were in good shape.

We came here for a day and rented skis. The rental process was chaotic and pretty concerning in terms of public safety. That’s the main reason I gave this place 2 stars. There was no regulation as to how many people entered the rental area at a time and I didn’t see much cleaning in the area either. Most people did wear a mask, but there were some individuals without it and it wasn’t enforced in the rental rooms as much as it was outside (which honestly isn’t as important). I’d appreciate if management put a gatekeeper on each side of the rental facility and allowed 20 people at a time instead of 200 like it was today. It’s very irresponsible and reckless in relation to visitors and the whole community. If you come with you own gear, you can skip the Covid-19 hatchery (aka rental room) and enjoy your time outdoors.

The wait at chairlifts was pretty long unless you went to the slopes for more experienced people. In 4 hours, we were able to go down only 5 times. And the length of the slopes can’t justify such wait times…

Unless Covid-19 safety improves, we will not be back. It’s too much of a risk right now if you’re renting gear on the spot.
dislikes: Inadequate slope length for wait times

reviews_attraction.text: This is a hidden gem and an amazing place to visit by any car enthusiast. Lots and lots and lots of AMC/Nash/Rambler cars both restored and awaiting their turn at the boneyard. Hundreds of beautiful vehicles from early 1900’s till 1980’s in a great shape. There’s a perk, too - all sorts of mannequins dressed according to the era they represent next to every other car. The ranch also has some European and even Canadian cars and Terry, the owner, is super nice and knowledgeable! You can tell how passionate he is about those makes and preserving the spirit of 60’s and 70’s. Last but not least, you are welcome to check out the collection of old Kelvinator kitchen appliances and explore the guest house inspired with the design ideas of 1960’s! I definitely recommend spending couple of hours here. Only by appointment.

Great museum to see while visiting Bozeman - especially if you’re a tech nerd or interested in computers more than an average person. The museum itself isn’t very big - just a few rooms. Someone wrote it was free - it wasn’t ($15 for two people), but still worth every penny. The rooms are separated by themes - from early arithmetic gadgets and calculators, to first PCs, to encryption devices and AI. You can even see the “brain” of the Minuteman ICBM and the Apple 1 board donated by Steve Wozniak. There are also early cell phones (Motorolas) and encryption devices like Enigma! The museum did a great job explaining modern tech and there’s a lot of reading to do while you’re there. If you want to continue on the subject after visiting the museum, watch “Halt and catch fire” show on Netflix ;)

Absolutely stunning! I’ve been to almost all big parks in Oregon and Washington and this park was one of the best if not the best one.

The two great starting points are Sunrise or Paradise Point if you’re here for the first time. The wait to get to Sunrise can be about an hour or so - that’s how many cars go there. So he mentally prepared.

If you want great views of Mt Rainier, snowy trails but also rivers and wild flowers - take the glacier basin trail and then hike up to the Burroughs mountains. It’s a long hike - about 11.5 miles so plan 6-7 hours and bring 1/2 gal water per person and some snacks. Also, charge your camera/phone. It’s a hard route but absolutely worth it!

Fantastic wild cat rescue center only one hour away from Indianapolis. It’s impressive how much the staff has done for these beautiful animals in the last 30+ years. And the animals are impossible to take eyes off. The price is only $10 and all the money goes into supporting the animals. All the tours are guided and you’ll be with other 8-10 people. The tours are about 1 hr long and are very interesting. Optionally you can also opt to stay one night at the owners residence and have a private tour of the other half of the rescue center and it’s facilities.

Nice place to hike both for individuals and families. There are low / mid / upper falls depending on how far you want to go. The further you go the more complicated it gets but it is worth it. Although for most people I’d recommend stopping at mid falls: upper falls are harder to see and are not more impressive than mid falls.

Overalls it’s a nice park with a plenty of parking and most of the hiking trails are shaded so you probably won’t need sunscreen.

Although the entire village is not the original settlement, it was recreated well and it was great to walk through the park and see Native American settlement and a 17th century village of first immigrants. There are some actors in the village who were dressed like people of those times and who you could ask questions and talk about life happening on your particular visit date. Really cool place to visit for all history lovers!

One of the best national parks I’ve been! Endless trails and paths to explore, beautiful mountains, waterfalls, and lakes. You can see a lot of wildlife just feet away and even camp with the permit.

Come early morning or weekdays to avoid crowds and to find a parking spot easier.

Dress appropriately, have a plenty of water, sun screen, and leave zero trash! You’ll love this park and endless ranges make it a must to come back.

Definitely one of Top-5 parks in Indiana. Lots of trails, picnic areas, and parking. There is even a dedicated horse trail and a pool! Unfortunately, due to Covid, many facilities were closed (pool and Wolf Cave), but you can hike your life away here and watch beautiful waterfalls, forest, and its wildlife. Be careful - there are snakes. The park is especially beautiful in the fall and less crowded. Definitely recommend!

Honestly, this is my favorite part of Grand Canyon. It’s incredibly beautiful and breathtaking and even those adjectives would be an understatement. The walk from the parking lot is about 10-15 mins and there are a few observation points nearby. You can’t go wrong with any of them - it’s stunning. Admission price is only $10 per car. It’s a must see if you are in the area.

In comparison to Turkey run - TR is better, in my opinion. Shades SP also has some nice trails with waterfalls and beautiful rugged terrain, but TR is like twice as impressive (and more crowded). I also recommend the Pine Hills Nature Preserve nearby!

Super easily accessible but usually crowded for that reason. There are multiple observation decks - i would say go to the right first and make all the way up to the highest point. The views are stunning, especially in the fall or during sunset.

Amazing place for all waterfall lovers. Make sure you wait till it gets darker to enjoy the lights on the waterfalls and take a hike to the top! There’s also an observation deck with an elevator that offers breathtaking views!

If you’re using north entrance or any other entrance than main - be sure to carry $2 in cash. Otherwise, use the main gate and pay $8 per vehicle. The park itself is very nice and the beach is beautiful!

The museum is very rich in history of racing and has lots and lots of cars to see from all generations. Plan at least two hours or so. The museum is good for all ages and offers some souvenirs as well.
Accessible via steps for pedestrians or via horse pathways it’s a great thing to see! It also has an observation deck with fantastic views. There’s another higher deck around the corner with a trail!
It looks solid, but there is nothing to do here more than 20 mins. All rooms inside fortress are empty and contain only posters to read. Can't compare to fortresses and castles in Europe.
Huge and very interactive. Make sure you see the German WWII U505 submarine and go mining. Some of the rooms have only written info and posters, but no physical things to touch / see.
Beautiful park with gorgeous gardens and fountains! In addition, it has a botanical greenhouse which puts some nice Xmas decorations in December and a water park nearby.
Beautiful road from Harbor Springs to Cross Village! I wish a had a convertible to enjoy it more. The route is especially picturesque in the fall (mid October)
You will love this place. It has nice shows about our universe and you should see Tesla coil in action. The surrounding park is great for hiking!
Amazing park for running and just taking walks.  Beautiful scenery with a lake and massive forest in the city. Ornithology center as a bonus.
Steps are free, elevator costs money :) There are about 330 steps to reach the top of the monument and enjoy amazing views!
Gorgeous overlook and it is worth hiking around for even better views. Come on a sunny day in the fall for maximum fun!

Keys View is beautiful. Make sure that you download offline maps because you will not have service in the majority of the park and it will make it hard to find some key spots... No pun intended, but maybe just a little. Seeing the sunset from here was absolutely stunning. There were nearby spots that we couldn't find because service was so spotty. But I'm glad we found what we could and saw the sunset from around this spot.

We wanted to come back here a few hours later for some astrophotography, but our hotel let us know that a few people and one woman in particular had gone missing within 10 days before our visit.... The woman's car was found with the front and rear windshields smashed in and no camping gear at all. Being 7 months pregnant, this is not a chance I wanted to take. And while I've heard of innocent accidents in Joshua Tree like heat exhaustion or hiking accidents, it's not a risk I wanted to take with just me and my husband going to shoot in the middle of the night.

These gondola rides at the Venetian are totally worth the hype! At first, I thought they were so cliché especially when I saw the line... But we managed to come in a non peak time when the line had died down. We went on the ride and ir was 100% worth it.

Between the picture as a souvenir and the live singing. It was romantic, relaxing and beautiful. The inside of the Venetian always looks like it's about dusk inside which adds to the vibe and atmosphere of the gondola rides.

I brought my then boyfriend (now husband) for his 30th birthday and the gondola ride was a nice relaxing thing to do in between all the craziness that is Las Vegas. The Venetian is conveniently located and is the perfect location from the strip. They have a great pool set up and the spa is just delicious.

A lot of people have recommended us to go visit The Flower Fields. As photographers, it was definitely beautiful. However, I don't believe the price and the value aligned. Almost $20 to see a field of flowers seems excessive and you almost want to take the cart ride to make it an experience and worth the money. As someone from out of state, I didn't really understand what was so amazing. Yes, they are beautiful. Yes, there are tons of flowers. And yes, they have made cool patterns with them. And I can see how the price must go to drip irrigation or even upkeep considering how dry California is. I just didn't really see the value behind it especially when La Jolla Cove is really close, you can see sea lions, and there's tons more to do.

Cirque du Soleil is incredible. Every show I've seen is to die for. My fiance really wanted to see this show especially because we loved O and LOVE. At last minute we dedicded to get tickets for Ká. The show was great. The length let it carry so there weren't luls. The stage was magnificent. But I'll be honest, I'd rather re-watch O or LOVE than this one. The stunts were great and the performance was awesome but it just didn't connect well. The staff let people arrive late with flashlights on which was so distracting and they usually don't do this. It made the story really hard to follow. Word to the wise, the crew members come out and scare you before the show. And not like other Cirque shows, like they straight up yell in your face.

I had low expectations but my husband really wanted to go and I'm so glad that we went! The story is amazing and the art is beautiful. The museum does a great job of adding dramatic lighting. The lighting made for some truly beautiful photos. There were also photographers in two exhibits that took pictures. It was nice that the pictures like at the Space Needle were free - it's a nice touch. When we went out to the gardens they actually had a presentation blowing the glass. It was nice to see it live and made me appreciate the art even more. The garden was beautiful even though it was raining. This also made for some beautiful pictures as you could see the reflection of the Space Needle in a lot of the glass that was wet.

Cool park in Seattle. You can get a nice shot (📸) of the sculpture there and even of the Space Needle. There's not a crazy amount to do here... So I wouldn't really plan it as a "must do" on your list when you visit Seattle. It's more like we went because we were going towards the coast to take pictures. We also took a tour with the Argosy Tours and was able to get a nice shot (📸) of the sculpture there too. For us it was 100% more about the convenience than seeing the actual sculpture. And it struck us as odd that there is another red sculpture very close to the Space Needle which isn't the same but very similar. It was a pretty close walk to here from the Seattle Center and that's one reason why we came out here.

Absolutely incredible performance! A few things to note before I get into the fun stuff 1. We purchased our tickets online from The Mirage yet we weren't sent e-tickets and no QR code either. This meant that we had to wait in the long will call line. They moved surprisingly quickly so that was nice. 2. There are strobe lights so people sensitive to flashing lights beware. Now to the great parts... The show carries from the very beginning. You do not feel time pass at all. It was absolutely incredible. You will find yourself bouncing in your seat singing along and enjoying every minute.

This place is so beautiful! After a 9 day cross country road trip in the middle of a global pandemic, this is exactly what we needed. Florida is crazy compared to the other states in terms of taking care of yourself with COVID but there were empty parts to the beach... It's getting to the beach that's tricky.

The sky was beautiful and we saw a perfect sunset. The waves and color of the ocean looked almost fake and we definitely got a few "postcard" shots. The pier is beautiful, and so peaceful. We had a great time at this beach and we're so happy we stopped here!

I am in absolute love! We knew they were around where we'd be driving on Route 66 but literally saw it randomly on the side of the road. The color was absolutely breathtaking, teal is my absolute favorite color and I CANNOT wait to print that picture out. It is such a beautiful sight in the middle of the desert! It goes on for miles and miles! Word to the wise, do not drone here! A gentleman came by while we were taking pictures and my husband's drone was resting on the ground. He told us that we couldn't be so close and that droning isn't allowed.

Really cool state park that's not too far from Vegas. Pack shorts, wear sunscreen, and bring plenty of water. Their is a visitor center but we didn't go. Most of it was worth checking out, I don't recommend the petrified logs... They're logs protected by a fence but not anything note worthy. It's nice that you drive through the park because you get short spurts of a/c and it's not as exhausting on the body. I'd bring a change of clothes, face wipes, towels, water, Gatorade, sunglasses, and a cap. Photographers 📷 lots of cool spots, worth the drive

For two and a half years, friends and coworkers told me I had to see Joshua Tree. So when I planned a cross country road trip for the summer and heard they had reopened from COVID, I knew I had to add it as a stop. It's beautiful, to be sure. The trees are so unique and beautiful. Watching the sunset there was amazing. All in all though, I'd say that Joshua Tree is hyped up. I think people see it as a cool spot to take Instagram pictures or to "rough it" but my opinion is that it's overrated. If you can, stop here, if not, no worries.

Definitely #1 place to take pictures of the sunset in the Los Angeles area. Biggest downside for any photographers out there is that it's really, really busy. There were so many photographers and models! Move quickly and be considerate. High tide makes it so you could get "stuck" on one side of the beach so keep that in mind. Great sunset shots and great moon shots too! Parking is paid, and really busy but the earlier (or significantly) later you go, the better

Beautiful park! Great views! Free parking, pretty easy hike (depending on the time of course) and great views! Absolutely amazing sunset, view of downtown LA (great skyline shot) and if you go when the moon is full, great view of the moon. Not busy at all especially when compared to other "photo spots" We didn't go all the way up, but plenty of people told us it was worth the extra 5 min. Really easy place to set up a tripod, great for time lapses and droning.

This is a photographer's playground, lots of fun backgrounds and scenery. Great framing and lighting all around the park.

The first time I went it was pretty empty (mainly just other photographers) and those that were in the park were masked but the next time I went there were a lot more people, a lot more families on the playground and walking about, none were masked or practicing social distancing.

Google says it's closed but it was open to walk around.

Great statue, close to a lot of tourist hot spots and great restaurants so you're not going out of your way. It's best to go during the day, or towards sunset. At night, there's a lot of harsh lighting and it's harder to shoot the detail of it. Directly behind it is the USS Midway Museum, and that makes for a great picture. Just in front of the USS Midway Museum is a parking lot - $10 flat parking for the day. And it's a nice walk from there to the statue.

It was fun but looking back I would have spent my time elsewhere. If you're going to go and want to see the Infinity Room, you have to go first thing in the morning. If you don't go to the Infinity Room you could do the whole place in an hour. And you should get tickets online because the line in the middle of the day is ridiculous. It's really close to The Last Bookstore and the OUE so you can cross a lot off your list the same day.

Amazing! So cool to see from the outside and even cooler to see from the inside. It's definitely worth it to go inside. Walking around is so surreal. Seeing the old language written on the wall, or the turns and tunnels from one section to another is amazing to see in person. And if you go all the way to the top there is an amazing view and you can even watch them shoot bread out of the canon.

Excellent stop for tourists. The Santa Monica is a great "quick" stop for visitors. Excellent views of the beach and great souvenir shops. The Pacific Wheel gives you stunning views of the beach, the pier and the ocean. If you walk all the way to the end of the pier, the breeze is absolutely delightful and there's a very good chance you might see a sea lion.

Great place to shoot 📸 a little hard to find but if you stumble upon the merry go round it's the trail just behind there. Lots of little nooks and crannies and a nice walk down with a great view. A surprising amount of people were there, mostly photographers and models. And it's easy to manage your way through the little caves and stairwells.

Went here to shoot some pictures a few years back - after hiking in California I can say this place really shows what Florida can offer in terms of natural beauty and the merge of nature and photography. This isn't the best example of that but it's definitely up there. Especially because of the opportunity for shade and rest in between.

The Bean! You have to go here! It's a must do on your list for Chicago. Very cliché but still very worth it. It gets packed really quickly so I'd go early or around sunset. It's an easy walk from other hot spots so it's very convenient. We got really cool shots from "under" the bean too. It was nice to check it off of our list

Photographers beware - the parking lot does not open until 9 am so if you're looking for a sunrise shot, plan accordingly. Also, take a look at your tides because it makes a world of a difference. The natural erosion and rocks are beautiful and the way the waves hit the rocks is amazing.

Very interesting place, a little too close to a not so great area but it was okay during the day. It's very much a world unto itself, and has a very genuine vibe. Authentic merchandise from overseas and that is very obvious. A lot of card shops and funko pop stores.

We went at the recommendation of my brother who's in architecture school. It was so much fun to take pictures here. The swings are so much fun and overseeing the water/bridge is so relaxing. It's a nice walk to Bayside too so it's nice to make a day of it

Incredibly clean! (Classic Boca - but much appreciated) this is definitely a much quieter area compared to the palmetto entrance, but parking is substantially more limited. There's definitely nothing like a Florida beach!

Pearl Harbor, a #1 priority for us.

A very emotional day, our Missouri tour guide was awesome. He said... reflect that you are about to go up the stairs as did the Japanese when they surrendered, 1st time Japan had to do such a thing... imagine you are going up the stairs to where General McArthur awaits for events to unfold... many boats, filled with reporters / cameras are taking photos...

On 12-07-1941, troops serving the US fleet at Pearl Harbor began a calm Sunday morning unaware that Japanese bombers were headed toward America's most important Pacific base. There, like a string of pearls draped across the docks and waterfront, was the majority of the US's naval might.

The devastating Japanese onslaught began at 7:48 AM, killing 2,402 Americans and wounding many others, sinking four battleships, and damaging military airfields.

The Pearl Harbor attack spurred America into WW II.

Aboard this ship... the surrender of Japan is signed!

As we approached the battleship, we noticed the statue of Chester William Nimitz, who lived from 02-24-1885 through 02-20-1966, playing a major role during WWII as Commander in Chief Pacific Fleet – Allied air, land, sea and the leading authority on submarines, overseeing the conversion from gasoline to diesel, acquiring approval to build the world’s first nuclear powered submarine, the USS Nautilus.

10 days after the attack on Pearl Harbor, Nimitz was selected by President Franklin D. Roosevelt to be commander in chief US Pacific Fleet, promoted to admiral, immediately departing to Hawaii taking command on the top deck of the submarine Grayling because every battleship in Pearl Harbor had been either sunk or damaged during the attack. On 12-14-1944, by an Act of Congress, Nimitz is appointed to the highest rank in the Navy: Fleet Admiral, Nimitz signed as the representative for the USA when Japan formally surrendered.

Our tour guide welcomed us aboard the Mighty Mo!

A new experience for us, Battleship Missouri was filled with details we did not know, the Mighty Mo retains all of the physical characteristics of her service.

We were told to look out for ‘knee knockers’ ‘head bangers’ to always face a ladder when we descend or ascend and to never lean on, or over the life lines surrounding the perimeter of the main deck.

The length of the ship is 887 feet 3 inches”; Beam 108 feet 2 inches; Draft 38 feet and its height 216 feet 6 inches. Its displacement is 58,000 tons fully loaded and 45,000 tons unloaded.

It achieves a speed of 32 knots, and we now know that a nautical knot equals 1.15078 miles on shore, so the ship can travel at approximately 37 miles per hour.

The Missouri was built in New York Naval Shipyard, Brooklyn, New York. The keel was laid on 01-06-1941 and launched on 01-29-1944, commissioned on 06-11-1944, decommissioned 02-26-1955, recommissioned on 05-10-1986.

Its main gun battery: Nine 16” / 50 caliber with a range of 23 miles
Secondary gun battery: Twelve 5” / 38 caliber with a range of 9 miles
Air Defense: 4 Vulcan Phalanx weapons system

Missiles: 32 Tamahawk Anti-Surface Missiles / Land Attack Missiles – 16 Harpoon Anti-Surface Missiles

Final Decommission: 03-31-1992

One interesting face we had never heard of is that on 11 April, 1945, a low-flying kamikaze Zero, although fired upon, crashed on Missouri's starboard side, just below her main deck level.

The remains of the pilot were recovered on board the ship just aft of one of the 40 mm gun tubs. Crewmen wanted to hose the remains over the side, but Captain Callaghan decided the young Japanese pilot had done his job to the best of his ability, and with honor, so he should be given a military funeral. The next day,

04-12-1945 he was buried at sea with military honors, wrapped in the Japanese flag.

The world doesn’t get to know of this honorable act because everyone concentrated on the main news of the day, the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt who dies on that day in Warm Springs, California.

Live and learn!

Our last photo was taken from a helicopter ride, Blue Hawaiian Helicopters!

Few national cemeteries compete with the dramatic natural setting of the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. Known as Punchbowl, or Hill of Sacrifice, it formed some 75,000 to 100,000 years ago during the Honolulu period of secondary volcanic activity.

A crater resulted from the ejection of hot lava through cracks in the old coral reefs which, at the time, extended to the foot of the Koolau Mountain Range

The name Hill of Sacrifice relates to the history of the crater, first used as an altar where Hawaiians offered human sacrifices to pagan gods and the killed violators of the many taboos.

During the reign of Kamehameha the Great, a battery of two cannons was mounted at the rim of the crater to salute distinguished arrivals and signify important occasions.

In the 1880s, leasehold land on the slopes of the Punchbowl opened for settlement and in the 1930s, the crater was used as a rifle range for the Hawaii National Guard.

Toward the end of World War II, tunnels were dug through the rim of the crater for the placement of shore batteries to guard Honolulu Harbor and the south edge of Pearl Harbor.

During the late 1890s, a committee recommended that the Punchbowl become the site for a new cemetery for the growing population of Honolulu, idea rejected for fear of polluting the water supply and the emotional aversion to creating a city of the dead above a city of the living. 50 years later, Congress authorized to establish a national cemetery in Honolulu with two provisions: the location be acceptable to the War Department, and the site be donated rather than purchased.

In 1943, the governor of Hawaii offered the Punchbowl for this purpose. The $50,000 appropriation proved insufficient, deferring the project until after World War II. By 1947, Congress and veteran organizations pressured the military to find a permanent burial site in Hawaii for the remains of thousands of World War II servicemen on the island of Guam awaiting permanent burial.

The Army planned for Punchbowl cemetery; in February 1948 Congress approved funding and construction began. Prior to the opening of the cemetery for the recently deceased, the remains of soldiers from locations around the Pacific Theater-including Wake Island and Japanese POW camps-were transported to Hawaii for final interment, first interment on 01-04-1949, opened to the public on 07-19-1949, with services for five war dead: an unknown serviceman, two Marines, an Army lieutenant and one civilian-noted war correspondent Ernie Pyle.

The National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific memorial pathway, lined with a variety of memorials to honor America's veterans from various organizations. As of 2005, there were 63 such memorials to commemorate soldiers of 20th-century wars, including those killed at Pearl Harbor.

Highly recommend a visit, reflect and honor those who have sacrificed their lives for our right to live our lives in freedom!

Our visit to Pearl Harbor was best in class. We learned so much about the struggle, the courage, the determination of all participants in World War II.

Our visit to the USS Bowfin Submarine Museum & Park was unique as I had never been inside a submarine before.

It was launched at Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, Maine on 12-07-1942 exactly one year after the Pearl Harbor attack.

Due to this historic coincidence, and in hopes of future success against the enemy, she was appropriately dubbed the "Pearl Harbor Avenger."
Bowfin was christened by Mrs. Jane Gawne, wife of Captain James Orville Gawne who was head of the Portsmouth Navy Yard.

USS Bowfin takes her name from the hard fighting, aggressive, and voracious fish found in fresh water from the Great Lakes down the Mississippi River, and as far south as the Gulf of Mexico.

As the last survivor of the family Amiidae, which dates back to the Jurassic Period, this living fossil is at home in backwaters and marshy areas.

Due to its primitive lung, it thrives in water with low oxygen content, and can survive for days at a time in little or no water. A more appropriate name could not have been found for an air-breathing diesel boat, this one soon to be legendary in the submarine force for her bold determination and insatiable appetite for enemy shipping.

As we walked about, the tight spaces, the concise use of every inch, the sleeping quarters... and the bathroom facilities are incredible.

Bowfin was reactivated because of the Navy’s need to expand the fleet to support United Nations led forces during the Korean War, the submarine was recommissioned on 07-27-1951 and, following shakedown training, sailed for the Pacific.

After arriving at San Diego, California, on 6 October, she worked from that port for the next two years, devoting her time to training operations and local exercises.

The nominal ending of hostilities in Korea in the summer of 1953 reduced the Navy’s need for active submarines and prompted Bowfin’s second inactivation. She arrived at San Francisco on 8 October 1953, and was placed out of commission, in reserve, at the Mare Island Naval Shipyard on 04-22-1954. The warship remained there until moving to Seattle, Washington, on

05-01-1960 to replace Puffer – SS268 as the Naval Reserve training submarine there and to begin a little over a decade’s service. Her name was finally struck from the Navy list on 12-01-1971, and she was taken back to Pearl Harbor, to serve as a memorial.

One of the photos shared features Kaiten, a one man Japanese suicide torpedo... Imagine piloting toward death!

With the mission to be a vibrant resource, strengthening a diverse community by educating present and future generations in the evolving Japanese American experience in Hawai‘i, the Japanese Cultural Center of Hawaii does an incredible job at accomplishing its goals.

Japanese in Hawaii are the 2nd largest ethnic group.

In 1920, they constituted 43% of Hawaii's population. Now about 16.7% of the islands' population - 2000 US Census, which separately categorizes mixed-race individuals, so the proportion of people with some Japanese ancestry is likely much larger

The greatest challenge for the Japanese in Hawaii came in 1941 with the bombing of Pearl Harbor. All Japanese -aliens as well as citizens- were suspect.

Community leaders were detained and sent to internment camps.

However, many continued to demonstrate their loyalty to the United States by joining the military or by supporting the war effort at home.

To demonstrate loyalty, many Japanese removed the Emperor’s photo which most used to display in their homes, removing family photos and artifacts that reminded them of home.

They were caught between a rock and a hard place because they too were attacked by the Japanese, as they lived in Hawaii and had made it home

We are rather interested in all things Japan so we chose to visit the Japanese Cultural Center of Hawaii. The Tokioka Heritage Resource Center honors Japanese heritage, embracing their diversity.

The collection is impressive, about 5,500 books in English and Japanese, including archival collections, oral history, transcripts and historical photos.

Manager and volunteers are available to help visitors, offering commercial translation, genealogical research and Japanese name consultant services.

We learned much about the story of the Japanese in Hawaii, from the first group who arrived in 1868 to work the sugar cane fields. Like most emigrants, Japanese left familiar environments for an unknown land across the ocean that was advertised to them as paradise yet encountering harsh conditions, long and arduous hours of work, plantation life that provided homes in camps, segregated by race.

The Japanese women not only labored in the fields but also cooked, washed and cared for their children.
.
Visit, it is worth every penny of the small entrance fee!

The oldest Catholic parish in the state of Florida and the oldest in the Archdiocese of Miami, property in the historic district on the National Register of Historic places. It was established by Spanish Jesuits in 1566, abandoned in 1572 when the missionaries were recalled to Mexico but they returned to Cuba in 1724.

In 1743, two Italian Jesuits from Havana opened a mission chapel on Key West for attendance by natives. Reverend John F. Kirby was sent by Bishop Francis X. Gartland of the Diocese of Savannah to Key West in 1851 and established St. Mary Star of the Sea parish in 1851.

The first permanent Catholic Church on Key West was dedicate don February 26th, 1852, on the corner of Duval and Eaton Streets. It was the 5th Catholic parish established in the State of Florida and the first parish in South Florida.

It is said that when visiting a new town, we should always enter a Catholic Church because we get to see society as it gathers to honor faith.

On Sunday, June 14th, 2015, we entered as people left one Mass and another was about to start, meeting and greeting those we came in contact with.

We arrived as one Mass was ending and another was in the works.

We sat for a while, prayed and left. As we go through the door, the most enchanting family is arriving, they have dressed their little boy with a white suit and I could not help but tell him he was gorgeous and the little kid stopped, we asked for permission and photographed him.

What is simply remarkable is that we went for breakfast and driving back they were leaving the Church, so we opened the window and called him and he starts running toward the car!

Highly recommend stopping and saying your prayers at this enchanting house of worship!

For years, the beach at the tip end of Key Biscayne has been a favorite of ours. In Spanish we call it El Farito, but the real name is Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park.

Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park is the home of this historic lighthouse which was built in 1825 and reconstructed in 1846.

The lighthouse is the oldest standing structure in Miami-Dade County.

This beach is ideal for sunbathing, swimming and to go for a picnic on more than one mile of sandy Atlantic beachfront.

The waters are crystal clear, providing a great opportunity for a long swim. The park has been renovated, offering two restaurants, many pavilions for family gatherings and interspersed tables for those who bring coolers.

There are rental for umbrellas, bikes, and all sort of water sports equipment.

Biking and kayaking are popular activities. Anglers can throw in their lines from the seawall along Biscayne Bay for some of the best shoreline fishing in the region.

Guided tours of the lighthouse and lighthouse keeper's cottage are given twice daily, Thursdays through Mondays. Two restaurants, Lighthouse Café and Boater's Grill, offer authentic Cuban cuisine, or picnickers can reserve a pavilion and fire up their own grill. Bicycles, beach chairs, and umbrellas can be rented.

Overnight boat camping is allowed in No Name Harbor.

Without a doubt, visit Cape Florida Lighthouse, as our pictures demonstrate, the views from up there are simply gorgeous as you enjoy -on a clear day- seeing Down Town Miami or the hotels on Key Biscayne.

The Philip and Patricia Frost Museum of Science has become a favorite place for us to visit.

The Museum of Science strives to share the power of science, delighting audiences with special exhibits, the Brain for example became a favorite of ours as we studied the powerful gift each human possesses, billion neuron connections that have achieved the transformation of Planet Earth into s wonder of history and art.

Located in Downtown Miami, the Museum is divided into 4 buildings, the Frost Planetarium, Aquarium and North and West Wings. We have the opportunity to learn about the living and solar system, the universe as we travel through the videos offered at the Planetarium, the physics of flight, light and lasers, the biology of the human body and mind... and so much more...

We have explored all that it offers several times, we are annual members and are allowed to take a guest with us, which has afforded us the opportunity to take relatives, kids and visitors to South Florida, making sure everyone becomes familiar with this great addition to what South Florida offers.

Frost Science is dedicated to education, offering summer camp so children find fun / educational activities for summer vacation.

The mission of the Frost Science is to inspire and connect people of all ages and backgrounds to enjoy science and technology, creating a better understanding of ourselves and our world and they exceed on expectations.

Without a doubt, don't miss visiting the Philip and Patricia Frost Museum of Science!!!
likes: Variety of topics (living, solar system, universe, physics, biology)

reviews_attraction.text:
We love history and St. Augustine, Florida is its cradle.

We visited Castillo de San Marcos, where the U.S. government relocated Native Americans from the plains and the southwest to St. Augustine’s 17th-century Spanish fortress.

Previously known as Fort Marion (as Castillo de San Marcos was called at that time) it served as temporary housing for Plains Indian men and women and some lived in tents atop the fort.

The first group — 76 plains Indians, Cheyenne, Kiowa, Comanche and Arapaho — came in the late 1870. With the Medicine Lodge Treaties of 1867, the horse tribes of the southern plains had agreed to live on reservations and stop their warrior ways.

Boredom with life on a reservation made them depressed and vulnerable to whisky peddlers.

In 1874, Cheyenne, Kiowa, Comanche, and Arapaho young men retaliated and rebelled against the reservation situation.

One by one, the chiefs surrendered to the U.S. Army. Herman J. Viola in “Warrior Artists” noted that the U.S. government was determined to prevent future such trouble.

The government “drafted a tough new policy designed to break the fighting spirit once and for all,” wrote Viola. They would be imprisoned half a continent away. This first group left St. Augustine in 1878.

If you have the chance visit St. Augustine as most places are excellent opportunities to learn about history.

The USS Arizona Memorial is #1 visitor destination in Hawaii. Millions of people from all over the world come to this majestic setting to see for themselves where World War II began for the United States on December 7, 1941.

Devastation & Hope

Imperial Japan won the battle but lost the war, devastating Pearl Harbor Naval Base, attacked by torpedo and bomber planes on 12-07-1941
@ 7:55 AM. The sneak attack attack sparked outrage in the American populace, news media, government and the world.

WWII Valor in the Pacific National Monument is located in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, 3,000 miles from the W. Coast of America and 4,000 miles from Japan, Pearl Harbor WWII Valor in the Pacific National Monument consists of 9 historic locations in 3 of the westernmost United States - California, Alaska, and Hawaii.

Of these, five are located within Pearl Harbor itself: the USS Arizona Memorial, the USS Oklahoma Memorial, the USS Utah Memorial, and parts of Ford Island and Battleship Row.

Access to the USS Arizona Memorial is suspended to address the structural integrity of the facility. Park staff and specialists are hard at work to restore the Memorial and allow visitors to honor the brave.

Highly recommend visiting!

John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park, first undersea park in the US, encompasses 70 nautical square miles. While the mangrove swamps and tropical hammocks in the park's upland areas offer a unique experience, it is the coral reefs and associated marine life that bring most visitors to the park. A glass bottom boat tour, scuba or snorkeling provide a closer look. Canoeing and kayaking are popular activities; fishing is permitted in designated areas. Walking on short trails, picnicking, or swimming at the beach. The Visitor Center has a 30,000-gallon saltwater aquarium and nature videos. Full-facility and Youth/Group campsites are available. Beach wheelchairs are available without cost.
The park is named after John D. Pennekamp, a Miami newspaper editor, whose efforts contributed to the establishments of Everglades National Park and the preservation of what would become John Pennekamp Coral Reef State Park.
We loved the tropical vegetation, we took photos of birds and marine life, admiring the mangrove swamps and tropical hammocks. We had a rather unique and interesting experience. The coral reef is simply gorgeous!

While visiting Las Vegas, at a NAPA conference held in the beautiful Mandalay Bay, we discovered the Shark Reef Aquarium and could not resist.

The displays are awesome, the tunnel that allows us to walk through the tank, a unique experience.

The Aquarium is not what we usually find at other aquariums.

It provides discovery through the senses as we are allowed to become part of an undersea ocean fantasy.

The Shark Reef Aquarium features dangerous and unusual aquatic animals from the world's tropical waters, taking visitors on a journey through an ancient temple slowly being claimed by the sea.

One of the exhibits holds 1.3 million gallon shipwreck where visitors experience an almost 360-degree view of sharks and fish, through an acrylic tunnel.

There was a spot where many congregated as guests are able to touch sharks, rays and horseshoe crabs.

We loved the experience and highly recommend stopping by to see it!

Hopi House is a gift store and art gallery. Built of native stone in a series of ascending terraces, this Mary E. J. Colter designed structure emulates original Hopi dwellings. It was intended to be a showplace for Native American handicrafts, a purpose which is still embraces.

Inside the dramatic building is a wide array of handmade goods, including rugs, pottery, jewelry, kachina dolls, sand paintings and the like.

The high quality is reflected in the prices, and the second floor offers visitors the opportunity to browse through even more spectacular objects.

The famous photography of Albert Einstein at the Grand Canyon was taken outside of the Hopi House.

Throughout the summer, Hopi and Navajo dancers demonstrate their skill on the stage in front of Hopi House.

We bought embroidered shirts, a treasure to remember this great adventure.

Almost immediately after the U.S. Navy established a base in Key West in 1823, the need for a lighthouse became evident.  Erecting a lighthouse was essential in assuring the safe arrival of both military and commercial vessels navigating the shallow, reef-laden waters off the Florida Keys
The current lighthouse opened in 1848 with a woman as its Keeper; nearly unheard of during the 19th century.  In the years following, the Key West Lighthouse underwent a number of upgrades including the installation of a Third Order Fresnel Lens, an extension to the tower which allowed the light to be seen from a greater distance, the addition of Keeper’s Quarters, and finally the electrification of the light.
If in the area, visit the Lighthouse and enjoy walking through history.

During our tour of Honolulu, we stopped at the Diamond Head (Lē‘ahi) lookout, on the eastern edge of Waikiki’s coastline.

Diamond Head is known for its historic hiking trail, stunning coastal views, and military history, the Monument is on 475 acres, including the interior and outer slopes of the crater.

A broad, saucer-shaped crater formed 300,000 years ago during a single, explosive eruption that sent ash and fine particles in the air.

Materials settled, cemented together into a rock called tuff, creating the crater, visible from the trail in the park.

From the lookout we could see all Honolulu, Waikiki Diamond Head and the gorgeous beach below...

Don't miss it, worth every second you get to spend there!

Mary Elizabeth Jane Colter was born on April 4th, 1869 and lived until January 8th, 1958, an American architect and designer, born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

As a child, Colter traveled with her family through frontier Minnesota, Colorado and Texas in the years after the American Civil War. After her father died in 1886, Colter attended the California School of Design in San Francisco -now the San Francisco Art Institute.

In 1901, the Fred Harvey Company offer her the job of decorating the Alvarado Hotel in Albuquerque, she began working full-time 1910, moving from interior designer to architect.

Who could believe that the State of Florida has a Caverns State Park?

Anyone who lives in Florida, flat land for the most part where six feet under there is water can't fathom the discovery of caverns.

And yet... there they are, the park's bluffs, springs and caves are referred to as karst terrain, and the caves provide habitat for the blind cave crayfish, cave salamanders and three species of cave roosting bats.

The land that comprises a large part of Florida Caverns State Park was acquired on October 11, 1935. We enjoyed our visit.

When you think you have seen it all, then something surprises you.

During our night tour of Las Vegas, we heard about the WATER DANCING concert at Fountains of Bellagio and wanted to see it.

What a delightful performance of dancing waters that make formation after formation by the rise and fall of water that depending on the lights hitting the fountain, achieve a mesmerizing rainbow of colors that delight visitors.

Without a doubt, make the time to see the magic unfold!

Trains, we love trains! We have traveled on Amtrak, Metrorail, and Tri-Rail. We have traveled throughout Europe, and trains provide comfort, space, an ability to read, play games, and view the world as it goes by. The Gold Coast Railroad Museum offers visitors an ability to witness how trains have evolved, how Presidents travel, all that is possible by traveling on a train. Highly recommend that you visit, take your camera!

During our visit to Hawaii, we had the opportunity to visit the Ali'iolani Hale, today the home of the State of Hawaii Supreme Court and where the statue of Kamehameha, the Great is proudly displayed.

Kamehameha is the person who achieved the union of the Hawaiian Islands and his story, or legend, is simply fascinating.

Highly recommend visiting Hawaii and learning all about it!

Royal Oaks Park is excellent, offering residents the ability to play games, enjoy the outdoors, and go outside for a pick-nick. The Roberto Alonso Community Center is located there, a place where many Town of Miami Lakes functions take place, to the enjoyment of all but in particular the Seniors of Miami Lakes. Our taxes at play!

From weddings, to concerts, to lectures, this Church is in an ideal location for grand display of excellence. With the Biltmore Hotel in front, the setting is ideal for gorgeous photography.

We have attended concerts and the acoustics are awesome.

Highly recommend visiting!

We took a helicopter tour to the Grand Canyon, flying over the picturesque and amazing views, landing and taking a bus to tour some more and go to the lookout where we ate, had refreshment, and admired the beauty of our surroundings.

Grand Canyon West is magnificent.

While walking through the shoreline we encountered the public art, Makua and Kila, a surfer and a seal, on Kuhio Beach, Honolulu...

Absolutely gorgeous, very appropriate... Highly recommend visiting!
A favorite of ours is attending the Irish Festival and Parade, which ends at this park. Tents, Vendors, Concerts, great music and food, the Irish Parade is a unique experience no one should miss!
At least once every year, we travel to Key Biscayne and visit the Seaquarium. The experience is unique and we highly recommend this attraction.

As parks go, this is an average one. The lake is nice, but the land amenities around it are lacking. The area is huge and there are small recreation areas around the lake. There are great places for fishing and recreational boating. There are various areas with lake access for swimming and shelters. All of this is nice.

However, to have as much land around this lake as they do and have no more camping options than they have is just sad. It's a poor use of space, in my opinion. There are ample places for them to set up options for backcountry camping. The Mountain to Sea trail runs right through here, and the only real camping options are paid camping spots in the state park. There should be a more extensive trail system with options for primitive camping.

In short, great for a family picnic. Nothing  more than average for the serious outdoorsman.

Love this trail! For what it is, it's a great location.

Do keep in mind, this is essentially just a greenspace carved out in the northern part of the Houston area inside the loop. But, its paved trails are a great place to unwind after a day's work on on the weekend. Great biking, and since it's flat, it doesn't require skill. It's also good for a family stroll.

Along the way you run across some great views of the skyline and pass places to eat or relax. There are several parks and picnic spots along the way too, so you can stop off for a break or pick out a place to drop a blanket and hang out for a while.

I was really surprised by this place. After all, it is an old landfill.

Great views of the surrounding area. It's the highest point in any direction for a long way. Makes for a great walk to the top on a pretty day. There are picnic tables and den he's up top.

It wouldn't call it hiking, if that is what you're looking for. It's a gravel trail up to the top of a manicured grass hill. But, it's a real big hill.

There are also pavilions and other things scattered throughout the park. It's a neat place.

One of the better state parks in NC. In my estimation, NC's state park system is lacking... at least in the eastern part of the state around Raleigh. This one is an exception. There are still not really options for backcountry camping like you'd find in this kind of state park in other states.

Do make it to the top of hanging rock, though. It's a great view and fun place to sting up a hammock and feel like you're on the edge of the world.

A fun little stop off in downtown Houston. It's small, but has some great seating and several restaurants with grab and go style food.

Pro tip: On Sundays parking is free in downtown. On a nice day, you can swing over to Market Square, grab some Niko Niko's from the kiosk or a couple of slices of pizza from Frank's right down the street and enjoy a picnic outside. Great place for a lazy Sunday afternoon.

This was worth the drive, especially when done in concert with Sunset Crater. The two together have a $20 day pass (for the whole car), and you can drive a 35ish mile loop through some amazing scenery.

The Pueblos at the national monument itself are decent, but I did not feel that Wupatki itself is the highlight of this trip. It's the whole day taken together that makes it exceptional.

This is a great spot, tucked away in North Durham. It is actually a city park, but has miles of good hiking (at least, for this area) along a nice stream. There are swimming holes, places to kayak, and even a working grist mill where you can buy fresh ground grits. Picnic areas are tucked away all over the place.

No overnight options here, but a great day-use space.

Trail is good. The summit is over-domesticated... But most are these days. Overall though, the trails in the park are still rustic.

When you get to the top, there is a gift store right before the last bit of summit. On a cold day, stop at the little concession bar there and get a hot cider. It's powdered stuff... But it feels like heaven after a cold hike.

Nice visitor center, but not many amenities otherwise.

The trails are oddly placed, and the maps available in the visitor center do not seem to be accurate. We walked this place all day looking for stuff that didn't seem to exist.

Nevertheless, the area is nice and there are a couple of overlooks that are worth the hike.

Great park tucks away right in the middle of North Raleigh. Good for biking, walking, picnicking, and tossing a frisbee.

It's rather domesticated, so don't expect a place to build a fire or camp. And the "trails" are pretty much paved walkways.

Nice lake though, pretty place to enjoy the day.

Probably the best state park within a halfway quick drive of Houston. I always enjoy being down here. The scenery is about as good as you can get in this part of the state. Trails are copious. Camping is a good option here. Great place for the kids. Just remember there are gators everywhere.

This is easily one of the nicest parks in Houston. It's a great place to bring small children, and it's a great place for adults. Plenty of seating and shaded areas. Several restaurants in the park, and many more options nearby. Great place to lay out a picnic or a blanket as well.

Odd little place out in there middle of nowhere, but it is a really neat museum for the kids... Or if you like rocks.

If your driving through the area, it's a fun distraction for a little while. Some pretty thorough exhibits inside on minerals and basic geologic info on NC.

A neat little oasis in the middle of the downtown. Great for getting outside if you find yourself working around the convention center and need some air. Lots of things going on there all the time, it seems. And, I believe most of the events that happen there are free.

It's a challenge to get to, but worth the visit for the privacy alone. If you e got a small boat, or a big one, you can scoot over to this island reserve and avoid the throngs on the beach just to the north. Great place for birding or fishing in a kayak.

Great little park tucked away in Raleigh. Many wonderful things in such a small place.

Pecan groves, and grapevines, and many other little secrets here. I picked a bag full of pecans for the holiday season this year.

Perhaps the best view of the valley and Phoenix around. It's high and on a clear day, you can see the whole valley and surrounding mountains.

You can drive all the way to the top too, so it's really for everyone.
An interesting place. A tiny amusement park. Free to walk around, and several restaurants. Could make a fun day trip from Houston if you're in the area for the weekend. Some decent looking rides.
For what it is, it's a decent little space. Not much shade, but there is a great picnic pavilion and tennis courts. Also some children's play equipment and half court basketball.
Pretty neat experience. The cisterns are a great piece of Houston history. The art exhibit in them currently is wonderful. It's pretty pricey, but we were glad we went.
Great park. Very large. Lots of places to picnic and walk. Great place to spend an afternoon, grill out, play some volleyball or softball. Walkers and joggers galore.
Very pretty area, but there were people everywhere. Lots of shops and restaurants on the walk. Felt more like a shopping mall than a historic district.
This place is remarkable. A free at museum that is top notch in every regard. I would highly encourage you to come here and bring someone with you.
It's smaller than you would expect, but it is very well maintained, and the site does well to communicate the rich history of the Alamo.
Great little pocket park for a picnic or to let the kids play on a playground. It was recently renovated and expanded.

This is the first river camp on the Suwannee, 12 miles from the Hwy 41 boat ramp in White Springs, or 9 miles from Stephen Foster. The 5 sleeping shelters are exactly like their counterparts at the other camps, perfect for overnight paddling. The bathrooms are even nicer than at the other camps, it's above flood plain and so is on a slab instead of moveable. The communal covered picnic table area is comfortable.

The most developed of the springs along this section of the Suwannee, the spring itself is beautiful. The last time we visited, cave divers were emerging from the crystal clear water. The area surrounding the spring is tiered with walkways, which comes in handy with the varying levels of the river. There are times when the entire area is underwater, and less interesting to play in.
dislikes: Less interesting for play when submerged

reviews_attraction.text: Island Acres is next to I-70, so there is background noise. But the trains across the river add a pleasant counterpoint without any crossings that require their obnoxious horns. The sites are pretty level, power is nice, the water is drinkable. All in all, quite pleasant, except that the gravel bike path is way too short. All activities require driving, unfortunately.

There are two campgrounds, Hasty below the dam with trees and electricity and water and coin showers, and the Point on the high ground with just fire rings and picnic tables. We stayed at Point and loved it! The lake view is lovely, sunset divine, and the site separation quite acceptable. The Wildlife Area is beside the Point CG, which is a great Gravel bike ride.

Nice sized sites, bathrooms have flush toilets and showers, lots of greenery, site numbers are spray painted on the ground. It's good the sites are roomy because finding level may be a challenge, and be careful of mud. A previous camper evidently got stuck.

Definitely worth visiting, walking around, marveling and imagining the fossils in the quarry rock. You walk over fossils millions of years old, helpfully encircled by small stones. And the quarry walls are cool in themselves. A great place for reflection.

Beautiful spring on the Santa Fe River, not too crowded. A delightful trio (two guitars and a flute, and a foot with bells) brought a simple elegance to the whole scene. Great on a Monday afternoon, it might get a little crowded on a Saturday.

Easy walk, gentle half mile descent to beautiful views of this iconic riverbend. The upgrades of the past few years really make the main view much safer, a railing lets you get right up to the edge in relative safety.

Suwanee Bicycle Association maintains great a great trail through Big Shoals, from Mossy Ravine to the Palmetto Trail and Long Branch, all connected by double track. All along the Suwanee River, some beautiful views!

A wonderful little state park. Go around low tide, and after a great hike through the woods you return along the beach. At high tide you will get your feet wet on the beach! At all times, seashore nature at its best.

Wonderful hiking trail along a river. The boardwalk kept us out of the mud and water, unfortunately the parts that weren't boardwalked were under water deeper than our shoes. The paddling from Louie's was great fun!

Lovely walks through the fields and woods. The Walk in Time is well conceived and implemented. And the barn contains many artifacts that give you further appreciation of the historical significance of the island.

Mountain biking, paddling, and lots of nature. The River campsites are far enough away from US 1 and the quiet is blissful. A great place to enjoy central Florida away from the over-developed surroundings.
Good signage directed us to the parking lot, and we had no problem parking our 24' van, and later turning around after our ride. It's dirt, but we'll graded, with no potholes or even any mud.
The Summer views are shades of green, not the panoply of colors in the Fall, but it is still impressive. The mountains roll across the horizon, and the trails are challenging.
An wonderful architecturally significant old theatre, with some incredible documents, it also is currently hosting an impressive art show celebrating the first amendment.
Camping in the woods, just a walk from an uncrowded beautiful beach. Plus challenging mountain bike trails, hiking trails, and don't forget the beautiful beach!
They've captured the history of the Beach and present it in an interesting fashion. Not just the little stuff, but whole buildings and a train!
A hidden gem of a zoo, a fascinating array of animals kept humanely and comfortably in relatively natural environments. A great place to enjoy!
The first river access in Florida, 2.2 miles from the Georgia line. A wonderful place to start a Florida paddle, or end a Georgia paddle!
Tennis courts, birds, community gardens, running path, Harbor Park is a nice reminder of what a wonderful community Neptune Beach is.
Easy access to the Intracoastal, and a lovely trail around the island. There are two piers for fishing and a kayak/SUP launch ramp.
A fun 7 mile mountain bike loop along the banks of the Suwannee and Withlacoochee Rivers, passing by the namesake tree.
Very impressive and well worth a stop and short walk! The Cascades really show the power of water to carve rock.
The shoals are a treat with its variety of water levels. The singletrack mountain bike trail is flowy and fun!

PRETTY COOL ! My wife organized tickets for 4 of us to look through this aviation & space museum in McMinnville, Oregon. We arrived here around 11.30am on Sunday, March 24th after driving from Portland enroute to Corvallis. My wife's son and his girlfriend who drove from Corvallis met us in the car park. Our admission price averaged out at $26 a person and we were not on any guided tour. After getting fixed up with some colored wrist bands at the cashier desk we were free to look at what we wanted. Of course the very thing I wanted to see was now filling my eyeballs completely.......the enormous Hercules 8 engined amphibious aircraft designed by the enigmatic Howard Hughes and completed in 1945. I have wanted see this amazing plane most of my life after reading articles and seeing newsreels featuring it when I was young. My thoughtful wife knew this and so we were able to fit this tour in on our way to Corvallis. The huge aircraft is simply astounding and constructed from birch wood even though it has the cruel nickname " The Spruce Goose ". We walked all around it and up a stairway to look inside. Unfortunately there is no way to venture very far into the aircraft for visitors apart from standing behind the cockpit and looking back into the huge store capacity of the fuselage. I had my photo taken by the nice museum guy looking after the info side of things inside. The rest of the tour was okay but nothing to get too excited about. We didn't stick around for lunch as the cafes didn't look very appetizing and the first one I approached the woman behind the counter said their latte machine wasn't working because they were out of the vanilla white powder to make the coffees. Whatever ! I guess unless you have paid for a guided tour you are completely on your own as no museum employees approached us at any time with information about the displays. The incredible Hercules was definitely worth seeing up close !
