Smith Rock State Park is beautiful. Tuff rock creates a canyon with the Crooked River flowing through. It is a hiker and rock-climber’s heaven. Dogs are allowed on leashes. No RV or car camping allowed but they have a hike in type camping option. There are tons of hiking trails. We walked down (0.1 mile path) “The Chute” from the RV parking lot and it lead to three main trails. Left is the river path, middle is the most difficult path called “Misery Ridge Trail”, and right is the 1.2 mile “Wolf Tree Trail.” We decided to take the path to the right with our 3 1/2 year old and 17 month old. We take them all over the place and they did well on this trail. We started early in the morning before the heat was unbearable and brought lots of water. Our 17 month old fell asleep (in the pack) on the pathway on the first hike. Towards the end of that path it did get steep for the little ones so you must use caution and have to keep them close. We saw quite a few people with hiker backpacks built to carry their infants inside. We saw some rock climbers and bikers, trails for horseback riding and many other options for adventure. Cooling off in the Crooked river was a nice refreshment and reward after a great hike on a hot summer day. The kids really enjoyed that part! We will have to come back when the kids are older to take on some more advanced trails!

This is a great tour! We got here just before they opened at 8:00 am. We signed up for their first tour which starts at 10 am. There were high wind warnings so we were notified that our tour could possibly be canceled. Kids played outside on the playground equipment prior to our tour which thankfully didn’t get canceled. The staff were friendly. Tours are $32 per adult. Kids 2 & under are complimentary. Kids are twenty something dollars. They offer a military rate. Prices are decent for what you get in the tour! The tour is approximately 2 hours long.
You walk down to the boat, boat takes you across the beautiful Lake Shasta and to the island. When you arrive on land the guides sort you into groups for each bus. The bus takes you up and around the mountain for a wild ride. Once you get up to the top where the caves are each guide gives you the safety speech and some information about the formations, etc. You get guided through the amazing caves and learn how all the formations were created, etc. it’s pretty neat! There are lots of tiny steps, and water on the floors of the caves . . . Bring some waterproof shoes, especially for the kiddos! My daughter got antsy towards the end of the tour. My 5 year old son did great!

Beautiful State Park within the Redwood trees. There are many hiking trails through the Redwood National Forest. Jedediah Smith Redwoods State Park stretches up California’s Northern Coast.
The park is populated with huge ancient trees and is a few miles inland from the Pacific Ocean. An Interesting fact is that this park contains seven percent of the old-growth redwoods left in the world.
In the 1820s a white man was exploring Northern California. His name was Jedediah Strong Smith. They decided to name the park after him (the first white man to explore the interior of Northern California).

The park was established in 1929. Family of a lumberman named Frank Stout donated money to save the redwoods. Hence, the name of the trail we explored.

I love exploring nature, getting away from everything and taking it all in but I have been spoiled by Oregon State Parks. Most of them have water and electricity plug ins. I was surprised that this park didn’t have any hookups at $35 per night. We decided to save the money on overnight parking and spend it towards a little dinner. We did come back early in the morning and explored Redwood trails.

From the trailhead fern canyon was about 0.2 miles. The trail is within walking distance of the ocean. There were plenty of open spaces to park our van because we got here really early in the morning. The road to get to the trailhead was windy and bumpy like many of the tourist destinations in the Redwood National Forest. We even drove through a stream running over the road! We weren’t sure if we could make it but then we saw a Honda Civic show us up and drove straight through it! The water was high but nobody got stuck! From the trailhead there are many trails to explore. We went into the canyon with our little explorers. We packed our almost two year old in a hiker pack and my four year old had his rain boots on. Rain boots is the way to go! My husband didn’t have waterproof shoes on so he got his tennis shoes and pants wet. Hiking up into a canyon made for a fun adventure. There were beautiful rocks in the stream- quartz rocks and all different colors. My son, being obsessed with dinosaurs found it fun that Jurassic Park shot scenes here.

This waterfall is amazing! I’ve been to many waterfalls in Oregon and this is at the top of my list of waterfalls to see in Oregon!
We visited while it was raining and had a blast! One of the roads to get to the falls were closed during our trip due to the wild weather (slide). Trees were down on the open road during our adventure but it wasn’t too hard to get to. Round trip hike is 3 miles. We take our kids on all the fun adventures and did fine. Hike down is pretty much down hill so the way back up is more difficult. It’s a really neat trail. There is a confusing point in the trail where you can choose to go towards the river or up the hill. We went along the river path and found the waterfall at the end. The bridge that goes over the river and above the waterfall is amazing. Walking over this bridge is exhilarating and will take your breath away as you glance down at the raging water flowing over the side of the hill. The bridge makes this hike magical! I highly recommend this hike! It was the perfect escape into nature!

You can reach this waterfall via the Oregon’s Niagara Falls trailhead. There are two waterfalls on the trail. The one pictured here is Pheasant Creek Falls that sprays over the footbridge you must take to access the other waterfall- Oregon’s Niagara Falls. Both waterfalls are amazing on a mid March day! The hike to the waterfall was all downhill. It took longer to go back up the hill. My five year old did great! There are some spots along the hike where you’d want to grip your child’s hand (if you bring kids). Trail was muddy since we went on a rainy March day. Lots of tree limbs, even fallen trees on the bridge shown below (just like the road driving here had tree limbs on it during this season).
Wear some good gripping hiking boots that you don’t mind getting muddy! See my review of Oregon’s Niagara Falls Trailhead to see photos of the other waterfall on the same trail!

We hiked Drift Creek Falls a few weeks ago and thought it was amazing! These two waterfalls all on one trail was pretty amazing as well!
dislikes: Fallen tree limbs on the trail

reviews_attraction.text: A short drive up the mountain from The town of Astoria will take you up to this beauty. There is a $5 parking fee. There is no additional fee to climb up to the top of the column which makes the parking fee worth it! Don’t be the crazy lady who parks at the end of the hill to avoid a parking fee! We saw a lady do that! It’s quite the walk to get to the top of the mountain! 😆 The view is amazing in itself! There’s a gift shop where you can purchase a woody paper airplane for about a dollar. You can fly your airplane off the top of the column. The climb to the top of the column is pretty crazy! My husband and I don’t have a fear of heights but when you have two kids to bring along with you, it can get pretty nerve racking when others are trying to pass you! The staircase is spiral and narrow. There are some resting platforms along the way. It’s a workout if you have some extra weight to carry! Be careful!
likes: No additional fee for column climb

reviews_attraction.text:
We went to Shasta Lake Caverns a day or two prior to this cave. Shasta caves is lead with a guide. This cave is much different. Subway Cave is an underground cave formed from Lava. You guide your own way and it’s very dark. We stopped here as it was closed and decided to check it out. Another couple was here at the same time.

We didn’t grab our flashlights and wasn’t sure how far it would go. My little ones and I didn’t want to go all the way through because it was too dark for a cell phone light so we went down and checked it out and went back the way we came. It’s just like the lava tube caves in Bend, OR.

When the gate is open there is a large parking lot available. Nice little stop.

We brought our 3 year old and baby along for the journey! The hike was pretty extreme on a hot day. We didn’t realize how many rock surfaces you would hike over and how long the hike actually was. When you are packing some extra weight with you it’s always going to be more difficult but once we reached our end goal the sight of the blue pool was amazing! The pool is such an extraordinary blue. People were jumping into the water from a high elevation. I wanted to hike over there but it was too dangerous with the kiddos. The water is also extremely cold! We found a small break off the trail to cool down. I can only imagine how breathtaking it was for all the daredevils who jumped in!

This is a really big and beautiful park. There are two children’s playgrounds. One playground area is meant for children aged 2-5 years old and the other is open to all ages. There’s a small pavilion next to it. There’s a huge pond filled with ducks and has a fountain in the center. There’s a pool area up on the hill and trails to walk along. They hold events here in the Summer. This seems to be a favorite place for dog owners. We noticed many people walking their dogs. Overall, this is a nice place to take your kids in Coos Bay.

The Wooden Shoe Tulip Farm has an annual Tulip Festival with fun for adults and kids. The event usually takes place from March until the end of April- during their full bloom. There are some free activities once you’re there. There are lots of photo boards, food carts and their own little cafe, and different activities for everyone. You can also pay additional money for your kids to jump around in the bounce house, ride around in a little tractor train ride (also fun for adults), and more. Adults can taste great wine.

We had a great time exploring this film museum and making a little film with a film scene set they had set up. We love the movie “the goonies” so seeing all kinds of props they used on the movie was pretty neat. We took a picture in front of the Goonie Truck, pictures of the mansion across the street, tried to guess movie quotes written on pieces of paper taped onto the ceiling and walls, and did some other things. Some of their film sets weren’t working so we got in for $12- kids are free.

This place was amazing for my toddler! There are lots of fun activities for the little ones. It’s hard to find fun, playful places for a three year old, but this is the perfect place for toddlers! You pay the admission and can ride all the rides as many times as you want. It’s a really neat place! There are different fairytale themed areas all over- Alice in Wonderland area, book reading places, slides, dragons, carousel, hill sliding area and much more!

We were lucky this state park was open in the winter! A couple other state parks we visited were closed on our little road trip! The only sad part about our stay was the showers were closed down due to vandalism. Somehow one of the showers out of all of them remained open so we still got a little trickling shower out of it. It is sad that people can ruin things for the rest of people! We enjoyed our stay and had hookups, no issues.

The garden area has a playground, picnic tables, & tennis court on the way up to the gardens. We were here in Spring and not a lot of blooming flowers yet. Fun area for kids, not a huge garden but Dunsmuir is such a neat little Train town along the river.

Very neat bridge. The glass bridge and beautiful structured bridge takes you over the river and through a trail to gardens. We went to the gardens during an off season (no flowers) but I’m sure it’s very aromatic and pretty when it’s filled with flowers.

We stopped at this little visitor center and explored the forts that had been rebuilt to look like the previous ones destroyed by fire. The fun part for my four year old was completing the packet for becoming a junior ranger.

Nice little hike on a nice day. The Natural bridge is where the river rushes beneath a rock formations. There are informative signs explaining how this has been formed! I won’t ruin your learning experience.
There is so much to see in this Zoo! It is enormous! There are lots of fun kid playing stations that my toddler really enjoyed! We didn’t get there early enough to see it all!
Not the biggest casino in Oregon but they are building onto the property- adding hotel rooms and other things. It’s a nice stop when you are exploring the area.
Nice little swimming hole. People there had a big group, pop up tent and picnic on the beach. Nice little stop for a dip and onto the next adventure.
These Falls are beautiful! There aren’t too many waterfalls around the coast but these are great waterfalls to hike into!

Stunning! The place is vast, beautiful, well organized and such a pleasure to visit with kids. There are several well organized sections - California, Americas, Australia, South Africa etc.  All with excellent representation of native plants. We caught magnolia blooming season and it was marvelous. It’s very easy to visit with kids - paths are stroller friendly and older kids will have plenty of activists to do - reading plaques, learning about plants, playing by the fountains and looking up fishes in the pond or exploring prehistoric gardens. Everything is nicely labeled with a lot of interesting tidbits and facts. Highly recommend coming several times a year to catch various seasonal exhibitions and blooms.
Restrooms are plenty and clean.
Parking is on the street (come early or drive around until find a spot).
Stag is very helpful and pleasant.
There are docent tours several times a day.

It’s a beautiful place. Quite a gem! Very easy to find. Parking lot is small (Alpine road) but free. It’s got restroom, area map. There are several different trail. Ridge trail/Hawkeye loop is my favorite (see map below) - about 5 miles. Elevation is minimal so it’s a fairly flat hike. Morning can be foggy which takes away from scenery but makes your hike easy and pleasant. Otherwise lots of open space, so don’t forget your hat and bring plenty of water! There are parts on Hawkeye and Ancient Oaks trails that are shaded.
No dogs allowed but horses are welcome.

An amazing place to hike. Great variety too - you see forest, boulder rocks, open spaces etc. Can spot wildlife. There is a waterfall with a viewing place as well but it was rather dry when we visited. Hikes are mostly easy to intermediate. There is restroom at the entrance and at campground (which also has running water).
Parking - $10 at either entrance (their old and brand new one). New entrance has EV chargers (check PlugShare for details). But you can also park for free right outside of old entrance. Parking is limited.

What a wonderful place to visit with family/kids. Well, any animal lover will enjoy it greatly. Big number of animals to see, learn about their habitat and discover something new. Making reservations online was easy. Staff on site is very helpful. Everything is clean, COVID- safe, everyone is masked and distancing. Stroller friendly.
Some areas are closed but that’s perfectly understandable. Gondola was a lot of fun. Separate are with California native animals was a blast to see. We hope to come back soon!

Loved it. This is where locals come to ski/board. Great variety of trails for all skill levels. Easy and plenty parking. It is usually not crowded here unlike larger resorts. Family friendly. Food court is so-so, but if you want something little more upscale, there is a great restaurant just across the street. Rental place can be crowded in the morning, so come early. We bought tickets online - there is a separate line to pick up tickets which makes it quick. Will come back for more skiing fun!

Awesome place to bring kids. All animals are well visible, fed, happy and joyful. Great variety of wildlife to look at. Staff is doing a great job with COVID related restrictions - reservations, masks, limited crowds, distancing. Everything is marked and clear.
Parking is easy, especially if pre-purchase online. As a perk, they have free EV charging for Tesla and other EV.
Bathrooms are super clean. Staff is very nice.
Hope to come back soon again.

Excellent place to hike. You get variety of terrain - from shady forest to exposed ridge with beautiful views. There is some elevation and then it’s mostly flat up top.
Difficulty - moderate.
Parking - free, off highway.
No restrooms.
Dogs are welcome on certain trails (watch for signs).
Main loop is little over 4 miles but you can easily double that by adding extra trails.
Stroller friendly - no.
Overall highly recommend it.

It’s a huge park with lots to do - large green space to run around, big playground with water feature, tennis and basketball courts, cafe and library nearby. You can watch people practicing Tai-Chi, other martial arts, playing sports. Parking is big but gets full on weekends as park is very popular.
Restrooms available. Parking is free. EV charging stations by library.

One of my most favorite hiking places period. Beautiful scenery, multiple hiking trails, you can keep hiking endlessly!
Gorgeous views of ocean and hills.
Parking lot is free but gets full on weekends.
There are two portable toilets next to parking lot (up top).
Trails range from easy to moderate and can be done with kids (not very stroller friendly though).

Absolutely stunning! Well worth $15 admission fee. Gorgeous tropical plants, ocean vistas, waterfalls. Very helpful staff. Ample parking, restrooms are clean. They even have complementary umbrellas in case if it rains. Gift shop has plenty of educational materials and gifts, including seeds for various tropical plants. Don't miss this wonderful place!

Fantastic little garden with plenty of well labeled plants. Can visit the actual house and have a tour. Otherwise can stroll around the garden, visit various areas with different flowers and plants. Some plants are for sale.
Parking is free.
Restrooms available.
Staff is very nice and helpful.

Beautiful park. Good medium intensity 2.5-3mile hike to reach the top. Perfect place to see sunset over the Bay Area. Have some water for yourself and your pet. There is a water fountain and portable toilets at the entrance. Parking gets full quickly but can park on the street next to it.

Very cool place to visit with kids. They have ton of stuff for kids to play with - an old historic carousel, really cool train, a model of a fighter jet, big lawn and a big playground. They sell snacks, hotdogs and burgers by the train station too. Overall awesome place to check out.

Great place to visit with kids. You can see historic buildings, bee hives, say hi to animals (alpacas, sheep, goats) and have a nice easy hike along Stevens Treek trail.
Parking is limited, but easy to find a spot on street next to golf club (5 min walk).
Stroller friendly.

What a great place to visit with kids. Lots of space to roam around, a big playground, lots of farm animals in the barn, ton of various farm birds. Multiple different gardens are fun to explore.
Parking is free. Restrooms available.

Excellent historic park. Nearby (5 min walk) is TwoStep snorkeling area. One of the best snorkeling spots on the island. Come here for tropical fish, corals, turtles and dolphins. Parking, restrooms available. Shade is limited.

Very cute lake park. Great for strolling, jogging. Two playgrounds for kids, bocce field, picnic areas. Two Parking lots $6 for a day. But can park on the street for free (in the back of the park, not highway side).

Awesome awesome awesome. Beautiful place to hike, bike, run. Great views. Can go with a stroller. Parking is really tight so get there early or park on the street (but will have to walk 5-10 mins to the entrance).

Permanent exhibition is great. Select rotating exhibitions are usually incredible. We came for Oscar de la Renta one and enjoyed it immensely. Definitely climb the tower to enjoy the views of the Park around it.
Nice place to visit to learn some history, view Golden Gate Bridge from below and enjoy city skyline. There is free parking. You can hike up through a beautiful garden all the way to the bridge.
Calm waters, plenty of fish and sea turtles. Lifeguard available. Plenty of kids snorkeling safely. Parking in abundance, restrooms in place. A great place for family snorkeling and swimming.
What a gorgeous place to visit. You can walk around the estate, enjoy the garden, take a hike up the hill. Beautiful place to bring visiting friends and family.
Nice place. There is a parking lot if you are going for a hike. They organize various events in the barn. There is a very clean restroom on premises.
Great hiking spot. Lots of dog walker. Few cyclists. Plenty of flat surfaces but also few steep area (if you want). You can watch whales from here.
One of my favorite places on the island. Beautiful beach, fantastic views. Restrooms, showers and picnic tables available. Parking gets right.

It's not a big space, but it's got a lot to offer. The trails were all built by the local mountain biking community in conjunction with the land managers. Lots of fun, twisty single track to keep you engaged. Definitely not for beginners! There are lots of sharp pointy rocks making it a good idea to wear guards/pads. Great hiking and trail running too, as the trails wind their way back and forth up the hill rather than just going straight up. Beautiful views of Batiquitos Lagoon and the ocean from the top.

I went for a early morning, muddy hike with my friend at the Calavera Nature Preserve. It was a beautiful space, where you can see what the countryside was before the city of Carlsbad decided to fill in or top off every other Hill. There are lots of nice hiking trails, although I wish there was still mountain biking available here. In all of my years of mountain biking, I had never been to Calaveras, and now that is closed off to mountain biking, I am sad I never explored the area.

I took my toddler granddaughter to Pecos Legacy Park playground for an hour of playtime. We had the playground mostly to ourselves, as it was a cold and cloudy day. She ended up having a great time, climbing all over the play structure and sliding down all of the slides. I even got into the action! The slides here are quite steep and high. Play structure is probably more intended for older children, but since my granddaughter is adventurous and Intrepid, she didn't seem to notice.

Stonesteps is one of those truly magical beaches in Encinitas. The stairway leading down to the beach is not for the faint of heart and the route backup isn't for people who are grossly out of shape. The beach itself just north of Moonlight Beach, is fairly narrow and at high tide you will most likely not find much Beach at all. The Bluffs here are beautiful and provide a Quick Escape from awareness that you're in the middle of a major metropolitan area.

Go Karting is fun but hard work. You will get an arm workout and your stress level will be pretty high when you finish. The wait can be pretty long, so don't expect to be able to just show up and race. If they have a party scheduled, you probably won't be racing. There is a concession stand, but expect very high prices (e.g. $3 for a small bottle of water). The staff is friendly. If you can get a Groupon, it makes the price a bit more reasonable.

Whether you stay in the canyon and walk up the river bed or you climb the hill to the top of Lopez Canyon, this is a beautiful hike that will make you forget you are in the middle of a major metropolitan area. One thing to be aware of is that there tends to be a lot of poison oak down in the Lush and Greener areas near the river bed. If you don't know what poison oak looks like, it would be good to check it out before you go.

What can I say, it's a pier. It makes for a nice walk out to the end, but there's not a whole lot to see once you're out there except for the San Clemente coastline with prison like apartment complexes lining the beach. There are some restaurants, but I don't know about the quality, as I don't eat that sort of food. In other words, don't expect healthy food, but rather mostly fried or standard American diet type Food.

Urban park with natural features including lots of poison oak. Beautiful throughout the year and well worth your visit. Hiking trails here vary between wide roads dirt roads and single track trails. Some good mountain biking is available as well especially if you connect it with San Clemente Canyon. You are likely to Seahawks soaring over head but probably not a whole lot of other wildlife except for small Critters.

I'm not quite certain why people think the park at the park is such an interesting place to visit. Other than the fact that it is attached to Petco Park, it's not like there's a lot of things to do here. I guess, if you're going to take your kids to a baseball game where they will be bored, then this park at the park will be something of interest to you. Otherwise there are many nicer parts in the area.

The Stewart collection is part of the UCSD campus and thanks for an enjoyable hike. Take a few hours to walk around the campus and enjoy all of the creative artwork. Whether it's the rock teddy bear or the house on the top of the engineering building, I find something interesting each time I go. Some of my favorite pieces include the talking trees, the snake path, and Stonehenge.

Small beachside grassy park with a playground, basketball court, bathrooms and paved walkway down to the beach. Small parking lot gets filled on the weekends, but there lots of parking along the streets nearby. There are several restaurants in the area as well as shops along Coast Highway. Coaster / Amtrack station and bus stop close by at Coast Highway and Lomas Santa Fe.

I never know what I will see at the Oceanside fishing pier. Throngs of people, some of whom put on various displays that draw attention. Skateboarders, people fishing, runners and walkers, families enjoying the beach, homeless people showering, lovers looking into each other's eyes, drunks stumbling around, etc.

While I was walking around Austin I discovered this Park and he was quite pleased to find myself in an oasis just off the beaten path. Even with all of the construction that was happening in the area this was a nice respite and there were lots of smiling people walking in all directions.

Nice park with large fields for sports, workouts or lounging. Not many trees for shade and the ones that exist (as of 2016) are still young as this park is fairly new. The playground is really nice, with a squishy rubber padded ground under the equipment. Lots of fun even for adults.

There is little that is endearing to me about Mission Bay Park (except for the kites.) An active waterway, filled with watercraft of mixed propulsion (human, cloth and motorized) to keep your head on a swivel. Mix in alcohol and the excitement begins to take on a variety of hues.

Torrey Pines State Beach is a great place to spend the day. Ample payed parking, lots of free parking if you are willing to walk. Bathrooms, lifeguards and good beach. Nice long beach walks are available too. Plus, with Torrey Pines Reserve, the hiking options are wide open.

Beautiful gardens to roam in and frolic around. The UC Berkeley botanical garden is probably more interesting if you are ready interested in the variety of plants that grow in California, but the San Francisco botanical gardens is far more accessible.

A small but very beautiful nature trail highlighting all of the coastal scrub plants. With a beautiful ocean view views of the Cliffside mansions, you will feel both awe struck and maybe even dumbfounded at how much money some people have.

Nice small park with lots of trees for shade. A slice of Encinitas history with Cottonwood Creek (one of the reasons that Encinitas existed so far back in history) Decent playground for the kids. Tennis courts, basketball.

I remember going to Old Sturbridge Village when I was a small child. I was always excited by seeing the blacksmith's and all of the people who were acting as if they were living in the 1800s. Educational but commercial.
A beautiful small park where the hippies come out to play on the weekends. Expect slack lines, parkour, acro yoga, drum circle, singing, etc. Nice beach below.
likes: Activities: Slack lines, parkour, acro yoga, drum circle, singing

reviews_attraction.text: Nice small park with picnic tables, skateboarding area, basket ball court, volleyball court and playground. Dog friendly. Only thing missing is bathrooms.
I rode my mountain bike up the trails from Harbin Hot Springs Which was very challenging. But it was well worth it. Lots of great trails
Nice park. Even though it looks like it came out of a box, it should be really pretty once all the vegetation grows in
If you are learning to scuba dive, then this is your place. If you are more advanced, you will probably be bored.

Loved the museum. Learned a lot about Walt  Disney's beginnings and his ups and downs. Saw early drawings and what led up to Mickey. Saw how all his movies came about through planning. Got to see a replica model of Disneyland as well. Only issue I've got is why charge $30 a person when there's only 17 rooms of just so-so displays? Then they add more to go see another building of drawings but you're not allowed to film or take photos because everything there is copyrighted? Really? Plus the souvenir shop is way overpriced. $17 for a fridge magnet? Are you serious? I'd suggest it for Disney enthusiasts but if you're just there expecting more for what you pay, you'll be disappointed.
likes: Activities: Viewing early drawings, movie planning, Disneyland model
dislikes: Facilities & Services: High admission cost, limited rooms

reviews_attraction.text: Overly priced for the size. The grounds ARE beautiful to walk but it's small. You're in and out within 15 minutes depending on how fast you walk it. Scenery is beautiful. Looks and feels authentic. It should be free admission due to its size and the upkeep money should be gathered from the tea house concessions. It was cheaper walking the Botanical Garden (which has 55 acres to walk). Definitely a tourist trap unless you're into Zen gardens and need to see it. Not very serene with tourists all around you chatting away.

Great park with a track all around for joggers, bikers, etc. Lake is nice and calming. Plenty of ducks and turtles and fishing available. Playground located on premises with a tennis court and basketball court. Just try to avoid being there late hours. Can be a bit unsafe nighttime. Police present during the day stopping speeders driving above 25 mph so be careful.

55 acres of nothing but flowers, trees, shrubs, and beautiful grounds! The garden features plants from all over the world and it's well worth the entrance fee! The redwood area reminded us of the Muir Woods! Take the time to enjoy every single inch of this place because it's truly a beautiful site to behold!

A beautiful Mission and the grounds are a great place to enjoy by walking, hiking, or biking. There's a nature trail that runs behind the church and Mission that takes you along the river and through the wooded area. Very relaxing place. Visit the church. It's beautiful but quaint.

Part of Espada Park located just above the Espada Dam. Has a pavilion and trails to walk along the river. The restrooms here are portapottys unless you drive back close to the entrances where there's a building with restrooms. Shaded area. Very nice.

Historical spot! If you've seen the intro to Full House, these are the houses seen in the background when they're having their picnic in a field! The park itself is called Alamo Square and the grounds itself are nice! A must see for all!

Love the new additions to the park. The walking paths are great. The fishing areas are terrific. Love the atmosphere. The only issue would be the restroom area close to Military Dr and having to see the oil refinery next door.

Great place to visit. Lots of history. Loved the courtyard area. Don't expect a huge place when you visit. It's a house. You walk through some rooms, you walk the courtyard, you're done. Love the sites though.

Nice park to spend family time together at. Gets packed with people. Lots of picnic areas. Good for fishing. Ride the Eagle train if you want to enjoy a tour around the park. The zoo is located nearby.

Nice park with developing trails and hills to climb! Water area for kids to play at! Biggest minus is the fact that it was built on an old dumping ground! Not too sure about being in an area like that!

A great looking pavilion located in Brackenridge Park. It's right next to a playground and a building with restrooms plus it's got a view of the river that runs by the SA Zoo. Great place for parties.

Great place to walk, jog, or bike! Deer are sometimes visible grazing! Long trails connect to a neighboring park! Only minus would be the planes that constantly fly overhead due to the nearby airport!
Great museum with nice artwork and sculptures. The exhibits are good but could be a lot better. In comparison to the Houston Museum of Art, it's light years away from even coming close.
Very small but cute playground located outside of the Mission Lago golf course. It's a covered area so the elements won't disturb you plus there's a few picnic areas to eat and BBQ.
Park is okay. Picnic tables are not covered so you'll be directly under the sun. The track is a half mile walk/run/jog. Has a volleyball area. Wasn't dirty so that's a plus.
Great view of Alcatraz and the Golden Gate Bridge from here. Parking is a ways from the location but not too bad. Could hear the water through the tubes.
Nice place to take your family for a picnic and/or have a party. There's a creek that runs alongside the park to fish in as well. Bathrooms are on site.
Great place to take your kids to play but is usually packed. Lots of seating areas for adults. The sites are nice and your within view of the Tower.
A nice memorial to a fallen Tejano singer who was taken away too soon. Her music lives on and so do her memories. Great place for fans to visit.
Always a great place to visit. The park was made for children with special needs but it's great for one and all. Love their Christmas decor.
So so park. Not much to do here. Has no playground area but does have a basketball court and baseball field. Shaded areas here and there.
Beautiful place to visit. Admission isn't that bad. Love the flowers, gardens, landscape, etc. A must for anyone visiting Corpus Christi.
It's an okay park with a decent playground. The grounds could be kept better though. Grass needed to be cut when I visited.
Loved it! Felt like I was actually in China! Tons of shops, eateries, and sites! Loved every minute of it!

Always a lot of fun for kids and adults of all ages.
We went early this year, so several of the caves were flooded and we weren't able to go through them, but there was still plenty to do. (Sadly, our favorite 'Lemon Squeeze' was among the closed).
It's a bit pricey for a 1-2 hour activity, but worth it if you only go once every couple years - And you could always walk around again if you have the time.

Always a lot of fun for adults and children.
After being a member for 20 years, finally visited the Butterfly Garden. I wouldn't go every time, but definitely worth it! I thought the insect exhibits outside were more interesting that the butterfly garden itself, especially the ant farm.
A Premier membership is definitely worth it, particularly if you can make quick trips. First hour of parking is free!

The wait is very long and the ride itself is nothing special.
You can look out the "windows" as it travels to Hogwarts, but it's really just screens with silhouettes of characters.
More fun going the other way too: Kings Cross to Hogwarts, like in the movies.

Great local zoo with a nice variety of animals and very walkable layout.
It is a pretty simple zoo with few extravagances, but great for a few hours with the kids.
Larger than its sister, Stone Zoo, with more animals and doesn't feel as cramped.

The pits and surrounding area are free to the public, so I definitely recommend walking around if you are in the area.
The museum is small, but not too expensive and worth the price for some history on the area and animals found in the pits.

Great park and museum.
It's free to walk around the park and see several of the pits.
Admission for the museum is not too expensive and worth it to read some history about the area and different animal remains found in the pits.

Really cool feature that has a lot of intricate detail showing different animals and scenes.
Definitely remember to look up during your visit to try and catch all sides of it. You'll notice something new every time.

Dark ride where you use a laser gun to shoot aliens and compete with friends for high score!
An older ride that is getting a little dated, but still a lot of fun. Still worth waiting for.

Fun ride with lots of references to various Simpsons episodes.
If you're a fan of the show, you'll probably ride it anyway.
For the casual fan, it's worth it if the line's not too long.
Definitely prefer 'Islands of Adventure' to the older Universal Studios park, but it's definitely worth it to visit both as they each have their own unique rides and themes.

One of the best rides in Disney.
Recreation of a safari, it's like a full immersion zoo!
You get to see animals in a more natural environment, not behind bars and glass.

Nice, open park with lots of room to spread out or throw around a ball/frisbee.
I prefer the Gardens, but the Common can accommodate more people and feels more open.

Great outdoor music venue.
Most of the free summer concert series are located here. Lots of room to spread out a blanket and hang out for the afternoon.

Very fun waterpark that has something for everyone.
Lines are pretty long, but move quickly.
Admission is pricey, but expected for a Disney park.

Great place to catch a ball game. One of the oldest parks still operating.
The food is wicked expensive, but normal for a park/stadium/arena.

Best part of the park.
Very immersive and makes you feel like you're in Diagon Alley.
'Escape from Gringotts' is the best ride at Universal.

Fun ride that takes you through cinema history and different genres.
Somewhat interactive with a live "tour guide" that narrates a portion.

Very cool place to visit. Ruins and great views.
Biggest issue: Difficult to get to if you don't have a car. (Bus only for public transit).

This pays respects to the former King of Thailand who was born in Cambridge.
Definitely worth checking out and learning a bit of history.

Great open space to hang out.
"Ball playing" is discouraged, but will be overlooked, unless the typical curmudgeon decides to report it.

A must-stop if you're in the area. The views on the dunes are amazing.
The first hill is a bit of a hike, but definitely worth it.

Fun if you've never been to a Ripley's.
Definitely pricey, but a tourist attraction in a busy area, so you have to expect it.

Small, but one of the best research aquariums in the world.
Worth visiting at least once a year, or when exhibits change.

Great theater full of history and popular tourist spot.
The hand/foot prints outside the theater are always fun to see.

Great place to hike (more of a walk) and enjoy nature.
Great views of the ocean, bay, and Golden Gate Bridge.

You need a timed ticket to get in, the easiest way to get same day tickets is to go to their website at 6.30am ET. We got 11am tickets and when we arrived, they were actually giving tickets to anyone that came. The line inside was very long, at least 30' waiting to get to the main exhibit, located in 3 floors. When we exited the main exhibit at 12.30pm, there was no line inside but the line outside the building to get tickets was 2 blocks long. I found the way the content was presented and the amount of people, very overwhelming. There was just too much in a small space, and it was hard to follow, I kept feeling I was missing things. The content is extremely important and interesting, I wished it was less cramped.

Beautiful place to visit if you like looking at antique books and the ornate building itself. They had an exhibit about the drawings that are done in court, it was very enjoyable and not crowded. It has an underground hallway that connects to the Capitol Visitor center, which allows you to not have to go through security again. We spent a little over an hour.

They have over 20 period rooms with a brief story of where they come from, very interesting and well organized, once you understand how the floor map works and where to go (you are basically walking around the outside perimeter of 2 or 3 floors). Not crowded at all. We visited them by ourselves and it took us about an hour.

Wonderful museum, the architecture of the building itself was impressive and the exhibits were very interesting. I was nice to see how they acknowledged the sad things that have happened to the American Indians and they did a comparison of believes and ideologies. Not crowded at all. We spent about 2 hours.

Gigantic museum with two wings, the east wing is all modern art, it had a Rothko room and an Alexander Calder room that were breathtaking. The larger, west wing, is more European art. The Garden Cafe was overpriced and the portions were extremely small. We spent about 3 hours to see the entire museum.

Very cool building, half of each floor belongs to the portrait gallery and the other half to the american art museum, which allows for a good break as they are all connected. Very interesting art, well presented and not crowded. One of the few museums that closes at 7pm during winter hours.

6 floors of interesting stuff! My favorite were: the big pieces of the Berlin wall, the antenna of the WTC, the FBI exhibit, the Capitol view from the terrace and the gallery that has very, very old newspapers with world events. The restaurant had very good food. We spent about 3 hours.

Great and small museum in a house that has very interesting architecture. Very friendly and knowledgeable host. We spent about 1.5 hours as the pre-columbian exhibit was breathtaking. Looking forward to coming back in 2018 after they finish the gardens' renovation!

Beautiful small museum, they had a very interesting exhibit about using industrial leftovers to create clothes and bags. Well presented, not crowded, the permanent exhibition was also very well presented. 45' was enough for us to see everything.

Parking is $6, you can use a credit card to pay, it's usually not crowded, several hikes available, you can spend 1 hr or 3, slightly steep at times, beautiful views of SF, stroller friendly, public restrooms available and also picnic tables.

It was mildly interesting, the lady that did the tour was running very low on energy and did not seem to enjoy her job. If you have extra time in DC stop by, but it's not a must. If you book the 9am tour, don't go before 9am, as it's closed.

It's basically designed to take good Instagram photos, very colorful but not interesting in itself. You are divided into groups but once inside you can take your time to go around it. You get to taste some ice cream, but not too much.

Great park for kids of all ages to play, they have swings for babies, for toddlers and one for special needs kids. It's covered in the soft padded flooring so it's safe for them to fall and it's kept very clean.

Cool museum if you like planes and space travel, very big, the cafeteria was closed so we had to eat outside. The annex close to the airport was 10 times better, less crowded, newer and had impressive planes.

Absolutely beautiful, it's free for residents, there are 2 entrances, it's stroller and wheelchair friendly, really well maintained, astonishing variety. The map is very useful and the staff is very friendly.
Good place to get information about everything that is open and available to visit, small gallery with the story of the founder and with some displays from each museum. We spent 1/2 hour inside.
Small but very cool gallery with very modern and different pieces of art. Well presented, not overwhelming, friendly security guards. Only the top floor was open, we saw it in about 30'.
Absolutely gorgeous, small, we spent less than an hour, but very enjoyable. Don't miss the park with the fountain across the street from it, which is also part of it.
Avoid it in March, when there are no roses. I can imagine it's beautiful when the roses are blooming, off season there is nothing to see. The garden is pretty small.
Beautiful garden, even in the winter, entrance is $5 and they give you 5 free postcards. No map available but it's small so you don't really need it. 45' is enough.
Highly recommend it, entertaining, well organized, it took us about 1 hr but you can easily spend more time, we bought tickets thru Groupon and got a big discount.
Beautiful place to visit, even in winter while it's raining. An hour was more than enough for us. Be ready for a 5-10' uphill walk at the beginning.
It was very interesting, kids would love it, and it's still fun for adults too. I got discounted tickets through Groupon. We spent about 1.5 hours.
Nice garden to walk around and see some art sculptures, in October it closes at 5pm, although the website doesn't show it. We spent 15'.
Small art museum, check what exhibits they have before going to see if you want to go. We spent 1 hour and it was enough.

If this is not the best museum about flight in the world, should be near. Is huge, full of experts explaining things, has a lot of tours... Wonderful. We spent here at least five hours but we felt like we could spend two days. We are not fans of the matter and that's the reason 5-6 hours was enough for us, but if I were a fan probably I'd be here two days.

There are two expositions about space exploration, one about WWI and another about WWII, one expo about the begging of flight, another about boing, another big room about the history of planes, another room where you can enter in different planes like an Air Force One, Concorde, 787 Dreamliner...

This museum is a six stars museum.

The South windmill, known as the Murphy Windmill, was the largest of its kind in the world, with gigantic 114 foot sails, each cut from a single log. These sails turned clockwise, unlike traditional Dutch windmills which turn counter-clockwise (early, terrifying, film footage shows repairmen riding the sails as they make their circuit). It was built to supplement the Dutch windmill between 1905 and 1908, funded by $20,000 from a local banker named Samuel Murphy, and donations of lumber and copper roofing from other local businesses. It has just recently completed a ground-up restoration, its inner workings re-fitted in the Netherlands by a centuries old windmill designer.

In 1902, the Park Commission authorized the construction of two windmills to pump groundwater for park irrigation rather than purchasing water at exorbitant costs from the Spring Valley Water Company. The Dutch Mill was completed one year later and pumped 30,000 gallons per hour.

Electric water pumps replaced the need for windmills in 1913, and the mill fell into disrepair. By the 1950s, the mill was in a state of ruin.

Towering emerald peaks guard the lush valley floor of Iao Valley State Park. Located in Central Maui just west of Wailuku, this peaceful 4,000-acre, 10-mile long park is home to one of Maui's most recognizable landmarks, the 1,200-foot Iao Needle. This iconic green-mantled rock outcropping overlooks Iao stream and is an ideal attraction for easy hiking and sightseeing.

Aside from its natural tropical beauty, sacred Iao Valley has great historical significance. It was here in 1790 at the Battle of Kepaniwai that King Kamehameha I clashed with Maui's army in his quest to unite the islands. Even with Iao Needle serving as a lookout point, Kamehameha defeated Maui's forces in a ferocious battle that ultimately changed the course of Hawaiian history.

There is a well-marked, paved pedestrian path leading from the parking lot to view Iao Needle and the ridge-top lookout provides incredible views of the valley. The needle is sometimes covered in clouds, so an early start is your best bet for a good view. Families can also take a rainforest walk or explore interactive exhibits at the Hawaii Nature Center, which is also located within Iao Valley. Restroom facilities are available.

This is a must do when in Maui.  It is very stunning and picturesque.

Been in Hawaii for over 40 years and can't believe I have never visited this amazing island treasure. It is more about the architecture and design. The guided tour is well versed and you learn so much about the life of Doris Duke and what led up to this amazing adobe.

From the moment you arrive, you can feel that you are in a very special and unique place. Every room is something exotic and eclectic.  So much in the tour to see and experience.

I recommend going on the first tour of the day. As part of the ticket price, you can visit the Honolulu Academy of Art Museum afterwards for no additional charge.  Take advantage and see all other amazing collections there or have lunch at their amazing restaurant. You also can visit the Spalding House contemporary art museum on the same ticket, so you can spend a full day on the price of just one admission.

Parking is challenging in the area, but across the street from the Honolulu Academy of Art Museum is the Honolulu Academy of Art School and they offer parking in an attended lot for only $5.

You must book your tickets in advance to visit this amazing site, so plan ahead and book right away.

This is a walking tour with steps. If you have any handicap, you should inquire further about this activity if it is appropriate for you.
dislikes: Not fully accessible for handicapped visitors

reviews_attraction.text:
This is a fantastic museum with numerous collections.  The variety of art and different exabits is vast.  You can definitely spend a lot of time there.

My favorite part was the cultural tribal art from around the world.  So many exotic and captivating items to look at in one location.  You can spend hours there just looking at every detail.

Not much for modern art, but if you are, there is plenty of all kinds for your viewing.

During the visit, there were Monet and Gauguin exhibits going.  Again not my favorite, but amazing to see so many items all come together.  However, because of the popularity, it was a zoo of viewers to contend with.  I recommend researching when it is slowest if you want to fully enjoy the exhibits without having to be elbowed, wait for bad picture takers, or listen to noisy chit chat by disrespectful visitors.

Communication by staff was very poor and sort of unfriendly.  They ask you to hold you backpack or bag in your hand, but don't tell you why. Finally was told there was a bag check, but only well into the exhibits.  Of course there seems to be numerous people disregarding this supposed security measure.

Check it out for sure, but try to plan the time of your visit as best as possible to avoid the masses.

Opened in 1971, Kula Botanical Garden was developed by Warren and Helen McCord. The garden is located on a unique 8 acre site featuring proteas, orchids, bromelaids and native plants. The natural setting provides unusual rock formations, waterfalls, ponds and a panoramic view of the valley and west Maui mountains. You will enjoy an aviary, koi pond, bird sanctuary with the Hawaiian Nene goose, and picnic areas.

This is a great place to stop after visiting the Haleakala Nation Park.  It is just a short drive after the park on the way to west side if your are making a full day trip to Ulupalakua Ranch.  They do offer a AAA discount, so be sure to ask for it if you are a member.  Surprisingly, they do not offer a Kamaina discount.

The location is set on a hillside, so it is an uphill walk.  Those who have walking issues might not want to attempt this.  There is a paved main path, but the rest of the trails have stepping stones or nothing at all.  Were appropriate shoes.

It is a very enjoyable garden and has lots of beautiful flowers and plants to admire.  I wouldn't go out of my way just to go here, but if doing the scenic drive and it was along the way, would defiantly make it a point to pull over and enjoy it.

I think this is a definitely a must see when visiting San Francisco.  It has the best views possible with 360' of viewing and photo opportunities.  There is a very small admission to go to the top of the tower, but it is totally worth it.

There is very limited parking, so I would plan ahead.  You can walk to it from Little Italy or the hillside facing the Piers, but it is a hefty hike.  Even though a bit of a hike to take on, it is very enjoyable and worth it for the experience.  For those who may have health issues, I would say to not even attempt it.

Avoid the weekends, because it is busier then.  Not sure what times of day is best, but we went after lunch and it was a bit busy, but manageable.  You might have to wait a little for the elevator ride due to the age and capacity of the lift, but it moves right along.

We accessed it from the back walking up form Little Italy, but regretted not walking down the front through the zigzagging walkways leading back down to the Piers.  No matter what, San Francisco in my opinion is a walking city if you are up to it, but Uber is everywhere with less then a 5 minute wait if you get lazy.

I have lived I Hawaii for over 40 years and this is the first time I have stepped foot at this amazing historical location. I regret not going before because I feel I really missed out.  I almost dare to say that it is better then the Iolani Palace.  There is a guided walking tour that really is full of amazing historical information and paints a complete picture of those that lived there and things that led up to their possessions and related historical facts that you just can't get out of a history book.

You don't need much time there, but I would allow a total of 1.5 hours to fully enjoy.  There is so much to see and study inside the house and the surrounding property is very beautiful with all the tropical landscaping.

It is very inexpensive to visit and they do offer different discounts, but it is so inexpensive, it is almost unnecessary.

Location is easy to get to, but parking might be a challenge depending on time and day of the week. There is a park just behind that has parking spaces and you can walk across the field to the site. It is a rainy area, so an umbrella might be a good idea just in case.

I am not a big art fan, but this was a very nice museum with a surprisingly large and with extraordinarily diverse collections.  It wasn't what I expected from the area and by the looks from the outside of the building which is rather plain for a museum from my other experiences.

There was a little bit of everything there.  Some classics, lots of modern art, native American cultural art, as well as Asian art.  Everything we very well spaced out between 2 buildings that allowed you to really enjoy each art piece on display.

I admit, I am not really into modern art, but they did have some interesting stuff even though I just don't get it at all.  The Asian art which is my favorite type of art was amazing.  They have some incredible items that were really impressive.  Although native American art is so so with me, I enjoyed the collections that they had.

Defiantly visit this art museum when in town.  They do offer a AAA discount if you are member so remember to ask for it if you got your card on you.

If you like or love nature and want to get out of downtown Portland, this is a great place to do and a wonderful outdoor experience.  There are both paved paths and hiking paths to take in the greenery all around you.

One tip, make sure you plan where you want to go if you are going to visit this attraction.  It is large and has multiple entrances, so depending on what you want to see there, do your research.  We took a Uber to the back entrance and missed out on some of the interesting parts, but enjoyed it all the same.  Taking an Uber from the city is cheap and quick to this back entrance and would assume it is a bit more to go to main entrance where some points of interest are.

It can be damp, so wear good walking shoe and bring an umbrella or poncho with you just in case.  The paved path does have lots of joggers and speeding mountain bikers, so pay attention because they were kind of rude in their presence and seemed to pop up unexpectedly at times.

This lovely botanical garden is a great way to finish off your day after visiting the neighboring museums.  Lots of open air and easy to walk paths to take it all in.

It was a bit early for it to be at it's full spectacular being that we visited in late March, but was plenty of amazing plants and flowers to view.  One special surprise was that the cherry blossoms were at their peak and in their full glory.

The large varieties of plant collections ensure that there is something for everyone to enjoy. Walk through the world of plants and feel like your are in another place.

The trails are a little confusing and not clearly marked, so it can be a little frustrating if you are trying to follow a path with a direction in mind.  At times, the map didn't make sense and gave the feeling we might have missed something.

In all, this was an most enjoyable activity and would do it again as well as recommend it to others.

This place is something most people don't think of as a historical place to visit.  It is an important part of Hawaii's history leading up to modern times, but it wasn't until recent years did become open to the public for free tours every Thursday.

The tour space is very limited, so it is a good idea to plan in advance.  You can easily book online to confirm available space.  Again, it is free, so this is a no lose deal.  The docents take you back in time to really help you understand everything about the property and events that have happened over time.

Being located next to the State Capital, Iolani Palace, and State Art Museum, you can make a day of it just touring Hawaii's history in one walkable area.

I don't recommend this for young children as it will be boring for them and they will disturb others who are trying to listen to the docent.  This is a very adult and mentally mature type of activity.

This is a small but very interesting museum.  The mission house is very interesting and has a lot of historical information to absorb as well as amazing furnishing from the past.  The main museum is small, but has one of the best gemstones and geological collections I have seen outside of the Smithsonian.  The seashell collection is also amazing.  So many different and exotic specimens to look at.  Another interesting feature are the different lava displays.  There is no better collection of examples of different lava anywhere.  The staff are very friendly and almost bed over backwards to show their “Aloha Spirit” as well as being very informative.  It is a hefty but enjoyable walk from the center of Hilo town, but worth the view walking back into town when you have completed your tour of the museum and mission house.

This is a must do and see when visiting Hawaii.  It has some of the best panoramic views of Waikiki to the Eva plains.  If you can get past the construction cranes ruining the views from all the new developments, it is an amazing view point of picture taking.  At lease Diamond Head is unobstructed for now.

It is very easy to get to via car and right outside of downtown Honolulu as well as only a few miles from Waikiki.  The memorial it's self has an amazing pictorial history of the wars with a focus on WWII.  It is just an amazing construction to pay tribute to those who served during those times.

You don't need much time there, maybe an hour tops depending on how much looking around you want to do.  Once done, it is easy to get back on to what ever other site seeing you are doing.

Visit this nice little attraction on the water front of the river next to downtown Portland for something different.  It is really worth the visit and gives you a good glimpse into the history of Oregon's riverboat days.

This is a good activity to do just about any time, but we went first thing when they opened and got our own private tour by one of the very knowledgeable docents.  He really went into great detail about all aspects of the boat, the things that happened back in the day and current facts as it was related to why they were there and how they existed.

It won't take up much of your time, but will fill an hour or more.  This attraction is great for both adults and kids of all ages.

Don't forget to ask for AAA discount if you are a card member.

This free, very accessible, and beautiful activity is a must when in Portland if you love nature and flowers.  The rose garden is neatly planted with an amazing variety of rose to enjoy both their colorful glory and fragrant smells.

Although it is easy to walk and accessible to most, walking shoes would be highly recommended as this is an outdoor activity and it could be wet.  Umbrellas might be a good idea as well, just in case you get a drizzle when you go.

Being located in Washington Park, you can access this garden via the free shuttle that runs every 15 minutes.  You can make a full day of it visiting all the other sites and start off by taking the HOP transit to the starting point at the Zoo and then riding the free shuttle the rest of the way.

Well this is a very long drive to see very little.  Although very pretty, there isn't much along the way to see and once you get there and take a few pictures, you have a long way back with again, not much to see along the way.

Lock your cars and don't leave valuables in plain site or in the vehicle at all.  Lots of warning signs and Hawaii tourist sites like this are notorious for car break in's as well as smash and grabs through the windows.

The homeless camps along the way with the derelict cars is not an enjoyable sight as well as all the trash along the roadsides. One of the worst kept areas on Oahu in my opinion.

Be respectful of the local culture out there.  It is a way of life for those who live to live so far away from town.

This is one of the nicest parks I have ever been to in Hawaii.  It has lots of interesting areas to rest, play, and enjoy.  The ponds and paths wide around with different views at every bend.  The pagodas a other structures throughout the park add lots of interest.  Being located right next to the bay, the ocean backdrop adds extra tranquilly.  This is a perfect place to escape and relax, contemplate, or just enjoy nature.

The Holy Virgin Cathedral, also known as Joy of All Who Sorrow, is a Russian Orthodox cathedral in the Richmond District of San Francisco. It is the largest of the six cathedrals of the Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia.

It is breath taking and amazing if you are so lucky to be invited in.  That being said, it is not something you should flock as a tourist and need to be respectful to it's purpose as a church.

Kind of a neat cave, but not much to see and don't need a lot of time.  Rather shameful to see all the rubbish and broken glass for what looks like people partying in the area.  Be sure to secure your car if you park and spend anytime.  High risk of auto break-in in Hawaii.

Lovely area, but sad to see trash like soda cans and broken beer bottles as well as fishing lines scattered around. Be careful to lock your car and don't leave anything visible in the cabin as there is a high rate of car break-ins in places like this around the island.

This is a fantastic little zoo that is free and well maintained.  It is totally worth the stop and time visited.  Allow about 1-2 hours visiting time. Very impressed with the exibits and how the animals are kept. This zoo far better then the Honolulu zoo.

This is very unique winery with some very good and unique wines.  Cute little showroom that is comfortable and relaxing.  Staff are very knowledgeable as being friendly.  It is a must stop to see this hidden gem if heading up to the volcano.

Very nice park with lots of great picture opportunities of the Windward coastline in Kaneohe bay.  Be sure to lock your car and hide your not leave anything visible to temp a car break in when you park to visit.
Very nice large park near Waikiki beach under Diamond head.  Great for excising, taking a relaxing stroll, pick nick, horsing around.  Activities almost every weekend at the park.
Sadly, the State has let this place get rundown looking, but they did have other priorities because of the lava flow in Puna. Hopefully they will fix it back up soon.

I'm sure a lot of us have gone to this bizarre but captivating museum at least once or twice in their lifetime.  We have visited this museum on at least two occasions and always captivated with all the bizarre stuff people get into or by some calamity, have become celebrated in one way or another.

The museum was crammed with a lot of fascinating articles, exhibits and worth the price of admittances.  As always, I relish looking into the historical aspect of a lot of the places we go to in order to better appreciate what the place is all about.

"Robert Ripley" delved into the uncanny stories of people's lives and has been called a liar more often than anyone else but has never failed to establish the truth of every allegation.

His museums have literally opened up all over the world and changed hands so many times that it's impossible to list everything so I just emphasized a few notables in this person's fascinating past.

In 1890, Robert Leroy Ripley was born in Santa Rosa, CA on Christmas Day.

In 1908, he quit school before graduating in order to support his widowed mother.

In 1914, he took his first trip abroad to Belgium and France.

In, 1918, he published "Champs and Chumps" cartoon and is regarded as the first Believe It or Not cartoon!

Since 1922, Ripley visited over 201 countries over the next fifteen years.  Ripley was nicknamed "the Modern Marco Polo" by the Duke of Windsor.  His travels took him to the four corners of the world.

On one trip alone, he crossed two continents and covered 24,000 miles - 15,000 miles by air, 8,000 miles by ship and more than 1,000 miles by camel, donkey and horse!

In 1927, Ripley stated that Charles Lindbergh was not the first man to cross the Atlantic by plane, drew 170,000 letters!  Many of his readers demanded proof of his unbelievable statements.

This cartoon made Ripley so famous that postmen forwarded his mail even without a full address.  Envelopes simply addressed, "To Rip" or "To the World's Biggest Liar" were all delivered.

In 1929, his Believe It or Not! Cartoon went from being published in 17 papers to worldwide distribution and his first Believe It or Not! Book was published.

In 1930, he began his 14-year run on radio and his 19-year association with radio show promoter Doug Storer (future president of Ripley's Believe It or Not!).

In 1932, he traveled to the Orient and the first and most successful national Believe It or Not! Contest was held.

In 1933, he opened his first Odditorium in Chicago, Ill. at the World's Fair.  His wild and weird collections brought in nearly two million visitors.

In 1934, he purchased a 28- room home on an island in Long Island Sound, off the shore from Mamaroneck, NY and named it BION (Believe It or Not!) Island.

In 1936, he opened Odditorium at The Texas Centennial Exposition in Dallas, Texas.  In a national poll of newspaper readers Ripley was voted the most popular man in America, President Roosevelt came in second.

In 1937, Charles Schulz's first ever-published drawing, a sketch of a cute little dog that would later become famous as "Snoopy," appeared in the Believe It or Not! Cartoon panel.

In 1948, he created a TV show and celebrated his 30th anniversary of Believe It or Not!

In 1993, the 75th Anniversary of Ripley's Believe It or Not! cartoon was celebrated; "The Life and Times of Robert Ripley."

From 1993-1997, Asian expansion took place with openings of museums in Thailand, Korea, Jakarta and Hong Kong.

In 1996, the Guinness World Records Museum franchise rights were acquired.

In 1997, the first Ripley Aquarium opened in Myrtle Beach, S.C. and by 2007; over 10 million guests visited the aquarium, which is still the state's most attended paid attraction.

In 2001, Ripley's three Moving Theaters were converted to 3-D presentations.

In 2007, Ripley's Believe It or Not! museum made a triumphant return to New York City's Times Square after an absence of 35 years.

There are now 30 Ripley's Believe It or Not! Odditoriums in operation around the world.

I'll start this review by saying, what's not to like about this place!  It's stunning to see the thousands of flowers during the month of March when this small farm is covered in yellow Daffodils.

Over the years, we have made this trek numerous times and have always enjoyed the walk through the side of the hill while admiring the daffodils.

"The Story Behind The Flowers!"

Mary McLaughlin Lucot, was born in 1881 and Jesse McLaughlin, was born at the Daffodil Hill site in 1893.

In 1887, Arthur Burbeck McLaughlin and Lizzie Van Vorst McLaughlin established McLaughlin Ranch, now known as Daffodil Hill.  The ranch was purchased from an old Dutchman by the name of Pete Denzer.

Denzer planted daffodils, which he brought over, from his native land.  The yellow daffodils were Lizzie's most prized possession and every year she divided and replanted the bulbs to increase the size of their garden.

The McLaughlin's continued the way station, renting rooms and serving meals (breakfast for 25 cents) to the travelers and providing feed and shelter for their animals.  For many years, the loft of the barn was used for "Saturday Night" dances at the ranch.

In 1912, Arthur passed away and a year later, their 17 room, 2- 1/2 story house burned down.  A small cabin was built for Lizzie before she passed away in 1935.

The original bunk house and larder room has been remodeled into living quarters for the present caretakers.

Following their mother's death, Jessie and Mary decided to plant daffodils in her memory.  Daffodils were planted every year, just a few at a time and soon people began to stop to admire the blooms.

As groups of tourists grew, so grew the plantings until the few hundred planted annually, grew to a few thousand.  Since then, 5 to 6 thousand new bulbs are planted annually, both daffodils and tulips.

The property covers approximately 6 acres of daffodils, 300 varieties, & 400,000 blooms.  The number planted depends upon donations received each year from tourists who stop by.

There is no admission charge, but old yellow teakettles and pots around the property are there for donations, which we have made over the years.

In 1981, Jesse passed away followed by Mary in 1973.

The property is now taken care of by Mary's two children, Arthur Lucot and Mary Lucot Ryan, their spouses, her grandchildren, great grandchildren and great-great grandchildren.

Daffodils are still being planted by the thousands each year in memory of their parents, grandparents, great-grandparents and great-great grandparents!

540 acres at Daffodil Hill, which is part of the ranch are walnut trees (1500 bearing trees), which have been planted to help pay for the taxes and other operation expenses.

The family depends on hired crews to pick the walnuts but the family continues to "knock our trees by hand, truck them to a commercial processor to be hulled and dried and delivered to Diamond Walnut Association before December 1st."

According to the family, November, December, and early January, is spent planting daffodils.  The rest of January into February, the family "cleans up, bench and table repair, fence work, painting, and a lot of weeding and raking of leaves."

By mid-March, the family states that their ready for guests.  You can meet and see their extended family and friends donating their time to say, "hello," direct traffic, sell postcards and answer questions.

Much of the landscape around the old homestead is covered with several varieties of daffodils.  The McLaughlin's descendants have continued to personally plant several thousand new bulbs a year.

In the past several years an average of 16,000 daffodil bulbs per year have been planted by the Ryan brothers and their families, great grandchildren, great-great grandchildren, and great-great-great grandchildren of Arthur and Lizzie.

It is estimated that today, Daffodil Hill is carpeted with approximately 300,000 bulbs when in full bloom.

This is one of those places that not many people have visited and for us it was by coincidence.  While in the Monterey area several years ago, we happened onto this place and stopped in.  This butterfly sanctuary is only of the few remaining places that have been preserved for the Monarch Butterfly to call home.

Once there was millions of migrating butterflies but because of man’s encroachment, many of the places that these magnificent creatures called home are endangered.  During our visit, we were asked to sign a petition to save this site from redevelopment into another residential complex.

We did get a chance to see a few Monarchs flying around and observed “clumps” of them on several eucalyptus trees.  Our children was thrilled to see them fly around and asked questions about their life cycle.

Since out last visit, we have stopped in over the years preceding our first visit.  I guess the petition worked because the sanctuary is still here.  If you’re in the area, it’s worth a stop into this place!

On October 29, 2013, a count of only 3,400 butterflies was made on the returning Monarchs at the Pacific Grove Monarch Sanctuary.

Pacific Grove is known as the "Butterfly Capital of California" for the annual migration of the Monarch butterflies.

The black-and-orange butterflies spend much of the fall and winter in the local Monterey Pine trees, roughly from Halloween until Valentine's Day.

Residents of Pacific Grove help the butterfly's habitat by planting purple and yellow flowers, such as lantara, yellow aster, Pride of Madera, and Mexican Sage, in what are called Butterfly Gardens.

•	City Ordinance No. 352 makes it a misdemeanor to kill or threaten a butterfly, punishable by a $1,000 fine.

Pacific Grove's George Washington Park is part of the original overwintering habitat and the City is trying to reverse this decline with an aggressive campaign of tree planting, mulching, and trail improvement.

The proliferation of Australian eucalyptus trees, first introduced into this country in the 1850's, has provided a tree that is not only well-suited to sheltering Monarch clusters, but also provides the butterflies with a convenient nectar source since it blooms in winter.

Monarchs cluster in the eucalyptus trees at the Monarch Grove Sanctuary, as well as in eucalyptus groves at Natural Bridges State Park in Santa Cruz, and at the North Beach Campground in Pismo Beach near San Luis Obispo.

After arriving at their destination, the monarchs cluster in large masses to conserve heat.  Their flight muscles do not function well unless the temperature is above 55 degrees.  They rest on the trees, resembling dead leaves, until sunlight warms them enough to fly.

On warm days, the butterflies leave the trees entirely, seeking out nectar sources with which to replenish their energy reserves, but always returning well before evening to once again cluster in the trees.

A female Monarch may lay hundreds of eggs; she deposits these pin-head sized eggs on the underside of milkweed leaves, where they will hatch in 4-5 days, depending on the temperature.

The newly hatched larva feeds voraciously on the milkweed, accumulating bitter chemicals from the host plant which help protect the Monarchs from predation by birds.

The mature caterpillar usually leaves the milkweed to seek out a bare branch or similar sturdy surface.  It attaches itself by spinning a silk button from which it hangs upside down in the shape of the letter "j".

After two weeks, the chrysalis becomes transparent, signaling that the black and orange butterfly within is ready to emerge.  The chrysalis splits open and the Monarch butterfly carefully emerges.  A female Monarch has approximately 6 weeks to seek out nectar, mate, and lay eggs before she dies.  By March, most of the butterflies have departed on the spring migration.

Since 1939, each October, Pacific Grove has celebrated the arrival of the Monarch Butterfly with a welcoming Butterfly Parade, featuring school children dressed in wings.

Over the years, I have traveled across this "old bridge a bazillion" times and seen the changes to the surrounding area, some good and of course others not so good.

My fondest memories will always be driving across the bridge to witness the panoramic view of both side of the bay and on a clear day, it was quite spectacular.

I was on this bridge after the center span collapsed during the 1989 Loma Prieta Earthquake, taking a photo of the collapsed portion of the span (attached in my profile pictures) and wondered if they were ever going to replace this bridge, which they did in 2013.

The drive across the "new span" is inspirational as well as a tourist attraction for being the only bridge in the world with a "center suspension system."  I've highlighted the conception of this man made phenomenon.

In 1850, the idea of a bridge linking San Francisco with the cities of Oakland, Berkeley, and Alameda "was proposed."

In 1868, the ferry service made five round trips a day and eventually came under the control of the Southern Pacific Railroad.

In 1869, railroad executives who built the western portion of the transcontinental railroad considered the idea of a bridge but because of the challenges involved never took shape."

* Demands for a bridge were the result of economic and social changes in the Bay Area, including increasing popularity of the automobile.

* The original plans for the Bay Bridge included a key system with railway access across the bridge.

On August 18, 1869, Emperor Norton, a well-known San Francisco character issued a proclamation ordering the construction of what is now the Golden Gate Bridge and the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge.

In 1921, the San Francisco Motor Car Dealers Association financed an engineering report on the feasibility of a link consisting of a tunnel and a concrete causeway.

In 1927, a study concluded that a bridge spanning the bay was technically or financially non-feasible, although it suggested a bridge could be built.

In 1928, Congress authorized the City of San Francisco to build a bridge but it was stalled as a result of objections by the Army and Navy.

The design chosen for the bridge was a combination of linked structures that constituted an historic engineering challenge.
