It included a cantilever span of 1,400 feet in the East Bay crossing, two 2,310-foot center suspension spans, two 1,160-foot side spans in the West Bay crossing, and a tunnel carrying the upper (six lanes for fast traffic) and lower decks (three truck lanes and two interurban track lines) through Yerba Buena Island.

In 1929, the creation of the California Toll Bridge Authority and it was their responsibility of connecting San Francisco and Alameda County with a bridge.

In 1933, construction of the Bay Bridge began on the longest bridge in the world at that time.

* More than 8,300 men worked on the original Bay Bridge.  The workforce was not unionized except for eight unionized crafts.  The average wage was $7.75 per day, and all the workers were men.

The odds were if a man worked on the bridge for more than a year and a half he was likely to suffer at least one serious injury.  There were a total of 28 fatalities during construction."

The final bridge cost was approximately $77 million, $6 million under the estimated cost.

In 1936, the new Bay Bridge was completed and the Bay Area celebrated completion with a four day festival that began in Oakland before the opening and concluded in San Francisco after the opening.

* As expected, as soon as the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge was built, it immediately became the favorite way to travel between San Francisco and the East Bay.

In 1937, the Golden Gate Bridge opened.

In 2013, after decades in the planning and construction, the Eastern Span was replaced with a new design, including the world's longest Self-Anchored Suspension Span.

The new Bay Bridge cost an estimated $6.3 billion dollars making it one of the largest public works projects in US history.

I completed a review on Golden Gate Park but because of the parks immense size I'm only able to cover "some of the many notable attractions" which we have visited over the years.

There is no other place here in the Bay Area where you can see an "authentic windmill" other than at Golden Gate Park.  The grounds are kept up and over the years, a tulip bed has been added which highlights these icon symbols of a bygone era.

This review covers the windmills, which is located on the western end of the park.  Over the years, I've seen these windmills deteriorate because of neglect and the weather, but have since been restored.

The windmills at this park played an important role, which I never knew until I researched its early beginnings.

At the turn of this century, San Francisco's coast was lined with barren, windblown sand dunes. Almost no plants could survive the shifting, inhospitable environment and there was no evidence that this desolate wasteland would one day be home to the spectacular gardens and fields of Golden Gate Park.

In creating Golden Gate Park, one problem existed for early developers and that was how to provide the enormous quantities of water necessary to transform the dunes into a lush paradise.

Initially, the "Spring Valley Water Company" supplied water for the development of the park, but it was expensive and only irrigated 75 acres.

In 1873, "Wells" were drilled along the San Francisco coast which indicated that there was fresh water.  A proposal was made to build a windmill right on the dunes and to use the prevailing westerly winds to pump water from beneath the dunes and into the park.

In 1901, plans were made to build a windmill 300 yards from the ocean.  This windmill could take advantage of the prevailing winds to pump water for the park's irrigation system.

In 1902, authorization was granted for the construction of two windmills to pump ground water for park irrigation.

In 1903, the Dutch Mill was completed and pumped 30,000 gallons per hour.

In 1913, motorized pumps were installed to augment the production of the wind driven system and maintenance became a thing of the past.  With the windmills no longer performing a primary function, their maintenance was neglected and they eventually ceased to operate.

Over the years, noticeable insect and water damage has taken place, making the gallery unsuitable for visitors.

By the 1950s the mills were in a state of ruin.

In 1964, Eleanor Rossi Crabtree, daughter of Mayor Angelo Rossi, initiated a campaign to save the North Windmill.

In 1980, as a result of Crabtree's campaign, the North Windmill received cosmetic repairs, and the Queen Wilhelmina Tulip Garden was created on the adjacent grounds.

On December 6, 1981, the Dutch Mill was placed on the San Francisco Designated Landmark list.

In 1993, after bringing in a windmill expert and designer, damage estimates were assessed and the urgency of repair to the South Windmill.  It was concluded that immediate action should be taken.  A reception was held at the South Windmill which revealed plans for the construction of a Community Center Pavilion.

In 2000, the concept of a Campaign to Save the Golden Gate Park Windmills was born.  Also that same year, the Murphy Mill was placed on the San Francisco Designated Landmark list.

In 2001, the "Campaign to Save the Golden Gate Park Windmills" presented restoration plans and a call for support to the Recreation and Park Commission, which was accepted.

Years of natural wear and tear, as well as visible beetle and water damage has seriously placed a damper on the appearance of the windmills.  The cap of the South Windmill was removed and shipped to experts in the Netherlands in the early part of 2000, and is expected to return after being fully restored.

A complete restoration of both windmills and the surrounding environment will also include a rebuilt windmill tower, pump mechanism, and sails among other items.

This is one of those places that not many people have visited and for us it was by coincidence.  While in the Monterey area several years ago, we happened onto this place and stopped in.  This butterfly sanctuary is only of the few remaining places that have been preserved for the Monarch Butterfly to call home.

Once there was millions of migrating butterflies but because of man's encroachment, many of the places that these magnificent creatures called home are endangered.  During our visit, we were asked to sign a petition to save this site from redevelopment into another residential complex.

We did get a chance to see a few Monarchs flying around and observed "clumps" of them on several eucalyptus trees.  Our children was thrilled to see them fly around and asked questions about their life cycle.

Since out last visit, we have stopped in over the years preceding our first visit.  I guess the petition worked because the sanctuary is still here.  If you're in the area, it's worth a stop into this place!

On October 29, 2013, a count of only 3,400 butterflies was made on the returning Monarchs at the Pacific Grove Monarch Sanctuary.

Pacific Grove is known as the "Butterfly Capital of California" for the annual migration of the Monarch butterflies.

The black-and-orange butterflies spend much of the fall and winter in the local Monterey Pine trees, roughly from Halloween until Valentine's Day.

Residents of Pacific Grove help the butterfly's habitat by planting purple and yellow flowers, such as lantara, yellow aster, Pride of Madera, and Mexican Sage, in what are called Butterfly Gardens.

* City Ordinance No. 352 makes it a misdemeanor to kill or threaten a butterfly, punishable by a $1,000 fine.

The Monarch Butterfly (Danaus plexippus) is a widespread tropical insect that ranges as far north as Canada.  It cannot withstand freezing winter temperatures and to survive, they migrate to safe overwintering sites that are neither cold enough to kill it, nor so warm that it wastes precious energy flying too much.

Monarchs east of the Rocky Mountains spend the winters in high mountains in central Mexico. Monarchs west of the Rockies migrate to locations on the central California coast.  They may travel as far as 2,000 miles, covering 100 miles per day, and flying as high as 10,000 feet.

Historically, most of the western population of Monarchs settled in the fog-shrouded Monterey pine forest of Pacific Grove.  These trees provide the micro climate needed: proper humidity, light, shade, temperature, and protection from wind.

Pacific Grove's George Washington Park is part of the original overwintering habitat and the City is trying to reverse this decline with an aggressive campaign of tree planting, mulching, and trail improvement.

The proliferation of Australian eucalyptus trees, first introduced into this country in the 1850's, has provided a tree that is not only well-suited to sheltering Monarch clusters, but also provides the butterflies with a convenient nectar source since it blooms in winter.

Monarchs cluster in the eucalyptus trees at the Monarch Grove Sanctuary, as well as in eucalyptus groves at Natural Bridges State Park in Santa Cruz, and at the North Beach Campground in Pismo Beach near San Luis Obispo.

After arriving at their destination, the monarchs cluster in large masses to conserve heat.  Their flight muscles do not function well unless the temperature is above 55 degrees.  They rest on the trees, resembling dead leaves, until sunlight warms them enough to fly.

On warm days, the butterflies leave the trees entirely, seeking out nectar sources with which to replenish their energy reserves, but always returning well before evening to once again cluster in the trees.

A female Monarch may lay hundreds of eggs; she deposits these pinhead sized eggs on the underside of milkweed leaves, where they will hatch in 4-5 days, depending on the temperature.

This Aquarium is the 3rd oldest in the United States and has comes with a venerable history in Hawaii.

On March 19, 1904, the "Honolulu Aquarium," as it was referred back then, opened for the first time and was a gift from Mr. and Mrs. Charles Montague Cooke, Sr.

The Aquarium opened with 35 tanks and 400 marine organisms, and the internationally renowned Biologist, David Starr Jordan, proclaimed it as having the finest collection of fishes in the world.  Considered state-of-the-art at that time, the Aquarium received positive comments from such notable visitors of that era as William Jennings Bryan and Jack London.

In 1904, a trolley was built next to the "Queen Kapiolani Park" and the Aquarium was an attraction of the new trolley line.

In 1904, Frederick Potter, a clerk for the Honolulu Rapid Transit Company was transferred and became the Aquarium's 1st director.  Despite his formal training in marine sciences, he was a vigorous supporter of Hawaiian ichthyology and served as Aquarium director until May 1940.

* The Potter's angelfish, Centropyge potteri, was named in his honor.

In 1912, a marine biology laboratory was built next to the aquarium and Dr. Charles Edmondson was the 1st director of this lab.  He was also the first professionally-trained marine zoologist to live in the Hawaiian Islands.

In 1940, Spencer Tinker was appointed the 2nd director of the Aquarium.  He was known for his books on Hawaiian fishes, Pacific crustaceans and other marine life.  He directed construction of a new aquarium building.

* At his retirement in 1973, Tinker's butterfly fish, Chaetodon tinkeri, was named in his honor.

In 1949, construction of a new Aquarium building was started about 100 yards south of the original Aquarium site and was directed by Tinker.

In 1955, the new Aquarium opened as the "Waikiki Aquarium," and included a saltwater well to supply the display tanks.

In 1974, the research function of the Aquarium moved to two new institutions: the Hawaii Institute of Marine Biology (HIMB), and the Pacific Biomedical Research Center.

In 1975, Dr. Leighton Taylor was appointed the 3rd director.  An ichthyologist (branch of the zoo that studies fishes) by training, Taylor was on the U.H. Zoology faculty and understood the need for a new aquarium vision committed to education, conservation and research, and he realized the need to diversify revenue sources.

In 1978, Taylor was responsible for the development of the education department, volunteer program, library, research facility, Aquarium logo, gift shop, Friends of the Waikiki Aquarium (FOWA) and first exhibits master plan.

In 1986, when Taylor departed the Aquarium's present mission statement evolved from his vision of what the Aquarium could become.

* The Waikiki Aquarium was the first aquarium in the world to maintain the chambered nautilus and the first in the United States to breed them.

The Waikiki Aquarium has received several awards for its research and conservation efforts, including:

* 2008 Keep It Hawaii Award.

* 2003 Munson Aquatic Conservation Exhibit (M.A.C.E.) Award.

* 2003 Edward H. Bean Award from AZA for Long Term Tropical Pacific Coral Propagation Program.

Our visits:
In my previous review of the "Honolulu Zoo," I mentioned that we also frequented the "Waikiki Aquarium" in conjunction with the zoo on most of our visits here.  For me anyway, just being on the island is enough but when you have children who have "ants in their pants" lounging around isn't an option!

That's all part of the parenting experience, to enjoy your children grow up.  This aquarium is pretty nice, although small by comparison to others on the "mainland," to have one on an island is pretty unique.

The "Chambered Nautilus" to us was the highlight of the visit and drew the most attention from visitors.  As aquariums go, it was a pleasant and an educational experience from the children's standpoint.
likes: On-site Activities: Unique marine life (Chambered Nautilus)

reviews_attraction.text:
Stow Lake is a "series of attractions" that I have reviewed for Golden Gate Park over the years, either by myself or with my family, during frequent visits into San Francisco.

I have visited this small lake on numerous occasions over the years, mostly just to see the place and how it has changed and just out of plain curiosity.  I have taken many walks along the lakes trail to appreciate the surrounding area and take in the tranquility of the lake.  My favorite hike will always be to Strawberry Hill Island.

Although the lake is small by comparison, it's unique in that it sits in the middle of this iconic park, which a lot of visitors miss unless they have read about it in advance.  This spot has always been a favorite spot to San Franciscans.

Stow Lake is touted as being Golden Gate Park's largest body of water and has been a popular spot for strolling, picnicking, and pedaling around in boats, which can be rented at the boathouse.

The lake has provided San Franciscans with an outdoor escape for more than a century.  The lake offers hiking and bike trails and is a popular destination for visitors looking to engage in active pursuits in the park.

A lazy afternoon may include a rowboat ride across the waters or picnicking, wildlife viewing, and even ghost hunting are also favorite activities of park visitors.

This lake was named after the Gold Rush era, lawyer William Walter Stow, who was a lobbyist for Southern Pacific back when railroad people had a lot of power.

In 1891, the Sweeney's Observatory was built as an elaborate castle like structure, which was actually a vista point back then.  Horse drawn carriages took visitors around the lake and up to the observatory until the great earthquake of 1906.

In 1893, Stow Lake was created and has been a part of Golden Gate Park for more than 11 decades.  The lake was created out of sand dunes by imaginative Park Superintendent, John McLaren and is the largest of Golden Gate Park's lakes.  Massive holes were dug out of the sand, carloads of clay were wheeled in and windmills were built to draw water from natural wells.

The lake has provided the people of San Francisco with a nearby place to escape from their crowded neighborhoods and homes, and enjoy the outdoors.

A boathouse was built along the north shore of the lake and was designed for leisure boating, as a promenade for horse drawn carriages, and as a reservoir for park irrigation.

Both bridges connect the lake shore trail to Strawberry Hill Island, where it follows the shoreline to the hill's summit, the highest point in Golden Gate Park at more than 400 feet.  You can still see the city through the thick groves of trees, but in the 1890s the hill provided sweeping views.

In 1906, the Great San Francisco Earthquake destroyed the Sweeney Observatory.

Today, just as more than 100 years ago, boat rentals allow visitors to enjoy a leisurely day on the water, gliding under the stone bridges and exploring the natural beauty of McLaren's vision come to life.

The more daring visitors of Stow Lake might want to stick around as dusk nears to investigate the legend of the White Lady, who is at the center of a more than 100-year ghost tale.

Free parking is available along Stow Lake Drive.  However, keep in mind that no cars are allowed on John F. Kennedy Drive on Saturdays (April to September) or Sundays (year-round) access is only available then from Martin Luther King Jr. Drive.

The Boathouse is open 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. every day of the week and ready to provide you with a vessel of your choosing.

There is also an on-site café at the Boathouse, which has coffee, sandwiches, or other snack available.

There are numerous picnic tables and BBQ grills to make your day memorable or bring a sack lunch and sit along one of the trails and enjoy the scenery.  The area can also be reserved in advance for birthday parties and other family gatherings.

**In 1854 and despite floods, fires and epidemics, Sacramento became California's Capital.

The city of "Sacramento" started off in the mid-nineteenth century as an expansion from Sutter's Fort.  However, the Fort being some distance away from the Sacramento River which was the main means of transport along the coast of California during that time.

By the 1960s, the area had fallen into such a rundown state that plans were actually made to tear it down to become a part of Interstate 5.  As luck would have it, cooler heads prevailed and a decision was made to modernize the area as an outdoor living history center similar to Colonial Williamsburg in Virginia.  Several of the historically significant buildings were moved or reconstructed and those that were beyond repair were demolished.

Since the 1960's, Old Sacramento State Historic Park or Old Sacramento as it is more commonly referred to has been restored and developed into a significant tourist attraction.  The Old Sacramento Historic District is a U.S. National Historic Landmark District.

Today, with 53 historic commercial structures sited on 28 acres, the Old Sacramento Historic District covers the area between the river frontage and Interstate 5, between I Street and the Capitol Mall.

The State Historic Park comprises about a third of the total acreage of the district including half of the waterfront, a large grassy area and railroad features.  The world-famous California State Railroad Museum sits at the north end of the District.

The majority of the buildings date back to the 19th century and they have "reasonably still kept their original appearance when they were first built."  The buildings have required varying degrees of restoration to restore them to their original state.  Most of these historic buildings now house restaurants, gift shops, or other businesses catering to tourists.

Old Sacramento attracts over 5 million visitors annually and regular events include the Sacramento Music Festival (formerly known as the Sacramento Jazz Jubilee), Gold Rush Days, New Year's Eve parties and events, the St. Patrick's Day Parade, the World Music and Dance Festival and the Mardi Gras.

Here are a few "notable buildings:"
* B. F. Hastings Building, the National Historic Landmarked western terminal of the Pony Express and the first location of the California Supreme Court
* The Lady Adams Building is the oldest non-residential building and is California Historical Landmark No. 603.
* Sacramento Engine Company No. 3, the oldest remaining firehouse in Sacramento
* Old Sacramento Schoolhouse Museum
* The Eagle Theatre, which only survived from 1849 to 1850 but has been reconstructed
* Booth's residence on Front Street was the first governor's mansion after the Mexican-American war.

Our visit:
We have come down to this historic place on numerous occasions over the years and we even stayed aboard the "The Delta King," spending that night sitting outside of our room and eating a "pizza" while watching boaters on the Sacramento River.

There is a lot to see in this "cobble stone town" and a great place to take the family and do a little window shopping while the kids munch on candy from the local Candy Store!

During one of our many visits here, we took the kids on one of the horse and buggy rides around "Old Sacramento" and they had a lot of fun and the price for the rides were quite reasonable in my "opinion."

The Sacramento History Museum tells about the history of the area and how it came to be.  However, my son always enjoys the "War Museum" where he marvels at all the weapons and old uniforms from yesteryear.  Joe's Crab Shack is one of our favorite restaurants to dine after a hard day of touring!  Parking can get to be problematic during some of our visits here, but on this occasion it was an overcast day and parking was a problem

After our amusing visit to the Musée Mécanique (reviewed) on Pier 45, we walked out the back door of the museum which is a "waterfront dock" and you can either go take in another tour or continue on the wharf for some enjoyable cocktails or dining at one of the many sit down restaurants, which our family has come familiar with over the years.

We decided to take a tour of the USS Pampanito (SS-383) which is a World War II, Balao Class Fleet submarine.  This historic submarine also reminded me of our tour on the USS Bowfin Submarine in Honolulu during our most recent visit to the islands in April 2013.

In my opinion, both subs were fundamentally built the same way during that period, in that they were restricted in space with little or no room to maneuver.  Unlike the modern subs of today, these ships weren't equipped with "air conditioning" and from what I've read, got pretty warm, on patrols where you couldn't surface for a long time for fear of being spotted by the enemy.

I wouldn't do well as a submariner as they are affectionately called because of being "claustrophobic."  I think my kids got more out of these outings because of what they symbolized and did during that time period.

After handing over the usual "tourist dollars," but all for a good cause in this instance, we walked on deck and into this "hole" which led downstairs inside of this sub.

Other than feeling like a "mole rat" inside of a tiny hole, it was a great experience and gave you that feeling of what it must have been like to serve as a crew member aboard one of these ships.

Since I like looking into the backgrounds of where we have visited or plan to, this one was no exception and I found the following interesting tidbits:

USS Pampanito was built at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard, New Hampshire and launched in July 1943.

By November 1943, the Pampanito was commissioned and joined the U.S. Fleet.  The Pampanito's crew conducted sea trials and training exercises from November 1943 to January 1944.

After further trials and refinements, the sub arrived at Pearl Harbor, on Valentine's Day, 1944 where she underwent repairs, installations, and repairs to her wooden (lignum vitae) shaft bearings.

Many drills were conducted in the warm waters off the coast of Hawaii in preparation for war time operations.  She was equipped with 16 "Mark 14" steam torpedoes and 8 "Mark 18" electric torpedoes.

On March 15, 1944, USS Pampanito left on her first patrol.

She carried 70 Enlisted and 10 Officers and was equipped with 4" 50 Caliber Main Deck Guns, 40 mm Anti-aircraft, and a 20 mm Anti-aircraft gun.  The Pampanito's patrol usually lasted anywhere from 50-70 Days

During its illustrious career, the Pampanito went on six patrols in the Pacific during World War II and was credited with the sinking of six Imperial Japanese ships and damaged four others.  She was also credited with the rescue of 73 Allied POWs.

She was decommissioned on December 15, 1945 and reclassified as "AGSS-383."  From 1945-1960, the sub was "mothballed," but maintained to be reactivated if needed.  On December 1, 1962, she was then released from the Navy (IXSS-383).

On December 20, 1971, she was transferred over to the Maritime Park Association (formerly the National Maritime Museum Association).  On March 15, 1982 she was officially opened to the public.

The Pampanito draws over 100,000 tourists and locals like myself and is considered to be one of the most popular historic vessels in the country.

15,000 kids a year participate in Pampanito's educational day and overnight programs and the ship is a National Historic Landmark.

Hearst Castle has been transformed over the years, particularly to the construction to the "Visitors Center," which has been significantly enhanced!

In years past, the roads to this place were dirt roads, which is now paved.

This castle also reminded me of my visit to "Castle Neuschwanstein" while I was stationed in Germany.

That too, was a magnificent castle in its own right and off the beaten path.  I've visited many castles during my time, and still amazed at seeing them.

Each castle has its own distinctive way in the way it was built and a truly fascinating story behind them, this one is no exception.

The tours at Hearst Castle have also changed.  In years past (from my own recollections) they were a more lengthy in that you saw a lot more of the interior of the castle.  Now they are shorter and cost more!

Tours can be purchased at the center or on line.  The only shortcomings of coming here is they could sell out depending on the volume of people who show up with reservations made through their "on-line check-in."

The castle opens their doors at 8:00am until 5:00pm closing time.  Arrive early to avoid the huge crowds especially on the weekends and holidays!

We paid for two of the most popular "tours" which was the "Grand and Upstairs Tour."

The "Grand Tour" guides you inside to view the dining and study rooms among others and is the most popular among "first timers."

The "Upstairs Tour" takes you up a series of winding stairs and through hallways to see where the rich and famous stayed during their visits to this castle.  Of course there are other tours that I didn't mention.

Each tour will set you back $25.00 a piece and the tours last 40 minutes.

After purchasing your tickets you're free to roam the center to view their museum which tells you some history about Randolph Hearst and some old artifacts and memorabilia from that era.

There is a large gift shop with souvenir shirts, movies, books, etc. on your visit to the castle.

When tour is announced, a guide will announce boarding and will ask to take your "family or group" photo, which of course they try and charge you at the end for a nominal fee!  We always skip this part.

There are numerous shuttle buses waiting to ferry passengers up the winding road to the castle which is narrated.  We enjoyed our visit!

Dragon's Gate is the "official entrance" to Chinatown, which runs down Grant Street.

On December 5 2020, I visited this iconic city during the "coronavirus pandemic." I wanted to post pictures for others, especially for touristists contemplating a visit to the city by the bay.

This once crowded city is almost a ghost town during the pandemic as depicted in the attached photos (fisherman's wharf).  This once tourist attraction which drew "tens of thousands a day drew fewer than afew dozen or so during my visit." Chinatown has been hit very hard because of the pandemic with shops and restaurants closing their doors for good.  We drove thru this once busseling go to places which sadly was void of the usual pedestrian traffic you would normally see here.

California issued a "Stay @ home order" until 4 January 2021, which means restrictions to hotels, restaurants, attractions, etc., and of course the tourism industry.

"In a nutshell," for tourists coming here, void some of the major attractions, tour of Alcatraz, Pier 39 Aquarium, etc., the scenery of the "Golden Gate Bridge and bay" never gets old.  Dining here has always been great even with "takeout!"  "Yes the ambiance of sitting in the restaurant is absent but the food is very good.

For anyone planning a trip here call ahead because changes occur by the day until this pandemic ends.

Bottom line, it's been a terrible year which we all can attest to but can only get better with the new year and the impending vaccination.  To all my viewers stay safe. take care of one another, and have wonderful trip!

We spent several days here on Lake Shasta in early June before school let out!  We thought it wouldn't be as crowded.......

"WRONG...."

Everyone and their grandmother was down here renting a houseboat for the first week in June.

It took us awhile to load our houseboat, which we were sharing with our friends.  We rented a 12 person houseboat and after splitting the cost several ways, wasn't that bad.  Of course we all brought meals for everyone to share including beverages.

During our trip we wanted to see the much talked about Shasta Caverns.  Ordinarily your fee included the pontoon shuttle over the lake to the entrance of the cave.  There is no road access to this location.

Since we had a houseboat, we just anchored at a nearby beach and walked to the shuttle bus which took us up to the cavern entrance.

The cave itself was very cool and on a hot day was a nice relief.  Our guide was very informative and we learned a lot about the history of this cave.

We saw "stalagtits and stalagmites" and learned about the early explorers who made the initial cave discovery.  Our narrated tour took us up some steeps and narrow passage.  We had a good time and upon exiting the cave had a spectacular view of the lake.

This temple is located 10 miles from Waikiki and depending on traffic congestion can take anywhere from 30-45 minutes.

This attraction is located in the "Valley of the Temples." Parking here is very limited but you can park along the road, just heed the "no parking signs."

It's $5.00 admission for adults & $4.00 for senior's 65+. As you walk across a footbridge you get your first glance at this sacred temple. You also come into view of the temple's giant bell, which you can ring and take pictures.

The "highlight" is the giant buddha inside, which stands out to visiting guests who enter. You must remove your shoes prior to entering the room. The statute itself is the second largest outside of Japan.

There is a "zen garden" which is well manicured and overlooks the large koi pond. For a small fee, you can feed the fish but this also seems to work with the other wildlife.

There is an abundances of wildlife that we encountered during our visit to include, swans, ducks, wild chickens, turtles.

There is a small gift shop, which is located on the grounds and restrooms in the rear.

In closing, everyone is welcome and bring enough cash because there is no ATM machines on sight.
likes: Facilities & Services: Zen garden, Koi pond
Activities: Ringing giant bell, Feeding fish, Wildlife viewing
dislikes: Facilities & Services: Limited parking, No ATM

reviews_attraction.text:
Museums have always fascinated me and during a visit to Sacramento we just happened to see this one while driving through.  What caught our attention was a huge banner of a "Buddha" in front of the building.

On the day of our visit, there was construction taking place and was told that the museum is expanding to accommodate more pieces to its vast collections.

What makes this museum so unique it that it's not located in the heart of the city like most other museums we have visited in the past.  This museum sits near the Sacramento River and originally started off as a home "mansion."

You don't get the sense of how huge this place is until you step foot inside, then your overwhelmed at its immense size.  To see the museum's vast collection of paintings and artifacts was fascinating to say the least.

We enjoyed the Crocker's personal art collections and belongings.  On our tour upstairs, we saw numerous paintings depicting many scenes of California during its early days, paintings of prominent people, the gold rush, and the "Buddha" artifacts.

You would think by having the San Francisco Zoo, it would be enough, but we have another zoo across the bay, which in size, is not as enormous as San Francisco's but I think is just as enjoyable.

It offers residents in the Eastbay easy access for that "zoo fix" in most of us!  I like the easy access from the freeway (Highway 580) and the large parking lot which is in front of the zoo.

With this zoo, you are walking up and down small hills to view the numerous animals but "my favorite part of the zoo has to be the sky-ride."  I believe the San Diego Zoo is the only other zoo in California that is equipped with a "tram-like" ride over the zoo, but this one is a "ski-lift" type of ride, which I think is one of a kind.

The lift takes you over the lion's den and giraffe prairie and gives you a whole new perspective from above!

Another favorite attraction of mine is the meerkat exhibit where in the wild these animals live in large "clans" and to me is just entertaining to watch.

When our in laws came for a visit several years ago, we brought them here as part of their San Francisco tour.  They were impressed that such a garden existed within the city limits and thoroughly enjoyed it.  I don't believe that any of my relatives have ever traveled to the Far East like I have so, this was as close to the "Orient" as it comes.

I think what impressed them the most was how well kept the grounds were and the many flowers throughout the garden.  The day my in laws were in town, the "Cherry Blossoms" had not blossomed.  Although the usual San Francisco "fog" was out in the morning, it quickly burned off by noon time.

The garden's little gift shop which was also remodeled presented that distinctively Japanese style in its architecture and interior design.  Although there were many souvenir items for sale within the store, we just browsed and admired the unique collections they had.

For anyone who resides in California and has never made the stop at this dam or Shasta Lake for that matter, has to!  The drive up to the dam itself is worth the trip and picture taking is not an option here, it's a must.  The views from the dam are breathtaking and to see down the "spillway" from the top is inspiring.

The view of the lake in the background is awesome and in the winter months, the mountains are covered in snow and is another "Kodak Moment."  Other than the summer months, driving up to the dam can get pretty cold and a sweater or even a jacket is advised.

They have a visitor center, which also has the history on the dam with scheduled tours available, although the day we were here, they were closed?  "I can't recall what their explanation was but at the time, I really didn't care because just the walk partway on the dam was enough for us."
dislikes: Cold weather requirement for additional clothing

reviews_attraction.text:
We have visited this fort on previous visits to the San Francisco area and walked among the old "batteries" which still sits here.  Walking on these grounds gave you a sense of what it was like back in the 1900s, when these forts were active around the San Francisco Bay Area.

The old parade ground still exist but a "Children's Museum" (East Road) of sorts has been built on the grounds which we visited while our kids were small.  From the pier, you can see the Presidio, the Golden Gate Bridge, and the rest of the Bay Area when it's not "fogged in."

We also stopped into the "The Marine Mammal Center" which is located off of Bunker Road and along the coast.  This whole area which falls under the Golden Gate National Recreation Area is a wonderful place to take your family to enjoy the views.

If you visit Pearl Harbor, this is one of the memorials you have to visit.  "The Mighty MO" along with the "USS Arizona Memorial" is a must see.  We toured this awesome ship right after our tour of the USS Arizona Memorial and USS Bowfin Submarine.  We arrived early and was lucky to get tickets for the USS Arizona Memorial, but I was smarter and purchased our tickets well in advance for this tour.

To get the opportunity and privilege to tour this living museum was an honor and one that our family with not forget.  To this day, the Missouri continues to serve the public by telling its story for visitors from around the world and it's anchored in a fitting place here at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii.

While traveling south on Interstate 5, we saw a sign for this mission and decided to stop in.  The mission is quite large and has a rich history behind it.  On our first visit, we didn't stop in but a few years later, we actually toured the grounds of this huge estate and was impressed.

From the historic buildings, fountains, and gardens, they were well maintained and plaques told about their origins.  The only drawback on our visit was the crowds that came in droves, like the "swallows" who return every year.  The gift shop which is across the street had some interesting stuff associated with this historic site.

Our family took this journey south to see this museum because we're into military Museums.  The museum building itself is small but it opened up to a huge hanger and outdoor display of numerous aircraft's from WWII to the present.

This was a very nice experience, especially for my son who's into planes.  There were planes insides as well as outside and the SR-71 Blackbird was the highlight of the museum.  We both got a lot out of this museum and left with a deep respect to those who served this country.

On the day we decided to stop into see this lighthouse, before continuing our trip to the Monterey Peninsula for the weekend.  This lighthouse is located along highway 1 and was another place to see a part of the California coast and read about its history.

There really isn't much to see here in the way of a museum but the view of the ocean is amazing and a great place for photos.  Although it was a sunny day for us, we had to retrieve our sweaters because along the coast it can get breezy...

We have traveled all over the world and I have seen this sweet candy in a lot of places that I have visited!  Like having a little bit of treat from home.  Everything that you might wish you had for your sweet tooth is inside of this store.  There is a small cafe and wonderful exhibits of famous people.  The tour is very informative but the treats at the end is better.

Grew up fishing from this pier and enjoyed the company of other fishermen.  Although catching and landing a fish was easy from the pier, it was still alot of fun.  I was even lucky enough one year to see the whales migrating.

The Denver Downtown Aquarium is an excellent, high quality aquarium. There are a lot of variety of fish, with a highlight on North American species and even Colorado native species. There are a few sharks. The surprising part was that they have 3 tigers - I'm really not sure why the tigers are here and not the zoo. The indoor exhibit seemed a little small for a 3 full sized tigers - although we only saw one out. There is a really cool flash flood zone with live water and thunderstorm effects. At the end there is an area where you can touch stingrays! I would definitely recommend coming here with a family - it's great for small kids. There is also a restaurant here and you can host events here as well.

This is an amazing museum to visit in Detroit - especially if you're a Wayne county resident because the visit is free for you! I haven't been to the DIA since I went on a field trip when I was in elementary school, and I was pleasantly surprised because it is much bigger that what I remember. I believe there was an expansion done relatively recently. I did not get to see the whole museum, but from what I saw they seem to have a lot of variety. There is also a beautiful cafe in an indoor courtyard, where you can come just to hangout or do work. I would guess it takes maybe 4-5 hours to go through the whole museum. I would definitely recommend visiting the DIA!

This seems to be a really interesting art museum that showcases art focused on the fusion of native american and traditional western american art. I visited on a Saturday in the beginning of April 2021, which is soon after it reopened due to the Coronavirus lockdowns. Unfortunately it seemed that more than half the museum exhibits were closed or under renovation, which means I would come back for more. It took me about 45 minutes to casually and calmly view the 3 exhibits. There is not much to do or see here for young kids currently, but I imagine that will change once exhibits reopen. I would wait on visiting here until everything is open again.

This is a really cool area to check out any time of the year. During the summer they have some games and even concerts. I actually came during Christmas time when all the decorations were up. The ice skating rink is a little small and can get crowded but definitely a fun experience. The Christmas tree is beautiful and is always decorated nicely. There is also a section with some really nice small shops to buy some great gift items, clothing, and even sweets. A little further down a tent set up called is a very elaborately decorated bar with tons of board games (Jenga, Chess, Checkers) where you can hangout!

This is a wonderful public park along the Pacific Ocean. There is a nice Boardwalk to walk along with really cool educational signs that help explain the habitat of this watershed area. There was plenty of wildlife when I went including maybe 10 different types of birds, and I also saw signs that mentioned that during different times of the year there are a specific type of fish breeding in this area. It seems that the parking was free? Maybe this is because I came on a Sunday, or because of the pandemic. Bottom line is that this is a fun family friendly place to visit. It is also a very hot surfing spot.

Warning - you will have no service or will likely be roaming the whole time you're in the Death Valley park. This means be prepared with maps and download your plans before you get into the area. The park is a really great experience, all of the roads are well maintained and the locations are clearly labeled. I came here with my family and February and the temperature was in the 60s, and cool in places like Dante's point - so bring a light jacket during this time of year. There aren't many options for food so make sure you plan your visit with snacks and bring lots of water!

One of the most popular tourist attractions in Los Angeles. I think word is starting to get out but it is possible to hike to the top of the sign for free! You can follow a paved path all the way from the park at the base of the mountain. It is a wonderful and relatively easy hike for beginners and worth every step for the epic view of LA from the top. I would come either early before it gets too hot or in the evening before the sun sets. Just a heads up, there is a no drone zone all along the hike so don't lug one all the way up there to be disappointed you can't fly it!

What a wonderful work of art that nature has placed here for us! This portion of the Garden of the Gods is really cool, especially because of the information boards that are posted. Apparently this was privately owned property back in the days and you had to pay money to get admission just a view and take photos with this Balanced Rock. I'm glad that they decided to make it a public place, do your tax dollars pay for this. It is very easy for all ages to climb around here, just be careful because falling on the rocks wouldn't be fun. Wonderful to visit all year round.

I was surprised to find this so close to home in Westlake Village. I saw a bunch of baseball fields and a large area to practice I think football. There is also a YMCA which I think it is closed due to Coronavirus. However behind the fields I noticed that there are a few different trails that you can go hiking on, they are actually open right now and I did not get a chance to go very far on one but it seems like a really nice hike. I will definitely be back to check it out!

What a breathtaking view from this point! There's a wonderful small hike that takes you to the top of the peak, which gives you a great 360 degree view of the area. You can look down into badwater Basin in Death Valley, and look across to the other mountain range. It seems that it is at least 10 to 20 degrees cooler here than Death Valley itself. I would definitely recommend to 13 Mile Drive to get to here cast for The View even if you spend 15 to 20 minutes here.

This is a great museum, which seemed geared towards younger audiences - middle and elementary school kids. I came here on a day the museum was free and had a good time, it is very large so you can definitely spend an entire day here. I was there for about 3 hours. I would not say that the planetarium is worth it, it was essentially a pretty old video playing on a dome screen. The exhibits are well thought out and very fun to view.

Unfortunately The Visitor Center was closed by the time I can visit it oh, I wish that the hours were more accurate and updated on Google Maps. Google Maps says it's open 24 hours which it definitely is not however it was under construction when I had visited so I don't anticipate that it was open at all. I wonder when it is going to reopen. I've added some photos of the informational signs that we're outside of the building.

I came here on a Saturday evening and it was very very crowded. There are a lot of people just walking around without wearing masks and not really respecting your distance, so I would come here during non-peak hours. However the sunset from the pier is beautiful I've attached a photo for your reference. There are definitely a good variety of shops and restaurants right near the pier as well as the Lifeguard headquarters.

It was pretty busy on a Wednesday night at around 7pm, so it was very difficult to find parking surprisingly. Despite this, the park is so big that it was not at all crowded. There are a lot of nice trees and the grass is well kept. It's a great place to go for a walk or even to bring your dog so he or she can run around freely! I saw a few picnic tables too - this is definitely a cool place to come for a picnic.

The Garden of the Gods is a wonderful natural landscape that is a must visit! There are an excellent number or easy trails along the car path that you can walk around to take in the beautiful views. The visitor center is excellent with some great exhibits and paintings to educate you and your family about the natural history of the landscape. This is a great visit at any time of the year and fun for all ages!

This is a wonderful ISKCON temple, with a great location in Laguna Beach. They have recently restarted the regular Sunday lecture and prayer. Unfortunately there were many people inside that were not wearing a mask, but there is enough space for you to keep your distance. Parking can be tough as there is no dedicated parking, but it is relatively easy to find metered parking or street parking nearby.
dislikes: Facilities & Services: Lack of dedicated parking

reviews_attraction.text: This is a really incredible view to come watch the sunset. From one side of the lookout you can see Topanga Canyon, on the other side is Malibu and the ocean. If you climb up to the peak that is nearby you can see Santa Monica Palos Verdes and even the Catalina Island in the distance. Are all so informational post put up to explain all the Peaks. Wonderful piece of nature to explore!

This is an absolutely beautiful Temple located in the middle of Malibu. It has been open during the COVID-19 lockdown for socially distanced darshan, as the deities are kept outside. It has not been crowded on any of my visits and it is very peaceful. This is a must visit Temple in LA for anyone. All people are welcome to check it out, no need to be Hindu or even Indian!

Unfortunately despite planning to come to the top of this mountain, we couldn't make it because the road up to the top closed before 3 p.m. I don't think the hours are very accurate on Google Maps and could not find the actual hours to post an update the times. If you want to make it out to the Top, early and call ahead! I imagine the view from the top is breathtaking.

Wonderful green area in the middle of downtown Plymouth to come and hangout with friends or family. The fountain is always great to visit in the summers, beware there tend to be a lot of mosquitos because of the water I suspect. There is usually (once COVID-19 eases up) something going on during the weekends so check the downtown Plymouth website to make sure.

This is a great Overlook along the Garden of the Gods Road. You can stop here and walk around to climb around the rocks and enjoy the view of the mountains in the distance. I posted some photos of the view and some of the information signs that were in this area. It is very safe and good for all ages to experience. It is also wonderful at any time of the year.

Fenway park is a classic American ballpark. I've been to 5 or 6 games here and I am always super excited to go and love the atmosphere on game day. The stadium is well kept, clean, and is easy to get into and out of. The food isn't as pricey as it could be and all of the fams are respectful (enough). If you have a chance to go to a red sox game, take it!!

This is a really cool area to come to hang out with your family and friends. It's an excellent area for a picnic or even to go on a hike. The old Zoo structures and cages are all still there oh, some of them are even open so that you can go in and take some really cool pictures. I would definitely recommend bringing your friends are family here!

This is an amazing place to visit for a great view of Topanga, Woodland Hills, And the Warner Center area. There is also a great road to the water tower across the street which leads to some epic trails. I'm posting a photo of a swing - it's withing a 15 minute walk from here. Can you find it? I'm hoping you enjoy this scavenger hunt!

I am an alumni for University of Michigan and every time I come back to campus I have to stop throigh this museum. The temporary exhibits are always top notch! I would definitely recommend. Plus the admission is free and you can donate whatever you want!!

Kayaking fun all over this area. Many people choose to just hang out around the beach area which is cool, it's just that it is at the side of Gandy. I frequently kayak the north Weedon trail from here, and on low tide days we explore around the power plant as I've had encounters multiple times with manatees, dolphins, and sting Rays. When I've been about a mile off from shore I've seen large amounts of some type of jelly fish around the kayak.

An old classic for me, as I grew up in the Kalamazoo area, and I can remember going here back when they use to have a rocketship you could climb within.
Like in the past, this is still a great park for a visit. There is plenty of walking area, bridges, streams, and at least one playground for kids. I have been to many parties at this park as well, which it is also great for!

Amazing experience going up and down this river. On a single occasion I've ever seen an otter here!
Lot's of tubers and a good amount or boats as well. It's second favorite spring I've been to, Weeki Wachee my first, but it's still a 5 star as it is totally worth your time to stop here.

One of, if not my favorite walking park in Pinellas county. Great trails that are well maintained, have water stations and benches throughout the trails, and a great bird sanctuary. Every time I've been I've seen little gators as well from the walking bridges off of the yellow trail.

I haven't visited all, but I've been to many of Pinellas county parks, and this is my favorite. Great trees, lots of Spanish moss, elevation throughout the park makes it more engaging visually. Highly recommended spot here. Room for everyone too it seems, with many pavilions.

Excellent park, but be prepared for a hike(1.5 miles) to get close to the lower falls. There is viewing right away by the gift shop though. Beautiful spot,and I'd say the best way to go would likely be to rent a boat.
Barely had service on my Verizon service, 1 bar.

I've only been once, but I walk by often. I just think it is about as perfect of a spot it could be in, and the exhibit I went to was fabulously setup and organized. Clean building inside that is good sized, but not a mammoth like other museums can be.

I enjoyed my visit here, but I didn't plan enough time. There are hundreds of letters and stories from people there during the Holocaust, and from survivors that moved on. Fascinating, but if you like reading you'll need at least 2 hours here.

Very cool park, that has many tables lakeside to sit with your group and grill up a meal on their charcoal grilles.
We enjoyed the views on the walking trails there and got to see many alligators in the lake near the safe picnic table areas.

Such a great place, and a St Pete long time attraction. Make sure to plan an hour plus for here if you want to read about you are looking at in terms of trees, and plants. Exceptional spot to go walk around when the weather is 75 or below.

One of, if not the best kayak trails in the area. This place is a favorite not only for the trail, but because this launch is so nice, and there is a wash station and a bathroom right here as well. Highly recommended for kayaking here!!

Great place for a walk. The banyan trees being the highlight of the walk. I suggest morning walks when the sun is coming up, as it makes the lake that much more pretty when looking from the west side.
Great campground, actually kind of surprising how nice it is for being so close to a big'ish city. Look to try and get a spot on the water, they make sleeping pleasant, even in warmer temperatures.

Speaking from a kayaking stand point this is one of my favorite spots in the Tampa Bay area to do so.

Many spots to do so, with lots of wildlife on most of my journeys here. Highly recommended!
One of our favorite areas, in the Tampa Bay area to kayak. Beach front, little islands to cruise around out back, and close to Fort De Soto as well. Great bird watching as well, of course! :-)

Nice beach with easy access. Not perfect as you need to pay to park, and it is usually busy on nice days or during "season."
Good little snack shak between the parking lots.
Great smaller, local resort. I had a pass here for multiple years while living in Reno. The chutes were also one of my favorite snowboarding spots in all of Lake Tahoe.
Great park for what it is. There is some trash here, which isn't cool, but overall it's a great place to take an easy hike. Most times here I've seen some gators.
I've only used the place for a kayak launch, but it is a nice location, but no kayak wash. Conveniently close, walking distance from awesome downtown Dunedin.
The place looks and feels like a jungle on the disc-golf course. We also use the park for launching our kayak, and it is a very nice Pinellas county park.

Amazingly beautiful, but you'd better come early to get a parking spot!
Great Rock hopping from this large to other smaller beaches southbound.
Try to get here early if you want to guarantee a parking spot. Other than it being a little small, and busy, it is a great launch location.
Excellent local park, both for exploring their hiking trails or their kayaking routes. Nice, quiet place with lots to see.
Cool spot to visit, with some very old artifacts. Was under construction when visited, but was still worth our time.
Very pretty picnic area. There are grilles here for those looking for a great spot to do a picnic cookout.

Lot bigger than I thought. I walked around the entire park in a few hours but it was a pleasent walk. I have done some fishing at the lake as well but I've never caught anything yet or seen anyone catch anything so I wouldn't recommend fishing here. Maybe they should stock it better.  There is a stream nearby as well  for more experience anglers and you may possibly have some luck there.

Nice hike along the river with plenty of other trail options and varied terrain to keep you coming back for a new adventure. I walked along the river to the waterfall trail and had a good time and I woukd gladly do it again or recommend it to anyone who needs recommendations.

Cool little there and back hike. Very well maintained. Would recommend this short hike for some neat falls. Was not crowded and if you wanted you could see more of the area if you continued! Also some local history around the area such as a kilm

After living in Pittsburgh for 4 years I found a cold winter days and I went! I'm mad at myself for not going sooner! They have great art to look at and admire as well as a thorough scientific exhibits. I'll be back soon to check out more of it!

One of the nicest parks in Pittsburgh. Lots of things to see and hidden trails. Usually crowded but there is plenty of room. Can be noisy near the bridge but you can walk or run or bike all the way to the Monogolia River at Duck Hollow.

Flat patch of grass that turns into a sunbathing area once it get warm. Very nice view of the fountain at Frick and the cathedral with food and a carousel on the side. Has a large tent for actives and to escape the rain

Nice clean park with views of round valley reservoir in the winter. Went here with my dog and we had a good time. There are options to to walk down to the water as well. Be prepared for long up hills and downhills.

Busy since it was the first nice day of the year. It's expansive with all types of trails and activities such as dog parks and an outdoor stage. I enjoyed my walk here and would go again if I was in the area

Very nice clean and easy to see trail guides. Lots of things to see and although the parking lot may be full it isn't too crowded ok the trials. Big boulders to climb on as well that allows for a lot of fun
Playgrounds, pavilions, and the hiking trails. Nice place to bring the family or go for a hike or bike ride. There's also easy access to the river from here that has a nice current to enjoy
It's a canal trail so flat with nice views of the river. Loud place because of the cars but nice and I recommend this for biking or walking but if you want to hike go somewhere else.
This area is owned by rich doctors and professors around Pittsburgh as well as some Pitt university property. Nothing much to see but it's a peaceful walk if you're in the area
Nice area to hike with historical landmarks with detailed signs along the hike! Not a ton of trails but there is a really nice walk along the river to enjoy
Cathy is the best building in town and simply amazing it feels like Hogwarts on the inside. A must visit for anyone in the area or visiting Pittsburgh
Well maintained with a nice little pond with well marked trails. I recommend hiking to the top of heartattack hill for a nice view during the winter.
Small but pretty. All of the main trails are well maintained but some of the smaller ones aren't. Not that much to see if you're a fan of hiking.
Nice trails with a constant view of the creek. Rocky so bring good shoes. Went here with my girlfriend and we had lunch and had a good time.
Nice trail with an overlook that makes it worth the hike as well as cool boulders and you really can see the steel tower from the overlook
Clean and well kept. Went camping for an overnight and enjoyed it immensely because of the clear and well maintained camp areas
Nicest MLB stadium in the world. You can see that river and here the city and every seat gives a nice view of the game
Small park in the middle of Coronado that had tables for picnics and plenty of shade compliments from the large trees
Great rivers and hiking trails to explore. Be warned Kim trail is covered in Wood nettle. Overall a great experience.
Yoy can watch surfers here or just take in the beach. Can be busier than expected depending on the time of day
Great hiking and look outs, walk down the stairs about a quarter miles north to get up close to the rapids
Fences surround the park for safty but you have a nice view of the lake. Plenty of stoves for a picnic

The trail goes longer but at around the horses near Galaxy View Park I think at around there i circled back. On the way back I took the the top dirt trail. I tend to walk most of the time and sprint uphill action 20-30% of the time so this was great. You also get a better view of the valley and the nature preserve. I wish I would of took the uphill rugged route instead cause there's not as much people, bikes. You gotta be carefull with other runners with headphones  bikes, etc. sometimes. If you’re listening to music make sure you’re not blasting cause bikers will often give you a heads up when they’re approaching behind you. Great place to bring the whole family, for sure.

Heisler park is one of the main attractions to see when visiting Laguna Beach CA. Wether your just dropping by to see the sunset or spending the day BBQ hanging out at one of the benches. Some people even setup hammocks. You can walk along the path on the cliffs about 30ft drop safe enough for the most part. There's some  beach entrances I think 2 or 3 you can walk down. The water is so blue looks really good in the summer and winter months. If you keep walking south you can some of the best food in the OC at Las Brisas if not keep walking to Main Beach Park.

Mission San Juan Capistrano is a must with a similar feel to the ones up north with the rolling green hills. The experience is pretty awesome if you you park on the historic neighborhood side on the other side of the tracks. Plenty of parking, for sure. On your navigation it will suggest it for parking, just accept it will take you there. It can get packed when crossing to the mission. I’ve been here twice and there was places i didn't see last time. The ponds are really cool with carp fish.

Great place to go for a quick run whether you're looking to run east or west this parks trails will take you there. One cool thing about Hart Park is the trail that goes under glassell st and the 22 bride on over to Santiago Park in city of Santa Ana. I highly recommend taking someone with if u decide to take that trail. Towards the back of the park I love the uphill action towards the football field. The park is always being maintained by groundskeepers. Ideal location for BBQ.

Parking here to get to Mission San Juan Capistrano was pleasantly swell. Sometimes there's events at the mission like weddings so parking can be trough around there. Cool trail comes back from the other side of the tracks. There's a playground and a winnery look picnic area of type. Iit was a cool experience to go thru you really take in the hills and the stretch of railroad leading into the horizon. Something smells really good on one of the trains I think it was the red one.

Top of the world park is an amazing drive to get there and hike, with perfect terian for sprint uphill action and down hill. There’s trails for bikes but you do get bike persons here or there. The trail goes on for a while. I think I went down one mile or somewhere around there. I got a good workout.This trail is populated so you it's perfect if you just wanna get in a quick run/hike at most of time of day I would think. Please check park rules for more info.

CastAways park has a really long paved walk along the cliff. There’s a really cool war memorial up on along the of the cliffs. I decided on coming here in the early am at around 8am’ish. Not only did I find a good place to run, I also found somewhere to watch people rowe and even do some canoe fishing. Just a great spot to park and send a couple of emails before getting casting a few. Look forward to taking an early day from work to come here.

Cool little spot to enjoy a view from a cliff (protectesd by rails of course) Crescent Bay Point Park is not too big however, it's good enough to watch the sunset as it gives you a vantage point to see most of Laguna Beach. Parking is free as long as you park along residences nearby. Please be mindful and not block gates and drive ways for locals.

Santiago Oaks part lives up it's name, for sure. Multi-level trails give this park a A rating not to mention the beutiful view that extend to the city to Irvine park accords the way. Please keep in mind to stay on the trails as there are many dangers. You will get a great experience and even a view of the aqueduct dam thing. Take water.

Laguna Niguel lake is a nice strech of land that follows the lake with multiple views from the lake and up above the hill. Great for fishing with cleaning stations and even an amphitheatre in the back. The nature element is awesome. All that area is just beautiful for hanging out BBQ riding bikes, it's just awesome!

Main beach is a true gem located in the heart of Laguna Beach. You have the 133 and 1 joining with people and a lot going on at any given period. The city does a good job of keeping things moving and keeping the public safe. You can head North up to Las Brisas or head back down south for more restaurants and shops.

Vista park is awesome park with a great view of the Huntington beach. There's a gang of squirrels around all over the place. Pretty neat to see them running around getting close to you. This is a good place for a quick picnic better on the weekdays. Weekends are moderately full bit you should be good.

Parking is pretty straight forward right next to the pier. I really enjoy walking or jogging out the wedge from the pier its a good half hour walk one way. I like coming out here early for runs and walk along the beach for sure. Lots of nearby shops nearby plenty of places to rent bikes and scooters.

Peters canyon has the scenic views and hikes that really challenge you. The hill inclines are incredible one trail with multiple routes. The trail takes you from Tustin to Orange. No matter time of the year bring some water. I'm very fortunate to live nearby! You can bike run and some ride horses.

I really enjoyed this trail definitely gives you options on how to start and end. You can start off going uphill or going around to the right near the 405 which I'm not a fan of cause you want to take in nature not see cars zoom by. I really prefer going up and then back up when its flat.

Really cool place to park send some emails as are many parks in this area. The memorial is pretty cool. I didn’t take the walk down as it appears it leads to John Wayne's Yacht which I still haven’t found! I take a lot of these roads to steer away from the congestion at times on the PCH.

Good trail takes you out to Peter's canyon. Great spot to come out to. The times I've gone, it's been pretty chill and not too congested. I really like some of the benches near the trees. Good places to have a quick picnic. I don't remembered if they have grills out for public use.

Worked around here for around 3 years. The whole walk down Old Town thru Orange Plaza Squre Park at around lunch is always Popping. When I first came out here to interview from out of state I was hoping so far I could work in such a magical city. I love this place!

I got married here way back in 2014. Decided to walk thru on my lunch break when I was serving jury duty. It really brought back many memories and the place looks just like it did then. Also, fun fact this is one of the filming spots for legally blonde

Aliso beach has great parking options and plenty of beach for everyone. I personally like the south side due to it being secluded. The long stretch of beach is ideal for a good run. Also right at the entrance they have a park right next to the bridge.

I love how Laguna Beach had many of these little parks than sometime serve as a private viewing of the sunset or just escape PCH to maybe just chill and watch the ocean. There is also a place to sit if you're tired of walking. Love the view from here.

Cool little spot walking distance from Old Town Orange. I sometimes come here to read or just chill and catch some rays on some cement benches. Small park on the corner. A really chill spot to come hang in the AM.

Went here for a team builder event with our company. We had a small team and even though we didn't know each other really good (i.e. most of us worked remote) we really had a good time. I miss those days!
Really nice place to hang out! I tend to go early on the day as it tends to get packed at night. There is plenty of seating along with a glass area.
Great hike connected to Peters canyon hike. You have some many options as far as uphill action to just inclined kind of a hike.

Took the boat tour to Boca Chita Key. To book the tour, I had to call the bookstore. I managed to get 2 tickets for the 1:30 pm tour. I must say I found the Dante Fascell Visitor Center and the adjoining area quite charming. The visitor center itself requires some TLC, the elevator had lots of dust and leaves and restroom was a mess.There is ample place to sit around the marina and near the parking lot. The visitor center has a little museum and theater. Boca Chita Key was simple amazing. Visitors can go up the lighthouse for an amazing view. Visitors can also go for a quick swim as well.

Visited as the tide was coming in. On the way back had to wade across water to make it back to land. Good views from the lighthouse. They are so good, my wife and I forgot about the tide. We were busy taking in the view and taking pictures. While walking back got a surprise when the path disappeared and was submerged. I would say we had to wade through about 1 feet of water. This was around 11 am. After seeing us, several others made the journey to the lighthouse even though the path was submerged.

I love aviation museums and I wasn't going to pass on an opportunity to see another 1. There are 2 hangars with wonderful old birds and in between the two hangars there are several exhibits as well.as usual there is a lot to learn and take in while visiting this place. One nice fact I learned was when Apollo modules splashed into the ocean,  the recovered modules were placed in one of the hangars each time the modules returned to earth.

This is next door to Biscayne. They have a restaurant which I thought was overrated. They have a huge parking lot and the cost for entry to the park is $5. This is not a National Park and national park passes don't work here. They have a swimming hole which should be good for children though it seemed dirty to me. Visitors can play volleyball ball here. I think it is a good complement for Biscayne next door.

This is one amazing place. There are several places to visit that provide ample opportunities to take breathtaking photographs. There are several hikes and the vast majority of them are not strenuous. You can just drive from point to point in your car as well. Parking spots can be tough to find at some places. The gift shop at the visitor center is huge and has a wide array of things that can be purchased.

They have a large collection of paintings along with some pottery and ceramics as well. As is the case with several museums they have rotating exhibitions. This museum is also part of NARM. Since I am a member of the fine arts museums of San Francisco, my wife and I get free admission here. There is ample paid parking outside. After visiting the museum visitors can stroll by the waterfront.

We did not manage to get pre reserved tickets so we had to avail of the walk in tickets. We managed to get onto the 9:15 tour. An NPS boat takes you to the memorial and visitors have to return on the next boat. There is sufficient time to spend in the memorial. I maybe wrong but It appears as if the sunken ship might still be leaking oil.

The volunteers are the most amazing people and are very passionate. Depending on the weather the missile hatch may or may not be   opened. I have been here twice. The second time it was raining and since they couldn't open up the entire missile complex they showed us another section on radio communications.

There is an extensive collection of pottery, painting and even masks among other things. As is customary with most museums they have rotating exhibitions. At present there is an exhibition on prints by Frank Stella. Don't forget to go to the observation tower for amazing views of San Francisco.

As we were strolling along Duval Street my wife and I just happened to notice that the church was open. The church was empty with just a few people. It felt great to be be able to pray inside; it felt serene. Visitors can also light candles and leave a little donation as well.

This is great picnic spot. There is a nice beach. There are great views of Chinaman's hat as well as mountains from the park. It is actually possible to walk most of the way from the beach to Chinaman's hat by wading through water. I saw quite a few people attempting this.

Great place to visit and an amazing place for a stroll. The entire area along with the Old Sacramento Historic Park,museums and the river walk is a great place to spend a weekend with the family. Just be a little careful of the homeless people once it gets dark.

I has a very pleasant experience on this submarine. To start, I didn't have to pay the entrance fee since I am a member of NARM. They provide little IPODS for the Audio tour which is very Informative indeed. For a vessel so old, it is in very good condition.

The check in process was slow. The sail itself was fun. They take you out and then along the Waikiki beach. Good views of Waikiki and Diamond head. We saw some turtles as well. Drinks are available on board. Overall a fun experience.

Beautiful little church. Paintings inside the church are exquisite. The views from the church are amazing. There are clear views of the ocean from the church. There is a graveyard associated with the church as well.
The building is so well maintained. The lawns are so fabulous. The cats strolling around are an absolute joy. There is a gift shop where books can be purchased. The furniture inside is exquisite.
Stopped here on the way to Las Vegas. There   is a fountain and the park is well maintained. The day we went everything was closed inside the park so couldn't learn more about the place.
Been to this place twice. It is an amazing experience. There are several pullouts. Park the car and take a stroll in the woods among giant redwood trees.
Nice hike to the seal overlook. Ensure that you get a permit from the visitor center before you embark on the hike. There is a gift shop as well.
An amazing place to spend a couple hours. I have been here twice and have taken friends and family along with me. Everyone enjoyed the exhibits.
I loved the hike. I hiked all the way to midnight falls. Please be aware there are exactly 224 stairs to climb to get to the top of the falls.
This is one of the first viewpoints on 17 mile drive if you enter from monterrey. Every point provides a different perspective.
A good quiet place to sit and gaze at the bay. There are several places to sit. Doesn't attract a lot of crowd
Last year or so the place is messy because of a lot of construction. Otherwise a great place to hang around.
The trails are flat. The views are ok. Overall it is not as good as the Garden of the Gods.

Balboa Island Ferry is a short ride; affords a nice view of the area as well as quick access between two beautiful areas, Balboa Island and the Newport Peninsula, both very gorgeous areas. I like to ride the Ferry to feel the cool breezes of the water and take in the fresh air.

I like both Balboa Island and Newport but I feel much more at home in Newport as the people there are more approachable for me... Newport Peninsula has a special Beach town atmosphere  with a generous portion of party town vibing.

Newport Peninsula is the larger of the two areas. It has great Oceanfront sandy beaches that stretch north and south for over one mile. Also, Newport has two of SoCals nicest piers. Newport is well known for its many great restaurants, bars, pubs, coffeehouses, Marina's, parks, a great lengthy boardwalk, shopping of every sort, sports center, recreation, an amusement park, boat excursions, fishing, the bay and much, much more. All of this is a must visit when you are in this area. Also very close to Newport Beach and a million things to discover.

Balboa Island has a lot to offer also. It has a very nice business area which extends several blocks. The shopping is upscale and plenty of options. The Islands restaurants are popular; also lots of places for treats, coffees, teas, ice cream, for your pleasure. Homes on the island are generally very nice although the properties are very small... well, this is SoCal.

This small Ferry ride is a must for the memories and is great for taking photos. Remember the Ferry connects two of SoCal's great areas to visit, Newport Peninsula and Balboa Island. Both areas are fantastic to visit! Or maybe you will decide to buy a home there... you are worth the best!

I have visited this area several times in the last year. I like it!

Don't forget the weather is great all year round!

A very good day to you!

The Humbolt Redwoods area is one of the most beautiful places I have ever visited. To walk/hike/drive through this gorgeous area is like living in a dream. I recommend that you go for some of the hiking trails. As you hike through the beautiful forest you feel like a very tiny ant-sized creature; the redwood trees are hundreds of feet high (Avenue of the Giants) dwarfing everything else in the forest. They are so tall (up to 350ft) that often you can't see the top of these impressive trees. Some of them are thousands of years old. Some have survived fires. Some have been struck but lightning but recovered or had new growth atop the severed base. You will be thoroughly amazed at the story and drama of Humbolt.

There are many great walking paths and hiking trails which afford you great access to the special beauty and spectacle of this nature preserve. Please take your best camera, you will be glad you did! One tree cut in half by a lightning strike about 100 feet above the ground had four trees growing out of the remaining 100ft base (I named that phenomenon, "treeth").

The locals are friendly; they are very creative with wood carving (they live in a world class Forest). Be sure to visit some of the artful souvenir shops in Humbolt. You can find great gifts or something for yourself as a keepsake.

On that note, one of the trees in this park is so large that there is a souvenir shop in the hollowed out trunk interior (some of these giant trees get hollowed out by natural fires. Many of these trees are so huge they actually suppress fire and survive.

Humbolt is a feel good adventure waiting for you to experience the awesome.
