Oh my! The seats were so comfy and it wasn't as crowded as I expected. Such a neat experience I would recommend if anyone has the time for a movie with visiting the stars!
I loved my experience all around here. The lines were quick, the shows were great, service was super helpful, and the animals were amazing. I would love to come back!!
This is such a beautiful vineyard with an amazing selection of wines. The staff is very friendly, and this is a must stop if you’re on a wine tour in the area.
Such a great place to visit to take a look at the past. It's a neat free tour that I would recommend even with kids if you have a couple free hours!
This forest is so beautiful and has so many trails to try and things to see. There's an endless number of routes to travel. Totally breathtaking!
Gorgeous place for a hike!  Not too difficult, but don't go after it's been raining for a while. It was flooded when I went in the spring.
This is such a neat museum to bring older kids and go with friends or family. The pricing is reasonable and there’s a lot to see!
Such a great place for a day trip checking out all the shops and sights! Apple fritters would be my top recommendation!
Gorgeous year round hiking in this area! The scenery is beautiful and the trails are well marked and easy to follow.
Awesome park with a lot of space and a great playground. There’s also plenty of great parking all around the park.
I love coming here! Such a great natural area to take a breath of fresh air and enjoy the outdoors. Breathtaking!

The year 1704 brought an end to the peaceful village that originally stood here. In that year Col. James Moore of Carolina brought a small army of colonial militia and a much larger mixed force of allied First Peoples from different tribes to bring the Spanish colonial system to an end here. The invaders both sought slaves and an end to further Spanish expansion in the region. While the numbers remain in dispute, at least a thousand or more Apalachee were carried off into slavery with another thousand forced to immigrate under threat of enslavement. What you see here is a re-creation of what the village and fort are thought to have looked like.

I grew up in Tallahassee in the 70's and 80s and as a child who visited on a school field trip there was nothing here but an outline of where the council house had stood (it had been excavated), an open field and a monument or two. It was quite a shock to return for a visit a decade ago and find all this built.

It is a special place as well because I brought my father here a few times in his final years---one of his best friends and mentors was the chief blacksmith of the site. And when my father passed away five years ago my family held my father's celebration of life here in the conference center. The staff were extremely helpful and supportive and we gave my father a great send off.

As you visit the site imagine it as it was and how it was the single largest Spanish/native village and population center outside Pensacola and St. Augustine. Much of the remainder of northern Florida remained wilderness with scattered villages of various native peoples spread throughout. Only tiny vestiges of native peoples inhabited central and southern Florida.

You cannot really tell it from the tree cover today---back then it would have been largely cleared of trees for construction and for planting crops---but the site sits atop one of what are call the seven hills of Tallahassee. The Florida capitol sits atop another. You get some sense of the height from the photo showing the view looking straight down the site's dirt road to the modern W. Tennessee Street/HWY 90.

Being an outdoorsman trapped in NYC I love Palisades Park. However, unlike probably 99.9% of visitors I only get there by human powered watercraft, either a paddleboard or sea kayak. I generally depart from my home port of Manhattan Kayak + SUP (MKC) located on Pier 84 across the embayment from the Intrepid Sea Air & Space Museum (USS Intrepid) in Hells Kitchen. This is, at a minimum, a 14 mile round trip. I generally prefer to go farther and most recently (see accompanying photos) paddled to Greenbrook Falls within Greenbrook Sanctuary over the Palisades from Tenafly, NJ. Paddling there from MKC and back is a 25 mile roundtrip. To get there from within the park on foot or by bicycle you will have to follow one of the roads to a trail that gets you to the Shoreline Trail. The only complaint I have about Palisades Interstate Park is the lack of camping facilities, especially for through paddlers on their way somewhere else. This is not an issue for those with cars or even bicycles as they can get back to the main road and either go home or find lodging. The through paddler, on the other hand can be stuck unless they have made other arrangements. For example I tried last year, in vain to get in touch with park HQ to get special permission. No one ever got back to me. So instead I planned my trip and eventually showed up at Alpine. A friendly day camp counselor gave me the direct line to the assistant park administrator who squirmed but ultimately refused my request. Luckily I'd made arrangements with the lovely folks across the river at the Yonkers Canoe Club.

I have long loved this park, for multiple reasons. My favorite aspect of it is that it has some of the last natural forest left in Manhattan. Forest that has not been developed and then altered into a park the way Central Park, Union Park, Madison Square Park all are. Another aspect and probably the most important to me are the old growth trees to be found here. You just don't find them anywhere else on the island. Then there are its links to the First Peoples. The Indian Caves and several sites around Inwood provided meeting places, and hunting and fishing camps for Lenape and others over thousands of years. There is the site of the Tulip tree and the park's famous rock (I'll let you discover that by zooming in and clicking). Finally, in addition to all the terrestrial aspects I love coming here via kayaks and paddle boards, which I've done for years. I actually live down in Hells Kitchen and prefer arriving here that way to the subway. I do wish that many of the parks visitors would do a better job cleaning up after themselves (there is all to often a lot of garbage to be found thrown on the ground and little campfire sites where people party in the evenings, unchecked by the NYPD or Parks police).

I'm only writing this as a New Yorker recording Revolutionary War sites that have some form of recognition in New York City. There is such a dearth that I like to note the few there are. In this case there are at least five here 1) is the statue to Nathan Hale (you will find a plaque to his capture near Grand Central along Vanderbilt Ave and 46th St; and another dedicated to the vicinity of the poor lad's hanging at 66th Street and Third Ave. both are at eye level attached to the wall). 2) is a carved stone plaque in the sidewalk noting the approximate location of the the notorious Bridewell Prison and looking up and onto the grass you will find a cement or stone outline of the prison's foundation. 3) another plaque in the sidewalk noting the site of the British Barracks (photos of both attached to this review). 4) near the Bridewell another cement marker behind the fence in the grass talking about the Liberty poles and a flag pole referenced that stands back toward City Hall. And finally 5) a statue of Benjamin Franklin across the street at Park Row and Spruce St. adjacent to Pace University.

Really enjoyed a cool visit on a mostly cloudy day in November—high in the 40s F—meant no crowds. Being a native Floridian with a great deal of diving experience it was wonderful to see so many of the species I know so well from the northern Gulf of Mexico, from Sheepshead, to yellowtail snapper, to hognose snapper and sandbar sharks. The highlight of the live creatures for me was to see the sturgeon. So ugly and ancient that they are beautiful. It also reminded me of the most startling encounter I've had paddling my kayaks on the Hudson. Down between the Battery and the Statue of Liberty 10 years ago a six-foot sturgeon breached, and splashed just a few feet from me. I jumped out of my skin. Also, I actually really enjoyed the outdoor display of the Beebe and Barton bathysphere, something I read about as a kid. Our kids, of course enjoyed all the fish but got most excited by watching the seals, sea lion (and sea lion show), as well as the feeding of the sea otters and penguins. Good to see the aquarium making a comeback after Sandy.

UPDATE: This morning came upon Lou Diamond Phillips, Tom Payne, Aurora Perrineau, Frank Harts and crew filming exterior shots for Fox’s series “Prodigal Son.” Also on scene were the running black ‘70 or so Pontiac Lemans that Lou Diamond Phillips drives on the series along with the body-double car that lacks windows for shooting conversations between Phillips and other cast members in the car. (See photos and video)...Love walking around the periphery of the park, despise that it remains one of, if not the only, private parks in the city. I appreciate the many grand old trees here and the many plantings. Do also love the old architecture surrounding it, at least the homes dating to the 1840s and 1850s. And one never knows what to expect when walking by, as I do daily on my commute to work, as when I saw this set of about 10 classic or vintage American cars from the 1930s and 1940s parked for a film shoot.

While my first paddling trip was in 1973 or '74 on the Little Tennessee River before Tellico Dam was finished, my New York City paddling career started here, in the old, original boathouse building and nub of a pier back in the year 2000. It was the city's first boathouse of its kind, at least in modern times, and was a font of knowledge. By that year there were already many thousands of people a year participating in their free kayaking program. And it was here that I had my first paddle in a kayak and began learning the ways of the river, its physics and folklore, and the history of what was here before. I also got to meet pioneers of NYC kayaking like Ralph Diaz who introduced me to the folding sea kayak (I now own three). These days you are more likely to see me atop an orange paddle board, often with my SUP pup Pepper, but I still remember Pier 26 and the DTBH quite fondly.

I've been a New Yorker the last 20 years but I'm a native of panhandle Florida, home of the cradle of naval aviation and its Museum of Naval Aviation, an absolutely amazing place. I spent a lot of time there growing up and always asked to go if were near there. It is an absolute travesty to have a place with the volunteers that HARP does, its expertise the collection of aircraft it does and the potential in its facilities. Yet it seems to attract little from the City of New York. Transport to get here is one issue but that could be remedied. You would think the New York Department of Ed would do more with it or have a high school here like they have done with The Harbor School on Governors Island. I love, love, love this place. As another reviewer said it is a wonderful little unknown jewel of NYC.
dislikes: Lack of support from the city

reviews_attraction.text: So sad. Most of the reviewers here, and certainly the vast majority of the visitors to Worth Square, do not even glance at who it was put here to honor. And that is a shame because William Jenkins Worth was a fascinating character. Raised as a Quaker, he served a nearly lifelong career in the US Army during its early years beginning with the War of 1812. I knew of him because I am a born-and-raised Floridian and Worth fought in the 2nd Seminole War, which took place there. He also commanded troops and fought battles during the war with Mexico in the 1840s. Amazing his longevity in the service. So take a moment to look at the monument and note the names of all those different battles he fought in and you will see them stretch from the Northeast to Florida to modern day Texas and Old Mexico.

The history of the statue, that it was from one of the first foundries capable of a piece of such size, scale and quality in the US and how the statue has been moved around within the park are probably little known. Residents, certainly, take it for granted. I’m glad the sign with its history is here. I stop by and read it every few years as I forget the statue’s history. Washington himself would probably be dismayed to see the homeless and addicted that often sleep below his horse’s feet during the warmer months. “What sort of society has ours become?” He might wonder.

My kayak was moving and the light was getting faint at times in the early evening when I took the accompanying image of the Bronx side of the High Bridge, it reminds me of old Roman aqueducts found in Europe. I love the cut stone retaining walls and seawalls from earlier in the century or last century that are found all over the five boroughs. While it must have been back-breaking and probably low-paying work, I really admire the stonemasons that built these. They have left such an amazing mark and legacy for the city.

The Google Maps folks have done something quirky with this listing---it only shows up when you zoom in far beyond where the average user would zoom ---and it is another listing that pops up in searches, one that nothing can be added to. Well, one person has been able to add photos. Anyway, camped here many times when I was a kid. The last time was at the end of my scouting career with my troop in 1988. Beautiful place that, judging from the far more recent photos, has only improved with age and despite hurricanes.

Love the many markers and plaques, especially those embedded in the sidewalks (don't forget to look down) as well as the statues including Washington, Lincoln and the less often noticed Lafayette on the east side of the park. My favorite bronze sidewalk plaque is of the sites of First People's villages prior to European contact. It is at the east side of the park at the 15th Street crossing, N side of the crossing (there is more than one plaque there so look at all of them).

My wife and I paddled the length of the canal on weekends and holidays while visiting my father-in-law in NJ. We used my two-seat folding sea kayak, which I stored set up at his then home not far from Princeton. I did most of the paddling while my wife read and napped in the front. Makes me chuckle thinking back to the laughter I could sometimes hear from above as riders along the trail realized my wife was asleep.

A beautiful place, especially in the spring and summer. Having been there in person I now enjoy spying glimpses of it from the river when I'm kayaking and paddle boarding. We (the family) visited by riding our bicycles from midtown Manhattan up here. There was a good deal of arguing during the process of navigation.

Never been to a concert or event on top of the pier. However, paddling south one evening with my late pup Nixie in summer 2015, we happened upon quite the spectacle: a Barenaked Ladies concert. We only caught the last 45 minutes or so but it was a fine performance and the stage and lights were great.

Visited for a company milestone celebration in 2014. I'm no wine expert but we all seemed to enjoy it. The grounds are gorgeous and they had lovely facilities for a meeting as well. I especially loved the drive getting here from the Valley.

Sadly, ‘it’s a rare thing in New York City to find homes from pre-Revolutionary War Days preserved. Thankfully this one was and it has quite the story to tell. Well worth a visit. Especially to see the period furnishings and artifacts.

Pepper and I had Lady Liberty all to our selves last Saturday. Still no tour boats because of the pandemic. Normally one of the most crowded places in the harbor—-especially for those of us on paddle boards or in kayaks.
I've visited by land and sea (errr, river), summer, fall and winter. The lighthouse and bridge are quintessential NYC. And one of those rare spots in the city more resident than tourist.
I've eaten many a quiet, peaceful lunch here. Close your eyes, listen to the roar of the man made waterfall, and it can be easy to escape NYC, if for just a coffee or lunch break.
A beautiful place. Visited here a couple of times when my wife was working in Albany. My favorite time was seeing it in its winter splendor and snowshoeing.
One of the prettier sections of the river I saw when paddling from Shoelace Park kayak launch down to Concrete Plant Park. One of the quieter areas too.
The exteriors of these homes appear to have not changed at all since my last photo visit in 2009 (when my accompanying photos were taken).
Visited back in the winter of 2000. Very cold day. I've also seen it from below via my paddle board and kayak on quite a few occasions.

I really enjoyed the tour and am glad that the state park system is able to preserve the land. It is really beautiful. Our tour guide was very knowledgeable, friendly, and patient. I knew very little about The Hearst family and how they came into their fortune.  I do wish the tours included more. It is pricey to see such a small bit of the castle. I know the goal is that you go back multiple times to see all of what is available or add on to the tour you purchased, I just feel that they could add on a little so the tours don't seem so rushed. Our "45" minute tour was barely 30 minutes. They must include the bus ride up? I would not recommend these tours for children under 12 because it is hard enough for the adults to mind the tour guides and remember the caution "everything at the castle is part of a museum" do not pick the oranges, sit on the laps of the marble statues, or play in the water of the fountains.It was sad that there were multiple people not watching their children and allowing them to touch marble statues and veer from the carpeted path meant to protect the floor. The grounds were being treated as a play park and not a museum.

Bodie Ca, once known as the wildest town in the west became a mining boom town in the late 1870's, a run that lasted only 4 years. In its heyday, over 30 mines were operating and over 10,000 people lived in the town in the Eastern Sierras. Major firea destroyed much of the town and although about 10 mines remained, much of the population moved on. People lived in Bodie until 1944, when its last inhabitants moved on. The buildings that were still inhabited were left as is to rot in the elements over time. The state parks acquired the land and has done a fantastic job of preserving the decaying buildings and the history of the town along with it. Some of the buildings have been restored at the interior and serve as employee housing, however, youd never know it from the exterior. Fantastic  place to visit with the whole family.

And Sequoia...the parks were spectacular. The visitor centers were of course crowded, but once away from those, peace and solitude could  easily be found on any of thousands of trails. The cave tour is worth it and the JR. Caver for kids was fantastic and unique- according to my son.  I preferred being in the Sequoia part of the park amongst the giant sequoia, however my travel companions preferred the hiking in the canyons. The one negative about these parks is lots of people with no respect for the parks, others or the environment in general. I saw people picking flowers, off trails, littering out of car windows. I had never seen behavior like that in a national park before.
dislikes: Disrespectful behavior (littering, off-trail walking, flower picking)

reviews_attraction.text: A place of unique and tranquil beauty which is hard to wander through without feeling the guilt of knowing the Tufas are only visible due to human destruction and near annihilation of the Mono Basin area. Due to the save Mono Lake movement, in 1994 a conservation plan was creates to restore Mono Lake to 25 feet below the depth it was in 1944, before the feeder waters were diverted from the lake. If conservation efforts are successful and the Mono Lake Preservation project is successful, the Tufas will one again be underwater in leas than 10 years.

Its fun, I guess I am spoiled by the Santa Cruz Boardwalk and so it is hard to compare. I think if the rides were open it would have been a different experience. The City of Santa Monica reminds me of a smaller version of Long Beach. It was a nice day, a great just walking around. People were wearing masks. The beach is big and beautiful and the Promenade Mall was great.
Park at the pier parking lot for a $10
00 flat rate or on one of the many public parking garages. We had a great time.

We took a trail that is on their map but disappear in many places. Glad I downloaded the trail route onto my GPS. No water do bring double what you think you will need and tell someone where you are going. It was such a beautiful tour and a perfect day
Although we were there at the very end of the elephant seal season, we were able to see a lot of the seals they call weaners. These are the elephant seals that are babies and have been weaned from their mothers but haven't left the beach yet. The docent was very informative and delivered a fantastic tour. Well worth the $7.00. We will need to go back in the winter when the adults are on the beach.

I used to hike here when I was young and it is just as lovely. Yhe wild horses no longer roam the hills and a  disappointing difference is that there are now enormous mansions built on the edges of the preserve that can ruin the view.  The parking lot used to always be empty and it apparently is now always full. It has been 25 years, and except for the houses, its exactly how I remember.

The back trail was absolutely gorgeous, however, walking for so long on the road was a little unnerving. reviews_attraction.text: We had such a great on this horseback riding adventure. The rangers we came across were so friendly and helpful. Trails are well marked, it is obvious they are doing their best to keep people on trails and not lost in the mojave.

Just fantastic. We learned so much about the area and the efforts to preserve the truly unique coastal area. Can't wait to go back.
Love this park, open field and small playground right across from the beach. Bring mosquito repellent if you go in the evening
We choose this route on a whim and were so glad we did. It was so beautiful and was just the very beginning of the bloom.

You need half a day of walking to see all of the garden and you can go sit on the big lawn facing the downtown to relax and be at peace.

Located at Cannon beach this is a breathtaking spot which is loved by many. The beach weather is chilly (possibly all year round) so don't forget to get a jacket. The beach is easily accessible and there are a couple of convenience store/cafes nearby as well.

Still really cool to look at downtown LA. You can go inside the observatory and look at the different mini exhibits which is for free. I know for some other activities, there is a fee that you have to pay.

I was told that I could take a peek inside two windows overlooking the main body of the building.

Far be it from me to trigger controversy but I wonder:
It 'just that the Franciscan spirit which is inspired by this place of worship?

I am sure that this was an unfortunate misunderstanding but I suggest managers to make a thorough review of the "policy" management.

Esperienza molto negativa per la inqualificabile gestione del luogo di culto al quale mi è stato impedito l'accesso perché, dopo la celebrazione di un matrimonio, del quale allego ampia documentazione fotografica,  "non era possibile l'accesso perché riservato solo agli invitati al matrimonio". E' proprio questo lo spirito francescano al quale si ispira questo luogo di culto ?

(Translated by Google) One of the most impressive geological manifestations in the whole park. As much as I had already seen the other arches on a previous visit, I must say I was really impressed. The photos, however well done and even if in large quantities, fail to give even a fragment of the emotion that is felt when visiting it live.

Tips for the visit - The excursion is particularly demanding in the ascent - descent of a fairly large plateau of living rock. I am not saying that it is necessary to be superman but it requires a fair physical effort. The path is completely exposed to the sun, there are no shelters in the shade. All other suggestions that are found around the park, availability of water, clothing and adequate footwear are also valid (we also see strange guys around who face the park with beach shoes !!) etc. If you make the excursion at sunset, consider the route well and equip yourself for a possible descent in the dark.

(Original)
Uno delle manifestazioni geologiche più impressionanti di tutto il parco. Per quanto avessi già visto gli altri archi in una precedente visita, devo dire di essere rimasto veramente colpito. Le foto, per quanto fatte bene e anche se in grande quantità, non riescono a dare neanche un frammento dell'emozione che si prova nel visitarlo dal vivo.

Consigli per la visita - L'escursione è impegnativa in particolare nella salita - discesa di un plateau di viva roccia abbastanza esteso. Non dico che sia necessario essere superman ma richiede un discreto impegno fisico. Il percorso è completamente esposto al sole, non sono presenti ripari all'ombra. Valgono inoltre tutti altri suggerimenti che si trovano in giro per il parco, disponibilità di acqua, vestiario e calzature adeguate (si vedono in giro anche strani tipi che affrontano il parco con calzature da spiaggia!!) ecc. Se fate l'escursione al tramonto valutate bene il percorso e attrezzatevi  per una eventuale discesa al buio.

One can't visit New York City without dropping by this monumental consecration of modern art. They show most of the cubists and their fare share of avant-gardists. My favorite works of art are the Klee and Van Gogh paintings. Besides the 5 hours you will offer yourself in indulging these masterpieces, you must also stop by the restaurant which has quite a fine menu to please.

From a scientific standpoint, I'm really disappointed to see it getting hit by mother nature's elements daily. As a visitor of Central Park, I'm very happy to get a real lifesize monolith to look at because of the history that it purports.
Brought back in the 19th century from Egypt, it still stands tall today and the Hieroglyphs ornating it are still visible.

What makes this maze so interesting is the width of the corn corridors made so you could walk 3 people side-by-side. Bring a party of folks, split up in groups of 3-4 and try to find your way out first, such an exciting adventure.
I wouldn't recommend to kids because they might get scared and help might not get there quickly enough before they start panicking.

You might never encounter Sylvester Stallone during your lifetime but you can always take a picture with its iconic figure Rocky Balboa. As it is with the steps leading to the statue, you will be assailed by a horde of tourists and picture-taking pedestrians. Once you selfied yourself out, take a walk inside the museum.

They really made this attraction into a museum that is worth visiting. The bell in itself is great to see and getting to admire it gives you a sense of the history that it bears. Only problem for a tight schedule is the lineups waiting to go in and the airport-like security one must go through.

This is a seriously awesome park with a landscape view of the river and the opposite shoreline. It bolsters all of what one wants for a park. Langone has tennis and bocce courts, soccer and baseball fields and paths for all to roam around. Summertime sees this place bustling with activity.

A museum that garners a fair amount of memorabilia. It is centered mostly on the North American side of dance progress. Their swing dance collection was a real pleasure to see. It took us about 3 hours to complete the tour and we loved it. I wonderful if they change it from time to time?

A park can literally be anything but at this recreational area, you will love the scenery and the vastness of it. Bordering New Jersey and Pennsylvania, you must stop here when autumn comes by. The shades of foliage is breathtaking and to appreciate it you should try hiking in the area.

Great politicians have to be remembered and what a nice gesture San Diego has done to honor Bob Hope this way. People have to be proud of his efforts to further liberalism in politics throughout the years. On the scenic backdrop that is the ocean, you will have countless nice pictures.

Not being a trekkie per say but having had the chance to watch my fair share of the series, I wanted to see what they could offer on this visit. Boy, was I pleasantly surprised and amazed. Being guided through with apparent ease was what one needed to thoroughly reel in the knowledge.

Another great park in this tourist-friendly Boston city. You really don't have to be a history buff to enjoy this park. Contrary to what you'd read, the size of this park allows for many outdoor activities abd only if you feel like it, you can pay attention to the war memorabilia.

During big outdoor events there isn't much parking around so one must pay the 10-dollar par fee. What catches the eye at first glimpse is the well-maintained lawn where venues are held. From the parking there are a few walking paths and also includes a handful of paid attractions.

There aren't many outdoor sites that showcase this many sculptures. Trenton built this in 1992 to amass and display prominent pieces from United State artists. Seward Johnson's life-likes makes the park look alive and captivating. Have a nice visit in 42-acre of eye-catchiness.

This is where it all started. America the great left a trail of cobblestones for us to remember streets like these that were lined by city-dwellers dating back to the colonisation. What's special about this place has to do with the conservation of houses in exquisite condition.

To give historical significance to the tea party events is of utmost importance but having a ship replica built to remember the past is pointless. What makes the museum worth visiting are the historical tidbits, the fun-filled activities and the reenactment they have perfected.

Their tunnel rivals many I've seen but the beauty of what lies above your head is stupendous. I didn't chance the dive tour but people I talked to said it was stress free and spectacular. Give yourself at least 3 hours to look at all of the creatures packed in this location.

Think of it as a bench park with a statue at its center. Representing a hero in its own right, the American Revolution would not have had this ending had it not been for Revere. The area surrounding this comfort zone has a bakery, a church and some government buildings.

There was a mariage I attended in this cathedral and the pastor was the kindest I've seen. He was able to find the right words to unite and bless a family to become.
As for the church in itself, what really has me in awe is the quality of the stained glass windows.

Walking along this miles long, wooden floored area, you'll evidently lose yourself in the quietude of the sea. Storefronts are there to grab you as you stroll endlessly here and there. Food, oceanware stores and amusement plaza are some of the offers awaiting you.

Stunning area with a built-in pedestrian path. Inside this reserve, you can appreciate the earth's fierce hand at manipulating its features. There are trails that bring you from the road to the beach but you'll break in a sweat in no time for the paths are hilly.

Plan a two-day trip if you have kids because the amount of activities to enjoy will have you running all-day long. The quality of enhibits is remarkable as they delve in wonderous subjects like electricity and parts of the human body. Mind-blown everytime I go.

Not your usual tower but well worth the climb. To reach the Coit Tower one need to go from one wooden staircase to another or just follow the winding roads. Inside this museum, you will enjoy nice art and get to know how handywork was done quite sometime ago.

You don't need to be a Red Sox fan to feel the vibe that hits you when you enter the stadium. Stories of baseball feats and the green monster passed down from generations to generations of die hard baseball fans can be acquired while touring the premise.

Always showing its best colors and neatly spruced up. Having not been built upon, it has kept its historical significance for troops were stationed here during the revolution. The range of activities inside the park is as wide as the mind can thinks of.

A beautiful foresty area to visit. Its stream is majestic and to get the chance to come near it to hear all the fauna one can enjoy is a pleasure.
Taking long walks in Hedden Park really marks ones day with accomplissement.

The USS Battleship Iowa Museum,located at one the busiest seaports in the world-The Port of Los Angeles in San Pedro,California, is a terrific museum and battleship to visit and climb aboard!
The Battleship USS Iowa Museum is a maritime museum located at the Port of Los Angeles in San Pedro, Los Angeles, California, United States.
Family friendly with all current CDC protocols in place, The USS Iowa fights Covid like it fought all the enemies it faced on the 7 seven seas during its  commisioned years!

USS Iowa (BB-61) was the lead ship of the last class of U.S. Navy battleships to be built by the United States. The battleship was originally commissioned in 1943 and served during World War II, the Korean War, and through the Cold War. Iowa earned 11 battle stars during her career and hosted three U.S. Presidents, ultimately earning the nicknames Battleship of Presidents and Big Stick. Iowa was awarded to the Pacific Battleship Center on September 6, 2011 for display at the Port of Los Angeles in San Pedro, California – home to the United States Battle Fleet from 1919 to 1940.

Iowa opened in Los Angeles on July 4, 2012 to a crowd of over 1,500 supporters and veterans at Port of Los Angeles Berth 87.
The USS Iowa Museum offers daily tours, group programs, education visits, special events, filming, military ceremonies, and is in the process of starting an overnight program.

Daily tours include visits to see the largest guns on a U.S. Navy ship,officers ward room, President Roosevelt's cabin, armored bridge, missile decks, enlisted berthing, mess decks, helicopter deck, and other areas. The ship is located at the Los Angeles World Cruise Center and has over 2,100 parking spaces available.

Iowa has played various roles in films and television including NCIS: Los Angeles, American Warships, Bermuda Tentacles, and Dark Rising. Iowa is home to annual American-focused events including the City of Los Angeles Veterans Appreciation,a Memorial Day Celebration, and September 11 remembrance.

Scenic Yucca Valley,located in Southern California,features many intersting places to see and things to do.
We recently visited The Desert Christ Park that features the sculpting work of artist Antone Martin.This collection of steel and reinforced concrete sculptures features places from bible experiences of The Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ.
The project was unveiled on Resurrection/Easter Sunday in 1951and continued being added to through 1961.It was a collaboration of Antone Martin and Reverend Eddie Garver as a bench mark for "peace on earth and good will".
There is no charge to visit,free parking,restroom and a bench to sit on and have a pik nik or relax!
You can walk around the stunning sculptures in about 30-45 minutes so it makes for a nice stop on your Yucca Valley/Joshua Tree/ 29 Palms adventure!
There is lots of great photo/IG opportunities here of the park and the scenic views of Yucca Valley from the park.
Set on a beautiful hillside near Yucca Valleys Hwy 62,Desert Christ Park is open daily till dark and is a great stop for everyone who is visiting Yucca Valley,Joshua Tree,29 Palms and beyond!

Salvation Mountain,located near Salton Sea in Niland,California,is a man-made mountain 28 years in the making by artist Leonard Knight of Vermont,USA, covered in half a million gallons of latex paint!What started as a small monument to his Lord and Saviour,Jesus Christ, made of dirt and painted cement became, over time, a colorful eclectic sprawling adobe and hay-bale mountain complex, with peripheral found art pieces made of telephone poles, tires,car windows,glass,ceramic,wood as well as art cars and sculptures, all painted in a patchwork of stripes and color blocks of whatever paint was donated that week!
His work and Salvation Mountain has been dedicated by the State of California as a landmark of Leonard Knights lifelong work and place of artistic,cultural and spiritual importance!
When you visit also visit the nearby "Slab City" enclave of residents and art pieces for another addition to your desert art trip!
Dont forget your camera or mobile phone because there is lots of great places and things to photograph and 'gram here!

"Surreal and Fascinating..." thats what I was thinking about Salton Sea State Recreation Area,Mecca Beach and Bombay Beach,California. I Had a chance to go out to Salton Sea State Park and Bombay Beach to have a look and take some pictures. Salton Sea State Recreation Area was interesting with the huge lake.Just a few miles south was,Bombay Beach."Post apocalyptic" as one story I read called it and I gotta admit it was a fascinating place-I left a review and more pictures at my IG account "seetheusa" for more info. A great place for photo ops-its really hot out there currently (about 109!) So bring water,hat and sunscreen if you go!

Off Of Hwy 111....
Thats where the "Shiprock Monument" of The Cahuilla Band of Indians is located.
Its a great stop on your way to Palm Springs on route 111.
Located on the south side of the highway theres marble etched sign that shares some info about it.

A great mountain day visit location featuring beautiful scenes places to eat and lots to do.
Close to the I- 10 fwy,and near the friendly cities of Yucaipa and Mentone California.
8-29-19 UPDATE! My wife I walked from
Chapman Heights in Yucaipa all the LONG way up to Parrish Pioneer Ranch and enjoyed a great Cider Float-really delicious along with a slice of Apple crumb and ice cream-terrific.They've added more things to look at and BUY at Parrish Pioneer Ranch-take a trip up here and enjoy!

Santa Monica pier and surrounding area of Santa Monica is a great place to spend a classic day at one of the most world famous Southern California locations.
Great I'gram location for hundreds of great photos.Lots of parking,food and restaurants
and nearby shopping centers-
A world class place to have a great time!
