One of the most iconic churches in downtown and currently undergoing a refurbishment/renovations but you can still venture inside to see a magnificent example of Roman Catholic style cathedral.

It's free and worth a trip by and venture inside.

Awesome park with fantastic views of the bay.  A St Pete gem right near downtown.  The continuous views of the bay and constant breeze make this a very popular place.  If the weather is nice you just can't beat it.

What a fantastic park in Hillsborough county and not too far from the for limits. Plenty of wildlife to observe and a fantastic shaded trail along the Lakeshore. This is a great hike, about 2.4 miles.

Nice little park to take a break and grab some shade.

There is a decent amount of shaded seating do the park makes for a great resting area of you need a break while taking in downtown.
Nice area with restrooms, covered bench area and shaded parking spots.  Makes for a great starting point to jog,walk,bike roller blade walk your dog on the trail.
What a great venue for downtown Tampa.  Right on the Hillsborough river the Curtis Hixon Park is a perfect venue for concerts, art shows and any event gathering.
A nice park with a water area that kids can play.  It's a decent size and has nice views of the bay.

Beautiful views, fun park for adventurous & athletic people, not so much for young children & I wouldn't even bring dogs here unless you keep them off the dangerous big rocks & stay on the trail, very rocky, no developments or comfy/smooth walkways, just primitive & beautiful nature, nice swimming areas, great exercise climbing over big rocks. Climb down a rocky cliff to reach lake & swim. Bring solid hiking shoes will tear up sandles, a backpack to keep both hands free for climbing. Not the quietest, lots of noisy motor boaters from neighborhood, & playing music loud.
Gov needs to put a ban on noisy & smelly & polluting motorcraft,
water would be far cleaner & prettier & healthier for people & wildlife.
Less noise pollution & overall better.
Still very pretty, great place to suntan, rock climb, walk around, & swim!

Great park, very big space, small playground, more developed & appropriate for young children & dogs, great swimming. Please clean up after yourselves, I had to throw away 2 dirty diapers, just laying around...really...?Aluminum cans, cigarette filters, & bunch of other litter. Please do not smoke cigarettes in the park, nobody wants cancer & it is certainly not healthy for the children to breathe. Dogs are allowed. There is an entrance fee, but seniors get free admission. Thank you for not fishing/terrorizing the poor fish, or leaving fishing gear pollution everywhere, I see those fake rubber fishing lures left all over the rocks, birds & animals try to eat those things.

Great trail, huge loop could spend all day walking it, or go back several times & walk a new area, nice scenery, great way to get some exercise, pretty birds & flowers, nice views of the skyline. Basically just a nice pathway to walk, & view the city.
Urban atmosphere, if you're looking for a large, deep natural area, to really get lost in seclusion & explore nature...this isn't the best place to go, the green grassy part is just a very thin strip running along the path.
But again, it's a super fun trail if you just want to walk/bike/run/dog walk, with beautiful views of Houston, highly recommend checking it out!

Camping & sleeping overnight right on the shoreline with the loud waves, was great, nobody at the gate collecting money, I am not sure if you normally have to pay to camp? I was nervous about sleeping here at first but there are a lot of police officers patrolling all night long & in the morning, so I felt fine. Lots of other people camping as well. PLEASE, DO NOT LEAVE TRASH ON THE BEACH....who would do this...??? I was shocked to see a bunch of beer cans scattered at the entrance as if people had a party & just trashed the place, & didn't  bother to clean up at all, unreal.

I have not visited this park yet I just wanted to comment about the gentleman who answered the phone 8:30am Sunday just after xmas, 5 stars for him, he was SO extremely nice and very helpful with my questions about tent camping I often run into rude staff members at state parks but he definitely set a higher standard and restored my faith in park staff thank you it was a pleasure speaking with him. I look forward to checking out Lockhart State Park someday. All the state parks in and around Austin are very busy camping sites are all booked up.

Very diverse & very scenic! A little more peacefully quiet, depending on what day it is, more relaxing for everyone, as well as all of the ducks, birds, dogs, deer, & other animals in the area disturbed by loud motor boat & boom box noise, which also makes children cranky. Less motorboats on the lake in this area on slow days, water nice & calm for swimming, great beach-like area. Particularly clear & pretty water here, on slow days, when motor vehicles are not decreasing water clarity. A long, curvy drive, with hilly inclines, but worth it!

Beautiful park, if coming from the beach, please slow down, and try not to hit all the little white butterflies, they are...everywhere...during spring/March, flying all over the place, across the road.  Careless, stupid people were just speeding down the street, and smacking into them,  I saw them landing in the middle of the road, it was so sad. :(  The speed limit is too high, when all the butterflies are out, you have to curb your OCD for a few minutes, slow down to about 20mph at least, and avoid hitting them.

Nice trails, good size park, pretty nature area to explore. Parking however, is just on the street...? A little uncomfortable, not really much of a safe shoulder to park on, very busy street with fast speed limit & everyone zooms by, I felt like my vehicle was going to get hit, or you can get off the main road & park on the street in front of someone's house & creep through the neighborhood which is uncomfortable...this park is meant for the neighborhood residents to just walk to I suppose. But it is a nice park.

5 stars for the size, nice BIG park which is awesome, tons of different trails, could go back many times & walk a new area. East side of town, but still okay, once you get deep in the trails there are some really pretty natural areas, & plenty of space to explore, some cool bridges with neat overlooks, & some creeks for doggies to cool off which is great. Nice big parking lot, & they allow dogs off leash which is great. Lots of great rock formations along the southern creek near Walnut Creek Crossing.

Absolutely loved my campsite! I slept right on the edge of a beautiful, rocky cliff & could see the lake from inside my tent. Wonderful views! I was the only one in the entire camping area so the privacy & quiet was great! No mosquitos, nothing biting me at all, in mid August. Only $19/night for water & also a covered shelter 👍👍. All you can eat, big, ripe cactus fruits growing everywhere! Very comfortable shower, with 2 shower nozzles raining on you! I would love to camp here again :).

Never been here waterfall looks nice but please stop spray painting the rocks, I see from the photographs & it looks disturbing & tacky frankly, & there is nothing spiritual or cool about toxic spray paint invading nature, & killing insects that become stuck in it, rainfall also washes the paint chemicals into the soil. Should be erased & prohibited. Use a natural chalk or something that isn't harmful to the wildlife, looks more organic & pleasant, rather than gaudy & artificial.

Great, peaceful beach, that isn't crowded! Pretty shells. No admission fee, just $2.00 for parking. Lots of waves, water very rough & choppy, not sure if it's always like that. The only insects that bit me were ants, in the parking lot, no mosquitoes or midges. I went in early February. Please do not spread poison all over the ground to kill ants...I'm just saying, there were no mosquitoes or midges which was very cool! I'll take ants over either one of them any day!

Absolutely fantastic park, my dog totally loved it, so glad I drove over to check it out!
Open fields & secluded trails for a quiet getaway,  playground & sports activities, great landscaping, flowers, & cacti everywhere.
The only thing missing some kind of water for the dogs to drink, fountain or pond or something but just bring a bowl & water with you, no biggie.

Great beach access park they did an awesome job of building a huge boardwalk. Please keep it nice and do not spray paint all over it find something more intelligent to do.  There's also a great workout station with pull up bar, sit up bench, and balance beam. Blackberry plants growing everywhere here, the thorny vines with the white-light pink flowers.

Nice big park, wide open spaces, more quiet & peaceful location away from traffic. Just waaayyy too many portable bathrooms placed everywhere, really degrades the scenery, & I would never use those. All of that money would be better spent on park road repairs, less portable bathrooms, more road maintenance👍. Nice water views & great place to exercise.

Nice place for a walk or run. Technically not an off-leash park, leashes required. No sandy beach, water meets rocks. Lots of benches, trails & open field. Information plaques next to trees describing the foliage, pretty cool!

Hilarious lol, totally unexpected, I was on my way to Davis Mountains State Park, when suddenly out of nowhere I see a lonely Prada shop on the side of the road, had to pull over & check out this funny place.

Quiet, easy walk, no overnight camping allowed, very muddy after rain, go when dry, they should remove the portable bathroom makes entrance look really tacky & I would never use one. Great place for dogs.
Nice park, overlook views, tranquil trails! There is a thin creek, it had water in it, also a nice little parking lot at entrance. Please try to avoid bringing litter into the park area.
I am sure it is pretty but I like to hike alone, I drove all the way out here to just a blocked road lol... Why not open it up to individual hikers?  I guess there must be reasons.
Great place, one of my top favorites, beach access, nice mature & quiet crowd mostly seniors during weekdays anyway, free parking, beautiful boardwalk & picnic tables.

Not going to be open for a while, lots of flooding, woman over the phone said opening winter of 2019....? :(
No idea what all they have to do, & why it takes so long.
Enjoyed my stay 👍👍😍 Nice private campsites separated by foliage, not just big open field, very close to shoreline, short drive to the beach.
One of the most beautiful state parks I have ever been to! Great staff. Recommend! Would love to return during warmer months.
Pretty place. Please do not drive on the dunes, or even onto the beach...it's very disturbing! Park & walk those legs!

We got up early to get to Pikes Peak, and wound up at the gate before it opened, only 5th or so in line. The drive up to the summit is spectacular in multiple ways, as you cross through a variety of ecosystems and climates. Signs along the way keep you up to date on your elevation and there are a couple of exciting places where the road goes steeply uphill and around a corner,  looking like it just drops right off the edge.

At the top, the wind was blowing incredibly forcefully, and a ranger told us that it was -6 degrees with windchill! The summit has spectacular 360 degree views, and we enjoyed watching the cog railway arrive at the top.

Right in the heart of old St. Charles, this set of buildings represents the very first of Missouri's legislative centers. The visitor center is small, but has lots of information to share, and tours of the capitol building are on offer.

You're free to roam the grounds, which includes a lovely backyard area with river views. The yard contains gardens and plantings of all kinds, as well as sitting areas and plenty of shade.

The first capitol is an important part of Missouri's history, and the historic site preserves it wonderfully!

Worth taking the tour! The home is a wonderful example of the craftsman style, and is chock full of craftsman and Art Deco furniture and architectural details.

The home is also full of Benton's art and belongings, all lovingly cared for and preserved. While you can enjoy the grounds on your own, the tour is required to go in either building. This site is a must if you are a fan of craftsman architecture, art deco furniture, Kansas City history, Mr. Benton's art, or all of the above!

A beautiful State Park, which includes the wool mill, the Watkins home, and the surrounding farm. The house and mill are two separate tours, each taking around an hour, with one or the other starting at the top of each hour.

Both are well worth the time. The house is filled with period furniture and lovely architectural details. The mill is HUGE, and has the distinction of containing all of its original machinery, which is all very interesting to look at.

Allow 2-3 hours!

"A Telluride Tradition" dating back to the 70's, the free box is a bit of the old Telluride, the small town that existed before the boom. The free box is a place for people to leave usable household goods, clothing, and other items for passersby to peruse, and take, if needed. Great stuff can show up here, especially around the end of the ski season.

The box's rules are simple. Always respect the box, take only what you'll use, and don't leave junk!

Definitely off the beaten path, Illiniwek Village State Historic Site represents the only known settlement of the Illiniwek (Illinois) peoples within the state of Missouri.

A short-ish walking trail takes you around the property, including a couple of dig-sites where evidence of Native American housing, including old post holes, was found.

Aside from the cultural history, this area is also alive with wildflowers and signs of animal life abound.

One of only four remaining covered bridges in Missouri, the Union is the only example of the Burr-Arch truss design, represented by the giant wooden arches on either side which are the centerpieces of the whole setup.

While it suffers a bit from graffiti, this bridge is still a beautiful sight in a lovely natural setting. A bit off the beaten path, but the history is real and interesting!

A well-manicured, beautiful facility, with lots of history to share. The short video available at the park office is worth the time, as it does a good job explaining the history of the place and why it is important.

The cemetery and church are both pleasant places, and the grounds are all lovely. The story of the Confederate veteran's home is an interesting one!

A lovely grouping of preserved buildings from Hermann's early days. They represent the German heritage of the area, and proudly display German architectural styles, interior decor, and more. The gardens are attractive, and the surrounding neighborhood is pleasant. Make time for the guided tour, and be prepared for lots of historic information!

This historic site interprets the events of the Battle of Island Mound, which is important as it represents one of the first combat operations for Union colored troops in the Civil War.

This site is off the beaten path, and consists of a short loop trail with interpretive stops, a small pavilion for picnics or contemplation, and a bathroom.

The Tom & Huck statue, in the city where it all started. A simple thing that is worth a stop to see. Climb the big set of stairs behind the boys, and you'll be treated to views of the river from the remaining platform where the old Mark Twain Memorial Bridge set off for Illinois, and at the top you'll find the Mark Twain Memorial Lighthouse.

Really enjoyed my tour of the Truman birthplace home. It's a very small house, but they do a good job of covering Truman's early history and depicting what life in small-town Western Missouri was like at the time. The home and visitor center sit across the street from one-another, and the whole site is very pleasant.

WOW! So inspiring. Walked around this area for a couple of hours, absolutely stunned by the beauty. Could have spent a whole day or more here. Stopping to gape at people climbing the dramatic rocks at various places seems to be popular, and this area really has a lot to offer. Don't miss it!

Loved it. A big mountain, with lots of options for people of all skill levels. We were there in mid-March, and it was evident that it was getting late. The first two days were pretty icy, but midway through our stay Telluride received 20" of fresh snow, and the rest of our time was a blast!

One of Missouri's many state parks where camping is the focus, Weston Bend is ideally situated along the Missouri River, with plenty of forest, hiking and biking trails, a neat old tobacco barn, and a scenic overlook of the Missouri river.

Nice marina, lots of fun options and good selection of stuff in the store. The swimming beach looked fun, although we didn't have time to enjoy it. The petroglyphs are worth a look, especially if you have any history buffs in your group!

We arrived too late to catch the tour of the interior of the home, but the grounds themselves are lovely and worth a stop. In addition to the home, there is also a schoolhouse structure on the site serves as a nice mini-museum.

Take the stairs, or skip them and take the cheater's approach on the back side. Either way, make sure you check out the lighthouse and the accompanying views of downtown Hannibal, the Mississippi river, and Illinois beyond.

There's plenty to do at Cuivre River SP. Well cared for facilities are matched with beautiful natural resources like the lake, forests, and river, to make this a perfect place to enjoy a summer weekend.

Nice spot. Highway noise is present, but not overbearing. Green grass, some benches, and a sweet gazebo that was recently remodeled. It also happens to be the smallest city park in St. Louis. Must see!
Stopped by here on a Sunday in January. While the main road in the park was closed, we were treated to the sight of Bald Eagles! We saw many more in neighboring Grand Pass Conservation Area.
This historic site includes a nice short loop trail with signs and interpretive stops. Great archaeological information relating to the history of the salt extraction industry in central MO!
Tiny park, based around a named lake. The park itself is pretty unusual. There are private homes all around it, not exactly the 'state park' setting you'd expect. Not a lot to do.
Plenty of space, grassy trails that cut through the woods, a large pond, a covered picnic area and good restrooms are all here, as well as the Little Sac River Trail!
Positioned along the South Dry Sac Greenway, this park is a convenient pit stop. Minimal amenities, but I saw porta-pots, picnic tables, and grilles.

This is a very large park with excellent facilities for all bicycle types and endevours (road and mountain). Pine Grove campground is right by Highway 1 and Riverside campground is 4 miles further into the park. Sites 132 and 134 butt on a restroom so have no privacy and limited to 20 ft. WIFI is available in selected areas of the park. Nice camp store too.
dislikes: Lack of privacy at some sites

reviews_attraction.text:
This State Park would be great for equestrian use. Many trails are provided for horses and hiking. Canoe launch is available for river access. Picnic and playground areas are nice.
The main camping area restroom/shower building is being revamped. Temporary facilities are marginal and very cramped. Tight but clean and serviceable.

This is a nice enough park. The public restroom is clean and functional. The picnic pavilions have nice tables and the sun screen overhead is made of expanded metal so it is good for shade but will not keep out the rain. The large open grass area is good for dogs and games. My main complaint is the large number of ants!

This is a very nice nature park in the city. Traffic noise from I275 is a minor distraction until you get out onto the boardwalk area. (Sorry... No dogs on the boardwalk). There is a small but well done exhibit in the environmental center. I usually see some wildlife each time I visit.

This is a state forest. There is no piped water so the toilet facilities are vault toilets. Bring your own potable water. There are only a few camp sites...all primitive. The trails are multi purpose (hiking, equestrian and mountain biking). There are some nice picnic shelters.

Nice park with fitness trail, ball diamonds, basketball courts, tennis courts and a place for skateboarding. Picnic pavilions with BBQ grills are also available. This park is crowded on Youth Baseball days (Saturday and some Sundays). Good place to get out and walk the dog.

I've heard people complain about the $5 per car fee but I feel it is one of the best parks around and would not be as good without the funding this provides. Great beaches, kayak and birding and even a nature trail. The campground is also worthwhile.

Coming back from Key West we chose to use Alligator Alley vice the toll road to see more wildlife. The kids counted over 100 gators along the way. The preserve is one of the last strongholds of natural Florida. It needs our help to stay that way!

This is a nice park with playground, restroom and boat launch. Connected to the municipal marina it has fuel dock and guest facilities. Trailer parking is limited due to construction near the launch ramps (hence the three stars).

Nice camp sites, good biking and hiking trails,  a boat ramp, canoe and kayak rentals and a fairly well stocked store. Good separation between camp sites to provide a somewhat secluded atmosphere. I'd definitely go back.

A great piece of Florida history. French and Spanish colony to US state includes historical information on plantation life, massacres and recreational use of the land. Now it is a nature preserve and wild life reffuge.

This is a great park for camping, hiking, biking, canoeing and kayaking. Large swimming pool (seasonal) and gift shop/camp store. Lock up your food at night as the raccoons are quite talented at accessing the goodies!
Many hiking trails and the highest point on Orcas Island. Great views, excellent camp sites but make sure you pack your rain coat! Roads are steep so use lower gears and watch for bicycles!
Nice bayside park. Good place to walk and ride bikes. No restroom here...closest is North Shore park to the North of the pool or South at the head of the Pier. The dog park is close by too.
O'Leno State Park is a good place to camp. Good well marked trails for hiking or off road biking. Interesting historical site and geological information. A lot of water moves thru here!
This is a nice seaside park with picnic pavilions and good walking/ biking path. There is also a canoe/kayak launch point. I didn't see any restroom facilities near where I parked.
Not the prettiest cave I have seen but the highest and dryest. The standard tour had a great guide ... I didn't try the flashlight tour. Good footing and no crawling. I'm 6'3".
We had a very good day at the park. The trails are good but we did not see much wildlife. The human encroachment is quite evident but it still retains a natural atmosphere.
A nice quiet lake park with camping, boat ramp and a playground. Only four stars as nature trails are minimal. The lake is good for canoeing but too small for power boats.
All of San Juan Island parks are beautiful. This one has tent and small RV (less than 20 ft.) sites with NO hookups. Clean restroom with flushing toilets but no showers.
The lighthouse (1890) houses a very nice museum for its size. History, wildlife and ecology are all presented and the people there were pleasant and knowledgeable.
This is a fairly small park. The trails are gravel and pretty well drained (no high top water boots needed). Major problem is lack of public toilet facilities.
This is a great park for bicycle riding and walking. There is much more to it than what is visible from the parking area. It is a great picknic place.
Nice playground ... Good ball field ... Great tennis courts ... A lot of open space to run ... Good picnic facilities. Only problem ... NO RESTROOM!
I like Ikea furniture as I have a smaller house so their products fit better than the overstuffed and bulky items found elsewhere.

For such an important part of American history and for it being about 2 square miles, it is great that one can see this area easily in a car.  The visitor's center was closed on July 19 but they have another place where you can maps and info.  It is great to see where history was made.  The road that takes you around the area is marked and there are many signs and markers.  We took a nice drive along the whole area. First stop was the Muhlenberg brigade with multiple houses built in the style of 1777 (following Washington's instructions of the era). Along the whole drive you see markers where the troops from different states were stationed: New Hampshire, New York, Virginia, Maine, Pennsylvania, etc. Stop #3 is the National Memorial Arch dedicated in 1917 honoring the soldiers' perseverence during the winter of 1776-1777. 4: Wayne statue.  5 Washington's headquarters and office and his guards' houses.

Gran Quivira was the largest of the Salinas pueblos. When the pueblo was at its largest it housed 1,500 to 2,000 people. Because of its location between the areas where pueblo Indians lived and the areas where the plains Indians lived, Gran Quivira was an important trade center.  Today, one can see the ruins of a large church and large kiva, as well as smaller kivas, rooms, etc.  There is a good, paved path and many signs explaining what you see.  The bathrooms are heated.  The visitor center was closed due to COVID.  There are a few picnic tables.  One comment on directions.  From Albuquerque go to About ruins first (from Belen going SE), then to Gran Quivira, then to Quarai ruins to then drive back to Albuquerque on the East side of the Sandias.
likes: Facilities & Services: Heated bathrooms, Paved path, Informative signs

reviews_attraction.text: My second visit.  The first was over 10 years ago.  Three years ago they completely changed Graceland adding a large museum complex across the street.  It allowed for a large room with his cars, a large room with outfits of singers that were inspired by those of Elvis, one about his times in  the military, one with Elvis' outfits, one about his films with lots of movie posters, one about Lisa Marie, the beautiful collection of gold and platinum records, and a section where you re-live Elvis' start (they show a documentary there).   In the mansion, everything was as before with an addition of an area where they talk about Elvis' family and life (where before they had the gold anx platinum records. I think) and the racketball/ exercise building.
likes: Diverse exhibits (cars, outfits, military, films, family)

reviews_attraction.text: This place is unique and very pretty.  We were there in the summer.  The parking lot was full.  The walk to the start of where er the tent rocks are was about 40 minutes.  Once the tent rocks start, the path becomes very narrow- one person wide at times.  Most of the path is level.  When it starts going uphill , you can turn back.  Three of the 4 persons in the group did that and did not miss much.  I went all the way to the top (I ran to the top and back).  The views are pretty but you do not see any more tent rocks.  Driving from Albuquerque took about 70 minutes.  The overall walk- hike at the tent rocks took about two hours.  Do take water.  They have picnic tables by the parking lot. A short, 5 minute, side trip takes you to Cochiti lake.
dislikes: Limited additional views at the top

reviews_attraction.text: We went to the Amish Village and the Amish Farm and House.  We liked the Amish Farm and House more.  Why?  Both tours take you through an Amish house- a "church room", kitchen, boys room, girls room, parents room, and summer kitchen.  Both have a farm with animals.  But, the tour at Amish Farm was more complete.  Because we went there last, we would hear when they explained or showed something that was not covered in the Amish Village.  A few examples:  we heard a recording of people singing in church, there was more detail on their religion, and in the farm there was a blacksmith showing how he works.  But this one was pretty good also. Cost was $11 per person.

This center is that best one run by the state of NM.  They have over 700 events a year since the new director ( R. Avitia) took over about three years ago. We just went to see the Ballet Folklorico de Mexico.  The photos are from that show and the building and the Disney Performing Theater.  We also attend many of the Thursday night movies and a few of the plays and operas (including Spanish zarzuelas).  On top of that, they rent the place for weddings and other events.  My daughter's wedding reception was there and it was perfect.  I hope that NM state continues to fund the place.

I visited Dec 30 of 2020.  I was very impressed by the relatively new penguin exhibit.  Great job.  It would be excellent if they clean the glass (maybe add windshield wipers?).  It was great to see the penguins underwater and see them diving.  Other exhibits that were open were:  lions, mountain lions, elephants, giraffes, gorillas, rhinos, zebras,   flamingos, carybaras, warthog, birds, reptiles... Hipos, monkeys, and polar bears weren't out.  It is $5.50 for seniors and kids 12 and under and $10 for adults. You must buy tickets online and must be a NM resident.

Beautiful falls.  The distance fgom the parking to the first overlook is less than a mile.  Overlooks 2 and 3 are a bit farther.  Kids and seniors can easily make the walks to those overlooks.  There are also trails that range in distance from 2.5 to 3.2 miles.  There is a Visitor Center but it was closed on July 13 due to COVID (bathrooms were open, though).  We went in to the park with our Senior National Park Pass and didn't pay more.  Some history also- the Patowmack Canal to bypass the falls was started by George Washington in 1885.

The world's largest hot springs pool.  We spent 4 hours in the healing waters. Their main pool, the “big” pool, is 405 feet long and 100 feet wide at the widest point. It has 1,071,000 gallons of water, and is kept at about 90° F / 32° C and features a diving area and exercise lap lanes. They claim that this is the world's largest hot springs pool. Their therapy pool, the “small” pool is 100 feet long and contains 91,000 gallons of water. It is kept at a temperature of about 104° F / 40° C. They sell food and the prices were reasonable.

Vfery nice and historic ruins.  The Kuaua pueblo had 1,200 rooms and many are exposed (some are buried to preserve them).  There is a small and very informative museum.  The most interesting thing is that you can see the ONLY kiva murals in the US.  That was impressive (sorry, no photos allowed). Another important thing is that there is a reconstructed kiva that you can enter (but not in March 2021 due to COVID restrictions).  The pueblo is very close to the Rio Grande and you can walk close to it with great views.

The Henry Hill visitor center has a small museum but also a map with lights that show the positions of the Confederate and Union armies and how the first battle of Manassas evolved. That map explains the terrain and the battle super well.  It takes 7 minutes.  We saw the museum on July 14, 2020.  We had to wear masks.  The battlefield is set for the 1st battle of  Manassas with cannons set.  There are multiple markers and plaques with information.  We walked only part of the battlefield.  You can see it in 1 hour.

Large and very nice gardens.  It has over 1,000 acres.  On July 20, 2020, the temperature was on the high 90s with humidity above at 40% and that made it hard to enjoy the gardens.  But the flowers, plants, waterfalls, fountains, woodlands, ponds, meadows, and structures are fantastic. The du Pont house also had a bit of history.  Look at my photos.  Even though I gave it 5 stars, I have to say that Butchart Gardens near Victoria, Canada was better (fewer fountains, though)

We went on December 4, 2020.  It was a great sunny day but the wind made it too cold to walk the trails.  We drove the South loop snd then the North loop.  I recommend doing that instead of rushing to the "flight deck".  There were lots of ducks and a family of wild boars in the South lopp.  In the North loop we mostly saw birds-  sandhill cranes and snow geese.  We slso spotted a coyote ogling a flock of sandhill cranes but didn't attempt to get close.

I really liked it.  The tour takes you about 1,000 feet into the mine's tunnel and your guide talks about the mine and mining. It was a working gold mine years ago.  After the mine, you can pan for gold.  The photo below shows lits of gold but the large majority is in my wife's bracelet.  The negative is that there were no seats to pan for gold.  They turn off the lights in the tunnel and it gets completely dark.
dislikes: Lack of seating for gold panning

reviews_attraction.text: Nice little town museum.  Entrance was $5.  Lots of info on the town, how it came to be named after a TV show, how the show's MC and the stars of the show continued to visit T or C, and its history before and after the TV show.  There is something for everyone from huge mastodon fossils to branding irons.  You can spend two hours there if you read everything.  I recommend the two narrated documentaries.

What a simple yet beautiful park.  It is a rock arch 150 feet high and 100 feet thick and the walls are 90 feet apart. US route 11, Lee's Highway goes on top of the arch. The  bridge itself is great but adding the brook, recreation of indian village, and the waterfall makes this a 5 star.

The entrance on the E Jefferson street side is hard to find and there is no sign.  But the park and the trail was great.  The brook had running water and there were kids playing in the brook.  We even saw two dear a block from the park in a house's backyard.

The Belle Meade Plantation used to be a horse stud farm.  The grounds were great but the tour of the mansion was not worth the $25 per person fee for seniors.  I would recommend that you skip the mansion tour, specially if you won't go to the wine tasting.

Pretty park with a full size replica of the Parthenon, an obelisk honoring the founder of Nashville (James Robertson), and a pond/ water feature.  The latter needs upkeep because the water is green.  They are planning a monument to the 19th ammendment.

Hill used for religious pilmigrages.  The hill has three crosses as in the calvary.  There are great views from the top of the hill.  The climb up from the parking area takes about 30 minutes for someone with bad knees.

The entrance was $20 for seniors.  I thought it was reasonable for the size of the place and how completely they cover Cash's life.  There were videos, gold records, his outfits and jewelry, awards, and much more.

Very nice park with tennis courts, large green area, walking path, skateboard area, kids area with swings etc., good views, dog park, climbing area, and racket ball courts.  Great place to take sunset photos.
The place was closed due to COVID on June 30, 2020.  It's only open for scuba divers.  I managed to take photos.  The water is indeed blue and very clear.  The picnic area is small but a nice place.
June 30.  The road to the campsites was closed.  The lake looks like a largo pond.   The bathrooms in the Overlook building did work.
You need to pay to get in.  It has a good size lake but there is NO shade.  No trees on the Southern part.  (there are two entrances)

Best decision we made, this rafting company was great!

We took a Family Float trip as our introduction to rafting and it was amazing. Our guide Mike was THE BEST!!! He made everyone feel safe and a part of the experience. He helped us understand our roles, taught us so much, but most importantly made the whole ride fun!!!

The ride was perfect for beginners! Thrilling and calming, a chance to take in the scenery. We also got to see a mule deer drinking on the shore!

There are many companies to choose from, but ART was a great value and worth every penny. Every person we interacted with was kind and helpful. Avoid decision fatigue and pick this for your next rafting trip!

This was really a great experience with kids. Definitely park near rt. 19 and start your adventure with a boat ride. The kind guide will clue you on what to look for and the history of the park. Inside, be ready for up close and personal with Floridian wildlife. We saw manatee fed, got up close with 7 gators, so many birds, Lu the hippo and much more. It's a very walkable park. Plus the fish bowl is a jem of the natural beauty that is often being destroyed in FL.

Would recommend to anyone with kids or who wants to get to know the animals of Florida!

Getting it out of the way, the falls are beautiful and I am glad to have gone. I just wish spaces like this were public spaces, not private efforts designed to extract every dollar from your wallet. Every bit of this area is just stunning, it cost our family of 4 $50 to see it ☹️

The Broadmoor has invested in saving this tourist trap and has solved the potential parking challenges that the space would have. However, the shuttle service can be frustrating to leave. During the summer, plan on 30 min wait or more to get back to your car.

Out family planned a 2 hour ride as a part of out YMCA of the Rockies stay and couldn't have been happier! Our party had several first time and novice riders. Our wranglers were outstanding giving us directions and helping feel confident.

The ride was great for newbies, rugged parts made it feel thrilling, amazing views and memories for all of us. Stop by the gift shop and pick up a horseshoe with your horse's name on it,. inexpensive souvenir for the kids at < $5.

Make sure you add this to your visit, worth every penny!!!

I really want to give this more stars, because I really want to see Champaign-Urbana have a great children's science museum.

A number of people have put a great deal of effort into making great components of this space. Unfortunately it doesn't come together very well. It has seen very free updates and doesn't measure up to the children's museums in Decatur or Normal.

That being said, the staff are great and having a birthday party there is certainly a great time.

The short Observation Trail is a great walk with amazing views of both rock formations and the Shawnee Forest that stretches around in all directions.

You can climb on huge rocks with no guardrails, just common sense holding you back. For this reason, those with small children should be advised.

It can be easy to miss, but make sure you catch chimney rock, it's so interesting.

Wow, what an amazing place. It is such a great opportunity to see some geological wonders. So thankful this is made free to the public.

Go early, take the drive around the park and get oriented. Take in the southern sites of the park from some of the smaller parking lots. Then head to the Visitors Center and ride the shuttle in to catch the north side. You will love it!

What a gorgeous find along the Embrass River. The hiking is remarkably hilly for Central Illinois,  with great areas to explore quietly or enjoy the many park amenities with friends. They have a great playground and many picnic table locations. They also have camping on site if you want to stay longer. This was our return trip and loved the hiking with our kids!

What an amazing visit to this gem.  Visitors can explore so many varieties of plants in the this beautifully kept space. Through each door, visitors will find themselves swept away from the city around them and into natural wonders found all over the globe.

As a bonus there is no cost, but please take the opportunity to contribute to their great work!

Great addition to the YMCA of Estes Park. Great collection of hiking maps, indoor climbing wall, place to check out (& buy) hiking boots, fishing supplies and a cool gift shop.

One of the best things we found there was the gift shop has these great patches for all the RMNP hikes. Awesome way to highlight the accomplishments of your kids efforts!

How can you not love this place? It is an iconic Chicago experience which you should visit often. I love how they maintain older exhibits with exceptional care AND always infuse new exhibits to keep the experience different every time you attend.

The experience is great for young and old alike!
Science Rocks!!! 🔬👩‍🔬⚛️🌪️✈️🚂🐞⚗️🗜️

An amazing place to get out and enjoy the fresh air and beautifully maintained grounds. Hike through woods, explore sculptures, and so many fields. The kids play area is simply amazing. I think the only downside is the cost. We were fortunate to visit on guest passes with friends, but I could see cost keeping many people away 😞

An amazing park just got better with a splash play space added June 2018. It had a great walking path around the park, plenty of space to do almost anything. Cookouts, playgrounds for all ages of kids, tennis courts and so much more.

Easy walking distance to two custard places will complete your visit!

This is an amazing natural space in Urbana. Unfortunately, the park district has really struggled to keep the lake clean. Build up of nutrients has led to choking blooms on the lake ☹️.

The Lake House, walking paths, pavilion, playgrounds, and open fields still make this a great place to visit.

We enjoyed the stay at the campground. Well tended and folks running it were genuinely kind and helpful to all. There are some nice little trails of the campground. Decent bathroom facilities and the fire pits were well kept.

Wood for sale on site, bring cash (learn from our mistake)!

We actually just walked out front, as we arrived near closing time.  My last visit was almost 35 years ago, they have really upgraded the experience and Graceland museum grounds. You can check out his planes from the outside. Next visit we will have to check the times!

We don't have many water places in Champaign, so thanks to the Champaign Park District for maintaining this and for keeping it simple. You can put in a paddle-powered boat, go fishing or go for a walk. Only downside is some of the visitors seem a bit... sketchy.

What a fun playground! Our kids had a great time. Loved the separate areas, even with many kids there, it did not feel crowded. Wish we could have seen the vines all greened up in the passage ways, as that looked awesome. Proximity to the bathrooms also a bonus.

Great park for a variety of athletic events. Baseball fields, soccer fields, disc golf course,  and lots of parking options.

We had a cross country meet there and it was perfect.
Not the Nelson Park of the past! The Ropes course, miniature golf and batting cages were super fun and a great value. Looking forward to the water park under construction!

Under construction, but one food spot serving World of Coke and the Civil & Human Rights Museum (neither serve food) was really frustrating.

Many great views of the area.
Such a great gem hidden on campus! Really enjoyed the regular collection as well as the feature exhibits on display. A huge bonus was the student exhibit. #art
What a great way to take in the mighty Mississippi! Amazing views of the Memphis Skyline and a good bit of exercise. Got to see the flood waters up close.
A beautiful natural area with many walking and bike paths. Take your time to explore along the Sangamon River, prairie walks or in the line forest.

Seems nice, unfortunately we were there for a cold and rainy cross country meet.☔🌧️

Looking forward to a better visit next time.

Raven Rock State Park is kind of in the middle of nowhere, but only about an hour from Raleigh or Fayetteville and it's a great place for a hike or just to enjoy nature. The park is split by the Cape Fear River into a north and south side, where the south side has most of the trails and attractions and the north side has bridle trails. Most of the attractions from the south side of the park are on the river and use the trail network to reach them. Most of the trails are rated easy, being mostly flat and short with a few steep parts, particularly the stairs down to Raven Rock. The park has a very nice new visitor center where you can pick up a map or ask a ranger for information and view exhibits about the human and natural history of the region.

Although its called Lanier Falls, its really more of a rapid. To reach the "falls", follow the Campbell Creek Loop Trail which heads off west from the visitor center. After crossing a foot bridge over the creek, turn right and follow Campbell Creek to where it reaches the Cape Fear River and continue on until a well-marked spur trail to the right goes down to the falls. During the warmer months, this is a nice place to cool off in the water after a hike. Back at the visitor center, follow the Raven Rock Loop Trail, but don't turn right to go to Raven Rock just yet. Go straight on Fish Traps Trail and turn left on Northington Ferry Trail. The trail ends at the Cape Fear River on the other side of Campbell Creek. About two thirds of the way down the trail, there is a grave marker for Jesse Northington just off the trail. The Northington Lock and Dam was used for transportation across the Cape Fear River for routes between Raleigh and Fayetteville. Later on, a bridge was built over the river and the lock and dam was destroyed by a hurricane.

Back to the Fish Traps Trail, turn left and go down to the Fish Traps. These are some big rocks in the river that are just above the water level. They flood when the water level is high and fish get trapped on rocks, hence the name. If the water level isn't too high, its possible to hop out onto the rocks without getting wet. The Fish Traps Trail continues on a short ways to a big rock and a view of the remains of the Northington Lock and Dam. Head back up Fish Traps Trail and turn onto Raven Rock Loop Trail. Just before reaching the rock, there is an overlook with a nice view of the river below and a few benches to relax and enjoy the view. To get down to Raven Rock requires going down (and later coming back up) about 90 stairs. Once down, you will definitely want to take a rest before heading back up. The rock is quite long and its possible to walk a ways down along the river bank. There is a really cool tree here with an impressive root system over the rocks that is exposed. From Raven Rock its about a mile back to the parking lot. If you're really ambitious, you can take the Little Creek Loop Trail and enjoy two more views of the river - from the canoe campsite and the group campsite.

The north side of the park is primarily for equestrians, but hikers may use the trails as well.  I've only hiked the West Bridle Loop Trail, but there are a couple more small waterfalls here.  The first is a 4-foot slide on Avents Creek, just upstream of the bridge on River Road.  The trail crosses the creek here and you can see the falls from the road.  The second is Jumping Fish Falls, also on Avents Creek.  It is just upstream of the ford on the trail.  Although only about 5 feet high, it's very scenic and photogenic.  You can get up close on either side of the creek to get pictures.

Toms Creek Falls is a scenic 60-foot waterfall located north of Marion. It's an easy hike, less than a mile round trip and the trail and overlook has recently been made handicapped accessible. From exit 86 on I-40, go north on US-221 about 12 miles and turn left on Huskins Branch Road. The road starts out paved, turns to gravel, then back to paved. About 1.2 miles from the turn, there is a parking area on the right, just past a gravel road and right before the bridge over Toms Creek. Hike the Falls Branch Trail (#214) less than a half-mile to the waterfall. The trail follows an old roadbed, so it's an easy stroll in the woods. The trail leads to an accessible overlook with views of the waterfall. It's also possible to go past the overlook right up to the base of the waterfall and wade in the shallow water. The watershed is small so the water flow is always low, but its still a scenic waterfall with the water falling in a tall, narrow stream in several distinct sections. There used to be an old mica mine right next to the waterfall. It had filled with water but you could get into the entrance. On my most recent visit, it looked like the mine had collapsed and the Forest Service had Do Not Enter signs around it.

Lower Haw River State Natural Area protects a section of the Haw River from US-15/501 in Bynum south to Jordan Lake.  As a natural area, it is less developed than a park and as such there are few amenities besides parking at the trailheads.  The north trailhead is in Bynum off Bynum Church Road and the south trailhead is along US-64 eastbound, just east of the bridge over Haw River.  A four mile along the east bank of the river connects the two.  It is not an official trail, so it's not maintained.  And there are a lot of beavers in the area, so many trees across the trail.  But its easy to follow and a beautiful trail that stays right alongside the river.  We only saw a couple other people on our hike and we were here for about four hours.  Three tributaries flow into Haw River and you'll have to go upstream a bit to cross.  Pokeberry Creek, the northernmost of the three, has the most water and is the most difficult to cross.  Overall, a great hidden gem for hiking and nature and I definitely plan to come back again.

We visited Shark Valley on our first day in the Everglades.  It was a beautiful day, so we rented bicycles instead of doing the tram tour.  On bikes, we could stop when we wanted for wildlife photos.  And we stopped a lot.  Tremendous wildlife viewing opportunities along the tram trail.  We saw great blue herons, green herons, tricolored herons, snowy egrets, white ibises, wood storks, and more alligators than we could count.  About half-way along the the loop is the observation tower, where you can climb up for good views over the "River of Grass".  There's also a restroom here.  I would definitely recommend arriving early.  We got there at 830 and had no trouble parking or getting bikes.  When we finished the loop around noon, the parking lot was full and there was a 30 minute wait for bikes.

Rock Bridge Memorial State Park is right outside Columbia and a great place to hike and see amazing karst geology.  We hiked the Devil's Icebox Trail, a short trail that is mostly boardwalk and wooden stairs.  It first leads to the Rock Bridge, the park's namesake, a huge natural tunnel that you can walk under.  There's even a small waterfall under here.  A little bit further is the Devil's Icebox, a double sinkhole leading to two caves.  Connors Cave may be explored, but Devils Icebox Cave is closed to the public.  We didn't have flashlights or caving gear so only went a short ways into Connors Cave.  Overall, an awesome place for a hike and to see amazing geological features.  Bring a helmet, good flashlight or headlamp and appropriate shows if you want to explore Connors Cave.

Dismal Swamp State Park protects a portion of the Great Dismal Swamp in North Carolina.  No camping here as there's limited dry land in the park and the hydraulic bridge is the only access over the canal.  There are, however, many miles of old fire roads for hiking and biking as well as access to Dismal Swamp Canal for boating.  Kayaks, canoes and bikes are available for rent from the visitor center.  The Great Dismal Swamp, which George Washington called a glorious paradise, is a beautiful and unique natural area.  The Swamp Boardwalk behind the Visitor center provides an easy way to experience the swamp.  Our visit was cut short by a flat tire, but we'd like to return and explore more.

We visited Kings Mountain National Military Park while camping at the state park over Memorial Day weekend.  Military through the Ages event was going on for the holiday weekend.  We didn't catch the reenactments, but there were a lot of exhibits on wars throughout American history.  It was a lot of fun talking to the folks from different wars and a great learning experience.  We saw military rations and parachutes from World War 2, medical devices and remedies from the 18th century, and learned how different weapons worked.  We also hiked the 16 mile Kings Mountain Trail that connects the national and State Park.  Overall, a great place to learn about history and enjoy nature.

West Point on the Eno is a great city park in north Durham off Roxboro Road.  The park protects a beautiful stretch of Eno River with several hiking trails to explore.  The north-facing bluffs along the river support a microclimate cooler than surrounding areas that allows mountain laurel to thrive.  In early May, the blooms are beautiful.  The Eagle Trail on the north side of the river is part of the statewide Mountains-to-Sea Trail and provides access to Eno River State Park to the west and Falls Lake to the east.  The park also has several historical buildings on site, including the reconstructed West Point Mill, which is a functioning water-powered grist mill.

South Mountains State Park is one of the largest NC State Parks at more than 18,000 acres.  It is about 20 miles south of Morganton.  The South Mountains are a rugged range separated from the Blue Ridge Mountains by the Catawba Valley, reaching elevations of up to 3000 feet. With more than 40 miles of trails, it's a great place to hike.  High Shoals Falls is the most popular hike in the park.  The 80 foot waterfall is really beautiful, but use caution and don't climb the fence as several people have fallen to their deaths.  Chestnut Knob is another good hike, providing great views of the Jacob Fork River Gorge.  Overall, a great park and lots of fun to explore.

We took our dog to Lake Norman State Park for camping and hiking in December.  The Itusi Mountain biking trail was closed due to wet conditions, but the hiking only trails were open.  Alder Trail is a short loop starting from the visitor center and Lake Shore Trail is a longer loop from the campground.  Both stay real close to the lake and provide lovely views throughout the hike.  The family campground is very nice - spacious sites with adequate room between neighbors.  A short spur leads from the campground down to the lake facing west - a great spot to catch the sunset.  Overall, a great park not far from Charlotte and we'll be back to visit again soon.

South River Picnic Area is in the southern end of the Central District of Shenandoah just north of the Swift Run entrance at milepost 62.8.  The South River Trail starts from here and leads just over a mile down to an overlook for the falls.  The view here, however, is mostly obscured by trees.  To reach the base, continue on the trail a short ways and go right on the fire road.  The road leads to South River downstream of the falls and a short rocky spur trail leads right to the base.  It's an impressive waterfall, over 80 feet high.  But like most in Shenandoah, it can dry up so best to visit after periods of heavy rain.

Starved Rock State Park protects an unusual area of deep sandstone canyons along the Illinois River.  I visited over Memorial Day weekend during flood conditions and most of the canyons had waterfalls.  The park is extremely popular, being about an hour from Chicago, so recommend arriving early.  I got there right when they opened and saw few people on the hike out; it was a zoo on the way back.  There are 18 canyons in total.  The most spectacular canyons and waterfalls were St. Louis, Wildcat, and LaSalle in my opinion, but all are pretty.  The only downside was that the trails were extremely muddy, so plan to get dirty.

We stopped at Ferne Clyffe State Park while traveling in the Shawnee Hills.  It was a really beautiful little park.  The main waterfall wasn't flowing when we visited but the gorge is beautiful and its an easy hike.  We also hiked to Hawk's Cave, which is a massive shelter cave.  This was really cool and the highlight of our visit.  It was raining on and off so we hung out in the cave to stay dry.  We also visited Bork's Waterfall in a different part of the park.  Not much water flowing here, but another beautiful little gorge.  I really liked this park and would definitely come back again if in the area.

Old Fort Picnic Area is a forest service area along Swannanoa Creek.  Besides the secluded little picnic area, it provides access to a couple of trails, open to both hiking and mountain biking.  Youngs Ridge Trail leads steeply up to Kitsuma Peak with nice views looking west towards Asheville.  The summit is forested but some cliffs just to the north provide an overlook.  The other trail is Point Lookout Trail.  Formerly the route of US-70, the paved greenway trail leads to Point Lookout, a viewpoint for the Royal Gorge.  I hiked a loop of the two trails for a challenging 10 mile circuit.

Brumley Nature Preserve is one of the newest Triangle Land Conservancy properties to open to the public, having opened in April 2017.  It is also one of the largest at more than 600 acres with over 10 miles of trails for hiking and biking.  The South entrance of New Hope Church Road provides access to multi-use trails, while the North side is hiking only, so this side is better if seeking solitude.  Great place to explore, with a number of old ruins, cemeteries, and farm ponds.  It's quite popular so try to arrive early on a nice weekend to ensure available parking.

Wright Brothers National Memorial commemorates the birth of aviation.  Wilbur and Orville came to Kitty Hawk in the early 20th century to complete their experiments in powered flight, taking advantage of the Outer Banks' steady winds and isolation at the time.  The visitor center has a nice museum showcasing the brothers' ingenuity and perseverance.  A 60 foot monument is on the top of Kill Devil Hill.  And the flight line shows how far those first few successful flights made it.  Overall, a great place to learn about the beginnings of human flight.

We took our dog for a hike at Pinnacle Park and had a great time.  It was right after snow the park was winter wonderland.  We made a loop with East Fork and West Fork Trails to go up to the Pinnacle for stunning views of the mountains and Sylva far down below.  We also made a detour to Gina Falls and Fisher Falls.  The waterfalls are off trail and somewhat difficult to find, though Fisher Falls is visible from East Fork Trail.  The going was slow in the snow, but if we return, I'd like to also hike to Blackrock Mountain.

We visited Twin Falls for a day hike with our dog.  The Twin Falls refers to Black Fork Falls and Marsh Fork Falls, there is no "Twin Falls".  And the two waterfalls are about a half-mile apart so not really twins.  But they're both nice waterfalls and its an easy hike to see them both.  We also hiked Cliffside Trail to the view points of Cabin Creek Gorge.  There is also a pioneer farm with crops and livestock.  The donkeys seemed very interested in our dog, they ran up to the fence and sniffed each other for a while.

Historic Yates Mill is a Wake County park that protects the old mill south of Raleigh.  Yates mill was in operation for 200 years before ceasing operations.  As the mill fell into disrepair, concerned citizens worked with the county to restore the mill and open a park.  In addition to the mill, there are about 3 miles of hiking trails along the millpond and through the surrounding woods.  Note that dogs are not allowed.  A beautiful little park to enjoy nature and learn about this history of the region.

Jockey's Ridge State Park protects the largest active sand dune system on the east coast.  Located in Nags Head in the Outer Banks, it is one of the most popular NC State Parks.  Two short trails lead around the dunes, through maritime shrub thickets and to Roanoke Sound.  The top of the dunes has great views of both the ocean and sound, and give perspective to how narrow this barrier island is.  In addition to hiking the dunes, hang gliding lessons are available through a private outfitter.

Water Wheel Park in Idaho Springs is a small park featuring the historic water wheel and Bridal Veil Falls.  A short paved trail leads from the parking area on 17th Avenue under I70 to a view of the wheel and falls.  The historic water wheel was built in 1893 by Charlie Tayler, who attributed his good health to the fact that he never kissed women or took baths.  We stopped here for a quick break driving west from Denver on I70.  Great little spot to stretch our legs and enjoy the view.

We took our dog for a hike at Moores Creek National Battlefield.  The park commemorates the Battle of Moores Creek, a pivotal patriot victory over British loyalists just prior to the start of the Revolutionary War.  The visitor center was closed when we visited but the monuments and signage brought the battle to life hiking along the 1-mile trail.  The area is very swampy so prone to flooding and recommend visiting in winter before the bugs come out.

Red Rock Canyon Open Space is a Colorado Springs city park with miles of trails through beautiful red rock spires and ridges.  The landscape is similar to nearby Garden of the Gods, but with smaller rock formations.  Although not as impressive, it's also a lot less crowded.  Overall, a great place in Colorado Springs to take a hike and enjoy the beautiful red rock formations without the excessive crowds of Garden of the Gods.

Bridal Cave is a beautiful show cave open for tours on Lake of the Ozarks near Camdenton.  Our tour guide was Sarah and she did a really great job of informing us about the history and geological features of the cave.  The tour lasts about an hour and a couple of the highlights were the Pipe Organ, Frozen Niagara and Mystery Lake.  Definitely recommend taking a tour of the beautiful Bridal Cave.

Big Creek Falls is a beautiful roadside waterfall along US-19W right across the state line from Tennessee.  We made a quick stop while driving by.  The waterfall is visible from the road or a short path leads down for a better view.  There's a big rock in front of the falls for a straight on view or climb down to the base.  The pool in front of the waterfall looks like an inviting swimhole.

The staff at the center there are pretty much all relatives of someone who lived in Nicodemus. We had an amazing presentation by a young lady whose grandparents lived there. Much more than I expected and a significant piece of American history. Currently there are around 27 residents still living in the only continuously occupied African American settlement West of the Mississippi.

Clinton Lake Park is a marvelous multi use park and lake. There a great view from the overlook area, and it's a marvelous picnic area as well. This is in the federal (corps) area, so there's no entry fee. The state oak area does require a day or annual pass.

Clinton is a nice park and lake with a variety of things to do. Boating, fishing, camping, hiking, biking, disk golf, of road bike trails, etc. We were there today road biking. During the week there's very little traffic, so it's a great place to bike.

In the middle of nearly nowhere, this is a worthwhile stop. Yes, the statue is huge, and that's impressive, but the center has a wealth of information and interesting displays. If you're passing through, get off the interstate and drop in.

Lone Star is one of the oldest lakes around here. Predates the much larger corps reservoirs. Built as a WPA project and county owned. There's private frontage around half of the lake, but also public use areas and swim beach.

If you're a history buff, you'll love this place. It's a unique collection of restored buildings, museums, a theater and more. Arrow Rock played a big part in Western expansion and Missouri history. Nice campgrounds as well.

One of the great natural attractions. If you're in the area, you should allow at least a 2-3 hours to drive to rim and walk to the various overlooks. Plan on getting off your butt and walking a few hundred yards.

Unfortunately, it appears that Illinois is not doing well maintaining their state parks. Marvelous area, but many of the views are obstructed with undergrowth, and buildings are showing deterioration.
The Liberty Memorial has been part of Kansas City as long as I can remember, but when it was rebuilt and became the WW1 Museum, it moved to a higher level. It's a marvelous experience.
Great views of the Mississippi from the high bluffs. Decent campground except for the hay being put up in the adjacent farm field which sent dust rolling through for a few hours.
One of the most scenic trails in the region and part of the Lawrence Loop. This section runs along the edge of the Kansas River and always has people walking and biking.
Nice riverside park with a nice passed trail. No rest rooms and one shelter house. Good place for short outings, walking the dog or enjoying pleasant weather.
This is a great place to take you kids or grandkids to learn and explore the natural world. A bit aged but undergoing improvements. Otherwise a 5 star.
Another great place in the marvelous west Florida city of Venice. Besides being a nice city park, all the trees and shrubs are marked and identified.
We only stayed one night, but the camp areas were nice and it's a good stopping point. There's not a lot to see and do, but a pleasant place.
Very interesting geology and one of the few lakes in otherwise arid Northwest Kansas. Definitely a stopping place if you're in the area.
As with most Illinois parks the lack of funding is starting to show. The campground was clean and a good place to stop for a night.
Nice park and camping in the Hill Country area. We were there for the bluebonnet season in the spring. Lots of parks and wineries.
This is a fun stop and walk through history. Since there are several building, it best done when the weather Street is pleasant.
A great park with trails and attractions. Definitely worth a visit or two. Be sure to do the Bird Walk to see the water foul.
A very small state park that has more of a city park feel. The campground is quite nice and popular. Well maintained.
Definitely worth a trip. To really see the birds, you need to be willing to walk the 3/4 mile out into the reserve.
Typical of a number of Indian Missions. It's a fine old stoned structure, bit was closed when we were there.
A very nice park with a museum explaining the history of rail in the area. Great for a picnic or walk.
One of the nicest stops among this section of the trail. A park like setting. Rest rooms and a cafe.

This is a grate park. There are some areas with picnic tables and cover overhead. There is a good play ground and two playgrounds for differnt ages. There are nice paved and dirt parents throughout the park. It's a grate place to run. But the path go's next to the pond in some areas so you may want bug spray. I suggest bringing a table cloth and somthing to clean bird pool up with if you want to eat at a picnic table. Bring plenty of water because there is no running water at this park. The are porta pottys in the parking lot. My family and I have had a lot of fun here.

This park is good for social distancing there is a small play ground but also a lot of space to runaround the baseball fields. I went to this park to get out doors during the "pause" for COVID 19 I arrived at the park with my son and evan though there were other people at the park we were able to stay more then 12 ft apart while running around. I left out a star because at this time there is not bathroom or port a potty here. I assume that is because of COVID 19

My whole family likes to visit the museum there are always more exhibits then we can see in one day. The traveling exhibits are interesting. The geology exhibit has been one of my favorite exhibits since I was a kid in the 1980's. Our three year old likes the discovery area with the water tables. The staff is friendly and helpful. The volunteers are helpful and knolagable when looking for specific things.... Like maybe lepercons/gnomes in the exhibits👍😉

I visited Saint Mark's Episcopal Cathedral with my husband on a weekday afternoon. Everyone we met was kind and welcoming. We were given self guided tour books that explained the history of the congregation and the cathedral. We enjoyed walking around and looking at the rooms and acatucture. We were pleased to see places to go to pray quietly. The building is beautiful. Its well worth a visit.

The people I saw here were all friendly. There where many places to spend time alone in prayer. The Mass in the middle of the day was short and in a small setting. It was lovely. The Cathertal is beautiful and tours are available. The workmanship and acatucture and artifacts here are worth a visit to see eaven if someone dosn't hold the same beliefs the beauty and artistry can be enjoyed here.

This is a great trail for a bike, running, useing a running stroller or walking. It is a continuous paved trail from Island grove park in Greeley to Windsor/Timneth area and starts again in Fort Collians. There are occional porta pottys at trail heads. Being your own drinking water because there is no running water at any of the Trail heads.

This is one of the trail heads for the Poudre Trail. It is also a popular spot for fishing 🐟. There is a handicap accessible restroom in the parking lot. There are unpaved trails off of the Trail and free clean up after your dog bags and trash cans along the trail. This area is beautiful and has trees and access to the pond.

This place has a wheelchairs capable playground and swimgs♿. The play ground is good for all ages. The park has a paved walk all the way around it. The things I didn't like about Renaissance Park is that it doesn't have shade form trees or any type of public restroom.  It is a very nice park even without these things.

😀 this park has a nice playground, misting arches, historic buildings, a small swim area in Lake Windsor, a small outdoor theater and a paved walk around the lake. This is a fun place to spend time outside with children. The public restrooms at the park are ok but look a little old and dirty.

This is a small beautiful park. There are public restrooms available and benches to reset on. There is a fountain that kids can splash in small stage area and trees for shade. There are people here a lot and its a good place to bring our four year old durring the day to play with other kids.
likes: Activities: Fountain for kids, Play area, Shaded areas

reviews_attraction.text: The building here are wonderfully restored and keepet in grate condition I like how the path shows how thing have changed over time and all the local history that the volunteers know about. My 3 year old loves events held here like baby animal days and pets and popsicles.

This park has a grate playground and there are soccer fileds. There is not a barhroom with running water but it does have porta potties.
The play ground is good for kid who like to climb. There is a zip line slides swings and lots of platforms to climb onto.

This is a great place to enjoy nature year round. Tickets are required ti be reserved online before your visit. Masks are required. Staying in the one way path is required. Its still a nice place to get out to.
I love this park. The only thing that would make it better is bathrooms that are not locked.... And/ or a porta potty that is clean. The porta potty had human wast all over the seat. 😕
This place has an epic playground, a trail head to the Poudre trail, lots of open space with grass, large trees, a large pavillion for large groups and a historic building.
The play ground here is small. But it is a nice lake to walk around or run around with the kids because it is not too big and the path is nice all the way around the water.

A wonderful place to visit with walking trails benches to rest on bathrooms labeled plants and several different types of gardens.
Masks are required in the restrooms.
We could spend all day here and never see all of the exhibits. The food in the coffee is good and the ebents are intresting. We love the Japanese garden and the zoo.
Such a neat find in Minnesota. The ball curator was very friendly and knowledgeable about the history of the ball. Especially cool if you are a Weird Al fan!
My son and I had a great day at the museum. My son is two and loved all the hands on exsibits. Every time we visit there is something new to see or do. 👍😀
This park has a whealchair accesable playground. And it has frizbe golf goals. But it doesn't have public restrooms or a paved walk all the way around it.
The view from the stone bridge was grate. There are pathes for bikes and walkers. We saw some eagles around the river. This was a nice place for a walk.
There are nice walking trails here and so many signs to explain the history of the area. Its a grate place to be outside and learn about the past.
I love the dog park with the pond here and so do our dogs. I took off one star because I couldn't find a restroom. But the trails and beautiful.
City park is big and has a big playground. The only problem I have is that the bathrooms are locked in the fall and the winter.

Part science museum with interactive displays and part live and functioning research center. This place is really fun if you are into learning about the science of the weather and atmosphere. The NCAR building is an iconic landmark in the city of Boulder and is celebrating its 50th year anniversary. The NCAR building is also a popular destination for hikers since it features many different trails within its property. The road that leads up to the building is a steep 710 ft climb that is also a sort of makeshift proving ground for cyclists. I enjoyed the many wonderful and memorable displays such as the one that makes clouds and you can touch and run your hands through, the one with the plunger bulb on top to simulate mainstream wind patterns and the crazy pendulum one by the stairs. Guided tours are offered every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday at noon, but check their website to confirm. Our tour guide was monotone and droned on and on. but the tour is free. There is also a cafeteria to grab some lunch.

This newly remodeled park is the probably the best, in terms of fun, park that Ive ever been too. The main attraction to this park is the giant 30 ft tall tower. Inside this tower is a massive arrangement of ropes, platforms,  and other handholds and footholds that allows you to climb all the way to the top. The interior of this tower is large and spacious and I, as a 6ft tall adult, could fully stand upright and not feel cramped or confined.  At the top there also is a wide and large spiral slide that in it itself is a fun means of egress. The sprawling landscape of this park also had lush green grass, large shade trees, and the normal park accoutrements such as swings, slides and other playground type equipment. As for the namesake of this park, Paco Sanchez created the first Hispanic radio station in Denver and later became a social activist helping the poor and under privileged find housing, set up bank accounts and he even held office in the Colorado House of Representatives in 1968.

Whether you're into old cars, trains, planes, motorcycles or bicycles, this place is for you! Many of the vintage items either belong too or are on loan to the museum by a private owner. By each item displayed is a detailed description and history, which I found to be useful in explaining why the item is in the museum. Many of the cars and other museum items are for display only but there are are few items, such as the trains that can be interacted with. One of my favorite areas of the museum is " Biking through History " they have a large room with bikes from the early 1800's through the 1970's. Its interesting to see how the styles and mechanical aspects have changed throughout the years. They even have a tribute to Wilbur and Orville Wright who once sold and repaired bicycles before using bike parts to build the first "flying machine". This is an trip through history of transportation and something that everybody of all ages will enjoy.

Dillon Reservoir is a great place for the outdoor enthusiast. Fishing, all different types of boating at the marina and a recreation path encompasses the entire perimeter (around 23 miles) to allow popular activities such as hiking and biking. Dillon Reservoir is also the main water source for the city of Denver. Back in the 1950's when Denvers population was growing. Dillon Reservoir was created to accommodate the water needs of the growing city. The Blue River was dammed and the reservoir was created, In addition to the river water the yearly snow pack from the surrounding mountains keeps the reservoir full. In severe drought years when the water level is low you can see the old remnants of what remained in the area before it's was flooded and became what we have today.

The Money Museum is an interesting place to spend about and hour or so  if you are visiting the 16th street mall area. This free self guided tour allows one to see all the different forms of currency that has been used in the United States since the first forms of paper money were used. Other points of interest included the counterfeit detection test and the many different "edutainment" computer simulators which teach about the value of money, loans, interest, and inflation. If math, finance and accounting is your thing, then you will love this small interactive museum. Dont forget to bring your government issued ID since they will scan it and run it through a background search plus run you through a metal detector before being allowed to enter.

Since Quilting is a form of art, I viewed this more as an art collection rather than a museum. They had many quilts on display. I believe the quilts where made by a small group of woman on a small Asian Pacific island near Japan. This was the majority of items on display in the larger room, the docent said there was quilts in the smaller back room that were of the American civil war era. When I looked at them they seemed to be reproductions with a photo next to them of the original. This is understandable since a quilt from the civil war era would be very valuable and not be hung loosely and unguarded. Overall I found this place interesting and the ladies at the front desk were friendly and accommodating.

The area that Sloans lake is now occupying  was once farm land. Named after Thomas F. Sloan, a homesteader in the mid to later 1800s that used this land for farming and raising cattle. One day he dug a well and the nest morning his land was flooded by the underground aquifer and then eventually became knows as Sloans lake. This is a great park in the town of Edgewater and very large, many events are held here, namely the Dragon boat festival being among its largest. A great place to run,walk, jog or bike ride along the concrete path that runs along the entire perimeter of the lake. There is plenty of parking and this is a great spot to have a nice little summer picnic.
likes: On-site Activities: Running, walking, jogging, biking

reviews_attraction.text: Come take a quick 1.6 mile hike to the top of Mt. Galbraith. This 7,260 ft mountain boasts magnificent view of Clear Creek Canyon and Golden Gate Canyon as well as the town of Golden. First time hikers should wear light colored loose fitting clothing such as shorts and a t-shirt in summer weather.
