I love to come here on my weekends! I enjoy the fresh produce and the merchants.  I have found amazing soaps here, as well as vegetables! I love coming on a sunny day and walking around the market.  The people watching and the large varieties of food to eat, is perfect on a nice weekend day!

I liked the boardwalk, if you come to Atlantic City this is something you must see. Talk your time and walk up and down the boardwalk, there are plenty of stores, restaurants and people to see. The boardwalk is wide and there are little carts going up and down the boardwalk with people.

The tour was not the best. It felt rushed and did not get too much information from the tour guide. The house itself is very nice for a former plantation home in the DC area. The home is restored. The best part about the tour is, it's free. It's a great free activity to do in the area.

This is a great park for locals living in the area. If you do not feel like the driving far this is the place to go to. There are a few hiking trails and there is a small stream running through the park. Stop into the forest to escape the city and the suburbs.

Beautiful beach that is excellent for finding shells. The water is a lovely greenish blue. There are dolphins and a variety of birds to be seen here. If you have a boat take the boat around the islands. Great place to swim and to hand out for the day.

A wonderful hidden gem in the dc area. Come here and try the wines. Come with friends and share the meat and cheese platter with a bottle of wine to share. There are many spots to eat and drink throughout the vineyard. Staff was helpful and friendly.
This is a great local hidden gem in dc. There isn’t much here besides the steps. It’s a great place to come in the summer and enjoy the weather.  Bring your lunch or read a book.
Great place to visit.  Off the beaten path for tourist sites.  This is a good place to come for 1-2 hours with the family to see Lincoln's cottage.

Buy the family membership if you live here! Small but mighty, this science museum / planetarium occupied my children for five hours on a rainy Tuesday - and I had to drag them out of there :) Prices for one visit are expensive, but for $80 a family membership you get unlimited visits and four complimentary passes to the planetarium show. There are LOTS of toys to build with, interact with, explore with, etc.  If your child likes to build or create, they will want to stay all day.  The planetarium screen is frankly outdated, but they have new shows every season that are nonetheless informative and engaging. There is a cool gift shop with STEM items for sale, and a large indoor/outdoor area to eat a packed lunch (they do not sell food).  The bathrooms are clean, and the parking is free and easily accessible.  We will be coming here several times a year!

This is a huge, sprawling complex of playgrounds, splash park, picnic areas, ball fields, and paved trails that make for a very nice, if confusing, recreational area. There are several convenient restrooms and water fountains, and there's plenty of parking everywhere.

The splash pad is a nice new addition - it's small and simple, but it's a great place to cool off and it has a large shaded pavilion with picnic tables for parents to sit and watch their kids run around in the water.

The playgrounds are also very nice, although they are not shaded and can get uncomfortable hot in summer.

I want to love this location, but the island maintenance is currently underfunded and there's a lot to be done. Much of Kingman Island looks like a half-renovated parking lot; there's a lot of trash in spots, and several rusted dumpster trailers that haven't been emptied in a long time.  There are no restrooms, water fountains, or any indoor structures.  There are several picnic tables and a couple of interpretive nature signs, but mostly this is an island with untapped potential. I would love to see DC upgrade this location in the future.

This preserve might have been nice when it was created in 2015, but it is an overgrown mess today. There is no good reason to hike this trail, unless you want mosquitoes and ticks to hitch a ride back with you. There are plenty of better maintain trails in the area that have just as many wildlife viewing opportunities.

There is no parking lot, just a pull off space for cars that is often taken up by the corporation across the street. There are no bathroom facilities, no picnic tables, and no water fountains. I won't be returning.
dislikes: No facilities (bathrooms, picnic tables, water fountains)

reviews_attraction.text: I've completed two rooms here (Sherlock, and the very creepy Edgar Allen Poe room), and it's been a blast both times.  I would suggest going with a group of friends - it's so much more fun if you work through puzzles with your buds!  It's pricey for 45 minutes of fun, but it's a truly original experience and very memorable.  Parking is solely on busy streets, so Uber if you can or drive if you must.  The staff are excited to be there, and definitely add to the fun. All in all, an unqualified recommend!

This is a huge recreational area. It has tons of open green space, a large children's playground, a duck pond, a hedge maze, plus amenities like vending machines, bathrooms, picnic tables, and lots of paved trails to ride bikes or walk on. There are good photo opportunities for blooming flowers as well.

There is probably much more that I haven't experienced myself! There is lots of parking available as well. Definitely come visit and bring your dog and kids for a lovely day outside

Gorgeous aquarium right on the water - we went on Baltimore's "Dollar Days," a once a year event, so each member of our family was only $1. The organization is impressive, designed to take  you from the first to the fifth floors through the use of escalators.  It takes several hours to really see everything; my three young daughters were exhausted but happy when we were finished :) They didn't search our bags for outside food, so we were able to bring in our own and eat in the cafe!

I visited on a Wednesday afternoon and the place was perfectly empty and perfectly wonderful :) The staff is gracious and well-informed, the indoor and outdoor seating is authentically rustic and caters to families as well as wine lovers, and the location is beautiful. The wine is on par with local Virginia wines (not too bad, not too amazing), but you come to wineries for the ambiance and this one really delivers. I will go out of my way to visit here again!

This is a lovely park, with tons of open space, a frisbee course (disc golf), two small playgrounds, a pavilion for grilling and parties, an amazing little league field, and easy access to the Mohawk River bike trail.

Located next to Knolls Atomic, this is a fantastic place to access the bike path, or just to bird watch from the hills overlooking the river. In the winter there are no water or indoor facilities; in the summer there are portapotties.

Gorgeous park that has virtually everything: playground, splash pad, kayak launch, and even a mini arboretum. Plus, lots and lots of places to picnic, play baseball, tennis, basketball, or just sit and appreciate the beauty of this area by the river. Public restrooms are available. It's across the street from Jumpin Jack's Drive-In, so you don't need to go hungry either. That's also the place where I would park.

Come visit - it's beautiful!

It's hard not to love this place, nicknamed Chessie's Playground. It has amazing play structures, hiking trails, plus a FREE gorgeous splash park in the warm months. There's easy parking, and available restrooms from March to October. You can rent the shared pavilion for birthday parties through the Fairfax County recreation website. Oh, and the rec center itself is amazing as well, but that's a different review :)

This museum and education center feels brand new, and is an immersive experience designed to teach and explore Washington's life and accomplishments.  You walk through different scenarios and really feel like you're in the forest with a young Washington, or on the battlefield in winter, or becoming the first spymaster of the new country. There's a kids area as well, with costumes to try on and crafts to explore.

This complex is a massive, beautiful recreational area, with really interesting playgrounds, walking paths, a pool in the summer, and acres and acres of beautiful open space. If you are anywhere in the area and need a break from your travels and have children, or even if you just want a place to walk around for a half an hour, this is the place to check out!

Rest area on the George Washington Parkway and the Mount Vernon bike trail with lovely river views and plenty of shady grass to picnic. There are restroom facilities but no food or other amenities.  This picturesque location is busy on weekends,  but there is plentiful parking.  Park closes at dark,  which park service police will enforce in the summer!

Cute, but super small, nature preserve with a .4 mile circular concrete trail and limited elevation changes. Great for kids and strollers. No bathroom or facilities, 9-car parking lot, with a water fountain. There's a surprising amount of trash in the nature area - maybe a girl scout troop could clean it up as a scout project?

This is a gorgeous monument to one of our country's most enduring voices for freedom. The statues are on a grand scale, and the view of the Tidal Basin and the other monuments are outstanding.  Between this and the Roosevelt Memorial Park, the southern end of the Tidal Basin is the new must-visit location in the area.

Lovely free nature center, with outdoor hikes, ponds, and indoor turtles, crows and other small animals. They host birthday parties for a fee, with an animal presentation included. Nearby is an amazing Wizard of Oz playground, free petting zoo, and pay-for carousel and mini-train.  We think this place is great!

In our opinion, this is the loveliest playground in the area! Shaded, with interesting play sets, access to fields and a hiking trail, this park/playground is a wonderful find. The whole playground is shaded, with picnic tables and plenty of parking available.

There's no restrooms (just a portapotty).

Elegant, lovely memorial with limited parking and a beautiful overlook of Washington DC and Arlington National Memorial. There's not much to see besides the three spires, but it's an easy stop just beyond the Pentagon 9-11 memorial, and if you've served in the Air Force it's a must-visit.

Adorable local park with 5 miles of trail runs, fishing, kayaking, grilling next to the water, plus a playground for kids and a dog park for fur babies 😀 Truly beautiful location right off the park - plus a concession store, bathrooms, and friendly staff able to help. We love it here!

Fascinating, sprawling playground. Almost too big, in a way, especially if you are watching out for two or more kids, because they can get quite far away. It's designed with handicapped children in mind. It's usually packed on the weekends,with overflow parking required.

This is a very unique national park, where you can see live artistic performances, concerts and plays all summer long. They have a kid's theater in the woods, plus a larger adult venue. If you haven't seen Shakespeare in the woods, you're sincerely missing out!

This state park is for-pay. It has at least 9 miles of easy to moderate hiking paths, some that are gorgeous as well as wheelchair-accessible! There's also a playground, a nature center, and a variety of wildlife encounters.
Gorgeous, profound, a fitting tribute to a generation who gave so much. Every time I visit I'm amazed by the grandeur and the beauty of this massive memorial.
Truly amazing park in the middle of DC - 22 miles of trails! A horse barn. A nature center. A planetarium. An amazing time no matter when you visit.

I have heard about the Dripping Springs Natural Area in the mountains of Las Cruces the first month I arrived in New Mexico. A colleague told me that a 6-mile trail will lead you to interesting historical structures and dripping waters at the mountain top. As I have seen many beautiful waterfalls and relics in my other travels, and the fact that a long hiking trail on a hot summer day does not excite me, I forgo the idea of paying it a visit.

Until one Saturday.

The 6-mile trail is actually composed of four trails — the Dripping Springs, Crawford, La Cueva, and Fillmore trails. Among the four, the Dripping Springs seems to be the most popular. It is about 1.5 miles long (or 3 miles round trip).

On the way, I saw the first historical wooden structures said to have been built in the late 1800s. These buildings served as a livery, mercantile and chicken coop for the Van Patten’s Mountain Camp Resort and Hotel.

A couple of hundred meters away, I reached the dripping springs. Look closely on the photos below, you see people climbing up the rocks to get closer to the water drippings. The water is unfit for drinking, though. The reservoir behind the rocks used to supply water to the nearby Dripping Springs Hotel.

Few steps away is the Boyd’s Sanatorium, which was constructed in 1910 by Dr. Nathan Boyd. The buildings were operated as a tuberculosis sanatorium.

If you want to escape the city and see some amazing landscapes, visit the Dripping Springs Natural Area, in Las Cruces, New Mexico.  One last thing, driving up you will come to a point where the pavement ends. Be prepared.

Small garden, not so many variety of plants, and for a $7 admission fee, it is not worth seeing. I visited the Santa Fe Botanical Garden at the Museum Hill as it was just right across the Museum of International Folk Art. The entrance to the garden was a little confusing. If you don’t walk and check a small trailer that was placed sideways relative to the parking lot, you won’t see the ticketing booth.

After I paid the fee, I asked the staff at the Visitor’s Center how long would it take to see everything in the garden. I was told — only 10 minutes! I was surprised to realize that I just paid $7 for a 10-minute walk in the garden.

If not for the statues along the short trail, I would have left sooner.

The staff was right. I finished the trail in about 20 minutes (including the time spent taking these photos).

I have been to a number of botanical gardens around the U.S., and the Santa Fe Botanical Garden offered too few things to impress visitors. So if you intend to just see the garden, don’t make the hassle. Instead, I suggest that you spend more time with the other beautiful museums at Museum Hill.

It was no surprise that I was the only one at the garden. No one dared to visit the place on a Sunday afternoon. I saw some visitors who parked their cars, looked around, and then left without even bothering to go inside the Visitor’s Center.

I love Santa Fe, but I will never go back to this garden.

The sign in front of the museum clearly says it all, that they are open on Saturdays from 1pm to 5pm. Even if you check online, that same schedule is posted. I drove a long way to see this museum that, based on comments online, seems interesting. I thought it’s something that I could write about. But I was very disappointed when I arrived at the place on a Saturday afternoon! First, the front door was locked. I went to the side and checked if maybe the entrance has changed. Still locked. I checked the schedule posted on their front and side doors and both said they are open. Since I couldn’t enter, I thought I should just leave. Then I saw a group of people entered the side door. I hurried hoping I could get inside. However, a lady at the door told me that I couldn’t because it’s a private gathering. But nowhere online or at the doors that say they are close that day. I wasted my time traveling to see the museum only to be rejected! I will never visit this place. If you want to go, call them first. Do not trust their website because they do not update it nor any other links online that says they are open.

I drove by the Space Murals Museum in Organ, New Mexico a number of times, but never decided to stop and check it out. From the road, the museum is just like any small residential structure in the area. Nothing spectacular. Until you go inside.

Bored one Saturday afternoon with nothing to do, I finally decided to visit. So, I called the museum to check if they are open. Someone named Ben answered the call and told me that he’d be glad to have me. It was about 20 minutes of no-traffic driving from my place to Organ, New Mexico.

I entered the Space Murals Museum and realized that I was the only visitor that afternoon. Even Ben was not there when I arrived. He was at the back of the building cleaning the pond. After about 5 minutes or so, he entered the museum, saw me, and then apologized for missing to welcome me. I said “no problem” with a smile.

He then gave a short intro about the museum. He told me that it is privately owned by Lou Gariano. The owner has collected some NASA space artifacts and decided to share them to the public. Some knick-knacks were donated by space enthusiasts and astronauts.

I woke up at 4 AM on a cold Saturday morning and readied for my trip to the Bosque del Apache National Wildlife Refuge, about 9 miles south of Socorro, New Mexico. I had to drive approximately 2 hours and be there just in time for sunrise. You see, the 57,331 acres Refuge is the winter home of tens of thousands of birds – including sandhill cranes, Arctic geese and ducks. According to the Refuge’s website, as many as 14,000 cranes visit the place during the winter months.

“The Bosque is also home to over 32,000 Snow Geese and Ross Geese, dozens of Bald Eagles and Goldens, Great Blue Herons, Occasional Pelicans, Avocets, and many, many other birds. This beautiful Refuge is also home to small herds of Mule Deer and families of Coyotes.”

I had to be there before sunrise to witness the “Fly Out”. It is a one-of-a-kind event when the birds fly out from the refuge, and in doing so, the flocks cover the skies, literally. No wonder why it is called one of the most spectacular refuges in North America.

All the good reviews you read online about the Deming Luna Mimbres Museum located in Deming New Mexico are all true. First, Deming is a small town with a population of about 15,000. Second, it is located away from big cities and surrounded by flat lands and mountains from far distance. These two alone made me question how such a town can have a museum that houses many artifacts and art pieces, all well put together. Astounded, I was. Who would have thought that a little town in New Mexico called Deming would have such an interesting museum?

No question, this was the best museum of any small town I have been to. The selection of exhibits varies from old photos, to furniture, to WWII memorabilia, to musical instruments, to classic vehicles, to dolls and toys, to stunning rocks, minerals, and geodes. One room after another, every space filled to the brim with pieces of history.

The photos below don’t even describe the completeness of the museum. You have to be there to appreciate the offerings.

Aside from the gallery exhibits and artifacts to enjoy, the museum has so much things to offer both for the young and old. From ranching and farming history, to seeing cows getting milked, to watching sheep dogs being trained, to hands-on exhibits that kids love, Western artists, life in the old days — it is a great place to unwind!

When I visited the museum, it happened that there was an ongoing event — the 2015 Cowboy Day! So, with just a $5 entrance fee, I was in for a nice treat.

There is the historic Green Bridge. It is considered the oldest and longest Pratt through-truss bridge in New Mexico. Spanning 133 feet and 16 feet wide, it is also the second-oldest surviving highway bridge in the state, and the state’s oldest steel highway bridge.

They’ll teach you how to train dogs to become sheep dogs.

The New Mexico Farm and Ranch Heritage Museum is a true local treasure and a definite must-see when you are in Las Cruces!

The Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in Washington, DC offers so many historical rarities all in one place. The Lunar modules, Charles Lindberg’s one-of-a-kind Spirit of St. Louis, the Wright Brothers plane, Amelia Earhart’s plane, John Glenn’s rocket, the nuclear warheads are just few of the wonders inside.

The museum is well organized in a manner as to be appealing for both young and adults. Although in some displays it was elbow to elbow, but everything was worth it.

Be awestruck by the massive exhibits that hang from all parts of the ceiling.

The space art gallery has superb photographs and paintings of NASA’s missions.

Certainly, this is one of Washington, DC museums to visit when you are at the Mall, especially if you love aircraft and space like I do. Be there at opening time to avoid the influx of people. The admission is FREE.

Literally, you can get lost inside the The Saint Louis Art Museum in Missouri. It is a huge museum with so many turns and ‘hidden’ rooms. In short, it has a very confusing layout. A map does not help at all. There isn’t any signage pointing out to which rooms, so you can easily miss an exhibit if you aren’t curious of what’s inside a door in a corner.

Not minding the layout, the museum is something not to miss if you visit Saint Louis. It has an amazing collection of the German immigrant Max Beckmann, who died in St. Louis. It has artworks done by Native American to George Caleb Bingham.

It certainly is not a wasted time if you decide to visit the free-admission museum.

Paying $6 to enter this museum is not bad at all. The Geronimo Springs Museum in Truth or Consequences, New Mexico is small but alluring. Inside the museum building are small rooms that showcase various interesting exhibits.

There’s the Apache history room that has a life-size wax statue of Geronimo.

There's a room for stone tools, arrowheads, and pottery.

There is a room about ranching.

This is the most interesting room — an old Hardcastle Cabin, which was moved from the Black Range Mountains to this new location in the museum.

This museum is one of the nicest small museums that is located in a small town.

According to the official website, the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C. contains the “most extensive collections of Native American arts and artifacts in the world—approximately 266,000 catalog records (825,000 items) representing over 12,000 years of history and more than 1,200 indigenous cultures throughout the Americas.” With four levels of object collections, touring the huge building will take about an hour or two.

Begin your visit on the fourth level then go down to each floor as you follow the lifeways, history, and art of indigenous peoples throughout the Western Hemisphere.

The National Portrait Gallery in Washington, D.C. is a beautiful walk through all the meanders of our memory. The Presidential Gallery and the American Origins Gallery are galleries not to be missed.

Housed in the old Patent Office building, the National Portrait Gallery is connected to another gallery, the Gallery of American Art. Although separated from the rest of the Smithsonian museums, this is one of the best museums in D.C.

Here are photos I took in galleries where photography was allowed.

The Missouri History Museum in Saint Louis is a small museum that showcases the history of the State, and is located inside Forest Park. While the present exhibits are interesting, I think the number of items are too few to be housed in such a huge building.

Thomas Jefferson. Charles Lindbergh. The Louisiana Purchase. The Cardinals. The Browns. The World’s Fair. These are few of the things inside the Missouri History Museum.

Saying that it is beautiful is an understatement.  If you enter from Jackson Street near U.S. 343, you would immediately be awed by the deep gorges and the strong water current that flows through narrow channels. You would hear the sound of the water from the parking lot!

I have visited other nature reserves around Fairborn and Dayton Ohio, the Clifton Gorge State Nature Preserve is the best of them all!

The Carlsbad Museum and Art Center in Carlsbad, New Mexico is small, yet informative. It houses very authentic western art. From the Native American pottery collection, to the rifle collection, to the stage coach and the model train exhibit — the museum is worth stopping by.

Aside from the very friendly staff, there is no admission fee. Please leave a few dollars into the box by the front door.

When you travel to Truth or Consequences in New Mexico, stop by the Veterans Memorial Park. It is more of a memorial than a park, though. The place is a beautiful. You can get a good walk around the area while enjoying the view of the mountains in the background.

The main attraction is the trail with tablets along the way that describe each of the 14 wars in the U.S. history.

Just adoring the gigantic Gateway Arch from the outside is good, but going up to the top of the arch is better. You get to see a magnificent view of St. Louis, Missouri like you’ve never seen before.

You have to ride a small 4-seater pod up to the top of the Arch. So if you are claustrophobic, you may have to think twice.

This is a small but great park! Once you are inside the park, you won't know that you are actually in a city! The Run Falls speaks for itself. It is cascading and it has levels of waterfalls.  It takes some efforts going down to the stream from the trail. I posted a number of photos and a video. Check them out!

If you're traveling in Champaign county, the Caverns is a must see.  It is a guided tour that will take about 45 minutes. I am giving it 4 stars because the tour guide keeps saying it's the most colorful cavern in the country. I've seen others that are much more colorful actually.

Since it is only open to pedestrians, the bridge is hard to find because it is not along the main road. Your GPS would lead you to a small and limited parking space along the road. You need to walk a hundred meters or so, through the greens, to see the bridge.

This is a 90-acre reserve of prairie and woodlands managed by Greene County Parks & Trails.  It's unique feature includes a nature playscape in the middle of the forest.  It offers a number of trails.  So grab a map before entering the reserve for your guide.

This museum is about looking and understanding—looking up to the stars, looking out to the desert, and looking down to see ancient fossils. There are three primary permanent exhibits: Desert Life, Permian Trackways, and Light & Space exhibits.
Great experience with at the arboretum! My mom loved it a lot. We didn't see any butterfly at the butterfly shed, but it was still a great visit! Visit on a summer to see all the flowers blooming👍
Expect to see animals next to your car, so keep your windows closed. Since everyone stops at the sight of an animal, a long car queue is inevitable. Be patient.
Very informative museum, retelling the history of migration of the Chinese to Northern America. This is a free museum with two floors of artifacts.

Fantastic. Free admission (please donate), but get tickets online for a given time slot because it's too full. Takes more than a full day to see/read everything. I suggest this order: 4, 3, 2, 5, and the balcony view + restaurant on floor 6 when the weather is good or during sunset. As of 24 Dec, 500,000 people have visited! There's several movies and interactive displays, and a few live actors that rotate through the Old Testament section. It's clean an beautiful, geared toward ages 12+. Parking is tough, but the green line will drop you at the L' Enfant. They have stage performances ($$) and a research room where I assume they will start giving talks. When you enter, look up! The ceiling is lite up and changed from the Sistine Chapel to blue skies to stain glass window to a garden and much more. Complementary coat check  Milk and Honey Cafe was reasonably priced and was actually good, though the coffee is extremely dark.

Did the "Agency." Intricate and well-built room, with a high level of difficulty and a decent progression of clues, though some of the early things we felt could have been a bit more obvious. Also, we accidentally skipped a full clue (which we never even solved later) and still got through. Recommend ~5 people, we had 7 and that was about the max. There was 1-2 actions that you did that has a consequence, but what that subsequence was want apparent, though it should have been. Just remember when you do something you think is correct, don't ever touch it again

Loved the show here. Saw Handel's Messiah, and got the cheapest seats, and was not disappointed. Believe me when I say, there is not a bad seat in the house. But do not try the park nearby. If you Uber, when leaving walk a couple blocks away and have then pick you up there, as the traffic leaving is crazy. Also, if you want to buy snacks/beverage during intermission, get there right away or else the line will be too long. If you get there late, you'll have to stand outside until the designated break spots, so you'll miss a large party of the show.

$28 per adult, but free for military. The price was scary, but well worth it, and clearly goes to a great cause of preserving national history and raising awareness. You'll need 3 hours or so. You'll get a time on your ticket for the main house tour, but you should do the garden and slavery tours on the hour while you wait, and walk through the underneath sections if you have more time. Beautiful and enlightening. Great for middle school and older kids.

It's free to just walk around and through the garden. The house tour and slavery tour are what costs money. People said it closed at 3 but that might be winter hours or a specific type of tour. Last house tour was at 4:30. There isn't a lot, like at Monticello, but the history was still interesting and you could see/do everything in 2 hours easy. There is a lot walking trail around it, and places for a picnic.

A beautiful next to the 9/11 memorial park. You need to make this a stop in your visit to NYC. The park is free. There are a lot of little memorials around it for you to see. There is a memorial statue titled, "America's Response Monument" dedicated to the men and women who fought in Operation Enduring Freedom. Much of this park is still under construction, so there are fences up.

One of my favorite Smithsonians. It's free, and there's plenty to see. Give yourself about 2 hours to see it all. The Native American museum sore a great job of telling the stories of the various cultures that were originally in the Americas, and what their life was like. I especially liked the section about treaties with early settlers, and their impact on recent cultural.

I suggest you drive the "fish hook" and end at Little Round Top (see Big Round Top first). You will see the Battle from the Union's perspective as they held the hill. Read all the signs and try to image charging up that him from the valley below. Dog friendly. You can park right at the top of there is space, or you can walk about 75 yards from the next parking lot down.

I get it. Art is about expression. But just because you've done something unique and dramatic doesn't make it good art. Some pieces are clever, others are just weird for weird's sake. But it is free, and is probably worth a look. Only takes about an hour, most of the square footage is empty space so you can see it all really fast.

Free! Great place to chill for 30mins, plus there's a ship with great sushi and bubble tea. They also have popsicles with real fruit, and flavors like mango and pineapple. There's a lower parking lot at the second entrance if the first gets full.
Don't bring a stroller, there are rocky narrow stairs around the outside.

This site is free and work a work stop. The memorial is at the center of this humbling and well maintained cemetery. The inscription is very well done and honors a great military mind. If you're in Lexington, definitely stop in to see this memorial; it will only take you 10-15 minutes to see the whole cemetery.

Great for an afternoon, followed by the Rodin Museum and Eastern State Penitentiary. The first Sunday of the month is donations only. Not great for little kids, but middle school and up can appreciate it. Some of the American Modern art can be graphic for little kids, but that's what they call arts these days.

A great piece of American history about a great military leader who loved his state. He was going to lead the Union forces, until Virginia seceeded, and back then state loyalty was more important than national pride. He taught at and revitalized the university here, which eventually added his name to it.

A nice little park, there's a good basketball court and tennis courts that get used a fair amount. Also a kids playground and an overhang for BBQs and a nice large patch of well kept grass. In the back is an abandoned baseball field that is a little swampy and not as well kept, but still okay.

The world's best Air Force museum! Huge location with every major military aircraft from the Wrights Brothers to the Stealth Bomber. There's a fantastic rocket and space shuttle section, and an area devoted to space exploration where you can touch a real moon rock. I loved it here!

Nice little park area, small trail to the side, and nice big open field for kids to through a ball and play. There are a few (4-5) covered tables on one side for eating, maybe a small birthday area, but not really room for large groups. All in all, a fine park.

Decent park in the midst of a concrete jungle. Pretty much just an open grass field. Plenty of chairs, and good shade that moves around the edges throughout the day. There always seems to be enough room and not over crowded, even in a Saturday in the summer.

So much to do here: SA Zoo ($), Japanese Tea Garden (free), and some fields for sports, though I haven't investigated them yet. Plenty of parking, never too crowded, and open almost every day. Great for kids, just don't use a stroller at the Tea Gardens.

Not too expensive. It's a great place to bring kids for the afternoon to teach them some American History. There isn't much, but on a nice day it's like a stroll in the park, with cannons and waterfront. Definitely watch the whole movie inside.

The concerts here through the summer are better than Baltimore and are second only to the DC Verizon center, but are cheaper and more numerous. At you get your ticket, you get your parking ticket for free in the same manner.
If you're in Philly, stop by Old Town and the Alley. Only 3 stars because it was a lot less than expected. The best time is December when it has holiday decorations. Then it would be a 5-star site.
Traveling circus-style exhibits. A little pricey, but if you go to the inner harbor a lot, swing by. You'll know if you are interested after the rest the signs around the door.
Nice little stop to look at the turtles in the pond. There was a port-a-potty that we used as we drive through the area. Pleasant and peaceful, though close to the road.
Great place to spend and hour or two with family. Free to visit, and the butterfly house is $8. They have different things throughout the year to see.
If you visit at an off-time, the lines won't be the regular 1-hour wait, and you'll get to see some American history. It's free all year long.

A delightful jewel box of a cemetery that encompasses local history, horticultural design and modern usage.   Beautiful and tranquilly sylvan oasis of the dead for the living.

Certain elements concerning the unmarked graves of itinerant Chinese workers and indigent asylum patients provide a slightly controversial aspect to the place but the city's commitment to memorializing these areas at some point in the future remains laudable.

A modern and vibrant institution at odds with the traditional conception of a museum.   You're not going to find simply geographically labeled rooms with historical artifacts (American Museum of Natural History being the prototypical institute of this type)- instead you'll find an institution that exists very much within the continuum of an existing peoples and their future.  A model for future institutions of this kind.

The layout of the park is excellent, a well designed piece of Olmsted's legacy, but there is something undefinably "off" about the park.  Incidences like the unsolved dog poisonings, carjacking assaults, and the fact that two women have shown up dead in the duck pond in the last decade seem to have left a slightly perceptible taint to the otherwise seemingly idyllic urban oasis.

A rich and nigh unparalleled experience.  The facility does an excellent job of catering to the researcher and the tourist alike.   Long and generic institutional hallways hold untold treasures behind their simple doors- an explorer armed with a registered reader's card can find a world of incredible material stewarded by extraordinarily knowledgable specialists.

There is no finer assemblage of historically significant air and space material anywhere in the world.   The downside is, of course, its tremendous (and well deserved) popularity.  Always packed to the gills but the dedicated visitor can make the time to suffer the crowds for the pleasures of the holdings.  History and aerospace buffs will be in heaven.

Nice little museum in a vast and surreal space.   Multiple historic planes, including a Mig 17 in airworthy condition, and helicopters but the real standout is the dank and echoing hangar itself.  A comprehensive film details the history behind its purpose, construction and usage is a nice add on.  Very much worth seeing.

A compact but masterly little survey of global botany.  Multiple biomes and habitats coupled with themed sections provide a truly excellent garden experience.  The medicinal room is a true standout- a chance to see a vast panoply of psychoactive and medicinal plants growing in harmony.  Excellent volunteer staff as well.

Underrated and under visited, a delightful little smithsonian outpost off the mall.  Enjoy a world class museum with an essentially priceless amount of stamps in an atmosphere that isn't choked by the endless nattering and jostling of giant school groups of overstimulated middle schoolers.  Well done.

A truly great man is, unfortunately, commemorated with what can only be described as a blemish on the mall.  This is a profoundly misjudged, poorly designed piece of monumental kitsch.  The marble looks like nothing so much as faux stone concrete. Just a colossal mistake and a travesty.

A charming bit of Portland's past.   Built as a community effort by early Italian bricklayers and Mason's it still serves as a welcoming Catholic Church.  Frequent services done well and an admirable amount of outreach and services provided for the indigent members of the community.

Superb and infinite vistas that are marred by lame upselling for family photos and personal tablet rentals.   Most of the guides are personable and knowledgeable but the strange Stargate looking electronic information consoles are just kind of distracting and unnecessary.

The little museum that tries harder.  The permanent exhibits are fairly minor but well dons and comprehensive but they go above and beyond with their special shows.  Free to Multnomah residents it's a perfect place to bring visitors.

Get your tickets early at the kiosk because, with a little bit of planning, an exquisite visit awaits you.  The best view of DC.  Take in all the strange 19th century Masonic symbolism and reflect on the country's history and future.

Brilliant and somber memorial with a fantastic and moving commemorative monument.   The site is rather forgotten and under visited/ utilized which makes for a powerful and often solitary viewing and visiting experience.

A somewhat challenging and evocative memorial- like the "Forgotten War" itself stuck somewhere between the bombastic triumphalism of the ww2 memorial and the starkly powerful modern imagery of the Vietnam memorial.

Great trail that has been negatively impacted by overuse and lack of maintenance. The first mile and a half is bracketed on both ends by solid masses of decomposing dog waste   Spectacular views at the top. .
Often extremely windy and packed it's still a necessary stop.  See forever and acknowledge the sagacity of whatever WPA program built this structure this high up on such a promontory.
Grim and charmless crossing that has permanently marred the infrastructure and skyline of Portland.  Has its moments of beauty but mostly a drag on traffic and the skyline.
Really well done model for a modern memorial. Balances historical context with commemoration. Captures the man and the warp and weft of the world he witnessed and shaped.
Well done little museum providing a fairly comprehensive history of Astoria, the Columbia and the the economic and social consequences of the sea and her bounty.
World class collection of airplanes and space memorabilia. Not cheap but a great tour and a great experience.  Spruce Goose is just incredible inside and out.
Comprehensive collection of southwest art. Well curated and eclectic holdings testify to both an amazing woman and a powerful artistic tradition.
Still a masterpiece.  Get yourself a burger and a concrete from the original Shake Shack, enjoy the new pedestrian plaza and bask in its design.
Sort of the last hurrah of the old South Park Blocks extension before it jams into the new Park West tower.  Pleasant space with much to offer.
Contemporary and historic heart of downtown Santa Fe.  Remains an exciting hub of humanity that honors the past but continues in vibrancy.
likes: Cultural Value: Historic and contemporary blend

reviews_attraction.text:
We had a great time playing disc golf on Presidents day. The course is tight and very wooded with some very difficult shots that were fun to play. For as tight as the course is, it still allowed for some long holes. Everything is fairly well marked and easy enough to navigate. Perfect place to work on your accuracy or trick shots from difficult positions.

We did not have to pay park fees or disc golf fees. Not sure whether that was due to the winter season or Presidents Day holiday, but it was a pleasant surprise.

A great park with some different play sets compared to other parks around the area. There was nobody there while we visited and the kids had the park all to themselves.

Also, dont miss the rest of the park. There is plenty of outdoor space and tables/benches to relax on and dogs are allowed,  just supposed to be on a leash at all times. There are also BBQ's to use, however I did not see them (did not really look for them either).

Had a great hike with the family. The trails are always very well maintained and in good condition. Especially when you realize that as many as 20,000 people visit the park in a day at times.

There is something for everyone from just wanting to take a stroll or look at the falls to technical hikes traversing rocks. Park is also easy to navigate and no concern or getting lost for those that are navigationally challenged.

Good little neighborhood spot for little ones. I was not a fan due to the fact that it didn't seem very clean (sandy and mulch everywhere, old broken toys scattered around the playground) and the play structures are rather old and in need of replacing. But if you live right around the corner, it's a good spot to come to have the kids burn off some energy.

Love this spot!  It's very flowing and for the most part smooth. Trails are well maintained and this spot is typically more capable to ride when other trails are rained out and in need of drying. All levels of skill can ride this location as there are options and ride around spots for tricky sections.  Very fun trail system.

We attended the Open House this summer and my son absolutely loved it.  The local Alexandria Fire Departments each brought trucks each hour to show off to the children and also had some fun games and tours for the kids. Definitely perfect for families with children that are into Fire Trucks.

One of the nicer parks in the area. There are lots of fun things to do here like run/walk/hide, Mountain Bike, Put Put, Disc Golf, etc.

Only thing I don't like is that you have to pay for entry if you are not a Fairfax County Resident.

Definitely one of the best if not the best memorials in all of DC. The concept is great and it's just beautiful. Definitely an honor to those who fought in WWII and any veteran or American can be proud of this spot.

A well built playground that is shaded by very old large trees. My kids loved it. It is spaced out with obstacles for all ages and places for parents to sit without being removed from their child's vision or reach.

Better for toddlers when it comes to the play sets. But the rock climbing wall and large rubber mounds are great for kids a little older. Probably one of the coolest and most progressive parks in the region.
This was a cool water park for kids to play. My children really loved it and we intend to come back with some friends. The playground outside of the splash park is actually pretty cool as well.
Love this park and the events held here.  Especially proud of CC Bid and Bike Arlington for installing their bike station and vending machine!  Very cool concept and execution.
A nice riverside option for getting outside and into nature. The trails were pretty good even though many are uninspired. Would appreciate more single track type of trail.
This is a great museum. I am glad that they came up with the concept  because there are some exhibits that you would not really think of seeing that are very good.
Old, Sandy and outdated. Water features were not working. We left after a few minutes and went to the new Quincy Park Playground that was leaps and bounds better.
Great park! Whether it be for the 4th of July to watch fireworks, your Monday night soccer game or just out for a stroll. This is a very nice and clean park.
Love hiking here. Super accessable and easy to come out even if it's just to kill a little time and walk along the creek. Plenty of adventure for all ages.
Always a nice park. The fields are nice and it's a good spot for some beach volleyball. The new children's playground is really nice as well.
The park was cool at sunset and not very crowded. There are often people flying kites here throughout the day, so that is pretty cool.
A nice neighborhood park with bocce ball and many other amenities. Heavily wooded in parts, open fields in other parts. Lots to offer.
One of the "must see" lighthouses when in the Portland, ME area. I like the glass light fixture the most. It looks pretty cool.
Always enjoy coming to the National Christmas Tree each year. But it's a shame that they stopped the Yule Log some years back.
Wish there were more trails and it was bigger but it's a great place for walks or runs in the Haddonfield area.
Beautiful place and nice to ride your bike to or go for a walk. Restaurants are great, views are good also.
A must when in town. Visit at odd hours if you want to avoid a like to take a picture.

This place is amazingly fun. Don't bring a shiny new car if you are worried about scratches. SUVS or vans are good because you can open the door on a van or the back window on SUVS and get very close to the animals.  Now they have budgies, which are great for the kids.  Even without kids, the animals are interesting and you will laugh your way through the park.

This has always been a great park to take kids to.  You can combine a nature walk, looking at great exhibits, and some playground time all into one trip.  The nature center is very interesting and the kids love it.  The trails around the lake are well kept and offer some views of duck and turtles, sometimes more.

Very well done memorial.  Nicely maintained and a friendly staff.  One of those fantastic resources that most locals have never been to.  Every Richmond should take the time to visit and remember. Not much parking available, so plan on that.  Maybe park near Tredgar/Brown's Island and see them all.

Stopped here on a motorcycle tour of all the Virginia State Parks.  This is an incredible place for hiking and camping.  Really nice campsites within feet of the river.  Friendly staff, very welcoming.  The roads around the park are beautiful for riding.  A great motorcycle camping destination.

A surprisingly nice little park with a great view of the city.  Also contains a museum and a replica statue of liberty.  A little research on both of these things may surprise you if you aren't familiar with their history.  This is a place that all Richmonders should visit at least once.

Very interesting and thorough tour.  After visiting Makers Mark, no other distillery could come close.  This one, however, is worth visiting because if the sheer size of the operation.  The visitor center is very nice and the tasting is well done, though it could be more educational.

Absolutely well done memorial.  Easy access, plentiful parking, excellent tour guides.  Can be done with or without a guide.  This is a worthwhile detour if you are anywhere nearby and even a little bit interested in history.  Solemn, respectful without being stuffy.

Beautiful park.  One of the best in the Va. Parks system.  I have visited every one and this one rates high for beautiful scenery and attentive staff.  What a great location for a getaway!  Cabins are small and rustic, perfect for a few days in the woods.

Absolutely incredible.   They have really done a great job catering and presenting history here.  The staff is top notch and engaging.  I am most definitely not a harley guy and I still enjoyed seeing the impact that they had on motorcycling hidtory.

It's a nice little battlefield park that most people don't know exists.  Wedding site of Patrick Henry and was an important battlefield site.  It's worth it to drop in and check it out.  House is being restored and is open only on weekends.

A good, solid aquarium.  Nothing like the big name aquariums in larger cities but well done and worth visiting.  I would rank it #2 in the biopark trilogy.  The botanical gardens are exceptional and the zoo is a waste of time.

Nicely maintained.  Has an electronic narration that tells the story of the battles in this area.  Not much to see and much of it is off limits for walking through, though the berms and trenches appear to be well preserved.

Always a great experience.  There is an exhibit that I always love to see because symbolizes my fathers work prior to his death.  Even without this personal connection, the museum is well done and is a great place to visit.

Excellent collection of artifacts and preservation of history.  You never know what to expect in a small town museum.  This one is a winner.  Kudos to the folks who decided to preserve so much of our past.  Good job.

Very nicely done aquarium, a peek into the river life that surrounds our city.  Great for the kids.  Offers events in private areas (like birthdays, etc.).  Home of the otters, which is always entertaining.

Very well thought out exhibits with staff that seems truly interested in sharing their knowledge of the refuges.  This should be your first stop on the way to Alligator River or one of the other refuges.

Fantastic zoo.  Better than Baltimore or DC.  They are worth visiting and very good zoos, but this one is better.  I remember going here as a kid and I still enjoy it 50 years later. Ride the balloon.
Simply outstanding.  If you only pick one of the 3 biopark places, do this one.  The zoo is a waste of time and money and the aquarium is a nice, smaller aquarium that is worth visiting.
Excellent hands on children's museum. Better than what we have in Virginia.  Odd to see a Sharps receptacle in the mens room of a children's museum though.  That's a bit sad.
Great park adjacent to the school.  New dog park going in.  Horse facilities, walking trails, skateboard park, athletic fields.  Very community oriented and safe.
This makes a great day trip from the Richmond area.  Richmond also has a Children's Museum but I believe that the one in Portsmouth is much better.
Very nice park with open areas, a playground and a sports complex.  The historical area in the back is very well done.  Great for kids and dogs.
Great piece of history.  Can you imagine the horrors experienced here over the years?  I would love to return for the Halloween exhibit.
Nice access for canoes, rafts, etc.  Walking trails start here.  The river is wide and flat here as it begins to head into Richmond.
Great for boating.  Scenic ride on a motorcycle.  The visitor center is very nice.  Very friendly staff.  Good camping cabins.

What a tremendous site. Better in person than on television. Elevator was out of order the week I was there. I measured I walked 20 miles in one week. Saw 75 % of the sites while in town. Going back for more in September. Glutton for pain. I'm 70.  Enjoyed all the sites and National Parks. The Rangers were all great. The Mall Police are not friendly.  When at Arlington be respectful. The ladies watching the guest won't let you sit on a wall. Not even in destress.

Was tickled to death . I was born and raised a Hoosier. First time I visited the Park. Met Ranger Penny. So interesting, fascinating , and intelligent. I wanted to stay all day just to listen to her. Helpful, Kind, and Sweet. Only some of her Charms. Worth the 1200 mile drive from central Florida. Thank you Penny!

It was fantastic. Saw Deer and Bambi's. Quail and Eagle. Spent four hours of pure bliss and solitude. Peaceful , Delightful and Tranquility were top of the list. Never noticed another human. We had a great picnic lunch with all the trimmings. Brought a backpack fill with blankets and candles. In case the sun set.

I'm looking forward tp going back in six months. So Worthwhile and a Very Touching Ceremony. Has to be somewhat of a difficult job on a daily basis. Even if it is for a wonderful Honor. A little tough on the elder trudging up the hill to Kennedy's Gravesite then over to Tomb of the Unknown Soldiers.

Seeing this place that was on my list for years. Huge area of history. Take the children and explain what happened. So many battlefields in the south to see. Each one has a story. I Google each place I'm going to visit and read some. Makes me feel better when I visit, having knowledge.

Very nice Memorial to All that Served. My father served in a Submarine. Close to other Memorials helped me go. I'm not a puppy any longer. I learned things my father had never told me. Still an educational day and memorable. Than You to those that Served. In any conflict, anywhere.

I totally enjoyed listening to the Ranger here. Kept me interested the whole visit. Gave me lots of information I hadn't previously heard. Some Rangers have an interesting story or two if the are willing to share. The girl was unbelievably kind. I'm ready to go back.

A lot to see and do. Miles of walking today. Enjoyed the past three days. Some D. C. Law Enforcement act like your in their home. Real attitude. Not all. I was a guest of someone and had privileges. Careful who you ask directions. If he's nasty just walk.

Seeing this Memorial is still on my mind. So touching to read all various things etched in the walls. Easy , flat walking area. I was impressed with the layout . Nicely shaded area to refresh your heated day. Spent about an hour here. FREE FREE FREE .

Really gets back to Nature. Ranger were pleasant and kind. A nice getaway from all the political rhetoric and miles of traffic. Easy to find parking. ( FREE ) ! It was Beautiful. Pleasant sound of falling water.
The morning I arrived they were setting up or preparing for a big to do. The people on hand still had time to share stories and information on this park. Looked large. Made me want to milk the cows.
Had a beautiful day at Peanut Carters place. My third trip for us. Interesting as well as educational. Easy to walk through. Rangers were informative and kind. We enjoyed the hour walk through.
A Beautiful places to Staycation or Honeymoon.  Quiet  ! Something you can know longer find. No loud tail pipes, train horns or neighbors 5 houses away talk on cell phone..
This Park has so much to offer for all ages. Gorgeous place. Great camping sites. I Just have a hard time getting use to Nine to Five hours. I usually rise at four a.m..
I spent some time here. It was loaded with joggers and walkers. I assume it is a safe place. I'm old and barely make it from parking lot to Visitors Center. Rainy day.
Do the 160 Park circuit to get Passport Stamp. Loving all the Parks . Well worth the Three time Winner Award.! Actually my secord time around. Did this in 2006. Fun
I really enjoyed the Rangers at the visitors center. They were smiling and pleasant to talk to. They gave me more information than any place all day.
Enjoyed the visit . Nice hike up the hill to house. Learned a lot about the Ranger on duty. Rangers are sometimes the most interesting part of trip.
I could type for an hour . Not much needs to be said. WWII was the big one. You know the rest. They made a beautiful memories out of an ugly thing.
Spent the day dipping my toes in the water and butt in the sand. Great Rangers working in a beautiful setting. Lucky people !
Great place to tale the children. They love the live gun fire and Cannon. Full of History and Cultural Facts. Great Day .
I took 3 friends. One called it perfect. The other fun. The other (all around special) . It has everything you need.
Off the beaten path and not hectic area. Relax and stroll the area. The Cuban Friendship Urn was by parking area.
Been by here 50 times. Finally stopped. Happy I did. Huge. The local share there own version of what they know.
Nice area to visit. Some bridges take to long to open and close. But I never had a problem with this one.

The Seattle Art Museum attempts to be somewhat encyclopedic, and while it falls short at this goal, it still has plenty to vouch for itself.

A comparison helps illuminate the problem. The Met in New York has the square footage, donor resources, attendance, and collection to thoroughly catalog almost every period in the history of art. Yet even its collection is spotty, highly overrepresenting Europe and shoving African and Asian arts into their little enclaves. And while their modern collection is stronger than that of many standalone modern art museums, it still irritates some who want the Met to focus on antiquity and established art. The point here is that finding the right balance is perilous, and that to be encyclopedic is to commit to a gargantuan task.

The Seattle Art Museum is not currently positioned to do justice to the full range of human artistic expression, so it does focus somewhat. There's a big focus on ethnic minority artists, and the modern collection is rather sizable. Yet the museum still seems to stray into territory where it's not really an expert. For example, there's a section dedicated to Japanese art; while it's nice to explore art that's a bit less mainstream, I wonder why they dedicated an exhibit in the downtown campus when there is the Asian Art Museum just across town that would conceivably be better suited to Japanese art. The problem is not that they are trying to showcase a diverse range of artistic expression, but rather the fact that their thinking seems to be a bit unclear. The museum managers and owners don't really seem to know what they're trying to accomplish. And to the extent that they do, they don't really explain themselves. Why this exhibit? Why does this matter? I would like to see the literature grapple with questions about the social purpose of its art. Especially in Seattle, people appreciate art that's thoughtfully curated and intended to provoke thought about difficult topics. The photographic exhibit from Braddock, Pennsylvania does this well, but the reflections are limited to that space. I felt the museum lost a critical teaching moment about the wider significance of its collection.

The museum is a pleasure to peruse and will take three to four hours to get through with enough depth in each of the sections. The title cards are well-written and generally engaging, and are digestible for even non-critics.

It's not a huge museum, which makes it more manageable. I hope to see them expand in coming years, simultaneously talking on broader missions and narrowing their focus on their areas of core competency. The museum has plenty of promise. We shall see.
dislikes: Lack of depth in certain exhibits

reviews_attraction.text:
One can't help but appreciate what the folks at Frye are trying to do. They're a rare free museum and thus committed to the public good. And nor are their donation appeals intrusive -- they simply set up a box near the exit.

The problem: there's no "there" there. This is a glorified gallery, with a tiny collection. You can get through the place in less than an hour. I parsed through the first floor; I'm not clear if there was any more to the place but they didn't direct visitors upstairs.

The collection isn't particularly distinguished, either. I saw the PAN exhibition, a collection of copies of great works. Not impressive. A small place should show the very best, but they just don't have it. The pieces hailed from the late 1800s and early 1900s, a period interesting only because it illustrates the evolution of art to modernity. Context aside, the pieces were uninspiring -- undeveloped abstraction without classical beauty.

A successful museum will harmonize gallery and art. The Frye doesn't. The construction of the space makes it feel oddly empty. The galleries are large boxes, but the work in the PAN exhibit was roughly letter-sized. This mismatch lent an uncomfortable aesthetic. The spaces would be better suited to larger works. Moving walls (a la Whitney) would also work.

The small details fall apart too. The PAN logo, one they called custom-designed, didn't even employ basic kerning. Hard to believe that no competent designers were available in Seattle of all places. At least one of the frames was poorly constructed, loose at the corner. It looked like one you'd buy at Walmart. A museum exists to showcase beauty and it should only commit to details that accentuate that beauty. Sloppiness damages the experience.

If you're able, I encourage you to give to this and other arts institutions. They could use the funding.

I went here for a video game event a while back.

First off, let there be no mistake that the exterior architecture is edgy and beautiful. It's a testament to the kind of raw energy that Seattle was known for the '90s and I suggest people give it a bit more attention before writing it off as a piece of trash.

The video game event I attended was mediocre at best. The exhibit showed a wide range of games, but only some were playable and they covered only a tiny sliver of the massive industry. In an attempt to cover the entire history of video games they only briefly examined any particular period or title. The exhibit seemed to lack an overall theme or purpose, other than something vague about informing the public about video games. I wonder how carefully this was curated. If this purports to be a museum it should take its craft as seriously as one.

The exhibit was also tiny, occupying just a few rooms. This made it a quick trip you can pass through in an hour or so. Either EMP is painfully tiny or the other exhibits are larger.

During the video game event we had the chance to view some other galleries. We went into a Jimi Hendrix exhibit. It was mildly interesting but the small time we spent there seemed like more than enough to get the gist. For hardcore fans the museum must have real appeal. For the rest of it seems excessive.

The museum seems overly focused on pop culture at the expense of meaningful history or art. Perhaps that's related to the museum's status as a tourist trap that doesn't have to be any good. People will go anyways.

This is the nature of a privately-funded pop culture museum: the subject matter and curatorial approach reflect the interests of the benefactor. This one doesn't work for me.

MOHAI talks about the Seattle experience, in a way the internationalized Seattle Art Museum doesn't. It's a reflection of local invention and industriousness. If you only see one thing, watch the video in the second floor screening room, close to the stairs. It's a stirring, even patriotic reflection of what the city stands for, often too complimentary but certainly inspiring.

The museum is wonderfully curated, with an impressive selection of artifacts and helpful placards. There's a massive amount to see. Although it's a small building, the exhibits are numerous and compact enough to allow for several hours of serious perusal. They managed to get some pivotal artifacts, like the Sonics' 1979 championship trophy and the first piece of Microsoft software. These lend a certain gravity to the museum's collection.

With this focus on industrialization and commercialization comes considerable oversights. It tends to credit more than challenge efforts at industrial dominance, talking at length about their benefits while sidestepping environmental devastation, oppression of natives, and the greed of Seattle-based multinationals. A more balanced picture, less tainted by corporate donors, would do this city more credit. As it stands, MOHAI reflects the many ways Seattle has become just like everywhere else.

It's an okay park, not my favorite. It doesn't have the seclusion and intimacy of Central Park, nor the spontaneity; it's too formal, with rigidly aligned walkways and trees and benches and no sense of fun.

There are also way too many tourists at the arch, which feels immensely cheapened by how many people gawk at it.

It's a lovely place -- a real neighborhood park, fully residential and hard to find. They've got a little league baseball diamond with fan stands, open fields, a gazebo, a tennis court, and a few benches. This place is small and nestled away, but it's cute and the streets nearby get great views of south Renton below.

This is a commemorative lighthouse with some rocks and benches, not a full-fledged memorial and not a full-fledged park. I thought it would have names or history written down but all there is is a plaque describing how the lighthouse came to be. Not an ample tribute to an epic tragedy!

This tiny little park was the setting of the famous scene from Woody Allen's Manhattan. It is a charming and secluded place that you can easily mix even walking right past it. There are several benches in addition to the famous one. This is a great place to take a date.

It's a decent park, with long stretches and a good amount of pathways. But it's also very quiet, empty, and lonely. This is probably a result of its awkward positioning by the bridge and right next to a business park. It doesn't have a neighborhood feel.

I love taking the train over this bridge! So cool to look out to the south at Lower Manhattan and up north to Midtown. The city is stunning during the day (in all its grandeur) and nostalgic at night (with the wall of lights).

I can say confidently that MoMA is the best museum in the world. They offer an unparalleled selection of art that breaks boundaries and opens minds. The museum itself is designed with care, and the typography excels.

One of the most powerful experiences I have ever had in a museum. They reveal striking insights using primary sources. You will walk away convinced and motivated to stand against tyrants (like trump).
The architecture is every bit as remarkable and innovative as the art. The concrete and glass give it a stoic feel, and the river adds life. The art isn't MoMA level, but it's generally well-done.

This is an excellent place to lounge with a group on a picnic. If you care for the ugly new skyline menacing the south, you can check it from here.

This is really a place for the summer.
Being here gives you the unmistakable feeling of peace, tranquility, and remembrance. Come at night when the tourists are gone, the air is clean, and you can contemplate the message.
It's quite remarkable to look up at this landmark and to realize that it was once the world's tallest buildings. It has soul without being tacky, so unlike skyscrapers today.
The park is currently being reconstructed so it's in a lonely and haggard state right now. There are fences and construction all around. Come back in a year or two.
They do outreach to the local community with bagged lunch service. They also have an awe-inspiring cemetery that makes you feel one with those who went before.
This is a nice relaxing place to sit on a bench and watch people, especially in the summer. The view of the nearby Woolworth Building is not to be missed!
A grand and inspiring cathedral that reminds you of Europe. It's a shame tourists walk around and take selfies instead of experiencing it for what it is.
It's an iconic park with plenty of benches, lots of activity, people to stare at, and enough calm ambience to spend an afternoon or evening here.
Interesting and free to visit. They are extremely annoying when you visit the chambers; you're not allowed to stand whatsoever.
One of the most fantastic museums I have ever visited. Gives you a sense of wonder about space again. Awe-inspiring.
One of the most spectacular buildings in the city, not the least because you can see it for miles down Park Avenue.
A great playground for small kids. Adolescents can have some fun but this is mostly designed for kids ages 3-9.

Went sledding here last winter with all my siblings and our babies. Was way too much fun! The hill here is the perfect steepness, and it has a gradual flat base so your kids dont go launching off into the playground or the road (looking at you Old Main Hill...). The playground itself is pretty great as well, and is very new and has all the bells and whistles that spazzy toddlers like to play around on. Will definitely coming back here next time I'm in the neighborhood.

This is a good amusement park. Pretty easy to spend a day here doing roller coasters and the various theme areas. My complaint, however, is that Lagoon charges MORE than other large theme parks in California such as Six Flags/Marine World and the like. So, you get a fun day for the price, but it is a little bit steep for a park which doesn't have as much to offer as other cheaper (albeit farther away), yet better, alternatives.

Beautiful grounds welcome to ALL visitors. Down the street from my house where we go to watch the beautiful sunset from the grassy hill a couple times a month. Got married in the temple here and it has incredibly photogenic grounds for ALL FOUR seasons. A must visit for residemts regardless of religion, as it is extremely central in historical and cultural value to the state and local communities.

Pristine grasslands and marshlands with Bald Eagles, countless rare bird species, and freaky swamp critters.

I went for a walk here one day to clear my head, and I stopped on one of the paths for around 20 minutes because the birds were singing up some birdsong chorus I'd never heard in my life, a very unique experience. This area feels very wild while being fully accessible and easily navigable.

The park is HUGE, with a nice baseball field, soccer, with a nice turf field, and decent running trails or walking trails around. I like to take my daughter to the playground which is under a net, to protect from fly balls from the ballpark. We go on walks past the turf field, and there is a paved trail that goes through a couple walking bridges over a creek. We head over every few weeks.

Was really skeptical that there would be an actual beach along the river but THERE IT WAS. It's actually got pretty decent sand and a lot of little coves and areas to sit and hang out with your people. The river and swimming areas around the rocks are also pretty awesome looking. Lots of people were swimming and playing with dogs and kids along the shore. Definitely coming back!

The GW Masonic building is truly amazing. The 15 dollar ticket I've paid twice was more than worth it each time. Highly recommend the tour, as they take you to the various artifacts and rooms that house Washingtons belongings such as his family bible, freemason garb, and other personal items. The trip to the top of the tower and the view of the DMV is incredible as well!

I go here for the frisbee/disc golf. This disc golf course is the hardest one I've played- I'm a beginner, played for around a year. I suck at this course, but it's a really good one and has great trails and hills to hike around on.

The trails are clean and garbage free, few folks come out here summer. No noise really. Also no poison ivy from what I've ever seen.

Non-LDS and members alike will find many hours of activities and historical places to visit in the Temple Square area. The temple itself is the only structure that's actually closed to the public, but the church does TONS of public events and things like that in the area. Best Christmas lights and decorations you might ever see in your life too!

Suburbs of North Stafford meet the swamplands of "true Virginia". This is a beautiful area that is being rapidly built up into a much more family-friendly, welcoming area.

A boy scout in my troop recently did an Eagle Scout project here, and the park staff were great to work with. Look out for the nice benches we put in around the playsets!!

OTHER. WORDLY. I've been to some awesome zoos. But nothing compares to stepping into a LITERAL DESERT BIODOME WITH JAVALENAS AND ROAD RUNNERS running amok. I feel like a crazy person describing the experience here because of how sci fi futuristic this place is for creating the controlled climate environment.

Nice and clean area. It's got a sort of murdery feeling about the place I cant put my finger on. Theres random culverts and fencing around certain parts of the park due to a few converging waterways, but other than that it looks quite nice. Bathrooms didnt look very appealing but I didn't go inside.

The park is pretty decent. It's in a beautiful area at the mouth of the Logan Canyon, so there's a lot to look at. A ton of ducks and some geese as well. Noticed the sprinklers were going haywire and there was not paper in the bathrooms, though. The bathrooms in general seemed pretty derelict.

The zoo is a small one, but very well kempt and has great caretakers. The exhibits are pretty great and the zoo is, to me, a gem in Cache Valley. One of the more unique places in Logan for sure. Great family night or a fun date as there is much to see and do. A must for all residents.

The park has nice expanse of grass, a decent playground area for kids, tennis court, and has a nice path going through it. It's got a bit of a bug problem, but that's because of its placement near the lake. It's a really nice park overall, much like the other great parks in Orem.

A surprising amount of wildlife here even in the middle of summer. A lot of fun stuff to explore around here. The rock structures are small enough for kids to run around, and big enough to be a challenge to climb around. Will be coming back here next time I'm in St. George.

Park is amazing, huge spaces to do all the activities. There are fairs an dcity events here too. Just stay clear of the disc golf course during the summer unless you KNOW FOR CERTAIN that you aren't allergic to poison ivy. My legs itch just thinking about it...
dislikes: Poison ivy in disc golf course

reviews_attraction.text: Very quiet and quite a bit of wildlife over here. Saw a vole, a deer, and some squirrels (I have low standards) during my first run here. Veryblittle trash to be seen, nice bridges and paths, and a nice little stream runs through it.

Wife and I went to see the fireflies here (2nd and thirdish week of June) and it was great. Fireflies in the field to the west. Beautiful park, clean with great flowers. They allow dogs, and have dog poo bags which is nice I guess.
Excellent museum with a good amount of galleries covering different origins and genres. Wanted more historic American and Virginia art but was happy with the selection.
The park is one of our favorites in Logan, and  we usually go here at least once a month in the summers. Great for dogs and kids, EXTREMELY clean, and very well kempt.
Nice views and trails spoiled by piles of dog poo all over the place. Did a family photo shoot over here and was unimpressed by the cleanliness of the grassy areas.
Beautifuk park with great foliage, gazebo, volleyball sand, playground, etc. Just down the street from USU, so good hangout place.
Very eerie but respectful place, does a great job of honoring the men who served while giving a glimpse into the horrors of war.
Was hard to locate where the actual Signal Knob was because the sign didn't point the direction or orient very well.

Plenty of history is shared behind the great statue of Liberty.  Exhibits about the making of the French statue, transfer of the statue, erection of the base of the statue and maintenance of the statue are covered.  You can even take a picture and share what liberties the statue represents for you for their mosaic and living display.   Outside on the island you can stop and get food, snap pictures of the statue from below, or get a better view of the New York city skyline.  Plenty to keep you busy for a couple of hours at least.  If you want to visit the crown of the statue you will need to make reservations months in advance as the view is quite in demand.

Large museum spread across multiple deck levels of an older air craft carrier.  Plenty of war history, aviation facts, and aeronautical wonder can be found here.
Just the experience of being on an aircraft carrier was pretty cool.  Though being an old ship it lacked sufficient air conditioning on several of its exhibits such as on the bridge/control deck.
About half of the exhibits were targeted towards kids, the remaining for adults or kids making for a good mix for families.  Will visit again with kids someday.

Great park, but limited parking makes it overcrowded and challenging to enjoy...  during the fall season the park is so crowded that it is almost impossible to take nature pictures without other people in your shot.  Additionally, they have been draining the ponds early on lately which makes everything less attractive for the fall pictures.

Best playground in the Pocatello area hands down.   Plenty of varied playground equipment for different aged kids to play on for hours of entertainment.   Age specific equipment marked. Playground area is marked dog free, so plan on letting at least one person in your group stick outside the playground if you bring a pup.

Premiere starting point for bike trails and ridge 2 river trail system.  Baseball and softball fields, dog park, RC car track, skate park and quick access to food and entertainment downtown.   Great place to take the dog on a walk or run/bike a trail.  On of the Boise bests.

Fun place to visit with little kids.  Worth at least an hour of entertainment walking around and seeing all the birds of prey.  If you visit on a day with planned events, it's best scheduled on a day with good weather as many of the activities are outdoors.

Great spot to let your dogs run, just be careful as the area is fairly traffic ridden as well.

Recently the park has had an infestation of goatheads and ticks, so make sure you check your pets before heading home so you do not spread them around further.
