Nice big Park with a playground that was recently built and a dog park with access to hiking trails. The park also has a paved path throughout and a Amphitheater. It does have a 9 Hole disc golf course I believe but it is overgrown and not very good looking.

Nice off the grid type of Park with a lot of history attached to it. Every time I've been here you don't have to worry about crowds. Which is not fun for me when trying to enjoy nature.

I wouldn't recommend just because you will be crowding the park for me!

5/11/18 Nice park area but the friends of Zumwalt does not manage the park very well in my opinion. I believe I read they mow four times in the spring and once in the fall so you will be enjoying your day with ankle high grass or longer, like I did.

I sent a email to the administration with an inquiry and I never had a response. Obviously not too good of management.

I wouldn't recommend, they sure seem like they don't care. Judging by reading other negative reviews they need new management.

Great Park, a lot of different options if you like to walk, run or cycle this is the place. With tons of Green Space for a Day picnic as well as excess to the river for fishing. The walkway system connects to the university as well.

Great park, my review is based on access to the restrooms in the park which were locked multiple times I’ve been there. So I used the building. You got to go, you got to go, maybe next time you idiots will open up the bathrooms.
1/3/18 Very nice, welcoming people. 👍🏽 I contacted the Museum about an inquiry and was greeted respectfully. I would recommend stopping by and learning some local history, support the community!
Nice park when it is not under water! Has a restroom and baseball fields along with a sheltered Pavilions, one down by the water. This is a Historical Park being it is the first one in Albany.
Great Park, it's spacious and green with a awesome walkway path winding throughout. I ventured over here while at the Salem hospital it is directly across the street.

Very nice memorial WE ALL SHOULD VISIT.
When I went it was amazing there was a guy playing the bagpipes. Honor the people that gave us freedom.
1/4/18 Great history in this area with a few old structures still standing but may have been moved there. Some hiking trails as well.
Nice park but closed throughout the winter. I am sure our tax dollars pay for the park so in my opinion it should be open year-round.
Nice park with few people most of the time. I have noticed recently there has been some suspicious characters parked at the entrance.

Aeropuerto tambien.

The border patrol agent explained to the man with the Latin looks why he had been singled out at the train station. He spoke Spanish, had diplomatic manners and didn't wear Kevlar or battle gear. Unlike the agent I saw on the train a few weeks ago in Buffalo.

His novia, un mujeur, didn't seem obviously Latina, as if that were a thing I should be detecting.

The couple listened politely as the agent explained, a woman border patrol agent taking notes on a clipboarded pad.

Am Amtrak conductor observed the exchange, four people having an encounter in a train station where a train from Canada, the Maple Leaf, allowed boarding.

The Amtrak conductor suggested I board although, "I didn't have to right away".

I took a mental picture because I was too cowardly to start a Facebook Live.

I want to cross back into the United States without a hitch, like I crossed last night at the Rainbow Bridge.

I handed over my passport last night and the agent and I talked about Johnny Roccos, a popular Italian restaurant on Lundy's Lane.

He loved Rocco's. Said so and gave back my passport.

I was quelled today.

I stood down today.

I should at least walked forward with my passport extended and said in a friendly voice, "Buenos Dias. Que Tal. Me Nombre as Guillermo".

Doesn't that name sound rather guerilla?

I had just taken pictures in the gift shop of the newly open museum of the Underground Railroad Museum.

Museums are not neutral said a bright red tee shirt.

Neither am I.

I side with allies because supporting bullies is unamerican.

Americans, almost all immigrants except for Native Americans who crossed on the Siberian land bridge eons ago, love the underdog.

The undocumented are clearly underdogs.

And Americans believe in solutions that pass the four way test of the Rotary.

Is the solution fair to all parties involved.

Yes, let's stay the hand of terrorism.

I remember a visit to a courthouse town in lower Minnesota, not far from the border with South Dakota twelve years ago.

I remember four wind turbines as I rolled into town after a long, fun night in Mitchell, South Dakota.

My mother had taken pictures of the Mitchell Corn Palace when she drive across country in a convertible in her years as a young woman, experiencing freedom years before Thelma and Louise.

So I had to see it myself.

I learned that the designs on the walls of the palace have always been woven by Sioux Indians.

We are still working, I hope, on America's relationship to our tribal citizens although I am worried about the bad medicine lately from our great chief in Washington.

If the corn palace cannot be held up as an exemplar of diversity at work, show me a better example.

Let's go back to that courthouse town in southwestern Minnesota.

I stopped at a store owned by immigrants from Mexico.

I noted that downtown had foot traffic at sundown, all pedestrians immigrants from Mexico.

All the rentals downtown looked filled with families, rooted in Mexico.

I guess the families had established themselves by helping bring in the harvest for the Jolly Green Giant,  a tall laughing gringo who stands in the fields south of the Twin Cities laughing .....

You get it.

I wonder about downtown Worthington today.

Has the downtown become a ghost town due to deportations?

What has happened to Shelby, Michigan, a town that also supports a migrant population, this population bringing in the asparagus harvest for Oceana county farmers.

Has this town been cleaned out too?

We need Worthington and Shelby to be strong.

And we need to learn how to create American citizens again, often working with those who have managed to find a home among us.

Cold has returned to Genesee Street.

The wind blew uphill, steadily, just strong enough to have a wind chill.

We had a reprieve from winter, so I think, "Okay, deal with it".

A light dusting of snow sparkled under the street light.

I enjoyed the pleasant weather last night, and I made a twenty minute walk up Salina Avenue to Little Italy, an enclave with small Italian restaurants.

I wanted to have dinner at Francesca's, which looked quaint and a bit secretive.

I chose Biscotti's instead because I could see the twin spires of Assumption Church from the cafe's window.

I ordered soup, a sandwich.

Skipped the cannoli, saved the sandwich for later.

Skipped the gelato, which I couldn't eat alone because I have good memories of gelato and companionship.

I heard the bells of Assumption Church peeling at Six PM, ringing more than six times.

The bells were calling the faithful to a mass observing the feast day of Saint Marianne Cope, who founded one of the great hospitals of Syracuse.

I had interest in her story and had wanted to visit the church.

Why not visit on a special occasion?

I needed the weight of my body to open the front door.

Nobody uses it that much anymore.

The side door to the cathedral is more convenient to the parking lot.

I hope a deacon locked the front door after I made sure with difficulty that it was closed properly.

To call Assumption Church a church underestimates the immense structure.

I took pictures of alabaster statues in numerous side chapels.

The pulpit rose above the pews two stories.

The cantor climbed to its high altar up a spiral staircase.

A woman from Hawaii played a hymn from the islands.

Mother Marianne Cope had established a colony in the late 1800s to care for Hawaiian lepers.

The Hawaiian must have played in the organ loft high above us.

I searched for a musician around the cathedral floor and I didn't find her.

The priest identified who had played the ukulele, but the Hawaiian didn't so much as wave from the loft.

As a mass, the service didn't seem too much different than a Sunday mass.

And then the celebrant set out a relic of Saint Marianne and congregation lined up to adore it, each taking a turn.

"You may touch it. You may even kiss it", he instructed.

The line was long.

He hadn't granted permission to photograph it.

The owner of Glazed and Confused has walked in with a few extra boxes of his decadent doughnuts.

I heard him right, "Please give your customers a free doughnut".

The free doughnut was covered richly with shredded coconut.

Feast of St. Marianne, indeed.

I have my name tag on now as we leave the bus hub on the Fly.

Twenty four minutes of travel shall bring me to work.

The overhead lights are on so the surveillance cameras can film.

Doesn't the bus company know people are trying to sleep?

I'm just glad to have some variety this morning.

A woman marched into Cafe Kubal and ordered a brewed coffee to go.

Then she asked for change for a twenty.

And she got it.

A man recalled when the buses waited for transfers at the corner of Fayette and Salina Streets, exposing passengers to hot sun and cold rain.

He's been taking the bus that long?

A man was overheard asking a woman, "You can get there from here"?

"Yes"', she affirmed. "Absolutely"!
likes: Facilities & Services: Alabaster statues, high pulpit, organ loft
Activities: Mass, relic veneration, free doughnuts
dislikes: Facilities & Services: Inconvenient front door, no photography of relic

reviews_attraction.text:
Lee Ann Creager Stitches Quilts with Threads of Fiber, Tractors and Electrons.

This article first appeared online at Beyond the Breakers

By Captain Art Walker | on July 9, 2013 |

Let us now praise quilting neighbors. Let us begin with Lee Ann Creager, executive director of the Coopersville Farm Museum. Creager is holding up a bullet quilt she put together with the help of one of her quilting circles. Creager is all about circles, and the Captain has found himself in at least three of Creager's circles. I'm always giving a good word for the events her team and her produce at the Coopersville Farm Museum. That's because we discovered one another through social media back in 2009, and I was immediately charmed. She took a workshop on Twitter through the #Coopersville Chamber of Commerce and Laura Bergells of Grand Valley State University and she took off from there.

In social media, surely Creager recognized a way to stitch together patches of community with threads of electrons and data. I weave with Creager through at least two blogs, and I drop in to the museum for the agricultural art and the Jam Night. Look for the Jam Night first and third Tuesday of every month, on a custom-built stage built to look like a barn. Lee Ann Creager, let me turn in this article, my quilt panel today.

Turn up one night at the Coopersville Farm Museum, and you'll see it's as cozy as an heirloom duvet and as varied as a crazy quilt. The museum tends to stay open for holidays to be a center for celebration, a safe place for New Year's Eve and a neighborly place to enjoy the Fourth of July. On the Sixth of July, a tractor parade went forth from the museum, rolling toward a picnic on Crockery Lake in Casnovia, Michigan, almost thirteen miles away.  I'm trying to imagine all of those tractors passing through the Dutch, Mexican and Irish town of Conklin, which has a Dutch-American Mill, a Mexican-American grocery store and an Irish-American pub. It's quite an imaginary sight to see Creager weaving together the fields of clover, wheat, corn and apple trees with a thread of John Deere green. Tuesday, July 9th, 2013, around one hundred and forty quilts started arriving in the hands of their makers, right at 10:00 AM. I'm sure a community table had some coffee waiting and maybe some homemade cherry pie, now in season. There's often a table laden with good eats for the Jam Night.

I like the new attitude of the Grand Rapids Art Museum since Dana Friis-Hansen arrived from the south to put the institution on a more open path. Yet, I must express confusion. Coopersville Farm Museum has the Quilts & Their Stories show open from August 1st to September 28th. GRAM has the Improvisational Quilts of Susana Allen Hunter until August 25, 2013. The Coopersville Farm Museum celebrates a primary use of American landscape. The GRAM opens Masterpieces of American Landscape Painting 1820–1950 on October 20th, 2013. I'm just guessing with great hope of being right that Lee Ann Creager drove to downtown Grand Rapids to see the improvisations of Hunter. I-96 is a thread of asphalt that conveys east and west. The two museums are less than twenty miles apart, close enough to be stitched together.

I snapped an entire afternoon of pictures as the Dutch Apple pleasure excursion made its merry way south on the Hudson River.

I snapped pictures of tugboats, barges and yachts under way.

I snapped pictures of riverhouses built by Dutch patroons and indentured servants who had succeeded after working off their bonds.

At first, I had assumed that the woman talking on the sound system, noting fine points along the river, would be a total annoyance.

That attitude didn't last long.

Yachts cruised up close so the passengers could call out greetings and our guide returned the favor, greeting each boater by name.

She could give intimate details of the riverhouses with the great lawns spread out down to the water line.

Most riverhouses started life as Dutch designed houses, altered over centuries to look American outside and inside.

Many homes standing still in Albany hide a Dutch house inside.

She knew the riverhouses well because all her life, she had cocktails at one or attended a soiree at another or enjoyed a weekend getaway at a third.

Maybe she was the last socialite left on that stretch of the Hudson, keeper of the memories of the waterway?

She had a remarkable eye for birds, too. The bridge over the Hudson nears no besmirching marks of pigeon lime, so corrosive.

She pointed out the Peregrine Falcon box where the State of New York maintained a brood of raptors, raptors that feasted upon pigeons plucked out of midflight.

Every heron fishing in the shallows came to her notice and she helped us focus upon these birds in camoflaging plumage.

What looked to be a seagull flying in the wind behind our ship turned out to be an Osprey on the wing, searching our prop wash.

Because the Hudson thrives with eagles, she taught us to search the treeline up one hundred feet from the water for the distinctive white head of the bald eagle.

She called out to us the immature eagles on the wing, working the waters, not yet old enough to show the white pate of the species.

"Next launch, pack the telephoto lens", went down in my mental notes.

The Dutch Apple passed over the stretch of river where a sandbar thwarted the northward passage of Henry Hudson's Halve Maen.

A pier of rocks built by the Army Corp of Engineers still struggles to hold that sand bar in check.

We cruised a little further south than the appointed turnaround point, maybe because the pilot felt more relaxed on Labor Day.

One should experience the view of Albany with its post modern buildings and steampunk towers from the southern waters afforded from the top deck of the Dutch Apple.k6

Tomorrow is the last Saturday of Summer 2016, and more than four thousand Michigan beer lovers are about to celebrate Burning Foot, a beer festival at Pere Marquette Beach. Drink cold beer and keep from Burning your Feet in flip-flops. Meanwhile, sculptors Lee S. Brown and Chip VanderWier are planning to burn the everlasting hop. Seriously. Burning Man burns the man and Burning Foot will yearly burn the Hop. VanderWier and Brown are clearly the most active sculptors living and working in Muskegon, and it's Unruly and Pigeon Hill beer that keeps them working long into the night. Thirst quenched, desire unquenchable. Last night, Brown and I chatted during the opening of Nancy Crow's Bull's Eye Quilt show called, "Circular Abstractions". Brown talks the talk but he also sculpts the sculpture. He wanted to tip me off about the Hop Statue he erected with VanderWier. I was gratified that the man who prepared the Nancy Crow show in the great gallery had a moment to talk on such a big night.

I promised to go see it Friday afternoon. Now I'm disappointed I won't see it burning at night. The instant icon is surmounted by a hop blossom constructed of metal leaves, unmistakable for an artichoke but similar. VanderWier has been obsessed with Michigan's newest artisan crop, shown by a series of four panels celebrating brewing. The four are given proud exhibition in Unruly's tap room near Rebel Pies. Brown transforms wood into fetish objects. His eight support posts, spear tipped, remind one of the ancient posts of the sundial at Cahokia Mounds, just off the Mississippi River near St Louis. Lashed to stakes at bases, this tepee like structure easily passed fire and safety inspection surely. Each post of charred cedar has been assembled of three lengths, secured by metal joints. Nothing is going to buckle so don't worry. Brown and VanderWier have teams of engineers and installers who do it right.

Thanks to the staff of Happenstance Art House, I studied pinch pot making with VanderWier last week for a song. There's a quiet team of philanthropists who fund the happenings at Happenstance. VanderWier had fourteen of us happily working clay successfully in minutes. He demonstrated techniques by transforming two pots into an orb. Then the orb became a cube in his playful hands and then became a dragon whistle with feet, ears and mouthpiece added. Both Brown and VanderWier demonstrate that relaxed playfulness that is the magic in a sculptor's hands. I'm glad the pair choose to play in Muskegon.

I feel an afternoon nap slipping up to greet me. I would gladly succumb to it, but I am a guest of history this early afternoon.  Chittenango recovered the landing where canal boats paused for repairs and canal boats were constructed. The attendant collected a six dollar admission and reminded me of the four in the afternoon closing time.  I would have preferred to visit this site when a blacksmith and a team of ship wrights kept this site busy and full of life all hours of the night. A pair of cyclists from Australia signed in to the registrar. Other than that, the only life passes by on the far side of the canal on bicycles and by foot. History might not be the draw that once it was back in the days of station wagons. Parents might bring their kids by the wagon load to make sure they were properly exposed to history. Not this afternoon. Maybe the ghosts of the past are watching Fox sports on TV. Could we celebrate history by placing a brew pub on this spot. Make the brewer promise to use old recipes and techniques. Now that's history to toast with a lift of a stein.

I am now a historical actor. I caught twenty minutes of peaceful snooze of the deck of a barn that once serviced the canal boats. Although I think the current barn is a reproduction built to historical prints, drafted by reference to Dauggerotypes and tin types of the previous building. The site must have fallen into quite a state of disrepair. A canal boat that moored on this canal wall now lies in ruins below the water line. Which I believe means it was burnt to the waterline. Which probably meant that a person considered the Marcellus, a guess as to name, an eyesore and burnt it to the waterline, maybe with the help of fuel and a cargo hold stuffed with straw. Plenty of good ships were put to the torch after years of good service. I can think of two such wrecks below the waters of the Grand River near Grand Haven. One famous ship filled with flammable materials and even gunpowder went up in flames on the waterfront in Toronto.  Refreshments and souvenirs sold, pictures published in local papers, I wish I could remember the good ship's name. This might be here the ruins of the Sadie Hughes or the W. H. Marcellus, both owned by Mr. I. J. Laning of Chittenango. Stephen Coulthart somehow got down into the marl and sketched the remains, the detailed drawing now on display along the dock. I'm sure Coulthart despised what time and weather and maybe human stupidity had done to this fair ship.

Sunday finds me in the coffeehouse with all the arts and craft furniture made by Stickley furniture. The window allows the low winter sun of noon to shine deeply into the hall, a window that features a repeating motif in stained glass that reminds me of Charles Rennie Mackintosh or Frank Lloyd Wright. I am sitting in an arm chair that has arms made of quartersawn oak, displaying the long woodgrain of the oak. At the nearby Stickley museum, an exhibit explains the clever design that hides imperfections and joins. Not a bad place to enjoy a little sunshine cheer, sip a coffee made from beans ground and roasted in the house and contemplate the upcoming year. The thirteenth has arrived, so I cannot wish my daughter and the people I meet, "Happy Twelfth Night", a night best celebrated with a performance of William Shakespeare's Twelfth Night and the lighting of torches. It's too late to wish acquaintances "Happy New Year" because we are already a fortnight into the New Year. A fortnight equals two weeks, a fact I have no drive to look up and confirm. In Troy, New York, a gathering of pagans plan to soak bread in beer and hang the slices of bread in the apple trees after blessing the trees. The bread attracts the birds, who will frequent the trees until it is time to pollinate the blossoms with their flickering feathers. As much as I would love to see just that,  three hours to Troy in a rush doesn't seem to be the way to prepare my mind to participate in a pagan ritual, marking the end of Wassaling. Instagram brings me signs that the season progresses. A photographer posted a picture of a red headed woodpecker tapping on a tree trunk rooted on the shore of the Erie Canal, running through Camillus. He confirmed to me that he took the picture Saturday. It reminded me of looking for woodpeckers along the Thornapple River south of Grand Rapids, north of Kalamazoo. In between the two Michigan cities, the town called Middleville hosts the fest at the end of April. I wondered aloud in writing with my acquaintance if there were enough woodpeckers for a woodpecker festival in Camillus. Funny, you would think he would have gotten back to me on the inquiry.

While I was sitting on a bench in a rain garden, a man walked over to talk to me, “So, do you think we’ll get all the rain the forecast promised”. I can talk about the weather like a pro. “Sure, I think we’ll see plenty of rain”. He took an interest because he saw me taking short TikTok films of a library that was part of the Southern Food Museum.

The building had been sold to a developer for three quarters of a million and he was leading a work crew. The museum double their money and will soon have a boutique hotel full of hungry neighbors. I wonder now if the books had to be catalogued and boxed for easy transfer to the next library space. He took ownership in his role at the museum, and I soon learned I was talking to the curator of cooking for meats and butchery, Dan Roberts.

He knew meat, serving as an inspector for the USDA. The museum had become his dream job, a way to work in the field he loved without the stresses of a rigid job. He got to teach his family recipes to enthusiastic visitors. He drew no official salary and led the donor roll.

I love it when people take a liking to me and keep talking. I excused myself because I had the appointment, or so I thought, a half mile down the road. He said, “Bike Works is right across the street”. “Yes, that’s where the Youth Improvement Program fixes bikes. I’m going to Bike Easy”.
“Oh, I don’t know about Bike Easy. Let me know if they need a feed for a fundraiser. I love to build up this street. It’s easy to make up a bodacious batch of Jambalaya”.

I thanked him. “The South is Different”, I said, knowing it to be true from the writings of Tennessee Williams and Flannery O’Connor. “I bet the food is extraordinary at the Southern Food Museum”.

“We take our food seriously in Louisiana, sir”.

Maybe he might help develop a vegan cajun cuisine?

The train trip became a safari, at least as much of a safari as a land recovering from DDT and massive industrialization can muster. In the Serengeti, nature still populates the land with flocks and herds the way she has for hundreds of years. A countryside recovering from a Silent Spring when SET collapsed the food chain and almost wiped out the eagles can only be expected to field a minor display. But today, I was amazed. The train passed through a preserve at the north end of Cayuga Lake, the Montezuma National Refuge. I loved seeing hundreds of waterfowl swimming on the surface of ponds built for their welcome. I saw massive flocks of Canadian Geese flying overhead in chevron formations. Not the bigger flocks I've witnessed over Perry Michigan,  but still impressive. The train rolled on and we entered a swamp with hundreds of silver, barkless snags standing tall in the water. On the top of many, I saw stick fortresses upon which herons lay their clutches of eggs. Upon each one, as resolute as an Episcopal verger, I saw the outlines of a blue heron standing guard.  I'm not sure I have ever seen a rookery of this size before.  But I noted its location upon my map, west of Weedsport and near the rail line. I could easily return for a visit while the rookery serves as a nursery for little herons. As the herons reach back to the days of the pterodactyl,  I felt as if I were looking back eons. But this is the way the land prospered with wildlife in the 1800s. Hopefully,  nothing delays or puts at risk this return to Eden.

I enjoyed my Saturday visit to the Bundy Museum, thanks to the time I was allowed to spend with the Rod Serling collection. Everybody was agog with the fact that I saw the Talking Tina dolls face to face. I read from family copies of the Twilight Zone scripts, written by Serling for the first season. The annex makes for a common area for visitors. You can't sit down at the dining room table in the Bundy house during a tour, but you can make yourself at home on a bar stool at the lovingly restored bar. A vending machine has drinks and snacks to keep you sharp as you peruse the scripts and make notes. The bar opens for special events in the space, which have included a Rod Serling Christmas Party and film screenings and concerts.

The Bundy Machine celebrates the invention of the time clock. However, the Bundy Museum extends its mission by incubating collections for future museums in Binghamton. How long until the Rod Serling collection can stand alone as its own destination? I'm wondering if there's plans to secure the home where the writer lived while attending high school.

Definitely worth paying a visit.

Phelps Mansion has been preserved by the efforts of a woman's society called the Monday Club. Just because the society transformed to become the Phelps Mansion society, do not believe that the women's society doesn't have a presence in the house. The renovations, bath room modifications and even the ball room addition carry the influence of this 1800s society into the Twenty-First Century. The volunteers who guide the walks through the house have been well groomed. My guide has just finished her doctoral thesis for a history degree from Binghamton University, so Chelsea could really handle almost any question raised by guests.

If you love American paintings from the Hudson River School era, you'll love that the Monday club decorated the drawing rooms and dressing rooms with unmentioned members of the school. The club bought the house for ten thousand dollars around 1905 and literally gave to the house a priceless number of rare objects.

I hope to soon catch a concert in the ball room, which looks like a chamber with great acoustics.

I prefer to call this span the "George Bailey Bridge" as that's how I heard about it. The bridge has its own festival under the name of the name "George Bailey Bridge". The bridge shall accumulate meaning as time goes forward as a place where we contemplate our contributions to the life of those we know and those we haven't met. Adjacent to the Ludovico Sculpture Trail, the bridge makes a great place to begin a walk when one needs to think and put the world at a distance. The sculpture trail has room for more sculptures, and I am charmed that the first female mayor of Seneca Falls and the first female police officer of Seneca Falls have been honored here with sculptures. Experts might make comments on the quality of these sculptures but I'll be honest. I love their honesty and hope I'll see hundreds more installed along the trail.

For the tenth most populous town in New York State, this museum stands equally with MOMA or the DIA or even ARTIC. I love how it rambles between the Johnson designed main galleries and the mansion called "Fountain Elms". Maybe Fountain Elms has gone too far too protect its collection of furnishings, carpets and bedsteads and divans? I felt a little the intruder peering about rooms where I should enter just three feat. This was a place of refugee and relaxation for the family and wouldn't it be nice if visitors could tune in by relaxing also? Maybe some relaxing, attractive yet fungible sofas in the halls? Seriously, I felt as if I were carrying microbes that would cause the furnishings to collapse into dust.

Ever hear that story about how engineers can't figure out how bumblebees fly but no one told the bumblebee? No one has told Rochester Contemporary that it has too small a base in Rochester, and yet the museum now owns the building. The Frederick Douglass Monument has a date to be moved to a prominent location in Rochester, again. RoCo has served as a workshop for exploring the implications of that act and deepening the relationship of the city with Douglass. I have heard everyone who wants one can have a little Frederick bronze in their front yard soon. That's totally cool.

Sadly, the house has closed for the winter, waiting only a few weeks to open on March 1st. The view of Van Cleff Lake from the front porch makes a good place to contemplate civil rights, which very well might be the foundations of all rights, including property rights. I doubt the lake existed when Elizabeth Stanton lived on the gorgeous prominence. The locks and the canal existed and so existed the post Civil War industrial might of this town so quiet on a Sunday. I hear the caws of crows and the cry of a bird in flight. To this add the trill of a bird I cannot see.

Franklin Square Park has grown up so fast.  Now we have a climbing gym, a Freedom of Espresso coffee shop and a Spaghetti Factory. I have yet to make it over to Burnt Acorn Brewing nearby or the Preserve, but the two fun spots for beer and community await so close to Franklin's statue. Plenty of raw industrial buildings to reclaim for mixed use retail & housing. Maybe they'll finally naturalize Onondaga Creek or finish the round the lake bike trail without upsetting the Eagles of Murphy's Island? Steps away and over a safe highway bridge, Little Italy awaits.

This is a fine example of a historic Green Space being set aside for the benefit of the public. Where Edith Farnsworth did her translations of poetry, one can now practice yoga. Where Lord Palumbo once established a impeccable English garden, you can help groom a woodland for permaculture and sustainability. I recommend that you take a yearly membership so that you can make the grounds of the Farnsworth House a relaxing getaway for your Sunday afternoons.

Mardi Gras World occupies a lovely perspective on the Mississippi River, and can be made much more affordable if you cycle to the world. Sure, you can take a tour but you can explore the gift shop and a small exhibit for free, too. Maybe you have some talent? Well, that's the best way to go through the door, to work in the imaginary world of the Mardi Gras before the floats disgorge from this fantasy warehouse.

I'm not sure what this refuge intends to become. It's part Prairie restoration. It's part land for the hunting of birds. It has trees, but it appears to be heavily forested. The Green River flows north of The preserve, but it doesn't flow through The preserve at all. I like it because it's a big patch of land they are letting go back To Nature. Plus there's a nice set of bluebird boxes in The refuge

Albright-Knox has been on my short list for Buffalo for years. The collection includes exceptional examines of abstract art, conceptual art and impressionist art. The masterpieces are given plenty of breathing room, too. Picasso's favors La Toilette might be the epitome of the collection but not the only major example of his age. The Van Gogh painting of the mill has an equal claim to fame.

Write well in New Orleans. Live well in New Orleans. Defend well the ethos in New Orleans. And if you are fortunate, might your papers dwell forever in the vaults of the Historic New Orleans Collection. Tennessee Williams allowed his papers to find many homes in the south. However, be sure that his papers are shared with the curious with total hospitality at the Collection.

I'm very impressed with the beautifully restored Stanley Theater, which has made a cool place to take in a screening of the Rocky Horror Picture Show. It's not every performance hall that can go off to camp like this. It's not every great hall from the roaring twenties where I can play on the stage as soon as I arrive.

I loved to visit Clinton Square for every festival from Juneteenth to the Polish Festival to the Bacon Festival to the Irish Festival. Sadly, the Tuesday morning farmers market won't be waiting for me next Tuesday at 6 AM. I'll have to go elsewhere for fresh tomatoes!

This gem lies on the Illinois River and you'll find it connected to a string of state parks all of which are free for your entry. I have yet to begin the complete exploration of all the canyons and bluffs. It says gorgeous in winter time as it is in summertime.
A lovingly restored Greek Revival home enhanced by the addition of a visitor entrance awaits those who wish to learn of Fayetteville's contributions to human rights.

The rock itself is nothing special. It is almost impossible to get a perspective of it from above. From below it is a muddy mess at the bottom which is the main thing you see from either angle. The most exciting part was watching my dog trying to pull a big stick out of the mud at the bottom. Anywhere near the stream or bottom of the rock get very buggy.

The rest of the conservation area does have well marked trails good for walking with dogs or children.
likes: Good for walking with dogs or children

reviews_attraction.text: Crawford Notch is a picturesque pass with an old railway along the west side. It is wider than Franconia Notch, and includes several easy to access waterfalls. The nearby mountains are less steep and less popular for hiking than the neighboring Franconia Notch. I think it is underrated and a good place to go when Franconia Notch is really busy, but otherwise I prefer Franconia Notch. Arethusa Falls and Mt. Willard are the places to definitely go.

Good sized falls falls for the area, easy to access and worth a visit in all 4 seasons. I have been during all 4. I actually thought the winter was the most interesting.
The height of the falls is modest but there are several places to view the falls along the base, and a couple spots near the top. Worth checking out during the winter, during the melt during the spring, and after a heavy rain.

The rock itself is nothing special. It is almost impossible to get a perspective of it from above. From below it is a muddy mess at the bottom which is the main thing you see from either angle. The most exciting part was watching my dog trying to pull a big stick out of the mud at the bottom. Anywhere near the stream or bottom of the rock get very buggy.

Beautiful falls, shortly off the road. There is a flat easy trail with a boardwalk to get you close to the falls. Accessible on the way up to castle in the clouds or with a longer hike from another location. The stream feeding the falls is relatively small, but the steep falls with cliffs on each side made it interesting.

Perfect stop right in the center of Crawford Notch. On the east side there is a small pond with fishing for kids. Picnic areas are on the east side of the pond. On the west side is a small store with ice cream and bathrooms. From both there is a broad view of Crawford notch on both sides. There is also plenty of parking.

An architectural masterpiece! It is so simple, but yet so beautiful how it reflects the city and looks different from every side.  Also fun for kids with sprinklers nearby and in a central location to parks and shopping.
In the morning the sun can bring angular light directly on it which is something to be seen

Interesting layout! But dated and expensive for what it has to offer. The chief feature is a circular aquarium tank that spans several stories with a penguin cove at the bottom. It has some very large turtles and many fish. Lacks dolphin/whale shows. The building is a dated too and looks like a cold war relic.

Hike starts at a nice elevation that you pass through mostly shady pine along clear stream in the ravine. Nice and cool for summer, lots of snow for cross country. Fairly flat to start. The notch features much of the same, and the peaks don't have much of a view after the long 4 miles to get there.

So much fun to tour the area with the family! It was a beautiful day and parking wasn't hard at all, nor was it overcrowded. We just walked along the peers and saw some of the best sites Boston has to offer, including the historical ships and buildings and boats sailing past!

Profoundly outweighed my expectations. I came at sunrise and it was majestic to watch the lights go out along the skyline and the morning sun reflect off the wake and the aquarium. It wasn't crowded either, mostly runners going along the lakefront. Great place to get photos

Really amazing cascades for the length of the hike! A short trail takes you to the base of the cascades and I really recommend going all the way up as there are several small falls along the length of it as well as pools. A hike the whole family can do.

My favorite park north of Chicago!
Open beach (not a swimming area but can wade on the shores), dunes, playground and sports field. The parking at the park is for wilmette residents only but you can park on the street

Biggest and most tourist of the beaches on Lake Winnipisaukee with access to boardwalk, train station, and restaurants/arcades. Dated bathrooms. The historical monument is small but really this is a beach.

My favorite city park in Manchester! I like its proximitt to the ricer in the middle of downtown.
I dont't like how small it is and that it does not connect to any kind of longer heritage trail
Decent park for a walk, parking is a little difficult. Probably the large size of the park is its main appealing feature, the tower is decent with good views of Boston.
Trail is decent but terrain is a muddy lowlands full of bugs. To get a view of the old canal you have to climb down a slippery bank. The rapids are the main appeal.
Ice skating rink is decent (a little overused when I went), but it is also fun as a fountain in the summer to cool off! The water was warm and my 3yo loved it!
Quieter than similar himes, with great views. I did the east side on the manning trail which reminded me of the welch dickey loop with less people.
Modern, beautiful, and amazing! The boardwalk goes around a large lake and there is a playground with outdoor fountains for kids to run in
The best viewpoint on the highway! A majestic view of the mountains lining the valley. Best at sunset. It wasnt open this winter however
Open green space with flowers, statues. A pond and birds. Fun for the whole family. Not many public water fountains or bathrooms.
Its a short hike to a series of impressive waterfalls. The water has a foamy tinge and views are limited so I give it 4 stars.
Great park! 2 playgrounds, swings, ball fields, a pond with a 1 mile trail around it. A green island in the city.
A big rock (which there are many of in the area) with poor views of cannon cliff because trees are in the way.

In observation of Veteran's Day I visited the newly-opened Soldiers Memorial Museum in downtown St. Louis (after it's two year dormancy for an extensive rennovation). The facelift has created a fine interior with modern exhibits that capture and explain major themes of WWI, WWII, earlier conflicts, and few on post-war conflicts. The narratives do a good job covering many aspects of war and how it impacted the soldiers from St. Louis, the home front (food rationing, manufacturing, employment), and soldiers' lives. Relatively little is spent on describing the wars themselves. The narratives focuses on individual sailors and soldiers and provide a high-level overview in everyday language, so people from all backgrounds and virtually no knowledge of the wars will be able to understand. War is a horrid, ruinous affair -- hopefully visitors will tour this museum with great respect for the men and women who have served, and with a vision and ambition to avoid war in the future.

Edwardsville has a beautifully restored / preserved home, the 1820 Colonel Benjamin Stephenson house, with an excellent docent-led tour. The family has an interesting history reflected in the (comparative) opulence of this pre-civil war frontier home. The decor, furniture and fixtures have been collected to accurately reflect the home of this period. In addition to the docents (in period costume), there were two young girls demonstrating typical household skills -- candle making, milling corn meal, grinding sugar, and baking corn bread. Superb! Note there is an admission fee, but it's well worth it.

Aviation enthusiasts, movie buffs and historians alike will enjoy, off well-trodden paths, the Historic Aircraft Restoration Museum at the Creve Coeur Airport in Maryland Heights. You'll find four hangars of vintage aircraft, mostly biplane from the golden age of aviation. Two shining stars are the WWI JN-4 from the film "The Great Waldo Pepper" (Robert Redford, Susan Sarandon, George Peppard), and a WWI British Sopwith Camel (which, for you fans of the comic strip "Peanuts," is the aircraft Snoopy flew to combat the Red Baron).

Housed in the historic Curtis-Wright Hangar 2 (listed in the National Register of Historic Places) is the Greater St. Louis Air and Space Museum in Cahokia, IL, which houses a considerable amount of aviation and aerospace memorabilia and photos. Not many places where you will see a pilot license signed by Orville Wright! They also have several vintage space suits, models, and a few aircraft and engines. Sad to see there are insufficient funds available for the repairs to this fine old building which houses so much history.

This home rates low in historic value because of the somewhat forced association with renown Ragtime composer Scott Joplin. He rented this home for two years (1901-03) and it was thought he wrote "The Entertainer" here, for which there is little reliable evidence to support the assertion. Making note of this house is akin to saying "George Washington slept here." Joplin was an enormous contributor to American music, with Rag influencing almost all subsequent American music. But this house has little to do with it.

Another of St. Louis' premiere sites, the Missouri History Museum offers both permanent and rotating exhibits pertaining to the state's history. Among the permanent fixtures are the replica of the "Spirit of St. Louis" aircraft which Charles Lindbergh flew on the first trans-Atlantic flight; and an amazing sculpture of Thomas Jefferson. It also hosts many of the city's cultural events and lectures. Great little gift shop too. Parking usually proves difficult, so expect to drive around a little.

Operated by the National Parks Service in downtown St. Louis, the Old Courthouse is a Federal style building was completed in 1828 and is most noted for being the location of the landmark Dred Scott case in 1846. After years of court battles, the U.S. Supreme Court in 1857 ruled against the Scotts, saying they did not have grounds as citizens to sue. Today the courtrooms and offices house exhibits on life in St. Louis throughout the years, plus of course the Scott case.

One of the city's premiere attractions, Grant's Farm offers families a wonderful afternoon with a free tram ride through the large animal sanctuary, an elephant show, many other exotic animals, horse stables, gift shop, feeding baby goats, a carousel, good food... loads of fun! Best news for families: admission is free! There is a modest charge for parking, so load up your van and go. Many individual attractions inside are free, while a few have small fees.

One of St. Louis' premiere attractions, the museum showcases a huge collection of representative pieces spanning many periods, genre, and geographic locations. It is free to everyone, certainly a rarity in today's world, because citizens elect to shoulder costs so that everyone has the ability to enrich their mind and soul through art. Traveling exhibits are usually quite good. Photos are of the "Sunken Cities" exhibit.

Situated across the street from Grant's Farm,  President Ulysses S. Grant's home (White Haven) is a well preserved U.S. National Historic Site. Park Rangers provide brief, informative tours of the property and interior of the home, and there is a self-guided museum within the old barn. Interesting collection of artifacts, as well as a curious personal history of the North's most prominent general and future president.

Among the numerous historic homes in town, this is unremarkable by comparison. The third floor was was under repair so fully 1/3 of the home is unavailable. The home is attached to a toy museum, as Mr. Field was a noted collector -- and even this collection is modest and not outstanding. The fee was excessive for the tour. In brief, other historic St. Louis homes are much better maintained or have better collections.

The Botanical Garden is one of the city's top attractions, particularly in the Spring, when many of the flowers are in bloom, as well as during the many festivals and special events it hosts. Allow plenty of time to enjoy your stroll so you're not hurried. The gift shop has lots of distinctive, cool things too. There is an enclosed greenhouse for orchids, as well as the enormous glass geodesic dome, the Climatron.

Not only does this park boast more acreage than New York's Central Park, it has some of St. Louis' nicest destinations - the Zoo, the St. Louis Art Museum, the Jewel Box, the Muni theater, golf course, Boat House w/ restaurant and paddle boat rentals, jogging trails, and the planetarium section of the Science Center. It is absolutely fantastic!

The first cathedral built west of the Mississipi, the Old Cathedral is an important part of St. Louis' history. The cathedral itself is simply yet elegantly appointed, and it offers the traditional adornments with the exception of stained glass. There is apparently a museum in the basement, but the hours are fairly limited.

A very good museum detailing black history from slavery to emancipation to modern times. Life-size mannequins of major historical figures are accompanied by narratives of their contributions. Most stirring is an actual slaves quarters from a MO farm, brought to the museum from its original location.

An excellent little museum, particularly for the true historian. The exhibits trace Churchill's career with interesting details and a handful of artifacts, including one of his paintings. Would really benefit from having more artifacts, but all said, a quality tour.

A premiere children's destination, the Butterfly House allows the little ones to roam the 8,000 sq. ft. all-glass conservatory with thousands of butterflies in tropical temperatures. There are also exhibits on other insects and a large gift shop with nice gifts.

This zoo differentiates itself in its sheer expansiveness. Animals such as zebra and giraffe, for example, have huge acreages in which they can range and roam, and there is an awesome overhead tram and boat rides for visitors to get great views of the animals.

The museum carries a mixed collection of artists, some quite notable (a Chagall, Kandinsky, Warhol, Lichtenstein), but they are few and none particularly notable. One full floor is dedicated to the Jesuits, for those interested in Catholic art and artifacts.

Extraordinarily well maintained home rich in St. Louis history. The home is lavishly appointed with period furniture and fixtures. Of all the historic homes in town, I believe this is the best. And gravy for the goose, there is no admission charged.

Reasonably well maintained historic home owned by Missouri Gov. Bates in 1850. Unfortunately the interior is only open on occasions, but it's quite interesting. The grounds include the home, the separate kitchen building and several outbuildings.

Hold on to your seats, here's the scoop on the Jefferson Barracks Telephone Museum!  It's actually pretty interesting to see how the technology has changed since the earliest years. And there are a LOT of artifacts. So be prepared to be dazzled!

The Tower Grove House was built in 1849 and has been preserved and restored, with a considerable amount of opulent furniture and personal items. It makes you feel as though you stepped through a doorway to the past.
While comparatively small, this cute little museum plucks at the nostalgic heartstrings of America. It contains memorabilia, roadsigns, and neon from yesteryear. Fun little trip down memory lane.
This is an exceptionally well preserved stone fort with wooden interior structures  replete with powder room, quarters, and functioning gate. Impressive in stature and sheer size of the walls.

+ Enjoyed kayaking on the lake -- at the time of our visit, it was $8 for a single or $10 for a tandem for a two-hour rental... definitely enough time to navigate around the lake more than once.
+ If you've got your own water craft, you can canoe, kayak, paddle, or use a small electric motor with your jon boat. Nothing bigger or noisier.
+ Campground was comparatively quiet and well-kept, with ample space and shade for each site. We stayed in Oak Ridge, which is, as far as I can tell, the same campground as Pine Grove (shared entrance & host, one shower house for both; it's just that the former is situated primarily among oak trees and the latter, primarily tall pines.
+ We drove through the area where the original springs and hotel were located 100+ years ago -- not that impressive. There's places to picnic here; a few points of access for the Deer Run Trail; and an archery range; but the playground equipment seems pretty outdated
+ Lots of hiking crammed in to the park -- we didn't do any hiking, but there's trails along the lake, prairie, and forested parks of the park. 10+ miles total, and the longest (6.6-mile moderate-difficulty Deer Run Trail) can even be broken in to smaller, easier sections, if so desired.
+ Check-in for camping was kind of confusing. Permanently-erected sign at the park office indicated if arriving after 3:30pm, we should make camp and check in the following morning. Typed sign hung on office door indicated that our campground would have a sign-in sheet near its info sign at its entrance, along with an envelope to include payment (we reserved & paid online, so no need to do that much). When we went searching for that sign-in, the campground host was nearby and didn't need us to sign in or anything, as we'd already made the reservation and paid. TL;DR: easy enough, if not slightly confusing.
+ No swimming permitted in the lake -- kind of a bummer, but the trade-off is that the park and lake are probably a little quieter than they otherwise would be.
+ A few other picnic areas are situated in the park, with their own bathrooms or latrines, playgrounds, and parking.
+ Lake stocked with largemouth bass, bluegill, sunfish, trout, catfish, crappie... I think there's more, but can't recall at the moment.
+ Pretty remote. First, pretty regularly had no cell service (data or voice)--not that that's necessarily such a bad thing. Also, the nearest Walmart is about a half-hour away, in Quincy. But, that night sky.... wow!
+ Everyone we encountered working there (concessions/rental store operator, campground host, & park ranger) was very friendly!

Pretty cool little hub for outdoor activity in the area. Three separate parking lots help serve this location, providing ample parking. Access to three different paved paths for walking / running / biking / rollerblading / skateboarding - the Moab Canyon Pathway heads east, along UT-128 for about 2.5 miles (though we did witness some braver cyclists venturing out onto the highway beyond there), as well as west for nearly 9 miles, over the Colorado River, past the entrance to Arches National Park, on up to UT-313. The path also heads back southeast into Moab, though that appears somewhat impeded at the moment by road construction on 191.

Other amenities & features include fully-functioning restrooms, a small playground consisting of a few different rock structures for climbing, a small green "field" for lounging or yoga or whatever.
likes: Diverse activities (walking, running, biking, rollerblading, skateboarding)

reviews_attraction.text:
Protip #1: Never pay for parking, there's almost always free street parking to be found, so long as you don't mind walking a bit.
Protip #2: Children's zoo is free to enter for the first hour it's open in the morning (at least that's been the case during our two most recent visits, in 2016-17)... an employee actually turned is on to this as we arrived early one morning and were attempting to decide what to hit first.
River's Edge is phenomenal, especially when the elephants are nearby.
Sea Lion Sound and the Fragile Forest are excellent exhibits as well.
And I could go on... so much to do and see here, and it's free!

One of the more unique arches in the park, primarily because of its shape, but also because you can get quite close to it. Also came to the Windows section for some stargazing & mediocre astrophotography a couple days after visiting during the daytime, and this arch provided a nice setting for that (though I'm sure it gets a little busier at night than what we experienced, as it was chilly outside and a waxing gibbous moon almost directly overhead). If you're driving this far back to see Double Arch & The Windows, there's no reason not to swing by Turret Arch, as well.

Playground seems to be quickly becoming small and outdated in comparison to others in the city's system--not sure if there's a long-term plan to upgrade it, as it still seems relatively new.
Two baseball fields, a basketball court, and decent-sized pavilion.
Immediately adjacent to both Glen Travis Park (trailhead on the other side of the main parking lot) and Jack Gettemeyer Park, both of which contain Dardenne Greenway trails, and connect to the Woodlands Sports Park to the southwest, as well as Dardenne Park & the city's golf course located north of Mexico Rd.

Trip to the top of the arch is pricey, but still pretty cool. The updated museum was pretty cool, though my nostalgia does make me miss the old one I remember visiting on grade school field trips. The new entrance is quite spectacular to behold in person, and the improvements to the above-ground park are pretty cool as well. We didn't walk south of the arch, but between the monument and where we parked on Morgan Street, the native wildflower garden is a vast improvement on the garage that was there before.

Worth the drive - we were heading from 70 to Moab and had some time to spare, so we decided to take UT-128 instead of US-191, and detoured through Castle Valley. We weren't quite sure what to expect, but this was just one of several places affording spectacular views of the surrounding area. Several of the side roads seemed unpassable (unless you're intending to drive off-road in snow), but La Sal Loop Rd was clear the whole way, and definitely worth the extra hour or so the whole trip took.

Hadn't been in 15+ years, and it has grown massively! I like that they preserved a bunch of the fun stuff I remember from when I was a kid... the kinetic sculpture near the entrance; the "shadow room"; the Van de Graaff Generator; the 3-story slide; the slightly-more-recent Children's Village ... The new exhibits they've added are even more fantastic, with numerous STEAM-related activities and plenty of fun for all kids and most adults.

Short little trail consisting of a boardwalk built around the dinosaur tracks. Each type of tracks has a sign identifying them, plus a little extra info. This particular site was easy to access (the other one located a little farther down the road might be a little tricky if you're in a car or something with 2WD), and we spent a total of about 20 minutes or so at this particular site, and our kids were quite fascinated by it.

Playground that my kids have enjoyed, but not the latest & greatest compared to others in St. Peters or elsewhere in SCC.
Paved, ~3.5-mile trail that connects to Spencer Creek, Covenant, & Laurel Parks (and all the way up to 370 Lakeside Park, if you fancy riding/walking along Spencer Rd. for a bit), and loops around a little pond west of city hall and its parking lots.
A few ball fields
The Cove

Camped here on multiple occasions. Getting a spot (at least during the fall months) can be tricky, particularly if you need 2 adjacent, so plan a few months ahead. Since there's no RV/trailer camping, it stays relatively quiet. Nice serene lake, decent hiking trail, access to Katy Trail. Only drawback is the unsightly (especially at night) Ameren plant directly across the Missouri.

Pretty underwhelming as far as parks go... you've got the Lewis & Clark monument & Boat House, which includes a museum. A barge you can walk on to for a more up-close view of the river... a couple cabooses...
A decent place for the various festivals it hosts throughout the year, though parking & traffic can definitely be a pain, though that's not exactly the park's fault.

Didn't hike the entire trail, but parked for the overlook, and hiked a short distance down into the "canyon" to get the full effect. Very good. Word to the wise: probably not best to view/photograph in the early morning hours (in our experience), as the sun doesn't illuminate the whole area particularly well for the first couple hours after sunrise.

Great state park to spend a day at. There's plenty of hiking to be done, the castle ruins to view, and lake access too. My only wish is that a campground could somehow be incorporated in to the park, because it's a bit of a haul to stay at Lake of the Ozarks SP with the intent to hang out at Ha Ha Tonka

Awesome view of the dam and surrounding environs; one of the larger overlooks, with multiple vantage points and even some seating. Not a terrible hike from the visitor's center; we did about 3 miles to hit French and Wildcat Canyons and the overlooks in about 1 1/2 hours.

Fantastic place to swim/play in water. The campground leaves a bit to be desired ever since The Scouring (not a whole lot of shade, and feels like an RV parking lot), but I don't don't it'll rebound. Pretty close nearby to several other fantastic state parks, as well.

Pretty busy area, but still worthwhile. The hike here isn't remotely strenuous, and the shape of the formation allows you to get even closer, whether you want to stand and stare up in amazement at the larger arch or climb up into the smaller one.
Such an amazing museum, too bad it costs as much as it does, especially since there's really too much to do in a single day. I especially like the U-505, transportation gallery, & science storms.
dislikes: Too much to do in one day

reviews_attraction.text: It's a good stadium for a good baseball team. Don't go as often as we used to because tickets ain't cheap and concessions ain't cheap, but it's still a good place to catch a game.
Cool statue of a couple iconic characters in American literature. Right on your way if you're hiking up to the lighthouse or checking things out around Main St.
Nice little park with some paved walking trails, a couple playgrounds, sand volleyball & basketball courts, and a few different pavilions.
One of St. Charles County's many fantastic county parks. Plenty of hiking, and the opportunity to wade or swim in the creeks is unique.
Playground seems small and outdated. Access to Grant's Trail is a definite plus. Large, open space where ballfields are located, too.
Parking situation isn't great, but it's a fine playground as a destination if you're walking or biking on the Dardenne Greenway.
Good park for fishing, picnicking, or kayaking. A playground, too. Not a whole lot else, otherwise, but still a very nice park.

Efficient and historically interesting way to get across Lake Michigan. Wi-Fi is available but the free level is not very useful. Food is ok and what I expected. It is a four hour ride and you need to be there an hour before. Many different places you can relax during the trip. You can learn more at the Maritime Museum in Ludington.

Guthrie Theater is a great place to see a live performance. Every seat is a good one.  Use the ramp across the street to park. Make sure to make reservations at area restaurants as many times they are pretty booked after performances.

Excellent experience! Go for the tasting option that lets you sample everything. The cheese and meat tray is one of the best I have experienced as you get to select from many choices to customize it. White port was a favorite!

Historic White Pine Village provides an interesting historical glimpse of early times in the Ludington area. When we were there we did not see an interpretive guides which would have added a little more realism.

Scenic hiking area. Great for walking dogs or running.  Signage not the best so be sure to look at the map. And wear shoes that you are ok with getting dirty as there are some muddy spots along the trail.
Great place to explore. Went to Martin Luther exhibit and despite timed entrance it was very crowded and very hard to see things. Plus, such dim lighting hard to read the cards by displays.
Wow! Fabulous and impressive magic show in a brand new theater. Tristan is friendly and the caliber of the magic matches (if not beats) David Copperfield in Las Vegas. Highly recommend!
Great place to stop on our way through town. Several resident bald and golden eagles, along with a brief educational show were the highlights. Get there when they open for fewer crowds.
Very interesting private garden. Unique sculptures, water features and variety of flowers and plants. Little hard to find and limited tour times so check their website.
We didn't do the plantation house tour but we did walk through the main gardens which had a very diverse variety. Worth the time if you are passing through the area.
Nice park for dog walks.  Well maintained. Be careful of people driving through though as they often do not obey the speed limit signs which is unsafe and annoying.
Cool place to visit and about 60% of the items in the house are authentic to the family. The house itself is a replica of the original house which was torn down.
Interesting lighthouse to visit. Watch the video even if you don't climb to the top. Tip: take the walk along the beach on the way back...it is worth it!
Allow plenty of time to see everything. Lots of different tours you can take and much to experience. Gets very busy later in the day so get there early.
Excellent tour! Gives you a story that brings history to life. You can select the tour that interests you most. Well run and recommended!
Excellent place to visit outdoors and away from the strip. Botanical gardens and museum are great! Take a tour of the gardens if you can!
I have seen this show four times and love it. If you are a Beatles fan you must see the show and stop at the extensive gift shop!
You take a boat to and from Fort Sumter and the tours get very busy. Historical place and well worth seeing when in Charleston.
This is a nice city park to walk the dogs. Also many events are held here...saw good firework show during Lakefront Days.
Nice park in the middle of St. Louis Park. Well maintained trails and friendly staff. Lots of mosquitos so come prepared!
Wow!  This is a must see if you are in Wausau. Allow about two hours. Totally free and some very unique collections.
Amazing collection of art here is very surprising. If you are in town and are in to art you can't miss this one!
Busy beach but some of the best fireworks we have ever seen on July 4. We walked from Ludington House B&B.
Was here for a concert. Great venue to see live music! Highly recommended if a band you like plays here!
Cool place to spend a rainy day. Not far from the strip by Lyft. Would be great for families with kids.

Even though, it is super touristy, yet it is one of the best places to visit in Chicago. Waterfront, shows, amazing views of skyline makes it a perfect place to visit. Best place to relax after work. Good pickup point if you like to take pedal cabs. Parking can be nightmare. However, there are few on Wabash ave like loop auto parks which provide cheap parking spots. Definitely recommended for anyone in Chicago.

One perfect way to experience American falls. It is a prettiest way to get closer to falls and we absolutely loved it. It takes about 3 hours for the full experience and the price is totally worth it. To stand beneath the falls and experience the force of it, is a shear pleasure. Loved it and definitely recommended when visiting Niagara Falls.

Mountains behind the water brings this place to life. On a moody day, mountains cheer up the area with the breeze. It’s a great scenic spot on 73. Must visit. There is also free parking. Great place to Kayak if you own one. Entering and exiting can be little tricky as the entry point is downhill from the road and can be easily missed.

Like every other state park in Pennsylvania, this is also so beautiful. Best place to spend evenings. Great place for walks. It also offer boat rentals during summer. Few parking spots are available across the shore. There is picnic spot up the hill. Make sure to check the park timings at the entrance so you know when to get out.

It’s fun to stroll along the walk during evenings. Shops are declining day by day but it is still fun to just exploring things. Can be maintained well. There are also carriage rides available on Broadwalk but are definitely expensive. Paid Parking is available on every road leading to the walk.

One of the best parks in Manhattan. Always up for something and situated in right spot. Love to visit in holiday season especially. Ice rink is already up from November and several food stores. Good enough. Seating also available. Good skyline views. Great place to spend evenings.

This is the most beautiful park in Poconos. There is something for everyone. Take train rides, walk the trails, check the waterfalls, bike, kayaks, much more. Good for all seasons. Definitely recommended. Glen Onoko falls in the area are pretty but comes after deadly hike.

Love the views from here. Walk the trails for the view around the mountain. Can be really windy sometimes. Delaware Gap can also be seen. Restrooms are neat. Parking is available, few spots though. There are viewing spots all along the way from bottom of the mountain.

Oh we love this place. It can be secluded if we go to the south beach. The rocks and lake are so pretty. Easily can spend a day. Trails are neat. Walking on sand made us tired but worth it. Parking can be filled up pretty early. There are good food options around.

It’s a different experience. Place is a beautiful gallery with all folk art and mosaics. Beautifully organized and maintained. It’s kinda small for the price(10$ - non members). More exhibits and upstairs will be presented with tour guides.  No parking on site.

Great and huge park. Lovely way to spend evenings. There are tennis courts which are usually not completely occupied. There is a long trail around the lake, a beautiful way to spend evenings. There is also child play area. Few parking spots are also available.

Place is usually packed. Lots of parking. Service is good but on the track, it usually is not organized. We waited for very long time to get trained. Trails and everything are well maintained. There are people to help along the way. Recommended in the area.

A national landmark that is worth the visit. Kept clean and well organized. Place is self guided. Parking is available at Independence Hall visitor centre. Expect security check and lines at entrance and Bell. It is worth the visit. Above all, it’s free.

Love to go every evening. Beautiful place with so much greenery all around. Memorial stands tall adding beauty to the place. Best place to watch sunrise also. Parking is available behind the monument. Several miles of walking trails around the park.

It’s a nice place to sit and enjoy the evening. Divvy is available here and also lots of parking    Children play area and Benches are also there. Beach can be maintained well but it got some good spots to enjoy. Good beach in the area.

So many waterfalls. So many creeks. Beautiful trails. Lovely landscapes. This part of Adirondacks is so beautiful and I would love going every time. Drive on 73, 9N and 86 to experience it to fullest.
It’s a very pretty temple in a huge area. The architecture inside the building is extraordinary. Loved everything about the building. Food isn’t that great. Parking is available around the building.
Lovely place to visit in fall. Can be maintained well. Trail signs are not clear for first time visitor. And if people roaming with hammers don’t be worried. It’s to hammer stones.
It has great views of George Washington Bridge. Well maintained paths and free to visit. Parking spots are available. Great place to spend evenings.
Good place in the urban jungle. Totally feel like out of city. It has lot of play areas for kids. Adults can sit and enjoy the city views.
Beautiful park. Nice place to watch sunrise. Good spot for kayaking and if you own a boat, it’s the right one. Fishing is also available.
Ample parking. Beautiful views of NYC skyline. Long trails for walking and running. Nice place to spend mornings and evenings.
Great place for all types of services - car and others. Canteen food is good. Temple is well maintained. Parking is abundant.
Happening place in Central Park. Must visit. Great place to spend and watch. One or other performance will happen here.
Beautiful and lovely park right in the edge of the city. Love it. Great park to walk and spend evenings.
