They have a small flock of alpaca.  At least one of them appeared to be wildly hungry.  The others appeared to be slim.  They had recently been sheared by they certainly didn’t appear up to an optimum weight.
In the Zebra cage there was a Zedonk – a cross between a Zebra and a Donkey, a female Zebra that appeared to be in the early stages of pregnancy and a Zebra colt.  There didn’t appear to be a male so I am hard pressed to imagine what’s going on there.  They have a ‘Zebra Feeding Slide’ which is a rubber tire cut in half and nailed to a board.  You slide pieces of carrot down the slide where it lands between the steel cage and a concrete pad.  The animals need to dig it out with their hooves or pull it out with their lips.  There is a large nail sticking out of the end of the slide where little hands might be.  The paddock was uninteresting poorly drained.

The giraffe paddock was also poorly drained.

They have one Timberwolf.  It paces back and forth without cessation.  The enclosure is heavily wooded and brushed but uninteresting.  The wolf has worn two tracks.

The bison enclosure was filthy and poorly drained.  It had a heavy stench.

Along with these items park staff were roaring around in large carts.  The sounds of screeching wheels coming a stop or turning were common.  Be wary with children and the elderly if you decided to go to this place.

Legoland as an attraction in general was a great disappointment.  The tickets were rather expensive even when we bought ‘combo’ tickets online that were matched with ‘Sea Life Michigan Aquarium’.  It is a shame that Legoland is associated with the other attraction in that it’s negative reputation may rub off on the other worthwhile attraction.

Entry to the place was confused by two lines that had very small signs on them that stated ‘Have Tickets’ and ‘Need Tickets’.  Because the signs were so small they were easily missed.  Even during the short time we navigated the entry there was a lot of traffic down both lanes that ended up in the wrong line.  That seemed to have been overcome by the cashiers sometimes by just processing anyone who walked up anyway.

As I entered the exhibit my wife was stopped after being processed and so I was stepping up alone.  As I turned to wait for her I was gently verbally accosted by a manager who was standing there overseeing the low-level chaos.  She asked me if I had a ticket.  I turned to indicate my wife had it and was right there.  I received a quick apology and the manager went nervously back to observing the scene where a manager might normally intervene.

After entry to the exhibit we were greeted by a photographer who moved us quickly through a series of photo poses and then quickly indicated where we should stand.  We waited and then one set of double doors opened while the other remained closed.  We had to crowd through the one set of doors.  Things were made a little more difficult by a caregiver taking time to reaffix a child’s shoes in the midst of a stack of packages they had brought with them.

Once through this second line we were brought to a room where a brief overview of how Lego bricks are made was shown to us.  They had us play a game without correctly announcing the rules and so we were instantly in a situation where we were locked in a large room with a bunch of strangers and competing against each other in a computer game.  We were repeatedly told by the recorded voice of an animated robot to look around to see how big the place was we were in but the view on each of the four screens in the room, rather than providing a 360 degree view showed the same view.  The result was confusion and dizziness.  One more round of computer gaming ended the light ordeal and we were released through another set of doors – of which only one pair opened – into a small area where we ended up on another line.

It turned out that one of the main attractions of Legoland is a cart ride.  We waited about 15 to 20 minutes to get our turn.  During the wait I read signs that stated that there were strobe lights, scary images, loud noises and unexpected actions and that children might be frightened.  There was also a size limit that seemed to be applied rather loosely as some families had arrived with very young children and infants.  There was a choice available to walk through this part of the exhibit to get to the rest of it but it wasn’t announced.   I hadn’t seen any signage or warnings about the ride prior to arriving at the point where they expected us to ride the ride (which also did not appear to be noted anywhere).

We finally got to the front of the line and had to wait as they adjusted timing as the carts were moving through too fast and bunching up.

When we got our opportunity we were provided swift instruction by one of the operators.  It was too quick and not very friendly.

We started on our way and were provided ‘laser guns’ to shoot different things.  The things we were to shoot were laser targets affixed to ‘monsters’ (there was one), bats and other creatures.

Once off the ride we went to a large area where there was a nice display of various locations in Detroit built out of Legos.  Interaction was limited to pressing buttons to make various things happen.

I won’t be returning to this Legoland or, if I have occasion to visit one of the others, I will skip those too.  Nice idea.  Poorly executed.

The layout of this park is extremely attractive and promises a lot.

This particular trip I took into the reserve, however, was disappointing.  The reserve had recently been the site of a 'prescribed burn' intended to clear away underbrush and 'return nutrients to the soil'.  Something must have gone wrong or this science is not all its cracked up to be. The place was burnt out in many places.

The ants have been the first ones to return to the area as indicated by small piles of sand around the park.

The sink holes and ponds had been burned right to the edge.  The only thing left in a couple of ponds were lillies, many with singed leaves.  I can only imagine how many toads, turtles, frogs, insects and birds were negatively impacted by this practice.

The most shocking and welcome sight I had was when I went to the border of the reserve which butts up to the main Croatan National Park.  That is where the burning had stopped.  A fount of water was flowing out of the ground from a field and filling in a large marshy area.  Birds abounded as well as insects and plants.  Evidence of other creatures was around.  It was truly a contrast I will not soon forget.

Don't miss a chance to check this reserve out.  The pond is beautiful.  Be sure to wear bright orange in the hunting season, as the instructions state at the beginning of the hiking trail.
+++
I wouldn't call this a pond.  It is an extensive body of water.  It is a good sized lake.  Some waterlillies have entered it.  Otherwise it is a very beautiful example of the round or oval lakes that occurred in the area and throughout the southeast in the old days.  Many of them were drained leaving this lake to be important as a source of knowledge of interest.

The forest surrounding the Patsy Pond Nature Trail is a joy and a wonder to behold.  A section of it, however, has been seized upon by a small hunting group and each year or two they burn it out to remove the unique flora and understory plants.  They do that, they claim, to open the land to deer hunting because deer, they say, like the open areas.  Because the area is also part of a managed forest (where loblolly pines are encouraged to grow and planted in long rows, this idea about deer and hunting doesn't make much traction.  Shooting at animals while standing (more often sitting) on a trail drinking beer is not my idea of hunting.

One year I was in the area and the North Carolina Department of the Environment had a 'controlled' burn.  It torched a wide area.  Upon reporting the flames, which reached more than 120 feet in the air at times and emitted acrid smoke, no authorities took notice and did not question what was happening.

Disappointing to say the least - however this area butts up on the Croatan National Forest and this trail skirts at its deepest point.  That area is wild and has been for a long time.  I recommend the Patsy Pond Nature Trail as one of the entry points to that wilderness.  Bring all protective clothing with you.
likes: Wildlife in the adjacent national park
Patsy Pond Nature Trail as entry to wilderness
dislikes: Loss of unique flora due to burns

reviews_attraction.text:
The Westland Historical Village is an attraction that is both very useful and important.

There are picnic facilities here and a nearby path.  It is enjoyable to visit as a pass time.  It is a wonderful backdrop to any outdoor party.  Some of the buildings are available to hire for weddings and other events.  The barn and two of the buildings are undergoing continuing renovations.
The house referred to as the ‘Octagon House’ is a beautiful specimen of Americana.  It brings back memories of small town American life which was actually big time.  These were the homes of the people who owned and worked the land.  They were homesteads and functional as well as being ‘home’ to the hard working families that lived in them and used them.

The clapboard houses and wooden frames stand as testimony to the strong work ethic of the people who lived in them as well as the time honored and proven methods of construction.  They are warm in the winter and cool in the summer.  It would be great to see modern architects, builders and craftsmen and women revisit these designs and materials to allow us to take advantage of these energy saving, attractive and useful structures in today’s developments.

Inside the buildings are period pieces and inventions of the past.  My favorite is the Eureka vacuum cleaner which sits quietly on of the porches.  Eureka had its headquarters near here and was a leading manufacturer and inventor during its heyday.

Along with the buildings is convenient parking and easy access from Wayne Road.  It is well situated.

The picnic tables and open space invite children, and everyone, to play and take their ease with hot dogs and towering glasses of lemonade in the summer months.  During the cool of the year the houses and barns are back dropped by colorful leaf blankets from the nearby woods.  The winter brings hot cocoa and marshmallows and the quiet and cold of a winter spent celebrating Christmas and all holidays during the turn of the year.
likes: Facilities & Services: Picnic facilities, event spaces (weddings)
Activities: Outdoor parties, family-friendly, seasonal activities

reviews_attraction.text:
First of all - if you go here with children or older folks be careful!
As the sign says at the moat (yes, they have a moat - if you appreciate moats then I especially encourage you to visit this moat).

There are steep drop-offs and inviting places to climb so keep the kids on a close leash.

Having said that this is an adventurous location.  There is plenty to see and do.

During the Summer months the Park Rangers are usually good enough to offer a variety of interesting special items as well as regularly scheduled tours.  The last time I was there we were treated to the display of loading and firing a field rifle used in the Civil War.
I am pleased with the restoration of the place.  Though I wasn't alive at the time it was built I have to commend them on their accuracy in recreating the images we have in photos, drawings and paintings of the time.

Visiting here is truly an adventure into the American past.  You can get a real sense of history here and learn quite a lot.

The fort is old and predates the Civil War.  The forts battles during the Civil War, though brief, touched every aspect of the conflict - from citizen-soldier, to career military men from the North and the South.

It is a nice place to visit.  The people are very good and helpful and informative.  I recommend it as part of a day trip as the park itself beyond the fort holds a lot of attraction for me as well.

Excellent historical station covering a wide portion of Eastern Carolina history.  The natural areas are either pristine or have reverted to that state.  Birds abound here - both shore and inland.  Beware the currents here.  Fishing is good on sound and ocean sides but swimming and even wading is dangerous.  The shore drops off precipitously and the currents can be savage.  Something to see!

Well, it’s still open, kind of.  This aquarium has come a long way and recently a lot of that distance is down.  It has somehow been taken under the care of the Michigan Department of Natural Resources but the operation of the aquarium itself and the administration of it is not clear.

Once home to beneficial and basic science concentrating on the Great Lakes, lakes, benthic systems, riverine systems, ponds and marshes it is now largely a tourist attraction centered around the building itself.  The selection of fish on display are from myriad locations and show only a tiny slice of the wondrous variety of fish and creatures in the Great Lakes basin.

Hours are spotty to say the least.  Signage is no longer accurate.  Some of the tanks are empty and decorated in strange ways.

There is plenty of parking but the parking lot is in poor repair.  The Koi Pond remains off limits and poorly maintained.  The adjacent picnic area is maintained poorly so expect to see garbage left behind from whatever party breezed through their last.

The most disappointing thing about this location is what happened to the science.  It is a small aquarium and always strained to meet the needs of the community it is serving but at the core of it science was genuinely alive and being practiced by caring professionals who shared their knowledge and made discoveries on a regular basis.  Today’s aquarium shows little of that vitality.

It’s a nice place to visit and look at but I’m not one to have to spend my time imagining what a place used to look like and used to be before it became a shadow of its former self.  Don’t expect too much and you won’t be disappointed by a visit to this location.   Handicapped access is difficult and offered on the side if it is open.

I continue to be wary of this institution.  When I first arrived in Detroit they had an overwhelming display of Hudson River paintings and other items, like an amazing collection of armor from the Middle Ages.

Apparently loans took place and some paintings are on loan.  I don’t know if they are gone forever because 10 years is a long time for a travelling show or loan of an art piece – especially from a location like Detroit which is in dire need of these connections to our past and national identity.

As for the removal of the armor I hope that this knee jerk reaction to changing social standards will be addressed and the fine collection put back on display.  If not in the great hall then in some location where they can be closely studied.  There are one of a kind pieces with connections in history that are duplicated nowhere else.  It is a shame to have them locked up in a closet.

What is there is of general interest and good.  The Asian exhibit, though it has been redone at great expense remains anemic.

I am greatly pleased by their outreach programs.  They send teams out into the communities in Detroit and surrounding it.

The building itself is beautiful and inviting.  The cafeteria is very nice and well apportioned but expensive.  You can bring your own lunch and eat in there and I recommend you do so.  There is also a central location in the building that I recommend for lunch or dinner.  The food and drink they serve there is a little pricey, so, again, I recommend bringing your own.  There are places to sit outside on the grounds as well.

This is a wonderful location for a school trip, a personal trip or a research outing.  I can only see it getting better as time goes on.
likes: Cultural Value (Hudson River paintings, armor collection)
Facilities & Services (outreach programs, beautiful building, inviting atmosphere, cafeteria, seating areas outside)
On-site Activities (school trips, personal trips, research outings)
dislikes: Cultural Value (removal of armor, anemic Asian exhibit)
Facilities & Services (expensive cafeteria, pricey food and drink)

reviews_attraction.text:
I often go here for research.  They have a wide variety of plantings outside and their greenhouse specimens are impressive in number, type and quality.  The greenhouse is a great scientific resource.  The grounds are perfect for families and class trips for all ages from elementary to college.

The Matthaei Botanical Gardens is a window on the world.

There is plenty of parking at the location – unless – there is an event in progress.  If so – go early or go late to ease the parking problem.  Events include special bonsai sailes, orchids sales and others.

The arboretum is a real treat.  They have a nice selection of standards and rarities of plants.  They are arranged tastefully and the entire enclosure is attractive.  They have thre water features.  A waterall, large metal tank and an oblong pond at the base of a trickling wall.

Two of the water features have fish in them.  Their Koi are especially beautiful and the goldfish are some of the largest I have seen.

By far their desert plant and arid plant display is one of the greatest.  The plants are in excellent health and placed in an easy viewing manner.  I was especially pleased to view the ‘living rocks’ that are there.

It doesn’t stop there however.  Out back during the warmer months there is an extraordinary garden of flowers.  The breadth of species that grow in Michigan is quite astonishing.  Along with that there is a large outdoor play area for children.  Still more awaits afield as there are prairie grounds to observe and an adventurous hiking trail along a stream and ponds.

The Tridge is certainly a unique place to visit.  I came upon it the first time at night and was not prepared for it at all.  It is a great idea and I wish it was in practice in other places – like across traffic intersections.

You walk up one leg of the Tridge and you get to the center where you can decide whether to go left or right.  It’s not as easy as choosing between the Yellow Brick Road and the Red Brick Road because there is no color coded way finding, but, that’s fine, normally if you find yourself standing over the middle of the intersection of two rivers you would generally have an idea of where you are going.

The Tridge is located at the point where the Tittabawassee and Chippawa Rivers come together in a confluence.  When I was there that first time I saw it the bridge was lit up.  It is very attractive.  The waters below reflected the white lights in blue relief and it was something to see.  At that time I could not tell there were two rivers joining there.

I returned during daylight and found a fine collection of trails and walkways.  There is a dearth of vegetation on the Isabella Street side but that could be taken care of by planting some trees and bushes.  The rest of the area is very attractive.  There is a canoe and kayak launch site.  While I was there I saw people fishing at dawn at the point between the Tittabawassee and the Chippewa.  I also saw a boat with two fishermen come down the Tittabawassee.

SEA LIFE Michigan Aquarium is a great place to go.  The entry fee is a little high but in line with other aquariums around the country.  If they brought it down a little I believe they would see even more traffic and serve a greater part of the community.

The exhibits are kept neat and clean on the outside.  There were just two tanks they seemed to be having problems with but it was obvious they were working on it.  The staff was welcoming and engaged.  We had a slight difficulty at exit getting our ‘free photo’ when we were directed to go back into the line to get it.  That was worked out satisfactorily.

They have apparently been actively engaged in breeding and helping wounded wildlife but I did not see anything specific about that in the exhibits other than some numbers posted at entry.

They have a wide variety of sea life on display and they all appeared in good health.  Most of the displays had plastic plants in them.  It would be nice to see more natural environments for the creatures and to examine them.

The viewing tunnel was very crowded.  There was no docent there and several patrons took the opportunity to rest and enjoy the tunnel while a single line file of other patrons had to navigate through along with carriages and mall baggage they might have with them.

Overall this is an excellent location to visit.  The children enjoyed it.  I would recommend by passing the play area.

This museum has a great deal to offer. It's arrangement is a bit odd but the materials they have are interesting and in good shape. They offer materials in regard to recent shipping industries, historical pirate information and objects as well as fishing information.

They lack a bit in specific parts of history like the near absence of the change that occurred in the area during the 1850's to 1860's when a regional industry based on kerosene, oils and tars extracted from the towering pine trees then growing in the area. In spite of this the information provided is generally true to life and records what instances they have focused on with a fair amount of accuracy.

Their materials regarding the local fishery are exceptional and excellent resource in determining how the present problems of the fishery have arisen. They also raise interesting points on how to solve the problem which you, the visitor, will be able to discern for yourself. The museum is generally well lit.

There are games for the children to play like a 'Treasure Hunt' which allows the children, or adult participants, to search for items throughout the museum. That is a particularly fun game, and my favorite, I recommend it highly. The museum is one of the focal points during the 'Pirate Invasion' which occurs annually during the summer months and is a celebration of maritime history, piracy and community!

Dynamite Park is a large park that is directly next to the Wayne County River Rouge park.
Dynamite Park is a rustic area.  There are just a couple of picnic tables and no lavatories.  Nevertheless it is a nice location for a picnic.  The park has several areas set aside as wildlife areas.  A visit here can give anyone an overview of the present state of natural recovery in most places in Michigan.
Deer, coyote, raccoon, opossum, hawks, fish and the occasional eagle frequent the place.  Look for tracks wherever you can.  During Spring and Autumn you may well cross paths with one or more of the wild residents.  This is an excellent place for birdwatching.  The birds that appear here range from waterfowl, to forest birds and meadow / open space birds.
On the edge of the park is a trail leading to ‘The Cliffs of the Rouge’ which is a natural wonder featuring a set of cliffs towering over the River Rouge.  A visit in any season will provide a unique natural viewpoint to be enjoyed by nature lovers and appreciated by students of nature.
Walking, hiking, snowshoeing and limited biking are all natural opportunities here.  There is plenty of open space for frisbee, baseball, football or soccer on the green fields near the water station.  The fields are not marked – these would all be impromptu games played with changing boundaries.  Have fun!

Science at it's best!  A wonderful display of native and imported plants.  Truly brings to life Thomas Jefferson's quote, "As for the soil of the Carolinas it seems that anything you put into it wil grow."  Kind guides and knowledgeable staff.

The JC Raulston Arboretum is a great place to conduct science.  They have a wide variety of plants and objects to study.  They have large facilities for meetings and conferences.  The architecture at the place is well done and interesting.  I like the trails and the way the exhibits and plants are laid out.  They provide details on what can be planted in the local area even if it is not native - that is - they provide common sense information on how to plant the plants so that they will not only survive but will grow and thrive as well.

I was pleasantly surprised by the number of pollinators I saw when I visited.  I also enjoyed the variety and beauty of the butterflies and moths in the place.  I was able to get some very nice photos during my visit.  The signage is well designed and holding up well.  They take care to keep the signs properly standing.  The cooperation between the scientists, docents and volunteers is a model to be replicated in other ventures - whether they are arboretums or other public attractions and educational operations.

Grand Circus Park is an interesting place to visit.  There are plenty of benches.  It is located in a very busy location.  It is a true circus as there is circular driving all around the park.  The crossings to the other streets are short and well identified.  Some of the cars enter the circus a little too fast.  Either they aren't used to the small street motion or they are being careless.  The park has been neglected for a long time.  It is great to see it being put back into use.

It's a great place to stop for lunch.  Whether you are having takeout or a brown bag lunch.  The last time I stopped there they had some example patio furniture around.  The pieces looked like something you'd have in your living room, so, I thought it a bit much but its a durn sight better than having the place empty.  There is some underground parking there but I'm not sure how it works or if it is still in service.

The Opera House is nearby and some great apartment buildings.  I am so glad they are being fixed up.  Most of them are still empty as people move back around the park I expect to see more people there.  Come on by when you're downtown.  It's got a great fountain, a giant statue and an obelisk!

I like to go to the Detroit Zoo to walk around, study, perform research and just generally have a great time.  The zoo itself requires a lot of walking.  There are two entrances, however, so you can start from the front or the back.  When it is running the Zoo Train will carry you around the periphery.  The staff is engaged and knowledgeable.  During the Spring, Summer and Fall the gardens throughout the Zoo are a joy to behold.  The butterfly house is a perennial attraction and the new penguin house is quite nice. Food can be a bit pricy but it is often worth it though we normally bring our own packed lunch.

It's a lot of fun to attend here.  The tickets can be pricey but - plan on staying all day and get your money's worth!  There are restaurants in the zoo that have very good food.  I prefer the American Coney Island over towards the tigers but the larger cafeteria-like restaurant towards the polar bears is also very good but the lines are usually very long.

I hope that in the future they focus more on breeding.  Right now they have many rescue animals and that is wonderful but for the most part they don't allow them to breed, or at least, allow it to happen.

This metropark is well laid out with lots of attractions.  I like the wild areas the best though they are cut through with lots of lawns that seem to never see use.  The trails themselves are acceptable but they are not well maintained nor do they offer anything in the way of signage.  I was there recently and along the walkway near the Huron River the brush and understory plants had been cleared just chopped away.  It was very unattractive.  They could use more shaded areas.

During events any shaded area is quickly filled up leaving most of the children (for whom the events are held) and seniors out in the sun.

There is a pool and pond attraction I have yet to visit.  I am looking forward  to checking that out.

This is a very nice park.  It located deep within a residential neighborhood.  There is plenty of room for picnics and even a public event.  There is just one portable public toilet here, so, if you have any event you would want to plan accordingly.

The parking lots are in good condition, however, compared to the size of the park they are rather small.  The neighborhood is quiet where the park is located.

There is a mix of play equipment.  Some classical slides and 'merry-go-round'.  One slide is super tall.  There is also a more modern play area.  There is plenty of walking space.  The ball field is in good condition for baseball and softball.  When dry the fields should be fine for volley ball.

A mixed park.  Outdated playscapes.  Well maintained grounds.  Bathrooms locked unless requested to be opened for a group.  Attracted latchkey teens and youngsters left to themselves.  Intermittent reports of violence in varying degrees.  Pavilions often littered with trash following use.  The park is large and generally featureless.  There is a grove of trees and wide space.

The dock is a good place to moor to.  There is a kayak loading point.  The trails are varying and of great interest.  No really wheelchair accessible to the water but can proceed far into the barrier foest canopy.  We enjoyed spotting the small alligators in the ponds - 2 to 3 feet long but they grow larger here.

I like to use this park when we are having a family picnic.  It is fine for business outings too.  The basketball courts are in good repair.  The volleyball court is good for practice and competition.  Easy to access but parking is best up nearby sidestreets.

The museum at the landing has great detail on the variety of animals on the island in the area.  The histories of Dr Sharpe and Mr Hurst in preserving the island were also represented well.  Right on site is easy access to kayaking and canoeing

The park is well laid out and cared for.  Great for running, jogging, walking and biking.  Plenty of play areas for kids.  The pond is pretty but don't fish in it.  Baseball fields and cross country tracks are great.  Plenty of parking.

A redesigne entry point, restaurant and beach access.  Reasonable rates to fish in rich waters.  The views are fantastic.  Service is friendly and knowledgeable.  A family friendly environment.  Newly renovated rooms.

Natural areas still in pristine state or restored with care.  Game and fish are abundant.  Lots of trails throughout.  Eady access at certain points.  Others are remote and primitive.  This is a national treasure.
Walking and strolling are two things you can do here.  The houses are sometimes occupied by living historians who tell stories about them.  The grounds are well kept.  There are lovely views.

Great non-standard souvenirs such as a mobile of large wildlife for babies.  Huge windows to look at the view.  Information on the wildflowers which you are sure to see when you are in Glacier. There is a hike to Hidden Lake and Hidden Lake Overlook behind the visitor center.  An interpretive hike around the visitor center, and the start to Highline Trail (which I would recommend doing all of, or just hike down about 3/4 a mile and back, the beginning and middle of the hike are the best so if you can't do the whole thing, hit up just the beginning) across the street from the visitor center.

Parking is awful (around 11-2, before and after that are better).  The shuttle is slow (all day).  Be patient.  It just comes with the crowded, short-season, popular national park territory.

It's fun to feed the ducks here. It's not often crowded so loading of boats isn't a pain. Another plus is that this lake is warm because it is so shallow.

The negatives, this is a muddy lake. All the carp have eaten all the vegitation so when you jump in the water in the middle of the lake you sink into a foot of sludge. And although there are beautiful views of Mount Timpanogos and the Cascade Mountain Range, photos aren't the best with the lake because it's a pretty brown lake.

That said, the boat festival (not sure the name of it) in the spring is fun. The winter has a holiday light show you can drive through which is fun. And if you don't mind brown water (it helps that it is warm), then this is a great place to waterski and wakeboard.

Very well put together museum and well kept. Also nice views from the deck.  The reason for the 3 stars was just that the museum didn't hold my interest enough, even as an adult.  Mostly likely because  I had young kids with me who did not allow me to read many of the information displays and so much of this museum requires you to read long displays in order to understand the display.  I don't think there would be many kids that would enjoy this museum very long.  The dinosaurs were cool.  I liked the erosion water/sand tank/display, but too many areas were too heavily focused on reading.

Loved this park.  There is tons of open space, tons of ducks and geese, fun water features, a skate park, and right next to this park is the Woodland Water Park.  My husband, son and I stayed at this park for a few hours enjoying the shade, watching and feeding the birds, as well as hopping in the skate park every once in a while.  For skaters, the skate park is awesome, but small.  I didn't like that it was fenced in, so it is hard to get out of someone's way if they are coming up/down the side.  But the bowls are nicely sloped, ideal for all skill levels.
likes: Skate park (slopes for all skill levels)

reviews_attraction.text: This visitor center was exactly what you want a visitor center to be, friendly and informative.  I wish this one were also a little luckier for me as I did not win the lottery for the Wave hike. Aside from that, my visit here was great. I talked with 2 workers, both had great recommendations for the area. I also like collecting stickers of places I have been and I was pleased that they both had stickers and that they weren't just the same boring GSE letters (although they did have those :) ). The facilities were also very well kept.

This place is a little out of the way on its own, but if you are passing by, definitely stop. I took my 2 year old and the 1/2-ish mile hike in was perfect for him.  Plus, it felt like a full-sized hike miniaturized since the 'switch-backs' and 'fin-bridges' were all minified.  Perfect for kids.  Plus there were rocks and small hoodoos that kids could climb on. I was also surprised by the perfect line of white rock to red rock back to white rock that went across the whole hoodoo valley area.  Super pretty.

It was a nice enough campground, but overpriced.  They didn't tell us that different camp spots were priced differently, they just put us in a $35 a night spot (others are $25 a night). Then everything is an additional fee.  Fee to use the showers.  Fee to use the RV dump.

The beach was nice, nothing special.  No cool rock formations or inlets.  Lots of seagulls and some storks which were fun to watch. Lots of seashells.  What we loved about this area is that the sunsets here are always gorgeous.
dislikes: Lack of unique features (rock formations, inlets)

reviews_attraction.text: So fun for families with really young kids or older kids.  I think for some mid range age kids they could get bored. My 2.5 year old was in heaven. They have a touch pool which I probably liked more than my son.  They have a tunnel under the shark tank which we both loved. The otters and penguins are both really fun to watch.  We also liked the fun rope bridge. The staff were all really friendly and knowledgeable. My only advice is to not come during a rainy weekend... So crowded!

Love this park in the canyon.  There is a stream that goes through, which is big enough to enjoy, but small enough that kids can play in it.  There are plenty of fire pits both in the park proper, and across the river. There is also a nice long (area-wise, not slide-able length) hill that kids can play on, and it gives some 'privacy' from the road-side of the park and the stream-side of the park.

We had a really nice time at the zoo today. 4 kids under the age of 5. They loved all the animals.  But they especially loved the play area for kids.  The playground looked awesome but I think it should have had a few more slides or bridges.  The rock formations look awesome but can't really be played on much.  It was too early in the season for the splash pad to be open but it looked fun.

I like this park.  It has a fun beach for kids, fishing and paddle boarding, and some grassy hills. The negative... WAY too crowded. The day it opened so many people posted about it on Facebook that it was an instant hit. You really need to get here early in the morning and save a spot on the beach if you want any sort of space when it's actually good weather to be here in the afternoon.

This is a really fun park for kids of all ages. There is a lot of grass and a big hill for rolling or ice blocking, and there are three different play areas, a little kids area, a big kids area and a splash pad. The park has tons of benches for adults to sit and it is dog friendly. I love that you can bring the whole family; there is something for everyone.

The buildings were nice; they had a good feel to them.  The 'gift shop' section was sad.  I just wanted a sticker but they didn't have any.  They pretty much just had a few photos, postcards, and some bat finger puppets.  The rangers were nice, but short.  They didn't give any details on areas and seemed to be a bit tired of talking about the same thing.

Of the national parks in Southern Utah, if you are only going for short hikes and view points, this park is less fun and less picturesque than the others.  However, if you are going for canyoneering or canyoneering-esque hikes, this park would rise to 4 stars.

Canyoneering - Rappel through Cassidy Arch

Canyoneering-esque - Hike down the Goosenecks.

We had a fun time at wheeler farm looking at all the baby animals.  This wad a perfect outing for my 2 year old.  I think if kids were too much older this outing would cost more,  paying for tractor rides and such,  but with really young kids I think the animals are enough.  There is also a little park area that is best for kids probably 3 and up.
dislikes: Limited park area for very young kids

reviews_attraction.text:
Quiet, beautiful, FREE place to camp for a few days.  Right along the banks of the river in the shade of the bridge.  There is also some fun fishing here.  Lots of little guys but a few big trout.

I wouldn't recommend taking any low clearance cars or large RVs, the road isn't the best.  It is overgrown with large pot holes.

Nice center.  Great rangers.  There was the regular help desk, then there was the wilderness desk.  I had a few questions that the regular ranger desk couldn't help with (road conditions, longer trails), so they referred me to the wilderness desk who answered my questions and then some. They were very knowledgeable.

Totally awesome swinging bridge.  Near Kootenai Falls (where they filmed scenes from the Revenant). It was a little eerie on the bridge since it does swing so much, it is pretty long, and there is a sign that you can only have 5 people on at once.  I definitely recommend this road side stop/hike.

Such a mellow environment and it's never crowded. It's fun like the zoo, but with less walking and a larger focus on the beauty of nature and natural elements.  Lots of flowers and art throughout, and all the structures are built with design in mind. I would definitely come again.

Perfect for family events or just hanging out.  There is a pond you can fish in, lots of ducks, a miniature Venetian garden area, as well as really cool swings and open pavilions.  We've use this park to play with our dog, have a birthday party, and have gone fishing there.

Nice park.  Lots of parking. Good water area for swimming.  Access to the river for kayaking or paddle boarding. A bike path. I wish there were a few more large trees.  There were many smaller trees, so in a few years I think this will be an even better park.

Great area for kids. There are multiple playgrounds with different features, some big fields great for ultimate Frisbee, and the scera pool is right there if you get too hot playing on playgrounds. Also lots of mature trees! This is definitely a great area.

There are lots of trees.  Two different jungle gyms for kids.  There's a nice bike path around the whole park and even a baseball diamond.  This is a really nice park to bring young kids. The only downside is the slides are warped bumpy

Pretty hike out to a lake.  I was surprised at how crazy crowded this area was.  Lots of parking but cars were squished in every possible location.  However, once we got on the trails, it was not very crowded, which was so nice.
Great park.  Not too busy. Had some fun museum pieces (log boat and barge) to look at.  River is of course pretty...green and blue.

This place was really cool! only $10 to get in, and worth every penny.  Has stuff about Presidents, the Pope’s, Day of the Dead, Egyptians, Celebrities, Antique Hearse (Horse Carriage & Automotive), info on embalming and cremation.  I thought it was gonna be morbid, but it was not at all.  Laid out very well! and with lots of info and things to see.  I was not expecting such a large facility, or the amount of things that I saw.  I originally found out about this place, after watching a show called Shipping Wars on A&E.  If you are in the area, I would suggest stopping by and checking it out.  I was told by an employee, that the owner of the Roy Rogers car is a Board member, and also owns the Batmobile, which has been displayed there before.  I would love to see those on a future visit.  Hope you enjoy it too.

This place has a mix of War Planes, Texas History as well as Flight Science and Flight History.  I can't say I have a love for Flight or it's history (still enjoyed the museum), and there was plenty of information as well as an up close look at these restored WORKING planes.  We went on a day when they were flying some of the planes, so it was nice to see.  There is a section for kids to enjoy and learn about how a plane fly's and how a pilot do their job.  They even had a Flight Simulator, where you can sit in a booth, and attempt to land a plane from Hobby to Bush Airport.  I didn't do very well, so don't let me fly your plane.... cause we won't make it!

1st time visit!  if you are looking for TABLE GAMES, you won't find any here!  (Maybe in the future??)  Went on a Sunday, and it was tough to get a parking spot (Both Areas).  The place was full, so there was limited spaces to sit and play.  Their slots also play some sort of Bingo on the digital screen, and not sure how that affect your winnings or money?

There are several non-smoking areas which is a plus and a small section for Higher Roller Slots.  There is a food court on one end of the building, with a few places of self-serve Coffee/Soda Bar.  2 bathroom areas, one located near the food court, and the other directly across from the main entrance.

I really enjoyed this museum and all the information about the cattle and horses that they cared for.  This place offered history of the people, land, animals and the owners of King Ranch.  I was told there is an actual ranch tour, but I only visited the museum and enjoyed learning about the history.  I spent about 45 min looking at everything and reading the tags on pictures and displays.  If you have family from this area, its quite possible that they work on this ranch, and their names may be included in the history at this museum.  You could even find a vintage photo of an ancestor.

You have several options with this company, and you can choose the one that best works for you.  There are 4 options included in the New York Pass, and we choose the tour called "Best of New York" which takes you all the way around the Island.  You will get the best pictures if you sit on the top deck in my opinion, but the drawback is listening to the audio landmarks because of the outside noise.  I would book again, and either pick the same or different cruise, just depending on timing.

This is a nice place to look across the town of Wimberley! as you can see a great distance while up there.  It is a steep climb up the stairs, and can take your breath away if you are not used to going up many flights of stairs.  So, take your time, and rest if you need to, because your legs may burn a little from the exercise.  They have installed Hand Rails up most of the path, so you have something to hang on to, but the view is worth it at the end.

This museum was small, but has a lot of interesting things about the Texas Long Horn, and local history.  You are first introduced by watching a short film, then lead to a 2nd and 3rd story viewing of memorabilia, history and art.  I really enjoyed the visit, and learning about how Texas has is genuine breed of Long Horns that are native to the land, and how a few ranches have preserved this type of cattle.

Fun and Cheesy is how I would describe it.  The 2 hosts do their best to get the crowd inside the bus, and outside the bus hyped up.  There are a few stops where you will find an outside performer that is part of the show.  It's a great way to see the city from an Air-conditioned Vantage Point, and take pictures as you ride along.  My tour was included with my New York Pass.

Nice place to learn about mobsters and some of the history of how some of the Vegas Casinos were started.  Also has modern history about counterfeit goods and drug lords in the modern era.

There is a bar in the lower level, and a few interactive feature if you choose to add on to your ticket.  Maybe on a future visit, I would try some of the add on, interactive items.

Very Beautiful place.  Different themes of Houston, under water, Asian, Frozen Lands and Dinosaurs!  These is also a small amusement park for small to teenage children.

Tip!  Go as early as possible to avoid entrance traffic.  Leaving can be a bit tricky, so be patience and courteous as everyone is also trying to get out of the same one lane exit.

This place is education for middle school kids to adults.  It’s interesting seeing all of the equipment used, how it’s done and the type of rigs that drill for the oil we use, at extreme depths in the oceans.  The Oceans Star was once a working rig, converted into a museum.  Inexpensive entry and a self paced tour.

Loved learning about the history of Dr Pepper, it’s bottling.  Also learned about 7up, Big Red, Snapple, and other brands that’s started before Dr Pepper.  There is are 3 floors in the main building, and across the courtyard you will find a soda shop and ice cream, along with more info about 7up and Big Red.
likes: Facilities & Services: Soda shop, ice cream

reviews_attraction.text: Nice museum, with an inexpensive entry.  Self guided, and is a great view into the early years of the oil industry of the local area.  There are a few models that demonstrate working machinery as well as stories of the pioneers from the local industry.  Total time spent was about 30 min looking and reading.

Cool local spot tucked in between some home, but is a future site to some sort of community center.  Not sure how much longer this place will be here, but it was worth a stop, to look at the Graffiti and the Talent some people have.  This is private property, so I suggest not crossing the fenced area.

Nice little museum, but not a whole lot for young kids.  I think geared for 8 year olds and above would be fair.  Nice setup if model trains, along with a caboose car, and a passenger car that you can walk through.  There is also a small building with an old switch board, for controlling the tracks.

Part of the 7A Ranch, and built to look like an old western town.  There is a game room for the kids, a cowboy museum, ice cream parlor and a church for weddings.  A few places to take photos with wooden cutouts.  Town is in need of a little repair, but still a great idea from the owners/builders

Small museum with a few trains, with history and model trains inside.  Office person will run toy trains and discuss history of the rail line.  Admission is free, but small donations make places like this continue to exist.  Keep history alive and provide a small donation for your visit.

It’s was a fully digital experience.  Great for young kids, or anyone curious about ocean life.  There is a small guided tour, then an area where you can read and watch short clips.  At the end is an interactive area, with 3D and hologram images of the things seen in the exhibits.

This place has changed a lot since the first time I visited.  This newer version is more informative, but not as gripping or emotional as it was before.  It felt more as if the changes are more about the post 9/11, vs the actual events and the personal stories of the people.
dislikes: Focus on post-9/11 rather than personal stories

reviews_attraction.text: Texas History and it's nice that with donations and care, these building were preserved for us to learn about.  Free entry, but like any publicly funded project, these types of places can always use your donations, so do your part to help, as any little bit helps.

Texas History and it's nice that with donations and care, these building were preserved for us to learn about.  Free entry, but like any publicly funded project, these types of places can always use your donations, so do your part to help, as any little bit helps.

Went on the tour and it was great.  JP was our guide, and he made it amazing.  Hope you can experience his tour, and find it just as amazing.  This is the second time I take the tour, and this was the best.  It was included with the New York Pass!

There is a free parking area in front of the sign, so you can park and take as long as you need to take your photos.

We used a ride share to get to the location and was about $5 from Harrah's Casino, then we walked back to the Vegas Strip.

Small Museum, said they were expanding, and takes about 30 minutes to experience the whole thing.  You do have to climb stairs, so if you cannot perform that task, you won’t be able to enjoy the exhibit.
The tour was nice and informative.  We were show a few of the places where the dancers practice, a view of the stage from a private space.  Spoke to a dancer, and saw a few other private areas.

I never really appreciated the Delaware Water Gap until I got out of my car and started exploring.  It has so many amazing (and hidden) waterfalls. I think they rival some of the ones I visit in the Columbia River Gorge  (granted, not as high).
The hiking trails are fantastic as well.  The NJ side of the River has some real gem hiking trails with mountain views and old ruins. I have also counted more black bears in one day on the NJ side than anywhere except Vancouver Island. And don't worry, I have hiked right up to them and they either run or just keep at whatever they are doing.  If one does approach you or, in the unlikely event of an attack, just make sure you can run faster than someone you are with and you will be fine. Also, if you are in the Gap area check out fantastic places like the Walpack Inn in NJ, or the Gem and The Keystone on the PA side.

This is a very lovely park and bluffs. I really enjoyed the views of Canada and Russia (or whatever I was looking at, maybe China?). The Spit was really neat and seemed to go on forever.  The further out you go, the better the views are all around, especially back towards Hurricane Ridge and the Olympics. The Spit is a great place to hike for people that tend to get lost because there are limited options for getting lost, yet if you do get lost, you should immediately stop hiking in nature and consider other hobbies, like maybe ukulele or something safe.
I also wouldn't suggest brining your little dogs here to swim because I didn't see any otters, which clearly suggests that Orcas ate them all and are likely hungry for other little furry creatures that might frolic in the straight of JDF.

This place is a gem. There are fantastic slices of nature here to take in. Now if certain folks could just stop coming here and ruining it. Please don't hike your extended family into the prettiest section of the forest and have a giant cook out and leave your trash, or a trail of trash. And yes, even when you hide it in some bushes or behind some rocks, that still isn't okay! And if you feel the need to spray paint on something please do it on a bridge or building, not the rocks and trees.

Not what it used to be, but still beautiful if you can get past the noise of people driving their motorcycles around in circles for hours.  And if you folks come to this park to picnic, because it is beautiful, please pick up your junk and throw it out, so it is beautiful the next time you come. And throwing your garbage down the hill or in the creek does not count as throwing it out. This is your park! Take some pride in protecting it and keeping it clean!!!

Nice little hike close to lots of places. Not too hard, not too steep, just nice.  I wouldn't go out of my way to come here, but would suggest it you live nearby or are driving through. I suspect you could turn this into as long of a hike as you want if you join up with the AT.

Great Rail Trail in PA. Connect it with the Lebanon Trail for a very nice bike ride. Then be sure to stop in at Snitz Creek Brewery to have a few fantastic beers. And make sure to hit the Mt. Gretna side trail and see what is happening in that neat little retreat community.

Fantastic park complex with various rental buildings, pavilions, picnic areas, great hiking trails, a small waterfall, lookouts over looking Long Valley, and nice open areas for activities. You can also get on the much longer Patriot Trail and go for as long as you desire.

Nice park once you get away from the noisy road. I like the incense the Disc Golfers Burn while they are playing. The smoke makes my dog really relaxed and friendly. Be careful at the dog park. There are often dogs in there. And there are tons of holes under the fences.
dislikes: Holes under fences at dog park

reviews_attraction.text: This park is so much more than it appears when driving by. There are several nice grass trails that go back into the farm and up along the powerline.   But watch for dog poop. Someone let their dog drop nuggets right in the trails. That's lazy! Move it with a stick.

A gem of a place to visit. To see where this man grew up before doing so much for our country and forests is quite amazing. To sit at the "Finger Bowl" where many a great meeting and floating dinner were served, is truly evoking. A must visit!

Lovely Park set aside by a wise man many years ago. Great paved loop trail for walks and biking. Beautiful Stream. Nice trees (how about Parks and Rec doesn't cut them down like at the other parks...grrr).
Allentown gets a bad reputation for obvious reasons, but it also has tons of wonderful gems from its days of glory. This is one of them. So are most of the parks including Cedar Beach and Trexler.
Probably one of the finest places for kids and families that I know of, and it is free. Please give a donation. And have a lovely time with your family. Just watch out for the Crazy Train!
This is no question one of the best places to see/hear a concert that I know of (and it is free!!) It is also just a great place to spend an afternoon with friends or family.
Short but sweet. A good bit of history thrown in as well. Interesting forest which I assume was planted. Dried pond bed above the dam. Nice in the evening sun.
The summer Tiki Bar is quite a cool place to explore. Not the cheapest, but really neat on a nice night. Haven't tried the food, but looks fun!
This places raises a lit up Groundhog to kick off the start of Groundhogs Day. Do they need to do anything else to earn 5 Stars?  I think not.
Not too sure about the Village, but the brewery in the barn is pretty darn cool. Haven't tried the beer yet, but what a pleasant place.
Allentown has great and amazing parks. This one is one of the best. If they could just safely connect all of them it would be the best.
Beautiful trails for a nice stroll. Often a few wet spots. Lovely river views. A gem of a place that we are lucky was made public.
Pretty little lake, but there is no shade to be found.  Go to tan, or go when it isn't blazing hot. Sun screen on the little ones.
A very fine park with ample parking, soccer fields, trail access, baseball, a pavilion and more. Outdoor concerts in summer.
Neat park with a few trails. Beautiful little creek with some high quality water.  Good for a walk or jog. Disk Golf.
Fantastic Trails in a lovely slice of earth. So close to reading, but makes you feel like you are somewhere remote.
Very Nice Park that hosts the most epic fireworks I have ever watched, and I don't get excited by fireworks at all.

Wow, wonderful place. It is now a National Park. 6th one in Utah. Lots of great history May 10 2019 is the 150th anniversary. Beautifully restored steam engine's. They have reenactments of the golden spike being driven in, throughout the summer. Check dates with times before you come. Remember to make sure your tank is full driving here there is no services. Bring a lunch with you. Check out Steam Fest in December. The steam engines really put off the smoke in the cold winter air. After you do Promontory Point, Drive down the dirt road and check out the Spiral Jetty at the Great Salt Lake.

What a Hidden Gem. Love the campsites. I love how dark it is at night. Nice touch for the park staff to bring out their telescopes to show us the Stars. Love walking through all the hoodoos. Kids had a blast and running around and having fun. Remember to take your blue lights and look for scorpions at night. We had the whole camp site looking for scorpions with us. The frisbee golf course is a nice touch also. Thanks for letting us rent the frisbees to play.

Fantastic park. Good road to get around. Bike and run with pleanty of places to park and rest. Good restrooms around area. Wonder places to hold a small or large picnics. Wonderful views of surrounding areas. Great play area's for the little ones. Plenty of space to avoid others having fun. Big pond to check out wildlife. Nice Big hill to tube down in the winter. Could not ask for a better park. Felt very safe while visiting here.

We were the only ones at this site looking for dinosaur tracks. Walked around in the hot sun trying to find them. We were not sure what we were looking for. But once we found them it was new and exciting. For those coming to visit, make sure you read the placard and look at the pictures before you enter where the footprints are, it will help you locate them.

Love the grounds, you always can find a secluded place to just meditate. Visitor Center is nice and very helpful. Missionaries here will answer any questions that any visitor would have. If you get a chance to go inside the temple, look at their architectural Wood & Decor. This was built in the 1800s and the first temple to open in Utah.

Great park. 2 baseball diamonds, softball diamond, soccer field, Big covered pavilion with lots of tables. Fantastic playground equipment for the kids to swing, climb, slide on. Bathrooms. Six Pickle Ball Courts, two Tennis courts. Good parking with handicap available. Nice grass to walk around on. Well maintained and clean.

I have driven passed Parowan for 45 years and never new the petroglyphs were here. Had a great time. I was surprised they let you get so close to some of them. I learned that the carvings were rather deep in the rock for the pictures. Very interesting learn something new will bring back the family later.

Great park. Lots of grass area to play and Big trees to find shade. Play area's for all ages. Wonderful splash park. Nice pool with good locker rooms. Place can get a little crowded at times. Plenty of parking with easy access. Views around area are fantastic. Summer event's are held here.

What a fun place to see. This has been under water most of my life. I have been here 3 times now. I have been in the winter and summer.  Remeber it is a dirt road 19 miles in and 19 miles out. Take food and water with you. Also take a walk and walk the spiral to the center and back.

Wonderful staging area to wait in before play. Nice gift shops and Food Shops. People are excited and happy to be there. Clean restrooms to use. People are excited for the shows to begin. Spectacular backdrop on plays with magnificent plays being held there. I must seeing for all.

This is a wonderful Park. Plenty of hiking trails to go around. You can see wildlife, petroglyphs, old Pioneer names on the walls. The red rocks are spectacular. You could Venture into small towns to get great food. Camping is wonderful. Go in the fall and pick apples.

Fantastic place. Nice City building with library. Wonderful park with ball parks, Giant playground with tons of toys. Nice bathrooms, huge grass areas with covered picnic tables. Even has a performing stage. Big parking lots. You will fell safe here.
likes: Facilities & Services: Nice bathrooms, covered picnic tables, big parking lots
Activities: Ball parks, giant playground, performing stage

reviews_attraction.text: This Barn is wonderful to have events in. I have been to a couple of weddings here that have been just wonderful to go to. Nice area for the kids to run around outside also. Great place to take pictures. Felt safe here also.

Absolutely had a blast camping in the camp sites. Well maintained bathrooms in the campsite. Fun things to do at the Flaming Gorge recreational areas. Love going inside the damn, experiencing the site's I saw.

Huge beautiful park. Plenty of parking. Nice bathrooms, basketball court, volleyball area, dog park, tables to eat on and spectacular 360 degree scenery. NOAA weather Park like this around. Beautiful!!!

Awesome Place. Great beauty all around. Wonderful camp ground with nice bathrooms, SUPER golf course, trails and roads to explore. Gorgeous anytime of the year. You get off Four Seasons at this place.
Never knew this place existed. Had a wonderful time exploring the apple orchard. Reading all the plaques around the orchard was wonderful. Great historic Pioneer Heritage here. Very informative.
Nice park with 12 covered picnic tables. Nice play area for the kids. Big parking area with easy access from main road. Nice walkway over wetlands. Very quiet the day I was here for lunch.
What a great place to learn about our past. Great dinosaur Quarry to visit. Could spend hours looking at all the fun things. Amazing we have such a treasure to come and see.
Great place to have the kids get out and run a little bit. The spring was well-maintained. I can remember when it used to be just a dirt path to get to the spring.
Beautiful Park, great historical feel to the park. Very calm and relaxing, love the water area. Also has great concert series here with wonderful performers.
Beautiful place, wonderful architectural building. Friendly staff directing you everywhere you want to go. Unbelievably clean. Great place to visit.
If you're looking to play soccer this is a fun little Park. No playground, no Bowery, no benches. Great for an open field play area.
Fun park. Fantastic play area for the kids. Place looked clean And we all felt safe here. Good parking. Nice tables and grass area.
What a great little place. Love reading all the plaques that told the story about the settlers that were here.

A massively, clean, well organized visitor center to get you prepared for your time spent in Colonial Williamsburg.

The parking lot is plentiful and the visual walking up holds a ton of curbside appeal with well taken care of paths, and builds, as well as a large fountain and sculptured map of the town.

Inside its spacious, equipped with an incredible gift shop, lines are spaced out and there's plenty of staff with smiles ready to greet and guide.

You've got many options once to the ticket booth that is explained to you while in line and posted. Knowledge is your friend on getting the tickets and passes that work best for you, your family, budget, and time frame.

A great easy transaction that'll get you started before you follow pathways from the center to the old colonial area, and-or, shuttles that offer you trips along the colonial parkway to both Jamestown and Yorktown.

I personally, would like to shout out to the incredible staff, particularly Laura McFarland, a supervisor who assisted us after one of the women at the desk who initially helped us (and I wish I would have caught her name), who pointed out we actually was supposed to have free access to the area with our stay in a connected resort. The Williamsburg Lodge, forgot to inform and did not send us out email notifying us that we got tickets to Williamsburg with length of stay. During our casual conversation with the woman at desk, she learnt that we were staying there and was quick to point out the mistake.

They very easily could have allowed us to pay and we would have never known the better, but instead, very quickly pointed out the mistake.

That meant the world to us and saved us money that we ultimately were able to give back to Williamsburg in other ways.

We appreciate the friendly, and professional staff, and will definitely visit Colonial Williamsburg in the future!

Been to The Pro Football Hall of Fame many times...

Great location that is easy accessible, parking is fairly sizable and can usually park pretty close. Awesome out door area which has a small turf field that they allow you to play on, great for throwing the football around with your pals.

Once inside there are numerous exhibits which takes you through a chronological history of the sport from the early days of football's origination in Canton to a Modern Day Room of recent players. You can see next year's Lombardi Trophy, all the previous Superbowl rings, and of course the famed Hall itself with the bust of those enshrined.

Capped off with a revolving theater, that showcases the latest seasons highlights and Superbowl, and ends, in an incredible NFL Shop with enough gear for everyone's favorite team and signed memorabilia.

The Pro Football Hall of Fame is a MUST go for any fans of the game.

Negatives-Things to look for :
Team events aren't always what they're said to be. I went for a "Raiders weekend", and they handed out HOF towels, which was a great gift, but had nothing Raider related. There also wasn't any great mementos regarding such, outside of the turf from immaculate reception which wasn't a positive. Team weekends were a huge let down!
Becareful to check for ongoing events, as sometimes the lots can be overcrowded due to such.  Took my grandfather once, and ended up having to park an incredible length away from building, he had to walk a terrible distance that he was incapable of doing, and we ended up actually going elsewhere for the day.
Outside of modern day changes, new annual bust, and the theater screening changes are not overly a ton, which is understandable.  I visit every couple year's to keep it fresh.

The Stonewall Jackson house was easily one of my top destinations in Lexington (Thomas Jackson Memorial Cemetery, VMI, Washington-Lee College being the others. )

It was an incredible step back into time to step onto the grounds, and inside, the home that has been fully restored to that of the time in which Jackson lived within. A place in which he was proud of, his only true owned home.

Though much of the furniture is replicated and the home has a history well beyond the time of Jackson (for nearly a half a century it was a hospital), the homes most humble beginnings and now famously known history is that of being the generals house during his years spent in Lexington.

The tour guides are very knowledgeable, and offer a fact based informative lecture on the homes history and Jackson's time spent within the walls.

There are a few select furnishings in the home that were actual belongings.

There is gardens behind the house, and a fairly affordable gift shop within, selling Jackson memorabilia.  The price of the tour is more then reasonable.

I very much loved this home and tour and think that absolutely anyone, but most definite, a history buff should absolutely visit. It's incredible to stand in the same space that was once filled with such a historical significant man, to our countries past.

The Columbus Zoo, simply #1 in America, period.

I have been going to The Columbus Zoo for 30+ years straight, within the last decade holding a membership, and after over hundreds of visits continue to keep coming back.

This Zoo is spacious and the viewing areas are set up for most exhibits in a way where seeing the animals is pretty easy for everyone.  Animals are many, very active, and are all for most part are in extraordinary visually stunning exhibits.

On rainy days, there's plenty of in door animal houses to spend your time in, and during the winter the most amazing display of winter lights you'll ever see.

Staff and volunteers are very knowledgeable and on hand, many interactive shows and animal talks, and the Zoo is constantly being upgraded and expanded.

Train rides, boat rides, water rides, rollercoaster rides, camel rides, pet the stingrays, feed the giraffes, just very FEW of the side options of things to do. Numerous dining options and an incredible amount of kids areas and things beyond just the animals that could never be fit into a single review

Hands down, the Best Zoo in The United States and a MUST visit for any Zoo lover.

I've been to quite a few museums in my life, including The National Smithonian's and I can say with confidence that The Dayton Air force Museum challenges any of those museum's for being among the best.

The museum itself is FREE to enter, with four huge bunkers. They start from the beginning and go through the end of the the Air Force, Flight, and hold a special section for Space and Historical Presidential Planes. Many Air-Force One's and personal jets are part of this unique collection. There are many artifacts and air craft that participated in particular wars.

The museum is extremely clean, all staff is incredibly professional, and the museum offers great education and entertainment for the entire family.

Food, restrooms, gift-shops all included amenities at the Museum.

You can spend at least an entire day, maybe two, if you are truly going to read every sign within the establishment.

The Air Force Museum in Dayton is comparable to none and is an incredible gem to have here in Ohio. I have visited at least a half of dozen times over the years and I've never once left unsatisfied with my experience.

Highly recommended!

The Park Fire Tower is one of Mohican State Parks main attractions!

While I am pretty certain (I HOPE, haha) that the tower passes all safety standards and isn't going to crumble beneath my weight what a thrilling experience making the climb. If it is windy at all, and often just generally as you're climbing it, you are bound to feel the movements of the old tower.

Many steps that are somewhat more narrow the higher you can go, I feel like coming down however is worse then going up, once at the top the observation tower is ultimately locked but you can stop directly underneath and take a look around. You can see for miles, in which will be some of the most breathtaking views of the park, you'll find.  You'll have a great view and photo opportunities.  Great spot to visit all year around but the best views come in the fall.

As long as stairs and heights aren't your enemy, I would highly recommend this to anyone who is in the general area, or, for that matter anyone who is willing to make the drive out.

The Magnum XL-200 stands at over 200 feet, and 70mph.

I think this is hands down the best value coaster in the park when it comes down to wait-versus-thrill.

It's almost hardly ever crowded and you can probably get on fairly regularly in under 1hr but I've been in situations to where I could ride it 2-3x in that amount of time.

Though it's now over three decades old, it's a total spectacle, when taking in the views of Cedar Point and beyond. The first drop is absolutely incredible as is the turnaround point.

The only downfall on this one is the end tunnels - in which you are hurled over the humps at a high rate of speed, if you're not prepared, and even so when you are, your legs are going to take an incredible beating. You're likely to come off the seat and slam into the bars a few times before coming to a sudden halt.

Brace yourself for the end, compare the wait versus the thrill, and this coaster is going to become one of your absolute favorites. It's rough, fast, high, and mean!

I LOVE IT!

Lee Chapel & Museum is easily my favorite location in all of Lexington.

It's an incredible well kept Chapel inside and out.

It is completely free of charge.

Once entering you are immediately met with the open chapel room and from afar will see The General's memorial - a sculpture of him laying in state - on each side you will see original paintings of General George Washington to the left and Lee himself to the right.

You're allowed to go into the room where Lee's sculpture is at state and eventually will veer to the left down to the actual crypts. The actual crypts host Lee among many of his kin, including Revolutionary War Hero, his father Light Horse Harry Lee, Wife, and Children.

His office is also in the lower room still intact and preserved just the way he left it the day that he died.

Outside you'll find his trusty mount Traveler buried near by.

An incredibly impressive place that anyone who finds themselves in Lexington must absolutely see.

First time in a Ripleys Museum.

The appeal of the outside on the Gatlinburg strip is hard to pass by, the detail is incredible, fun to look at and very inviting.

Once inside there's numerous floors of interactive and regular exhibits, that'll keep you busy for some hours.

I think we spent around 3hrs total, if you're trying to read everything. Fairly spacious, so, even on a crowded day it's mostly comfortable.

Lots of neat exhibits. Charles Mansons finger prints and criminal ID card, Annie Oakleys Trick Shot pistol, was a few of my favorite inside this one.

Though, for the price, I was a little disappointed that many of the exhibits are simply pictures and recreations that otherwise are actually in other museum's or just storytelling.
I preference if I go into a museum for me to be looking at the actual thing's.

Still, it remains one of the most visually stunning places on the strip in a town full of touristy trap shops holds most of the legitimacy.

Took a drive North to the small town of Milan, Ohio.

Often pass it but have never stopped, for those who still haven't, nestled on the end of town next to its canal  (which at one point was the second most popular canal in the world for transporting grain) lies the 1841 structure that was the childhood home (birth, ages 1-7) of one of the the world's greatest inventors, Thomas Edison.

A $9, 45minute guided tour offers a deeper glimpse into the homes history, which is still the original build and structure, as well as shows you the room in which Edison was born and houses some great Edison artifacts. The home is still owned and  operated by Edison descendants and runs soley off of visitor funding,  as its not part of the NPS.

Our tour guide was awesome, and it was defintely worth the drive and cost. I would highly recommend the trip for any history buff and anyone else really who cares about historic relevance.

The Stonewall Jackson Memorial Cemetery host nearly 150 Confederate Veterans, two Governors of VA, as well as many other notable individuals.

The center piece and most obvious individual, of course, is Thomas "Stonewall" Jackson himself and surrounding family members.

The cemetery is quite small compared to what I imagined, though, it is full of notable names and historic legends that made this one of the most hallowed and humble cemeteries that I ever had the honor of walking through.

I had only wished that I knew half of the individuals that were there, prior to me visiting, so I could have truly taken it in for all it was.

Very well kept, clean, and honorable place. I would recommend time for a long stroll to pay out respects and seek out notable names, if you truly want to take all of it in.

Very incredible cemetery.

This is a great Zoo.

Getting parked and finding the lot in general when we arrived was a bit of a pain and should be marked better, but, once out of the car and up the escalators to get in The Zoo, a very pleasant experience.

It is incredibly relaxing, well laid out, and absolutely beautiful. The mixture of the gardens and trees with the exhibits make it seem like an oasis and the exhibits here are some of the absolute best I've seen. Animals have ample space and don't seem cluttered, at all.

Nice Covid19 guidelines in place that I felt like most of the staff and general population was observing. Reservation times to enter was nice and non touch ticket scan worked out well.

Prices for food and drinks were reasonable.

Finally got to meet famous Fiona.

A great zoo, well worth the price of admission.

John Oliver Place, the first historical  stop on the Cades Cove Loop, offers a glimpse inside the first white settlers 200 year old cabin.

Having settled in the 1820s, and the Oliver family living in it for nearly a century, it is now under ownership of the National Park Service and one of the most visited spots on the trial.

Aside from some of the expected wear and tear a two century year old cabin might have, and bad tourist marks, the cabin is in fantastic shape and offers an incredible glimpse back into time.

If lucky a volunteer or ranger may be on site to answer more questions. Walk to cabin is  simplistic, maybe 5 minutes, and the views surrounding it are absolutely breathtaking.

Hands down the best place to do sampling in the entire area.

These guys and gals, are awesome.  Check ID and get band at the door, and, off to one of the round table you go. Host in the center, in which, after three days in a row of doing this I can say, they all were great !

The round table is a nice touch, as everyone is truly engaged and involved, having a great time. Host are always joking and keeping the group entertained. Just an ALL out A+++ experience.  My favorite place on the entire strip.

Moonshine is around $20/jar, band goes towards the cost of merchandise, the shop itself is great, also with great staff.

This place knows how to do business and has a great time doing it!

Major General Meade's Statue can be found on Hancock Avenue, looking out over the field in which Pickett's charge took place.
The statue stands at nearly 20ft tall with the pedestal included and shows Meade on top of his trusty mount, Old Baldy.

Meade is staring out across the field at his old foe, General Lee, for eternity, opposite the field on Confederate Avenue.

He forever sits at what has long since been known as the high water mark for the confederacy, next to the angle, in which had the union line broke that day may have been the end of our glorious Union. Having taken command just shortly prior to Gettysburg,  his finest hours would surly be on this Battlefield.

Not one of my favorite coasters...

Expectations were to high for this one, I think, while the design of the trains and track itself is visually pretty incredible, especially the keyhole over the entrance, the rest of the experience was fairly boring.
