Quiet small park off the beaten path. Part of the trail that traverses the Delaware River. Quiet and with bathrooms. Nice views of the Tacony Palmyra Bridge with fairly easy access to the bridge. My kids enjoy "walking to New Jersey (and quickly returning)" worth a stop by if you're in the area or exploring urban trails.

Great aquarium- lots of hands on and children's centered activities. Check their online schedule for special events. Consider getting a yearly pass if you plan on making yearly trips- pays for it's self after 2 trips. Also consider going off hours and you can pretty much have your run of the place.

Not ' in love' with Love Parks redesign. Seems sterile an uninviting. Nice place to stop and see City Hall and up the parkway. Hosts a variety of events throughout the year including the Christmas village. Try and go off normal busy hours because it can get very crowded.

One of my favorite places in the city. Great for people watching and views of the city / delaware/ ben franklin bridge. Check their calender of events for free offerings and check out the new enclosed pier right next door (Cherry Street Pier).

Great wooded and paved trails
A reenactment plantation, a classical mansion which now hosts weddings and other events, a horse farm, and a variety of 19th century houses- check it out!
Great riverside park. Easy walk to NJ and has a great interpretive space. Check it out. If you're in for a hike you can head north to Bowman's Tower.
Part of the state park. There's a small fee. No pets in the tower. There's a small elevator but does not make it to the observation deck.
The design upgrades with the fountains are great for kids. Year round activities in front of one of the cities most recognized landmarks.
A 'pay as you wish' location. Great for kids! The playground had a lot of easily accessible playground equipment. Worth the day trip.
No dogs allowed ! (I didn't see this on the webpage). Also unmentioned- the river trail was closed! Otherwise was a neat experience.

Nice activity- well set up.
This year had rides mini golf and amusement park like games. There's also food ice cream and a bar.
Went during the off season with few souls out. Good for shell exploration with the kids or just to walk around.

I have to say that I go hiking on many trails from central to northern NJ. High Point State Park's Appalachian Trail switching off to the 3.5mi Monument Trail makes for some of the best views. And if your daring enough, you can climb Veteran's Monument-- which can be accessed by vehicle or through trails. I happened to get lost briefly as it is confusing when you reach the point at the three trees with white, green/red and blue markings.
Luckily, a group from the start got lost and retracted back and we hiked back to our destination at Appalachian trail. So my solo hike ended up with a group one and to say the least,  a friendly group. I look forward to going this trail more often. I'd say the trail is moderate difficulty because of all the rocks and various incline/ declines. Also there's an observation deck before you get to the monument that's pretty sweet!

This place is breathtaking with speechless views after miles and miles of trail. I parked off Green Pond Trailhead and walked through Rockaway, Hibernia & Boonton -- what a workout. The trails are somewhat well-marked however when you walk up the gravel road, it is labeled trail but does not say how far the hawkwatch edge is. I'd say my walk was well over four to five miles one way. The site is really something to see and I can't describe it other than nostalgic. Check it out for yourself! Supposedly, there is a parking area near the hawkwatch but I can't say exactly where.

An exceptional park with miles of trails and well-maintained, as are most Morris County-based parks. While the landscape could benefit from some cleanup of old fencing and unkempt brushes, overall I walked half the mileage and am eager to complete the rest at a later date.

There are various entry ways in which offers ample parking, latrines, picnic areas, benches and even a playground with some workout stations along the way. I do a LOT of hiking throughout Morris and Sussex and this is being added to my list for location and scenery.

Having moved to Morris County a little under two years ago, I knew there was already much historical landmarks and nature trails. To my surprise, I walked down an unmarked path and came upon the former incline plane and this canal park. For a hidden park and upper trail path, I was happy to find this place that I will soon be exploring and visiting more. The incline plane has quite the history and the canal park offers information on this. I'm glad this is one of few not heavily populated areas.

First time & loved it! The ease of trail markers lining four different colored trails with wooden entrances, scenic outlooks to marshes & lakes within a peaceful, quiet landscape was fantastic. Various information reads along the trails provide species-related knowledge & since I love challenge, I tackled the Green Trail (advertised as 3mi loop); which is a 3.5 mi trail of moderate difficulty. I look forward to a group hike next time since this was a solo, unplanned trip.

If you love history and are unfamiliar with the story of the Liberty Bell, you will gain invaluable knowledge.  There's an outdoor historical information place off Market Street; which leads into the Liberty Bell Center. It's quite popular with affordable parking nearby & is rich in historical context. I went during childhood and as an adult,  the updated center & background stories provide a glimpse into the struggle for liberation & freedom.

I'm certainly bummed that the building was inaccessible as many abandon buildings left untouched offer insight and historical appreciation for what was left. The building itself appears in fair condition and has plans to become a county park with an unknown date of development. I can't wait until it opens up. At the moment, there are four historical information boards and several no trespassing signs.

As a train lover and enthusiast, I found a train heaven of various freighters and historical information. The visitors center displayed pictures in a 2nd Fl gallery, 1st Fl has historical data and that day the theater was closed. There are over 35 trains on display in the turnstile and along the walk from the mall's food court, you can walk down a wooden path to the train platform.

The best part of growing up in Belleville was Branch Brook Park & it's annual Cherry Blossom Festival. With events from its 10k run, bike tour, cell phone tour & Japanese cultured demonstrations, the park displays a variety of over 5,000 cherry blossoms-- making it the #1 in the U.S. Truly, it's a great place to go alone for peace or being your family for a fun day of adventure!

Hands down one of my top 5 destinations for picturesque, photographic views & exercise trails. There is plenty of information related to its history along the bridge, park trails & within the mini park in Poughkeepsie. There are entry points from Poughkeepsie & Highland. If you're seeking great photos or just a relaxing escape from life, you will not be disappointed!

This arena is quite world famous with displays of historical events throughout their halls of sports and musical achievements. The facility is extremely clean, staff friendly and the atmosphere was insane. I attended here for Rangers preseason last night and only have been to the Garden once before when I was a child. Pretty cool feeling as an adult.

I have to say this is one of the most beautiful parts of NY I have explored. I traveled for about 15 miles but it felt never ending and I wouldn't have minded because the views were gorgeous. From Port Jervis to D&H Canal to beyond, it was picturesque and tranquil. I will certainly return to meditate and just breath in the heavenly views.

While the area is pleasant for other things such as dining & relaxation, Cooper's Cave itself is nothing more than a hole. While history is attached regarding James Cooper, his writings & more specifically, The Last Mohican-- view of the cave is visible from behind metal fencing.

Pretty cool spot that offers benches to relax by the lake and a trail that offers views of three different lakevie. While the trail path is tiny, it is marked by blue & yellow markers to follow two separate paths. I came upon this location by accident and enjoyed the trail site.

Gorgeous lake views along small beach, area park with basketball/tennis court & fishing dock with benches. A quiet escape from busy downtown Bolton Landing with local events held in park; including movie nights. While parking is $5, street parking is free for two hours.

Probably nice during the spring, but in the rain it didn't look too well. It has two large areas of field for baseball and soccer. The parking lot is also a very large stone, unmarked area. It's pretty basic, nothing too exceptional, other than a dog park.

A nice, well maintained park in the Fords section of Woodbridge. I was surprised to see the recreation areas fenced in, requiring a permit to use fields. Other than this, there are two roller rinks, a jungle gym for children and basketball courts.

I love this park for the simple fact that it's trail is unmarked but very easy to walk along. The park is complimented with a long water stream, playground, field area and plenty of parking. Easily accessible through Dover and into Randolph.

I came upon this site by accident; however it was pretty nice to see a historical turntable. Hopefully they restore the trains and allow visitation to the trains because the tracks are shared with NJTransit and highly secured.

A humongous and beautiful landscaped park with a walkway, tons of parking, multiple playing fields and a playground. Some features are a kayak rental area, concert stage and plenty of grass for lounging and picnicking.

A public park located in Hackensack that requires permit for field usage and has multiple baseball fields. The park also offers a field house, playground and small walking trail along the Hackensack River.
So close to home with large open space for family fun & bbq grill stations for events. This park features a large playground with a two gazebos, a 0.8m track & a beautiful view of the waterfront.
A true gem with hidden trails and great environmental scales. While there are several playing fields for soccer and a small play area, the trails provide a serene escape.  You must check it out!
Amazingly structured driving/walking one-lane bridge with a D&R Canal Trail along Scenic Drive. There is a small parking lot, toll house and majestic views for photography.
Incredibly beautiful with landscape views that will np..we your mind. There are several trails that are accessible and information about wildlife in the area.

Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 1+
Sidewalks: Paved to and around park grounds
Seating: Benches around play area
Bathrooms: In building by Shelter 1 (largest shelter)
Picnic tables: Several in picnic shelters and throughout park
Grills: Several in picnic shelters
Sports field: Off-shore fishing, dock, and boat launch; sand volleyball; open fields

Because it's a county park, Island Lake has a lot of amenities city parks don't. Namely, there are several picnic shelters with huge grills and plenty of picnic tables. There are also several picnic tables scattered throughout the grounds. Picnic tables are situated so that guests have some privacy from one another.

Island Lake County Park is a long park that runs along the edge of Island Lake. At one end is the large picnic shelter, bathrooms, and playground. At the other end is the boat launch and dock. In between are smaller picnic areas and the other shelters. Trails weave throughout the park.

We fished off-shore for sunnies (those trusty boogers will always bite) and our kids had a blast. Where we were (not by the boat launch or dock), off the shore and for a few yards the water is shallow and clear. We were able to see the fish swimming around and trying out our bait. This made fishing even more fun for our kids.

After fishing for a while, we made our way to the play area. There's a lot of space to play: one continuous strip of playground on one side of the park and one big swing set on the other. A double seater spring rider sits in the middle.

The playground has sections to accommodate new walkers and seasoned climbers. Zoey (17 months) enjoyed both the tunnel and small slides made for little tots and the bridges and big slides made for older children. Aside from the occasional boost, she was able to make her way all around the playground on her own.

Titus (3) and Madeline (4.5) had a blast on the gross motor skills obstacles (ladders of all sorts, overhead glider, tunnels, horizontal bars). They also liked the variety of slides available (steep, short, covered, open).

The double rider takes the shape of an alligator (or other reptilian) and easily seats up to four kiddos (we took a picture with the three eldest kids and my husband on it). Next to it, the swing set generously offers regular and baby swings.

We visited Island Lake during the evening. It was incredibly shady, which is a nice change compared to most parks. There was little traffic despite it being a county park located off of a major highway. The grounds, including the picnic shelters, are clean and well-kept.

If you take your kiddos fishing here, be wary of the drop from some the off-shore spots. While the water isn't deep, the distance from where you're standing and where the water is can be at least a yard.

What may also make fishing off-shore a challenge are the brambles sticking out of the ground. Since there's a drop from where you stand to where the water is, plenty of roots poke out. Our lines got tangled more than once. Although they weren't hard to untangle, we did catch our kiddos trying to it it on their own. This was a safety issue considering how easy it would have been for them to fall in.

A final con is the wear and tear of the playground equipment. The park has been loved and well-used over the years, reflective in the appearance of its play area.
dislikes: Brambles and roots causing line tangles

reviews_attraction.text:
Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 3+
Sidewalks: Paved to play area with a trail around the park
Seating: Benches by play area and along trail
Bathrooms: A porta-potty by the play area
Picnic tables: One by the play area
Grills: One by the pond
Sports field: Tennis courts and open fields

My kids were so excited to get out of the car as soon as we pulled into the parking lot at Howard Johnson Park (1260 Woodhill Drive). Along with the popping color of the play grounds (that yellow!), there's an incredibly steep slide they were eager to try out.

The playground has a combination of mulch and synthetic flooring (the latter underneath the playgrounds themselves). It's also got two playgrounds: One for kiddos 2+ and another for kiddos 5+.

Younger kids can take stairs, a curved ladder, or raised steps to yet another curved ladder to reach the top of their playground. They can take any of these options back down or ride one of the double slides.

Even though this playground is meant for younger tots, the only way Zoey (16 months) could get up was via the stairs. Even Titus (3) struggled with the raised steps (they're tall and far apart). Madi (4.5) was the only one who could comfortably navigate the smaller playground.

Older kids have a variety of vertical challenges at the bigger playground, including a sideways ladder that connects one part of the playground to another. This feature is definitely not for the faint of heart; I'm not sure I'd cross it myself!

Also included on the big kid playground are several slides, a curved climbing net, and a climbing wall. Madeline enjoyed the challenge of the climbing net, but steered clear of the sideways ladder. Titus mainly used the stairs to get to the half of the big kid playground he could reach.

The swing sits opposite the playgrounds. It has the full assortment of swings: high back, baby, and regular swings.

Between the playgrounds and the swing set are a low-hanging hammock, double-seated spring riders balance beam, swirling seats, and other spinning equipment (both seated and hanging). Madi and Titus couldn't reach the hanging equipment but did enjoy spinning on the other features.

As is the case with most Roseville parks, the play area is in great condition. The parking lot also sits right in front of the play area, a convenient location, especially for a mama with lots of littles in tow.

Unfortunately, I found this park best suited for school-aged children. Most of the equipment is intended for kids who have a strong control of their gross motor skills and are physically tall and strong enough to confidently navigate obstacles such as the sideways ladder (which hangs about 12' above the ground).

Unless kids can cross the sideways ladder, or scale the curved climbing net, there's also no other way to reach the steep double slides. Because of this, only Madi got to try out those slides.

Younger kids who can't yet scale the big playground will quickly tire of the little playground. This is where we found ourselves near the end of our visit. Not surprisingly, we ended up swinging for the last 15 minutes or so.

While Howard Johnson Park is beautiful and well-kept, our next visit will probably be a couple years from now.
likes: Multiple playgrounds for different age groups
dislikes: Limited access to some features (e.g., steep slides) for younger kids

reviews_attraction.text:
Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 1+
Sidewalks: Paved to and around play area
Seating: Benches around play area
Bathrooms: In warming house
Picnic tables: 1 by play area
Grills: 1 large grill by play area
Sports field: Several including tennis and basketball courts (see full listing here)

Contrary to several of the pictures of the park on Google Maps, Wilson is newly remodeled--and beautifully so. Except for the warming house, it looks like the park in its entirety got a face lift.

The grill and picnic table are located right off the parking lot. Behind them sit the play area, which includes a playground for little kids (1+) and another for big kids (3+), a climbing net, merry-go-round (the contemporary kind), seesaw, a double-seater spring rider, and swing set.

The little kid playground has slides, a mix-and-match activity (think tic-tac-toe but with pictures), and some age-appropriate climbing obstacles.

There's also a cute little window for peek-a-boo or a puppet show of sorts. Zoey (17 months) enjoyed the mix-and-match activity and had little trouble making her way around this play structure.

The big kid playground also has slides (watch out for the double slide--it's steep!), stairs, ladders, and other climbing obstacles. Titus (3) had a little more trouble scaling this structure, simply because he wasn't tall enough to, while Madi (4.5) navigated it without any issues.

Contrary to the traditional climbing net, the one here at Wilson is geometrically intriguing. It's diamond-shaped instead of rectangular. Kids can climb inside or outside of it.

My kiddos found the merry-go-round especially fun. It's got several seats carved out, complete with handle bars if kiddos are more adventurous and opt to stand. Had I not been about 38 weeks pregnant at the time of our visit, I would have pushed them around in it a lot longer.

The swing set is generously stocked with regular and baby swings. There's also a strange-looking swing that seats two. It's kind of like they hung a shovel: kiddos can either sit on the neck or in the scoop of it (don't worry: I took a picture just to show ya!).

The double-seated spring rider takes the shape of a caterpillar and is still in mint condition (like the rest of the park). Even at my size, I wasn't concerned I'd squash the bug, per se.

The seesaw sits in the corner of the play area. Taller kids can ride it standing. Mine couldn't. They enjoyed [trying] to get it to work, but eventually gave up and opted to run around in the tennis and basketball courts next door.

With its renovation, Wilson Park has plenty of years of play ahead. I wish the picnic area was better stocked with grills and tables. Although I didn't get to check out the warming house, it looks like there are bathrooms located on site.

We visited close to lunchtime and there was only one other mom and child there. Considering summer sports activities and the range of sports fields located at Wilson, my guess is that it gets pretty busy here during the evenings.

Aside from its potential for traffic, the park is backed right up to neighbors' yards. Unless you mind being so close, there isn't much else missing at Wilson Park.
likes: Play area for different age groups

reviews_attraction.text:
Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 1+
Sidewalks: Paved to play area and throughout park
Seating: Benches by play area
Bathrooms: Between the playgrounds and splash pads
Picnic tables: A couple alongside play area
Grills: NA
Sports field: Several (see website for a complete list)

Madison's Place is built on synthetic flooring and stretches far down the side of the HealthEast Sports Complex.

The playgrounds come first. There's literally a playground conglomerate--the first I've ever run into. There's a huge mass of slides, climbing obstacles, bridges, ladders, tunnels, stairs, and spinners suited for the youngest walkers to the most experienced ones. There's no way any kid will get bored in less than 2 hours.

Next to the playgrounds is a row of sitting and hanging zip lines and gliders. Again, these were a hit for both younger kids, who could ease along with the help of an adult, and older kids, who could challenge one another to crazy dares.

Around the edges of the playgrounds are various equipment such as seated group spinners and spring riders. A sidewalk separates the playgrounds from the splash pads. It leads to a small building in which bathrooms and water fountains are located.

The splash pad for little kids has mini fountains and sprinklers. It's also far enough away from the big kid splash pad so kiddos aren't accidentally pinned down by one of those water-dumping buckets. Zoey (16 months) was comfortable exploring on her own in this area.

The splash pad for big kids is touch-activated and runs for about 15 minutes before needing to be reactivated (I personally appreciate this water-saving feature). It has fountains, "rain," rotating guns that spout water, sprinklers, and dump buckets, to name just a few things there.

All around the play area is luscious green grass that's perfect for lounging or laying. While there aren't trees big enough to offer ample shade, all you need for a comfortable visit is an umbrella or tent.

My kids loved Madison's Place. They didn't want to leave--and did the whole cry and beg thing when we said it was time to go.

I liked the variety of equipment available for play. The kids were almost always running from one thing to the next for the entire time we were there. I also liked how they could easily switch from playground to splash pad as much as they wanted.

As extensive and fun as the playgrounds are, there's a lot crammed into one space. It seemed to get crowded or even claustrophobic at times, simply because you're completely surrounded by play equipment, running kids, and chasing parents.

Also, as you can imagine, Madison's Place is a popular stop. It was very busy when we visited (as in parents and guardians sat all along the border of the play area--which isn't small), which added to the feelings of crowdedness.

Regardless of the compact structure, we're likely coming back for more of this playground-splash pad duo.
likes: Seamless transition between playground and splash pad

reviews_attraction.text:
Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 3+
Sidewalks: Well-paved around park
Seating: A few benches
Bathrooms: Inside warming house
Picnic tables: Several
Grills: 2 by play area
Sports field: Open field and baseball field behind playground

There are so many things I like about Lexington Park: its location, its size, its abundance of picnic tables; its compact design; its warming house; its climbing rocks . . . So many things.

On errand-heavy days, we like to stop by this park for a breather before heading home (or on more errands!). It's literally 2 to 3 minutes away from the library and Target.

For a park that sits on a busy road in a busy city, Lexington is surprisingly well-facilitated with a play ground, additional play area, huge swing set, sports fields, trails, and warming house. It's not often you run into a park with all these features done well.

The play and climbing rocks areas are laid with mulch. Most of the playground is either high off the ground or climbing-dependent, making it a challenging course for little ones.

Its got an ample supply of slides, monkey bars, climbing structures, and stairs. We've been here on several occasions, often close to 2 hours, and my kids have yet to complain of boredom.

Although Zoey (15 months) was able to navigate the playground on her own, I had to keep an eye on her and offer help. She had fun, but all play areas are best suited for older tots with a better grasp on their gross motor skills.

Right next to the playground is a huge swing set. It sports a high back swing, baby swings, and regular swings.

The additional play area has several features: a triceratops to scale (dino equipment = added bonus); a car to "drive"; a spring rider; a tire swing; a rock-play structure; and a balance beam of sorts.

Right between these two play areas is a good-sized, open concrete area (perfect for chalk drawings or hopscotch) and several picnic tables. Stopping for a snack or resting here while watching your kiddos play (in whichever play area they want) is made so much easier because of this central seating area.

Behind this area are climbing rocks. There are two artificial rocks sculpted to accommodate climbers of average to excellent skills. Titus (3 years old) can scale these with minimal help.

Behind the climbing rocks is a warming house. Inside is an open space to rent (or run around in when it's cold outside) and bathrooms.

Sports fields are located to one side of the park. I've seen the fields used for both informal and formal games.

There are two things you should look out for when visiting Lexington Park. The first it that it gets busy, especially after work hours and around special events such as holidays and the State Fair.

Consequently, the small parking lot fills up really fast. Plan to visit around these times or to park off-street somewhere around the park and you'll be fine.

Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Off-street
Age range (playground): 3+
Sidewalks: Paved to play area
Seating: Benches around play area
Bathrooms: None
Picnic tables: None
Grills: None
Sports field: Open field; full basketball court

As soon as we stepped into the park, I was blown away by what it has to offer. The playground, climbing net, and spinners sit on turf. The small (2 baby swings) swing set and diggers sit in a sandbox.

What impressed me was the variety of play equipment and the turf/sand combination. This makes for a broader sensory experience (especially if the kiddos are barefoot) and longer play period (for my kids, at least, who can play in sand for hours).

Madi (4.5) and Titus (3) were big fans of the circular spinner (pictured in main photo). They spun themselves and one another. Zoey (16 months) liked going up and down the elevated bridge on the playground. She also loved the swings (as always, she tried out and approved of both baby swings).

A unique feature of Eileen Weida is a netted bridge. Madi was extremely excited for this challenge (and had little trouble traversing it). Titus shied away from it.

Other equipment on the playground include slides, a climbing wall, raised steps, and ladders.

Right next to the playground is a big climbing net. The last few playgrounds we've been to have had this feature as well. Madi and Titus were super excited to be "spider-monkeys" again (spiders because they're in a "web" and monkeys because they're climbing around) and spent a good amount of time on this equipment.

The entire park (open field included) is fenced in, a nice feature if you're with professional escape artists. The field is pretty level and offers plenty of space to run around (there was a backyard football game going on during our visit).

There were several trees and a couple benches between the play area and open field, offering shady refuge.

Eileen Weida was pretty busy during our visit, mainly with unsupervised kids. They were friendly and mainly kept to themselves (one kiddo asked about my belly!).

I personally like having other kids around on our visits, as I think this does wonders for socialization. If you'd rather a quieter setting, consider visiting during school hours.

This park has both been around for a while and hosts a lot of guests. The play equipment (especially the turf), then, is pretty worn.

Some of the older kiddos got rowdy towards the end of our visit and broke something glass-made (at which we put our shoes back on). One of the adults in that part of the park did pick up whatever broke.

Eileen Weida has more quality than most of the other Saint Paul parks we've been to. If you don't mind being in a developing neighborhood (more good than bad), stopping for a visit when you're in the area is worth it.

Here's what you need to know:
Age range (playground): mainly 3+
Seating: Several tables and chairs on one side of the playground
Bathrooms: Yes
Outside food allowed: No
Party hosting: Yes
Price: Varies depending on when you visit. We went on a Thursday evening, during which they offer a deal. (See website for all prices.)

Lookout Ridge is a forest-themed indoor playground located on the bottom floor of Woodbury Central Park. It's behind closed quarters (bathrooms and eating/party space), which makes keeping the kiddos corralled much easier.

There's a lot more to the playground than meets the eye; it takes exploring to see all of the wonderfully hidden nooks and crannies.

At one end of the playground is a bouncy "house" complete with netting. My kids had a blast climbing in and jumping around this area.

To the far back of the playground is an obstacle course. It has dangling "vines," hanging "wrecking balls," and poles to climb over or under. This was Madi (4.5) and Titus' (3) favorite part of the playground.

Another side of the playground is well-suited for kids at least 1 year of age. There isn't much to it: A quick walk through a giant tree trunk to a few stairs which lead to a small slide.

Next to the playground is what I thought was the coolest feature: a "pond" of small critters and other small items (i.e. coins and amphibians). The critters are set in some kind of plastic so that they're seen and walked over but can't be touched. A boat sits on one side of the pond.

There are only a few entrances that lead into the playground. One is a climb up a rock mountain and the other a crawl up netting.

Once the kiddos get into the playground, it's hard to keep an eye on them. The playground extends up into a vaulted ceiling. From the seating area, I couldn't see where they were.

If I followed them from the ground, I could only hear them. The play area is surprisingly dark, making it hard to see much aside from the playground equipment.

My kids weren't comfortable scaling the playground by themselves. I think this is largely due to the fact that it was a dreary setting with a lot of playground cramped into a small space.

I personally would not return to Lookout Ridge. Even at the Thursday night discount price, it wasn't as fun an experience for my kids as other indoor playgrounds have been. The equipment is worn and ill-replaced.

If you're looking for an indoor playground to host a party, you'll have much better luck elsewhere (I really recommend Eagle's Nest!), especially considering you're not allowed to bring food into the premises. Woodbury does most things well, but their indoor playground has plenty of room for improvement.

PLAY AREA REVIEW ONLY
Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 2+
Sidewalks: Paved around park (not directly to play area)
Seating: Several benches around play area
Bathrooms: NA
Picnic tables: Several in picnic shelter
Grills: Several by picnic shelter
Sports field: See the website for details on what's here

As soon as we turned into the parking lot, all we could see were "allergies" (dandelion seeds) floating in the air, literally turning the air white. For people with seasonal allergies, wasn't necessarily a warm welcome.

The play area is a few minutes' walk from the parking lot down a well-paved sidewalk (unfortunately, the sidewalk isn't a straight walk from the lot; it curves this way and that).

On the way down we passed a lovely stone picnic shelter and plenty of open, grassy areas for lounging about or (maybe) even a game of volleyball.

The play area is split into two sections. One accommodates kiddos ages 2+ and the other accommodates kiddos ages 5+. Both are laid with sand, made of wood, and have metal slides.

Zoey (16 months) had a hard time navigating the smaller playground due to the tall steps and long drops. She was also uncomfortable with feeling wood under her feet (we took off shoes to keep them from trapping sand).

Titus (3) and Madi (4.5) were uninterested in the smaller playground because it's pretty bare: a single slide, bridge, some steps, and a tiny tunnel (less than a yard long).

Madi was eager to try out the big kid playground, but had a hard time doing much on her own. She was able to scale the curved wood ladder and take the steps up to the top of the playground. She also found the balance beam (her first ever) an especially fun challenge.

She couldn't, however, navigate the monkey bars, which comprised half of the playground. She quickly grew tired of this section.

Each playground has swings suitable for the intended audience. The big kid playground also has a tire swing, which Titus enjoyed; and a big digger, which Madeline enjoyed.

We were here for no longer than 20 minutes when we decided we'd had enough. None of the kids were comfortable scaling the equipment due to its composition and even when they did, there wasn't much for them to do.

I wanted to keep exploring in the city of Little Canada; but both of the two closest parks (one of which we've been to) looked just about as impressive as Spooner, if not less.

My guess is Little Canada's parks and rec system isn't as current as surrounding cities'. As is such, we won't be coming back unless we know updates have been introduced.

This park has beautiful bathrooms.

We're talking well-lit, odor-free, toddler-friendly bathrooms (as in a built-in stool at the sink and booster seat for kiddo to wait in when it's mama's turn to go). If there's a gallery for amazing bathrooms, this place needs to make the list!

Aside from the impressive bathrooms, here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 1+
Sidewalks: Paved to the playground and other park amenities
Seating: Ample supply of benches surrounding playground
Bathrooms: On the side of the main building
Picnic tables: A couple scattered by play area, including toddler-sized tables; more in the pavilion
Grills: A couple in by the play area; more in the pavilion
Sports field: Shaded grassy area by play area and a baseball field to one side

The playground, main building (with inside meeting space), picnic pavilion, and baseball field are all right off of the parking lot. The lake is a short walk down a hill. There's a dock off of one side. The park is well-paved to each amenity it offers.

Surrounding the play ground is plenty of seating, including two benches perched underneath a charming pagoda.

The play area is laid with mulch and suited for kids of all ages. There's a section for little kids, complete with baby swings (that also features a high-back swing); and a section for older kids, complete with regular swings and one of those hammock swings (I still don't know what this is really called).

Something I appreciate about this playground is the aesthetics: It's made of plastic made to mimic wood. The overall appeal of the play area is a fun treehouse paradise. Synthetic wood also means lesser chances of splinters or burns.

My kids' had two favorite parts of the playground: the climbing mushrooms and the crawl spaces underneath the playground for older kids. They also enjoyed the variety of slides, spring riders, and climbing obstacles (which ranged from easy to challenging to, at this point, impossible without help).

We went for a couple hours in the morning. It got a lot of traffic during our time there. This was a pleasant surprise for us, as we also got to socialize as a bonus.

Although we had no use for them on our visit, I like how there's an ample supply of picnic tables, including a couple just for toddlers. Casey Lake Park was impressive to the point that I've noted it as a potential spot for future birthday parties.

Here's what you need to know:
Parking:  Lot
Age range (playground): 1+
Sidewalks: Paved to play area and around park
Seating: Benches around play area
Bathrooms: Inside warming house
Picnic tables: A couple by the building
Grills: None
Sports field: Open fields, baseball field

Oasis is a pretty secluded park in a residential neighborhood. I failed our first attempt to enter the park: we parked off-street and were halfway to the play area before I saw it had a parking lot. Note to future guests: There's a parking lot!

The play area is in mint condition. The play equipment sits on a large plot of mulch with synthetic flooring at the base of some parts (i.e. slides).

There are several parts to the play area: a climbing-heavy playground for big kids; a toddler-friendly playground for new walkers; a swing set with baby, high back, and regular swings; a merry-go-round of sorts; and a set of some musical equipment. On the hills nearby are two bench swings, perfect for lounging.

When I say this had the tallest playground we've seen, I mean it: Even Madeline, our fearless adventurer, thought twice about going down the slides. She eventually tried the open slide. Zoey and I ended up going down with her on the closed one.

Overall, Madi (4.5) and Titus (3) navigated the big kid playground with minimal help from me. It has several slides, ladders, stairs, and climbing challenges. While there are several ways to get to the first level of this playground, the only way to reach the top most level is via a ladder on the first level.

By now, Zoey (16 months) was familiar with the play structure for kiddos 1+. It's the same design as those in many of the parks we've visited: a slide, mini tunnel, some drums, and a tiny climbing challenge.

Unlike structures at other parks, this one also came with a play area for the medium on which the playground sits. Unfortunately, Oasis is mulch-laden and this playground feature isn't as fun as it's intended to be.

The merry-go-roundish feature was one all my kiddos enjoyed, even though it isn't fast as Madi and Titus wish it were.

Not far from the play area is a pond. Although there's a good deal of foliage to slow down an escapee, there's no fence keeping kiddos from the water.

Despite the terrible heat, we enjoyed our visit to Oasis. I only wish it was better-suited to host parties (i.e. grills and more picnic tables).

Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 1+
Sidewalks: Paved to park amenities and throughout park grounds
Seating: Ample seating throughout play area
Bathrooms: Located in warming house
Picnic tables: Enough to seat around 50 in a picnic shelter to one side of the play area
Grills: NA
Sports field: See website for a complete list

Take my word for it: This park has pretty much everything.

Climbing walls, ladders, nets, and domes; tall slides, short slides, bumpy slides, and curvy slides; bridges; tunnels; weather-resistant instruments; stairs; steps; seesaws; monkey bars--

(Insert breath)

Sand play area; hammock; ramps; seated merry-go-rounds; high back swings, baby swings, and regular swings; regular zip lines and seated zip lines; and a bunch of stuff I can't even identify.

It offers more shade than the average playground and it's got synthetic flooring. Did I mentioned there are also real, flushable toilets inside a clean facility?

I might build myself a house in the woods nearby just so I'm local.

Woodridge Park is a dream. It's like the Mall of America of parks: Every type of playground equipment you could want is here. You could spend the whole day here and see only half of it. And, of course, it's ginormous.

It's so big, in fact, that I didn't even realize how busy it was until we returned to the parking lot on our way out and almost half of it (ginormous parking lot for a park, as well) was full of cars.

There are several playgrounds scattered in the play area accommodating ages from walkers to jumpers. All of my kids had a blast running around trying a little bit of everything.

One of their favorite parts was the roller slide. I think they spent a quarter of our trip riding it over and over again. They also loved playing the xylophones and scaling the outside of the huge tunnel.

We could have easily killed half a day at this park if it weren't for the merciless sun and humidity.

The park opened just this past fall and is in wonderful condition. It's definitely beloved and received plenty of traffic during our visit. At the same time, the spread of the play area keeps even busy times from feeling overwhelming

If you're looking to host a party or keep your kids entertained for a few hours, pack a hefty lunch, plenty of water, and head over to Woodridge Park. It'll do the trick.

Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 1+
Sidewalks: Well-paved to and around all amenities
Seating: A few benches in play area
Bathrooms: Inside community center
Picnic tables: In picnic shelter beside playground
Grills: In picnic shelter
Sports field: Tennis courts, full basketball courts, an ice rink, and open fields (check the website for a complete listing)

Richard Walton Park is located on the grounds of the Oakdale City Hall. It's beautifully furnished with a variety of sports fields and courts, a picnic shelter for large group events, and a bandshell. There are well-kept sidewalks coursing throughout the park.

The park has two entrances, one on either side of the playground. One lot is to the park specifically while the other is shared with city hall visitors. Both are about the same distance from the playground. As per usual, we only visited the play area.

Perhaps one of my favorite features here is the fact that it's fully fenced--a win for moms with runaways. A wide sidewalk cuts the play area into two areas: one for kiddos 1+ and another for kiddos 3+.

Zoey (15 months) had no trouble checking out the little kid playground on her own. Madi (4.5) and Titus (3) also had fun plowing through the structure. I like that it was basically an oversized climber you would find in someone's backyard. It was definitely fresh-tot friendly.

While the big kid playground is recommended for kids ages 5+, Titus was able to navigate nearly the entire course without my help. He avoided the uneven steps course and monkey bars.

All three of the kids loved the assortment of slides available. The playground is built in a circle, so they spent a good amount of energy running across its bridges, scaling its steps, and climbing through its tunnel. Each section of the playground has two swings to accommodate the ages of its intended audience.

During our visit there were several other families at the play area and the park itself was busy.

The few things we didn't particularly like about the park is the absence of a nearby bathroom and the lack of shade surrounding the play area. The last half hour there we spent under the merciless sun--hence Madeline's comment about winter. Slap on that sunscreen if you're planning to visit!
likes: Variety of sports fields and courts

reviews_attraction.text:
Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Off-street
Age range (playground): 2+
Sidewalks: Paved to and around the play area; connects to Roseville area trail
Seating: A few benches
Bathrooms: None (maybe a portable one come summer?)
Picnic tables: None
Grills: None
Sports field: A half court near the play area

This pebble-laid park has four play areas: a playground, a rock play area, a swing set, and another gross motor skills section.

Kids can scale the playground via stairs or climbing obstacles. If your little ones are well-versed in stair-climbing at the least, they'll be fine navigating the playground on their own (my 15 month old didn't need my help).

There are a variety of ladders and slides to try out. If your kiddos really love climbing, there's a towering net that'll keep 'em entertained for a while.

On the "main level" of the playground, there are tunnels to crawl through and stairs thrown in here and there to add to the challenge of traversing the playground, especially for young tots.

The rock play area is the biggest we've run into yet: It's got a ship-like feel to it with a "plank" on one side and a slide on another. There's also a "deck" where my kiddos cooked up dino delicacies (I had the choice of gorgosaurus or parasaurolophus meat). They enjoyed stuffing pebbles, sticks, and pinecones down the chutes to see where the items ended up.

Near the rock play area is a mini climbing net and a spring rider.

To one side of the rock play area is a small swing set with a high back swing, baby swing, and two regular swings. It sits in the shade of some tall pines.

The last play area has some spinners on which kiddos can stand or sit. Both my older kids got a kick out of these. While they didn't play on the other equipment in this area, it looks like it involves climbing.

Some final perks of Owasso Hills are the tall and short water fountains right by the entrance of the park; the roadside fencing; and a beautiful pagoda with benches underneath.

Finding the park itself was the biggest challenge, along with determining where the entrance was (there was no sign from what I could see, just a residential sidewalk running past the park). We drove around a few times before I decided on an appropriate place to park during our visit.

Here's what you need to know:
Parking: Lot
Age range (playground): 1+
Sidewalks: Well-paved to playground with trails around the park
Seating: A few benches in play area
Bathrooms: NA
Picnic tables: In picnic shelters
Grills: In picnic shelters
Sports field: Open fields

There are two sections to Battle Creek Regional Park: an east side and a west side. We ended up at the east side (2300 Upper Afton Road, Saint Paul) where the water park is located.

This beautifully-landscaped park has soft rolling hills and shady trees surrounding the parking lot and some of the picnic shelters. The playground is located across the lot from the water park.

There are two picnic shelters in this part of the park: A huge one that probably seats close to 75 people (I think there may be bathrooms located at this site) and a medium-sized one that probably seats up to 50 people. Both have picnic tables galore and grills.

The play area is a short walk down a hill from the parking lot. It's laid with mulch. There are two sections for different age groups: 1+ and 5+. Zoey (16 months) comfortably navigated the smaller playground while the other two (ages 4.5 and 3) enjoyed the challenge of the bigger playground.

The smaller playground has stairs, a tic-tac-toe board, tunnel, ladder, and double slide. There's also a steering wheel for your little driver to play with. The bigger playground has stairs, monkey bars, a climbing wall, tunnel, slide, and spiral climber.

To the side of the playgrounds is a set of swings complete with a high back, baby, and regular swings.

The most negative aspect of this play area was that it sits under the merciless sun. We visited around 3 in the afternoon and felt like raisins 45 minutes in. We ended up leaving earlier than we planned to because we were too hot to keep playing.

If you're planning an extended stay, find out where the bathrooms are and bring a big umbrella to hide under when you get hot.

We LOVE the vastness of the playgrounds at Lions Coon Creek Park! There are several playgrounds on site, each tailored to a different age and developmental level. This makes for long and frequent visits without ever growing tired.

There's a sand play area that is a nice change in pace from all the running, climbing, and maneuvering the playgrounds require. There are also several swings available for use, which comes in handy with how busy this park is when we visit (during the day). Due to its size, it seems to be a popular spot for local school field trips.

The playgrounds are about a two-minute walk from the parking lot, so come prepared with a wagon or stroller if you have little ones. You'll also have to cross a wood bridge and some small hills/dips before hitting the playgrounds. The walk to the play area is beautiful.

We haven't explored much of the rest of the park. From what I can see, there are portable bathrooms and shelters with picnic tables. If you're planning on eating or spending a few hours here, make sure to bring along sanitizer and bug spray (heavily wooded area).

We've been to this park several times, even had a baby shower here once. In my experience, the best feature of this park is its availability: it's tucked away from the main road and harder to find, which makes it readily available for private use without any reservations.

The playground is an older model, but big enough to keep kids entertained for a while. My kids (3 & 4) were able to navigate the playground without my help. The only time I had to step in was when they wanted to try out the ladder that stands from the ground to the slides.

There is a shelter with several (at least 5) picnic tables and one grill. Unfortunately, there is only a portable bathroom. I find this a bit ironic, as we're able to grill but have no access to water or soap for hygiene. You can definitely make it work, but it's rather inconvenient.

There is a large open field behind the shelter, along with a hockey rink you drive by on your way to the shelter. This isn't my first pick of parks, but it works as a last-minute outdoor meeting place.

Rosebrook is a beautiful park in a convenient location. It's got a small gathering room inside a building. Attached to the building is a clean bathroom with running water. Right by the parking, in ample shade, is a kid-sized pool, perfect for toddlers.

The playground is better suited for older toddlers (at least 3 years old), as it requires a lot of climbing. It's laid with mulch. There are plenty of swings, including baby swings and regular swings. There is also an area sectioned off for digging and moving rocks (or sand; I can't remember which).

To the far side of the park are several sports fields. There are also several tennis courts next to the playground with a sidewalk that makes accessing them easy. Be sure to check the Roseville website for times when the pool is open.

This is a neat little park whose playground is mainly comprised of lots of challenging climbing equipment. There are a couple of slides but overall, the playground was not enough to keep my toddlers interested for long. I definitely recommend for older elementary-aged children. My 4 year old liked it more than my 2 year old did. It is mulch-laden and heavily forested around half of the playground. There is a large swing set on one side of the playground and a huge number of sports fields and a tennis court on another. There is a portable bathroom right by the playground. My husband loves the scenic disc golf course on site.

This is a beautiful park with plenty of playgrounds to keep kids of all ages busy for several hours. Their arrangement of playgrounds (you'll have to walk/drive to get from one to another) accommodates little kids and middle-school-aged kids. The playgrounds are mulch-laden. It is extremely clean and not busy in the mornings we have gone. There are plenty of sports fields surrounding the playgrounds, along with sidewalks connecting the playgrounds and bike racks for any you may bring along. My only issue with this park is its lack of shade. The sun will be beating mercilessly down upon you, unfortunately.

As a mother of toddlers, this park wasn't as kid-friendly as I would have liked. It's got an older playground with wood frames, chains, and metal bars instead of plastic (watch out for splinters and burns!). It's sand-laid and has a bench for nearby seating. Where we were by the playground I did not spot any BBQ pits or picnic tables. It does have huge fields right next to the playground which made flying kites easy for us to do after the kids had tired of the playground.

Taft was a neat little park tucked away in a quiet neighborhood. The parking is rather far from the playground, so be prepared to walk a few minutes before getting there. The playground is sand-laden and a bit outdated. It is a good size for toddlers (2+) so long as you avoid some of the older pieces (the seesaw, especially!). There is very little shade surrounding the playground save for one side with a few benches for seating. No BBQ pits that I saw while we were there.

Great creative space for kiddos to explore and work their imagination. There’s space to refuel in the play area for tots that includes tables and a microwave. Finding parking can be tricky the first time you visit. In the Museum ramp, it’s $6 for a 3-hr visit.

My kiddos (ages 17 mo, 3, and 4.5) enjoyed the activities available for their size. Definitely a better deal for older kiddos. I highly recommend bringing your own food and drink so your kiddos last the day without you breaking the bank.

Beautiful new playground atop a hill, A mini trail around the softball field, and a small picnic area. The tennis courts are a bit rundown and, unfortunately there is only a porta potty, no bathroom/sink in a building.
Relatively clean grounds featuring African animals, large cats, primates, tropical reptiles/fish/amphibians, and some marine creatures. We love that it’s donations-based for visitors.

A great little park that's divided into 3 sections, 2 of which have an entrance to the 34 St-Hudson Yards Station(only 1 entrance is open). In the middle section of the park there's 3 large circular fountains where the water flows from the perimeter of the fountains to the center. There's also SO much seating everywhere, some of which lights up at night. You can't have a park without lots of plants, and this park has tons of it all of which look fantastic.  (Also water fountains to drink). It's a very relaxing park so give it a visit if you're in the area.

A big park located between the FDR Drive and 1st Avenue. The Park has a Running track with a futbol/soccer field, Handball and Basketball courts, Baseball Fields, and a Community Center with a pretty large pool. There's also a Pedestrian Bridge that goes over the FDR Drive to the Pedestrian/Bike path along the east coast. There's also 2 playgrounds inside the park and some art sculptures too. The east river plaza mall is nearby as well.

A long beautiful park that's great to go to anytime of the year. There's a couple playgrounds inside it, as well as basketball courts, and Baseball fields too. There's even a pond inside the park as well, where you can see geese hanging around. (For SOME reason someone removed the park from Google maps around Aug. 2016, so all images/reviews have been erased before that point.)

Nice plaza that has tons of seating and tables for your relaxation. There's bathrooms at the Southern part of the square, and Herald Square is a block north of this Square. The Empire State building is one block to the east. The B/D/F/M/N/Q/R/W Subway Lines and PATH trains to Hoboken & Journal Square are nearby as well.

A beautiful long park that spans from 128 to 141st Streets, that's fantastic to relax at. Getting there is really easy too, since you can take the B or C Train to 135th and exit right in front of the station. It's also great for a little jog or walking your dog as well. Lots of stairs everywhere!

Everyone in the surrounding area comes here. You can take a walk around, play handball, workout, play soccer & football in the field, walk your dog, go to the rec. Center, or just simply relax and read a book. It's always a great place with genuinely nice people all doing their own thing.

A cute park situated in one of the most peaceful parts of New York City. It's relaxing as heck to sit it, and the area is so safe I'm pretty sure you could take a nap and nobody would bother you. It's also a convenient little shortcut through the Manhattan College Pkwy.

Not really a park in my opinion, but more of big plaza. There's seating EVERYWHERE, which is convenient during lunch break(s). there's Halal food carts and fast food joints all around this park.The Fulton Center is nearby, as well as PATH trains to Newark and Hoboken.

SUCH A BEAUTIFUL LITTLE GARDEN!! You can really tell the people who manage it really put at least some sort of tender loving care into it. Not a single place where there's no grass, and all the plants look really healthy. Give it a visit if you're nearby!

A bit hard to get to with all the traffic surrounding it. Homeless people tend to be here late at night, so avoid it after sunset. There's only a handball court and some basketball courts and gets boring very quickly.

A fantastic waterfront park...but could use some improvements. For starters, there should be restrooms at both ends of the park. The food there is also overpriced with them having almost a monopoly in the area.
Everyone, no matter how old they are, comes here. Whether it's for the view of NJ and the GWB or to lay down in the grass. It gets filled with people always near the end of the week, and the weekend.
Almost always full of people and there's seating along all of the paths. It looks so great all year round. At the South end of the main path there's a beautiful big circle full of different plants.
Exactly what the name says. A somewhat relaxed atmosphere always arises when one sits down near it. This spot can be a tad romantic as well. For first timers it could possibly be hard to get to.
Beautiful fountain. If you stay for a little bit you'll almost always see a horse pass by. In fact it was technically built so horses could drink from it, back in the 1860s.
Fantastic views. Peaceful. Romantic. Relaxing. All of these things (plus many more) make this park a guaranteed getaway spot from the hustle and bustle of midtown or Queens.
Great little park to let your dog run around in. However there's poop everywhere, and the park is really just grass in the shape of a heart  and some seats on the side.
A great spot to sled on during the winter. It's nice to see people are respectful and have not tried to Vandalize the Statue that's there. It's steep so be careful!
A beautiful park that's far from the subway and (most) tourists. Tons of spots to lay back and relax. There's a dog park and playground inside the park as well.
It's cool to see and fun to play in when they let the water gush out in the summer. There's also lots of great pictures you can take of it too.
A bit on the small side, and a chunk of the Nannys in the area come here when it's open.  It looks nice overall and the locals take care of it.
Located inside Carl Schurz park, this playground is very expansive and has tons of different stuff for kids to play with. Also has restrooms.
Well maintained, but since it's in the southernmost part of NY it doesn't get a lot of visits. The park named after it is beautiful as well.
Lots of seats, but not lots to do for children in the area. There's just one little playground structure in the middle.
Nice looking park with a great view of Wall Street all the way down the Ocean. The park itself needs some sprucing up.

I heard about the panorama of NYC and made a day out of it in Queens. The Queens Museum of Art is not necessarily a big place. Not too much art in it but you can spend hours just examining the panorama. It's gigantic and they really did an excellent job documenting all the boroughs of NYC. It even moves with airplanes.

After the museum, check out the globe in Flushing Meadows Park and take a stroll.

The volume of traffic could be quite insane on this bridge and even more so if there is construction on it. There are two levels, upper for commercial traffic and lower for cars only. Lower level is your best bet when driving over. There is also a pedestrian walkway you could bike or walk over and catch a nice view of the Hudson River. Under the bridge is the Little Red Lighthouse.

There is always something going on at Madison Square Park whether it is an art installation, Big Apple Barbecue, or a crowd at Shake Shack. This is a great outdoor space walking through the city. You will never have a problem finding a seat because there are benches all along the perimeter. Wifi is free so don't forget to check in on Foursquare and update your Facebook status.

Located at the end of Hylan Blvd by the water near Fort Wadsworth is a museum dedicated to promote public awareness and scholarly study regarding the life and work of Alice Austen, one of America's earliest and most prolific female photographers. There are workshops in photography that are held over the weekend for those interesting in photography. Just check their schedule.

Grand Central Terminal is a hub for transportation but also a lot of people shop here. The New York Transit Museum has a little store that is a great peak into how great our transportation system is. This is really tourist stuff like MTA subway shower curtains and shirts with the N sign on it. But if you're interested you could check out the real transit museum in Brooklyn.

This place is crazy especially when there is a free night. The line goes down the block. It's better to just pay. If there is a special exhibit go early to avoid the crowd. On the last days everyone will try to see it. We didn't get to go down the slide as the line was easily a three hour wait. That's just ridiculous.

This bridge comes with many names, 59th Street Ed Koch Queensboro Bridge. You could grab this bridge along 1st Ave or from 59th Street. And it would dump you near Queensboro Plaza. If you are crazy enough to cross by foot or bike, make sure to hold your breath the whole time! There is way too much pollution.

Park Avenue Armory is a great event space. I attended the Ann Hamilton exhibit. It was pretty trippy and a multisensory masterpiece. This was an interactive space with swings that you could sit on and while you swing you could see curtains move from the wind. It looked like an ocean. There was quite a crowd.

Easiest park to find in New York City. Just follow Broadway or take a train to the station. There are many events that take place to find local artists selling their creations, local farmers selling their produce, seasonal markets and gathering for a flashmob or to unite people for a common cause.

One of New York's newest landmark on Hudson Yards that features an infinity staircase. If you want to go inside, you would need a time slot tickets which are available on their website. There is also elevator to the top of the Vessel for those with limited mobility and small children.
likes: Accessibility (elevator for limited mobility and small children)

reviews_attraction.text: Yes it is a real castle. Central Park has some real gems. You just have to go out and seek it. This castle is used for weather purposes but everyone is free to walk around it. It is very picturesque and the kids love it. Below is also the lake where everyone lets their turtles free.

Washington Square Park is really very nice. You have the arch, the fountains, lots of playgrounds, and green grass to sit and have a taco party. This is the heart of the village and NYU. It's very crowded but a nice spot to chill. There is always something going on in this park.

Battery Park has had some significant improvements over the years. Some areas are really nice now and they did a good job adding benches to enjoy the views of the water and playgrounds for the children. This is a good spot to start your walk around the perimeter of Manhattan!

Wonder Wheel in Deno's is just a classic ride and a must ride. The wheel gives a wonderful view of the Coney Island. There are swinging cars that swings along a curvy track in and out of the wheel. And the non swinging cars located at the edge of the wheels.

The New York Aquarium is an okay aquarium to visit. It's one of the smaller ones but if you only have a few hours then it might be a good stop on your list when visiting the Coney Island area. If you have small kids they will surely find this place a blast.

This is a great art museum in Brooklyn. They have new exhibits from time to time so you have to check the schedule. They do have special days where admission is free and also once in awhile have a dance party. Very easy to get to on public transportation.

Randall's Island is a bit out of the way. It's best to get here by bus or drive your own car. The Island is big and mostly used for sports such as soccer and flag football. They also host a variety of events here such as Meatopia and Cirque du Soleil.

We stumbled upon the Jeffrey Hook Lighthouse, aka the little red lighthouse, while we were walking the perimeter of Manhattan. It is located next to the base of the George Washington Bridge. This lighthouse was made famous due to a children's book.

This bridge connects the South Shore Staten Island to Perth Amboy where you could grab NJ Turnpike, NJ Parkway and Route 1. This is a nice option from taking the Goethals Bridge if you're heading South to the Jersey Shore or towards Philadelphia.

Nice park to walk to either from Bay Ridge side of the highway or Dyker Heights. It is a nice place to do some laps with some playgrounds for the kids. Also there is a place on the northeast corner to throw horseshoes.

The Planetarium is great for kids. It's as close to space as you are going to get. You must visit when you go to the Museum of Natural History. It's an educational show and very relaxing. Just try to not fall asleep.

This is a wonderful waterfront park with plenty of place sit and relax in Adirondack chair or a lounger where you could straight your legs and enjoy the view of the Manhattan skyline across the East River.
The eternal fart..erm flame. Reminds of the island from LOST. A hidden gem as you could see from the lack of reviews. Shhhhhhh...
Located in St George near the SI Ferry Terminal is a tiny museum great for kids to learn about science, history and art.
I love the new museum. And the views of the Hudson River and the Highline is worth the price of admission.

We got on the SnoExpress bus from the Springhill Suites (Maple St, Issaquah). The hotel confirmed the parking on the second level is free and we were happy to see many shaded parking. The ride to the Casino was comfortable and took less than 20 mins. The casino buffett was good and it has a great valley/mountain view.

Wonderful building to visit during the day and the night view is gorgeous. I recommended the following: (1) explore every floor by taking the escalator and stairs (2) try the free self-guided cell phone tour of the Central Library; asked the front desk for instructions. (3) visit shop from the 5th Ave entrance.

We loved the butterflies house and virtual reality experiences. There are so much to do and many exhibits/themes are designed for kids. Plan ahead and come up with a must see and to do list bc it will take at least half a day if your kid want to participate in some of the activities.

Amazing structure!! I was not able to find any ticket within the next three days (1/5-1/7) so I decided to try my luck at the kiosk in front of the Vessels.  Luckily I was able to reserve ticket for the same day but we had to wait for an hour for the reserved time slot.

Its is a short (~2 miles) hike to the fall and there is plenty of water access along the trail. One can get really close to the fall and we love the cool mist around the bottom of the fall.  Limited parking space so be prepared to park along the sidewalk.

Beautiful Downtown w/ plenty of nice shops and wide variety of eateries.  It is within 10 mins walk from the Bainbridge Ferry Terminal so an pretty awesome place to visit with no worries about getting stuck in traffic.
we took the eastern loop trail from the ferry terminal to get to the park.  The eastern loop trail goes through beautiful houses along the water front.  The beach has amazing view of Mt. Rainier.
I went there three times over the past 5 years and the ferry from NJ side does not have wait line so it may not be a bad option if you need to stop by Jersey for shopping afterward :-)
Playground with games for everyone. Ping-pong, large jenga, connect four, foosball, chess, corn hole, and much more. Pretty awesome to have this playground in the city center.
Several trails with beautiful trees and shrubs. Love the floating wooden walk path at the Foster Island. The trail was muddy after the rain so it can be difficult to walk on.
Nice paved road for bicycles and runners and nice trails for hiking. A couple shoreline area for kids and dogs. This is truly a great park for exercising or just kick back.
Beautiful park connecting Downtown to First Hill. It is also connected to the Convention Center where one can grab a cup of Joe and enjoy the spacious indoor seating.
This is a great place to spend a day with kids. There are so much to do beside the locks, botanical garden, salmon viewing, and beautiful view of the bay and canal.
This bridge appeared in countless films. You have to see this bridge and its lovely surrounding to fully appreciate one of the most iconic spot of central park.
Beautiful park. very nice trails and filled with wide varieties of shrubs and trees. Parking can be difficult on weekend so plan to arrive early.
Wonderful display of planes from different era. It is truly an awesome experience to be able to tour some of the commercial planes. Love it!
Beautiful trail along the lake and lots of interesting park installed on the park.  There is a museum buding with restrooms and snack bar.
Truly a sanctuary within a short walking distance  from the city. Quiet,  peaceful , and gorgeous view of the city and cascade mountains.
Beautiful spot to see sunset and city lights. The lights on the big wheel changes colors fairl frequent so we never get tire from it.
Pretty cool outdoor setup to enjoy and learn an varieties of bonsai.  We didn't know bonsai can get so large and over 500 years old.
Absolutely a hidden gem of Downtown Seattle. There are a good varieties of plants and flowers. The pictures speak for itself.
Beautiful garden worth checking it out when you're in Pioneer Square. Plenty of seats to kick up and enjoy the fall foliage.
Nice collection of cactus and orchids.  They have train set setup around Christmas so a fun place to visit for the kids.
My friends were surprised to learn that we have a fall in NJ. There is also a museum nearby and trails to enjoy.
Beautiful park to soak up the sun or nice long walk along the Alki trail. Great weekend get away from the city.

I absolutely love this place!  I’ve always heard amazing things and I finally went and instantly
Fell in love. Great place to take the kids! This beautiful place is free they do ask for donation. There is a Children’s petting area where they have some farm animals to feed. I believe this area is for viewing only due to Covid now. They also have other animals around the park to see bobcat, bald eagles, bears. They have a paved walkway that is stroller friendly. The gardens are just beautiful. Our favorite is the stepping stones in the Japanese garden. They also have a glow event that you do have to get tickets for which is worth every cent. They have fire pits and food trucks available the event took about 30 mins for us to walk through.

Went to the glow event this was our first time. Honestly was a little disappointed thought it would be nicer since it’s so expensive. The house was lite up which was beautiful. They had one fire pit open as well as a food truck. We got a few hot chocolates but they were boiling hot. They had a couple people singing Christmas carols on a bench near a fire. Tents available to tour and get gingerbread cookies. The event it’s self was not big. They did have a gun demonstration and you can tour the museum not the house. I brought my 6 year old and 9 year old who were bored. As an adult perspective who loves history it was okay I wouldn’t recommend it for kids. Just wasn’t what I expected

This was an amazing event! Honestly it’s really only worth it if you go ice skating. The lights it’s self takes maybe 10 min to walk through we walked through them twice. Tons of photo opportunities. There’s a shop for kids to get light up toys as well. The skating was a ton of fun especially at night around the lights. Tickets include skate rentals. It is real ice. Was not crowded at all when we went. If you’re not good at skating no problem they have little walkers to push around and little kids can sit and ride them. Staff is very friendly and they watch over the ice for people who fall. I brought my 6 and 9 year old we had a great time

Great time on rude tours. Unfortunately  we did not see any whales but we saw a few dolphins on our way back in. They gave us a free pass to come again which I love. It’s a two hour tour hour out in the ocean a hour back. It does get very cold it was 46 degrees when we went. Dress warm I would recommend warm socks and gloves. The wind is pretty strong out there. The boat wasn’t too packed they have it taped so you know how far to stay apart. Drinks and snacks are offered. They also do a picture in the beginning sold for $10. Staff was very friendly and informative. Excited to go back hopefully will see a whale next time

Okay keep an open mind when you come here. Don’t expect anything great but if you keep an open mind it’s a lot of fun. I have taken my kids here twice ages 4 and 7. This town is one of the coolest towns I have traveled to and this is a crazy road side attraction my kids love. It’s old you pretty much walk through a trail in the woods and there are corny special affects and dinosaurs. The whole thing is pretty corny but it’s cool if you have little kids.

This has to be one of the best museums I have ever been to. My kids ages 8 and 4 really loved it that they cried when we left. There are so many activities! It’s worth every penny. We went to see Thomas. Which was a great experience. They have s huge model train exhibit which was my kids favorites. They had tunnels where they could go under and see the trains. There was so much to do no one was
Bored. We will be back!

We go to this park at least twice a year. My kids always beg me to go. They have so much to do. Inside they have a huge play area my kids would love to do just that alone. They have many animals you can feed. There are many play sets as well. We always go to pumpkinville for the fall activities. They have moon bounces, slides, and hayrides. Each ticket gets a free pumpkin. It’s great family fun!

Beautiful spot wine tasting was okay they were out of a few wines. Not all the wines are from there but from other local wineries. There is a brewery on the other side of the winery I have not tried that yet. They also have cigars available for purchase. There are many spots to sit outside very relaxing with a great view. They have chickens running around and an area for the kids to play.

Really nice museum! Very informative! It is a little pricey and smaller than I thought but they do squeeze in a lot of information. Parking is validated with a ticket which is really nice. I brought my 5&9 year old honestly it was too much reading for them. They liked to look at the pictures and exhibits however went through the whole thing within minutes. My 5 year old was very bored.

Love this place! Remember it during my childhood and took my kids and it was just as magical as I remembered! Very very expensive but I believe it’s worth every dime. We couldn’t have had a better time. It is very crowded they do try to upsell you on shows. We just did the standard ticket and it was plenty. We were there for about 3 hrs maybe more. My
Kids ages 4&7 loved it.

Cute little farm! Kids and I went on Easter. Plenty of space to social distance. We enjoyed our time walking around the farm seeing the different animals. Best park is when the horses and pigs came up to us . They have a mile long loop trail to go one. Also the pillow jumpers were open which was a lot of open space for the kids to jump on. Over all really nice park

Beautiful hike! It’s about 3 miles total there are two paths you can take an “easy” way and a scenic way. I would recommend the scenic way there and the easy way back if you are able to do physical activity. There are many spots available if you need to stop and rest. The falls are breath taking. Remember to bring $5 cash for parking. They use the honor system.

This place is amazing! We did two tours in a day. Went during the day time and one at night for the winter fest. Both 100 percent worth the money.  Brought my kids 10&6 they loved it. So much to see! Staff are passionate and very kind and helpful. Such a great experience especially winter fest the lights on the ship are amazing pictures don’t do it justice

Great experience! Took the ghost tour with my 9 year old son. It was really special we didn’t know what to expect. The tour was very informative and fun. We lucked out with great weather and it was just the two of us in the horse and carriage. We learned so much about Frederickburg would love to do another tour one day during the day

Really cool zoo! Be prepared to have your car filthy! And full of spilled animal food! But overall great experience . The zoo isn’t just driving they have an area to walk around and see other animals that are not on the safari.  Our favorite part is the birds area where you can feed them
And they land on you!

Great winery! Beautiful property and very friendly staff. I came here with my son everyone was very warm and inviting. They let us roam around the property so he can look at all the artifacts. We had a really great time. I got a bottle of wine to take home which was amazing. I will be back!

Small museum but nice. IMax ticket is included which makes it worth it. Was disappointed a lot of the interactive exhibits were not functioning. Took my 9 year old he enjoyed it especially the imax movie. We went during the week so it was not crowded and social distancing was very easy.

Amazing experience my kids had so much fun! Staff is so friendly and helpful. My kids were so entertained playing and learning. The price is more than fair. During covid the navy museum was closed but we had a great time. Best deal is the combo deal.
