likes: Specific attractions (split rock, hole in the walk)

reviews_attraction.text: This is a very cool, short in and out trail that gives you an awesome view of the ocean. Plenty of area to explore along the coast once you get there. My friends and I spent about 30 minutes just exploring and taking in the views. Highly recommend if you’re going along the Oregon Coast.

This is a great park. It has plenty of mountain biking trails, an awesome frisbee golf course, and a very nice actual park. There is also plenty of space to hammock. My friends always enjoy the frisbee golf; it’s never too busy and it’s never too windy because it’s encased by trees.

This was a very nice lighthouse. The views were pretty nice, and the lighthouse itself was beautiful. It was pretty busy though, as you could not get into the lighthouse without paying. The cobble beach next to the lighthouse is the true reason to visit this area if you ask me.

Vista House was a very nice viewpoint. The information it gave was nice, and the view of the Columbia River was great. The parking, however, was a major headache. We had to park a ways down the road at a different viewpoint and walk. Nice place if it isn’t too busy.

This is your run of the mill visitor center. It’s pretty far away from all the stuff one would want to see when visiting Olympic, but it gets the job done. Plenty of information available, knowledgeable rangers, some nice exhibits, and a plentiful gift shop.

This is your average run of the mill state park. It’s nice enough and has the usual creek and surrounding forest. I camped there for a night. The bathrooms were adequate, the campsite wasn’t too expensive (20$ I think) and it wasn’t ever too loud.

I stayed at the campground two nights. Nice enough campground, and it had showers (which is a rarity with most campgrounds). You did have to pay for hot water (50 cents per 3 minutes) and the campsites are pretty small for the price.

This was a very nice natural area. The lighthouse was pretty nice, and the cobble beach was amazing. The other cove attached to this area was also nice; it was a regular sandy beach. Would recommend a stop if you have time.
This is a relatively nice lighthouse; easy trail up and a decent view at the top. Nothing too special though. Not too many lighthouses on the Oregon coast so might still be worth the stop.
The canyon itself was cool, but most of the trails were under construction so we could only see a limited section. Wish I could’ve seen more.

This is an amazing piece of art. There are layers upon layers of petroglyphs. The more you look, the more you see. It's not very big, but it was clearly an important place to generations of native people, since they kept coming back to leave their own mark on this rock.
In some places, you can see where images had begun to fade and were carved again. In other places, the previous images were covered by something completely different. You can tell which carvings are older based on the patina that has developed on them since they were created.
It's an easy, 25-minute (or so)  drive on paved roads from the main highway to Newspaper Rock. There is a parking lot, and the rock face is right next to it. There are pit toilets that are well maintained, and Newspaper Rock itself is fenced off, but you are close enough to be able see everything. Take some time to just look--there's so much to take in.

So worth the hike! The hike itself is lovely, and a moderate 1.9 miles. However, it's also quite rocky, so care is needed on the trail. My knees and ankles were sore afterwards from all the uneven parts of the trail. Also, the trail is a bit narrow and quite busy on the weekends. There are parking lots, with additional parking on the side of the road, if needed.
And with all that being said, the view at the top is incredible (as long as you have relatively clear weather). It is truly stunning at the top, and the ledge is big enough for many groups. You may have to work your angles and wait a bit for people to move in order to get the photo you want, but just staring out at the hills and forest is enough on its own. Rattlesnake Lake below is also very picturesque.

Great museum with a very responsible attitude towards its artifacts--many things have been returned to the tribes they belong to, and some have been loaned back, but others have been replaced with something commemorating the original item or replicas, with information about the original items/the repatriation of the originals.
I liked that this museum covers things native to the Pacific Northwest, and also things from around the Pacific, from New Zealand to Vietnam to Japan. I also really liked the cards scattered throughout that teach how to pronounce native words and how Pacific Islanders navigated.
Next time I plan to explore the upstairs section on natural history.

This is a fantastic place to view the falls. The trails are paved and beautifully maintained, with lovely gardens lining the paths.
There are 3 viewing platforms at the top--2 have great views of the whole falls, while the uppermost one is a bit obstructed, so you can only see the top of the falls.
Hiking down to the lower viewing area was much easier than coming back up, and the trail is steep, but well-maintained.
There are many informative plaques-- done explain the geology, some the history of the area, some the history of the power plant, and others explain the plants found in the area.
All-in-all, this is a beautiful area and well worth the trip.

Beautiful place to visit with lots to do and see. There are campgrounds, beaches, lakes, hiking trails, scenic drives, historical landmarks, and plenty of peace and quiet if you know where to go.
Watch out for the deer, though. They have no fear and will raid your campsite for food-- even things you would never expect them to eat. They also browse right by the road.
If you're camping, many of the campsites book very early, so pay attention for when they come open--they fill up fast.

There are many wonderful examples of bonsai here, with lots of information about the individual pieces and the art itself. Most of the trees are outdoors (some require more stable temperatures and are kept in a little greenhouse), and admission is free, which is great. I can't wait to visit during other seasons to see how the bonsai change.

This is a really great science museum for all ages. It's very interactive and informative, and the exhibits are well-thought-out. We spent hours in the puzzle/science hall, and the chemistry lab has great activities to help kids learn about chemistry. Plus, part of the building is an old power plant, with a turbine still on display.

This park has so much to do: swimming, fishing, a playground, large grassy areas, picnic tables, a sand volleyball pit, tennis courts, and a lake you can kayak and boat on (bring your own).
I hear it gets really busy in the summer, though. There are a few parking lots, but they probably also fill up on busy days.

Personally, I find this really really gross, and would have avoided it if I'd known I was right by it (but I snapped a few photos anyway because I'm weird). It's iconic (why, tho), but smells just awful. If it's your thing, and you want to see it, it's right there at Pike Place Market. Good luck!

This park only has a small set of play equipment designed for kids 5 and up. It has several picnic tables, a small pavilion, some  trails, and some grassy areas to play on. It's fine, but wasn't quite what I was hoping for a younger child.
It does have lots of shade around the perimeter.

This is a great little botanical garden. They have lovely walks, plenty of places to sit and mediate, and specialty gardens. Plus, it's free.
They also have a gift shop and restrooms. I will have to see what all the seasons have to offer. So far, I can say that spring is gorgeous.

Amazing place to visit. If you're there during low tide, the tide pools have so much to see, and there are often volunteers to explain what you're seeing.
The beach is lovely, to, but don't expect much in the way of swimming-- unless you like cold water/bring a wetsuit.

Lovely botanical garden with well-planned landscaping and easy, well-groomed trails. There are many places to take nice photos. And it's free to enter. You have to pay to visit the Japanese garden, though.
Also, the parking here is limited, but free if you find a spot.

This park was cool on a hot day, has nice views, a large pavilion, and restrooms. The equipment is good and there are grassy areas to play on with a paved pathway. There isn't much space in the parking lot, but you can park on the street is you need to.

I like that this park has a dog park and a wetland area. They have a small but fun playground, and some grassy areas to play on. There are trails around the park that seem to be somewhat popular for getting in a little exercise.

This is a gorgeous and fascinating hike--but always stay on the trail, since it can be dangerous if you leave it. The trailhead is nice, with plenty of parking, pit toilets, and informative signs/maps.
This is a large, nice park with lots of facilities: a good playground, large grassy areas, a large pavilion, and a beach area where you can swim. There is also a designated area for fishing.
Gorgeous views, with good facilities (some campsites are more primitive than others, though), lots of trails to hike and beautiful drives. The park staff is helpful and knowledgeable.
Hogle Zoo is a nice little zoo with very accessible exhibits and a good selection of animals for its size. It's very clean and they are very caring towards their animals.
Beautiful nature park with neat, easy trails and lovely places to explore. The Nature Center/gift shop is informative and the employee there was friendly and helpful.
Nice wetland interactive trail on boardwalks. It's not a long trail, but there are several areas with benches and a birdwatching tower (currently undergoing repairs).
Lovely area with several trail options to explore. It's close to civilization, but remote enough to enjoy the natural surroundings and get a little outdoor therapy.
Large park with lots to do: there are baseball diamonds, grassy areas, picnic tables, playground equipment, and an area to access the river.
Fun little park with good equipment to play on, for all ages. There is also a short trail and a grassy area.
It's a nice little park. The water was still on (we went on Labor day) and the park was pretty quiet.

We stayed in the north Campground where are the sites were nice but we were close to the highway which made quite a bit of noise in the evening and night.  Campground has a mix of open and wooded sites and has some hiking trails connected. There are both toilets and a shower house. We enjoy Wisconsin Interstate State Park most for its beautiful and rugged short hikes. There is a Beach area although the beach is full of grass and small. At the beach there is also picnic tables and shower facility. There is a small playground with a slide climbing wall and four swings. The Ice Age Nature Center is worth a stop. There are several interesting exhibits about the natural history of the area as well as a good video to learn about the Ice Age and geology. The potholes are smaller on this side of the river however the park is all so much less busy than Minnesota Interstate State Park which makes it worth the extra few minutes Drive.

This is a large park with 50 miles of hiking on various types of trails. Superior hiking trails along the river are particularly beautiful .  Lots of water  exposed rock and wildflowers are visible along the trails. Biking hiking horseback riding trails are all available. Good trails for cross-country skiing in the winter . The Swinging Bridge is a great attraction near the Park Visitor Center. Beneath the bridge is a rock Beach on the river. The beach also has a lot of great exposed rock faces and surfaces to climb on. We stayed at the campground and we're happy with the location relative to all of the points of interest in trailheads. The park could use some maintenance and the water main is currently out so there is no running water anywhere in the campground or the rest of the park and the dump station is out of service. Porta potties are available in many locations temporarily.

This is a highly visited state park with a lot to offer. There are some gorgeous waterfalls to hike and see as well as camping Beach volleyball court swings and some other hiking in natural sites to see. The campground showers are very clean and nice. The campground itself is large with some electric sites and good access for large rigs. The roads are paved and level making them great for kids to bike around. The sites are large and private with good shade trees. Sadly the park experience some severe flooding earlier this year in many hiking trails around the lake as well as the beach itself are closed for repairs.

Beautiful mid-size State Park with easy access to Lake Geneva. Campground is gorgeous with lots of electric sites. The campground shower facility is very nice. Our favorite part about the campground or the large campsites with lots of grassy area behind the gravel pad for kids to play. There is a somewhat small amount of hiking trails throughout the park but they are all fairly easy and well maintained and bring you through several beautiful parts of the park. There is a lot of picnic areas with beautifully maintained grass and lots of parking throughout the park. The playground is excellent.

Small but beautiful State Park perfect for kayaking and camping. There is also a few miles of hiking through the forest and some picnic areas. At the main picnic area there is a volleyball court ball field and playground. The playground has equipment for ages 2 to 12. The beach is small but the water is mostly clean. However there is a lot of goose poop on the beach sand. The campground has water and a dump station. The campsites are wooded but open allowing for plenty of Breeze and some water views. As result of the breeze bugs are not very bad in the campground.

Beautiful Park with extensive trails and a Long Beach. Pets are welcome on one section of the beach and the other is pet free. Hiking trails explore the dunes where there are some uncommon wildflowers and other sights to see. The Nature Center is small but has some interesting exhibits to learn about the dune ecosystem. There is a ton of parking including one parking lot 4 which includes many RV and trailer parking spaces. The trail near the Nature Center also has three historical replicas showing what three stages of early human life was like in the dunes area.

A beautiful well-maintained State Park. Lots of hiking trails some of which are handicap accessible and marked with interpretive signs. Other trails seem to be seldom-used and are very narrow which makes for a good Adventure. Many beautiful flowers trees and rock outcropping along the shore. The Beach area is not large but it's clean and beautiful. The beach area has picnic tables and a changing room. The park does not have a lot of development in it and the camping is hike in only. However the roads are paved and the picnic areas are well maintained and clean.

We stopped at the Brule River State Forest site near Brule with the DNR headquarters. We hiked on the 1.6 mile Stony Hill hiking trail Loop. The trail is nice but very buggy and the Overlook has very limited visibility due to the trees and brush. The picnic area is in a small loop with limited parking and vault toilet building. There are several picnic tables and outdoor grills available in a nice grassy area with shade trees overhead. There is a canoe launch as well. The campground As Nice wooded sites with a little bit of privacy for each site.

This is a smaller State Park of only about 500 Acres but still has some very nice features. The campground is nice and well-run with private campsites in with shade from mature tree cover. Most of the sites are electric. The campground is in the center of the park and connected to all of the parks hiking trails. Although there are only a few miles of trails several have nice views of the river and lead to other interesting parts of the park such as an old growth forest preserve, Beach and playground, and boat launch.

Fort Fun Park is a large wooden playground located behind the aquatic center. The playground has areas appropriate for all ages of children and also has some handicap accessible features. There are many areas to climb, many towers and slides, swings and picnic tables. There is also a picnic shelter and a pair of sand volleyball courts. Only reason for 4 stars instead of 5 is that the structure is aging and needs maintenance to clean it up and repair many small features.

This is a fairly small children's museum with play area on two levels. There are many toys and exhibits to play with featuring local culture. Museum is orderly with friendly staff. There is a gift shop attached. Food is allowed but only on the first level. Large clean family restrooms. Exhibits are mostly design for ages 5 and younger. Good parking in two adjacent parking lots and on Street. $9 per person admission. Good place to spend a rainy afternoon.

The historical town and buildings are cool. The cave system tour is really excellent. We enjoyed the campground a lot including the nice private sites and paved Road through out. There is also a dump station. However we are giving only four stars to the park because the hiking trails almost all share access for horseback riding. There is a large amount of horse droppings throughout almost all of the hiking trails in the park.

Such a beautiful County Park. The park is rather busy even during the week however parking lots are large. There are RV spaces available. Restrooms are available on site. Walking pads are well groomed and connected to the State Park trails. There are some trails along the cliffs but if children are well-behaved they are not dangerous. Fun places to climb on rocks and stack them into formations on the shore.

Governor Dodge State Park is a large and beautiful State Park. It has many amenities including beaches hiking and multiple campgrounds. The beaches are on clean Lakes and offer canoe rentals in addition to picnic areas and clean sand beaches. There is one hiking trail that leads past a waterfall that is definitely worth seeing. There are also horse trails and biking trails around the park.

Gorgeous hiking along cliffs, rivers, and waterfalls. Observation tower is fun, but limited views due to surrounding tree canopy. Campground is nice with lots of trees and privacy. Shower house, vault toilet houses, and rv dump station. Concession area has playground, sandbox and trail heads around a large parking lot. Beach is small but beautifully clean water and sand on Loon Lake.

The park headquarters is a small building and includes information desks with very friendly helpful Rangers and a small camp store with lots of Peninsula State Park souvenirs such as mugs t-shirts and hoodies. Although there are several campgrounds they can be difficult to get into without making reservations far in advance or showing up the day of and getting a site for the night.

Very cool UNESCO ancient historical site. Limited hiking and walking around the historical Village site and some picnic tables and grills. Excellent informational plaques for a self-guided tour through the site. There is a manual water pump and and clean pit toilets. Good parking lots. Definitely worth a stop and interesting for the whole family.

Great tour of the mine, and a lot to see on the surface without paying for the tour.  Our 3 and 5 year olds loved it.  Beyond the mine there is nice hiking, lake access, biking on the Mesabi trail, a new day use area near the new campground east of the mine area with picnic areas and fishing pier.

A practical but beautiful state capitol building. Guided tours are available during limited hours but self guided tours are allowed as well. Visitors can access the observation level on the 18th floor for nice views of the town. Both chambers of the house and Senate are also open to view.

Excellent modern wild west theme playground. It has large areas for tots, preschoolers, and older kids plus wheelchair access and features. There is also a splash pad, public restrooms, picnic shelters, and reservable party room. There is a nice parking lot and additional street parking.

A favorite state park on the North Shore. Not nearly as busy as Gooseberry Falls but absolutely beautiful waterfalls, lakeshore, and lots of hiking. Very nice, private sites at the campground, but no trailer dump station. Hiking is strenuous and not accessible at all for strollers.

The nature center building is worth visiting, especially with young kids. Friendly, knowledgeable staff. The beach is gorgeous and protected from wind. Nice walking trails and some uncommon wildflowers. Hike to the point for beautiful views.
Amazing park with playground with modern equipment, lots of picnic tables and grills, picnic shelters, volleyball court, restrooms, basketball hoops, Fishing Pier, Beach, and new boat launch.
Interesting historical site with an informational plaque explaining additional history of this location. A small parking lot and boat ramp. A good place for kids to wade into the water.
Nice staff and paved walking paths. We pushed a stroller with no issue. Museum teaches a little about the geology and a lot about the native people and traditions of the area.

There's a bit of everything to do here including an off leash dog park, soccer fields galore, a few playgrounds, rock climbing and during the summer there is a concert venue which usually has pretty well-known bands. Parking is definitely not an issue during the weekdays but it does cost $1.00 The only real issue is that the park is used as a cut-through to avoid traffic so you end up with a lot of people that drive much faster through the park than they are supposed to.

Nice open park for the kids to run and play. Couple different play structures within view of each other, set up for different age ranges. There is a covered picnic table area and bathrooms close to the primary playground. Nice, easy and flat walking trails around the outer perimeter of the park which are good for strollers and walking dogs. Doggie waste bag dispenser located by the parking lot. Most notable, this park is absolutely beautiful during rhododendron season.

We've been coming here for over a decade. The exhibits are a lot of fun, though most of them haven't changed much, there are some newer exhibits worth checking out. My kid has yet to get bored with most of the older exhibits here. There are always new projects/experiments to try at the Tinker Tank which was a lot of fun for my son and we were able to work together to test theories. The Imax seats are uncomfortable, if you plan on watching anything longer than an hour.

There's a really large, well maintained playground for kids of all ages. The open field is great for soccer and getting the kids to burn off energy unless there's Frisbee golf being played. The Frisbee golf course is pretty fun but not as extensive as some others around the area (and you do have to play and maneuver through the other people using the park). The trails are muddy during the rainy weather but shaded and great to use during warmer weather.

Large open park space with Frisbee golf. There's a community garden area just past the parking lot with plenty of large cans for compost. Lots of shaded trails along the creek and open area trails for enjoying the sun. This is an on-leash only park but the trails are very well maintained and open for walking dogs. The trails do connect with other longer public trails with horseback riding and bike riding available.

This has always been a good place to get out and walk shaded trails with dogs. There are different levels of difficulty with the trails and some I wouldn't recommend trying with kids or dogs. Most of the trails drop down to the lake and there is a bathroom and picnic tables at the bottom. The playground is being updated but is a large play area and definitely keeps kids busy.
dislikes: Some trails unsuitable for kids or dogs

reviews_attraction.text: During the week this is a wonderful area to come have lunch or walk the dogs without a lot of people around though you will have to deal with the pushy seagulls and pigeons. There's a boat launch, kayaking rentals, and playground for kids. Weekends here are a lot busier and parking can be difficult to find near the beach.

Busy but well maintained, open area park. Play structure is basic with six different height slides. The playground is close to the parking lot and the bathrooms. There are also volleyball courts and soccer fields available for use. Not the best park for walking dogs as there's a lot of kids in a condensed area.

A very well maintained and clean park. Two separate playground areas with a basketball court and small water park area (for hotter days) over near the northeast parking lot. The main problem with the park is that parking is chaotic and sometimes limited depending on soccer games.

The playground has been recently updated with more safe and usable play equipment for children of all ages. Tennis courts, baseball field, skate park and bike riding trails for the older kids. Covered picnic areas and BBQ grills near the lake for a nice view of the water.

A great park for taking your kids or walking dogs. Lots of shaded trails and creeks around the outlining area of the park. Open field and animals (horses, goats, and ponies) for kids to stay busy and entertained. There's a tire swingset but no playground equipment.

The miniature golf course is updated and always fun to play. Definitely fun for children. It can get a lot busier on the weekends and you will have to wait for a short time between holes. There are some okay shaded areas to wait.

Smaller beach area for picnics and playing in the water. Parking can be limited and the beach can get crowded at times. There are a few trails to walk behind the lighthouse. Kayaking is popular along this stretch of coast.

One of the Seattle city parks that are close enough to downtown but stays fairly quiet and less crowded. Nice views of Lake Union and Gas Works Park. There's a water park here for kids during the summer and playground.

A very pleasant area to bring your children to learn about marine life and explore tide pools. The trail down to the water can be steep and the rocks are slippery so good boots with traction are recommended.
I've been to several other Japanese gardens and this is by far the most authentic and beautiful one I've ever been to. A new perspective every few paces you walk.
Areas of the park are currently under construction/maintenance. Trails for walking dogs and hiking. The playground equipment is newer and well maintained.
Lots of fun activities for kids. Not much shaded areas during the summer heat but there are a few hiking trails around the outer edge of the park.
Fun and shady park for kids. A few picnic tables and lots of bench seating around the playground. Litter and graffiti are the only issues here.
The playground is small and outdated, but shaded. Lots of trails to explore and a nice shady trail system that is perfect for walking dogs.
A nice open park with playground. Fairly decent trails around the park for dog walking. The public space tends to be messy from litter.
Absolutely beautiful place to photograph. A bit of a walk down from the parking lot but worth it. Bring food and enjoy the view.
Even with all the smoke from the fires and the heat, it's still a beautiful area with lots of historic information available.
The park is less crowded in the evenings but the mosquitoes are very prevalent when the sun starts to go down.
Lots of spacious areas to walk. Kid's play area is new and gives the little ones lots of things to do.

Sunrise is only open for a brief period of the year when enough snow has melted in the summer and before the storms of late autumn. It is the highest point you can reach by vehicle in the park,  and has full service facilities including a ranger station,  restaurant, gift shop, and restrooms.  Many of the most magnificent trails in the park originate from Sunrise.  Mid July is often the peak time to visit for wild flowers at Grand Park. This area is generally busy, especially on weekends, but has ample parking. An excellent place to watch the night sky, as well. The food at the restaurant is good, but limited to burgers, hot dogs, sandwiches, and soups, with desserts.  It is pricey but satisfying after a day of hiking.

This hike is one of the best day hikes in Mt. Rainier National Park. The road up is gravel for about 15 miles or so, and only open once the snow is sufficiently melted. This is a very popular trail, so go early! It begins as a part of the Wonderland Trail near Mowich Lake. After less than a mile you'll encounter a fork with markings for Tolmie Peak. The trail is fairly easy going to Eunice Lake. From the lake a huge V-shaped switchback will take you to the fire lookout. On a clear day you get views of Mt. St. Helens, Mt. Baker, Glacier Peak, and a real closeup of Rainier. In July many of the wild flowers were in bloom throughout the meadows beyond Lake Eunice. Overall, a fantastic hike that's not too difficult!

There is something for everyone at the SAM, from galleries of contemporary American art,  old European masters, an extraordinary collection of Native American works from the Pacific Northwest,  to ancient Hellenic and Egyptian pieces. The reservation system is in 30 minute time windows which allow visitors to space themselves out well, and provides a contactless admission system. Don't worry about your coat, they have a self coat check at the door. Maps and additional exhibit information is made available via easy to use QR codes placed throughout the museum,  and plenty of friendly staff is throughout the gallery space to offer help, or answer questions. A great place to spend a day with the family!

The Sol Duc Trailhead is a pathway to some of the loveliest areas of the Olympic Peninsula,  from the famous falls a mile up the road to the solitude and splendor of the High Divide and it's views of the Hoh Valley, Olympus, and the other great peaks of the Olympics. Alpine lakes are in abundance off this 18 mile loop, in addition to lush forests. In spring and autumn mushrooms will abound,  while in the summer huckleberries and blueberries dominate the upper slopes of this trail. One of the best trails to experience the diversity of the Peninsula as well as to experience wildlife.  And there's refreshing hot springs just down the street when you get back from your hike or backpacking trip!

This trail near Leavenworth offers incredible views of Dragontail Peak and Colchuck Lake, as well as Stuart Lake. Rated as difficult, the trip to the lake is about seven and a half miles round trip. Come early, as parking fills quickly and parking on the roadside is strictly prohibited by the forest service.  This trail is one of the routes into the core zone of the Enchantments area of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness view Aasgard Pass, to the left of Dragontail Peak from Colchuck Lake. The route up to the pass is extremely difficult, requiring good backcountry navigation skills. Camping at the lake is by permit only except for a period in the off season from the end of October to May 15.

One of the newest additions to the trail network surrounding North Bend, the Mt Teneriffe trail is approximately 6 miles long with around 3300' gain. It provides mostly gentle grades, but is quite long. What makes this area five stars is the vast array of hiking options. Teneriffe, formerly Kamikaze, Falls is also accessible from the trailhead,  as well as two different connections to nearby Mount Si via the ridgeline trail near the top, or the Talus Loop about a third of the way up the way to Teneriffe.  The trail does thin out once you enter the forest on the ridge line, so be sure to look for the black blazes marking the way to the top. Pit toilets available at the parking lot.

This relatively moderate hike up to Summit Lake is about 6.5 miles roundtrip with 1300' of elevation gain offers rewarding views of Mount Rainier and the Cascades Range, as well as two alpine lakes. In June and July the forest floor is covered in Queens Cup. Wildlife can be abundant in the area. It is not uncommon to spot a black bear, marmots,  or even a mountain goat. There are many campsites available for backpackers at Summit Lake. Be sure to register at the Carbon River ranger station if you're going to do any camping.  Be advised, the road up to the trailhead is very rough. It is doable in a sedan, but something with AWD and more clearance is highly recommended.

Mt Rainier National Park is an amazing place, from the alpine visitor centers at Sunrise and Paradise, to the many smaller entrances to the park. For amazing views of the mountain, go to Tolmie Peak off Mowich Lake, or practice your mountaineering skills on the way up to Camp Muir on that seemingly endless snowfield. Ranger Falls off the Carbon River entrance is a spectacular spring waterfall, and Narada Falls on the way to Paradise is just as amazing. Rainier has something for everyone. Most importantly, when visiting the park be sure to stay on trails and leave no trace. The wilderness is fragile, and should be preserved for everyone to enjoy.

First, the last couple miles of the road up to this trailhead are pretty gnarly. The road is narrow, steep, and potholed. Watch out for traffic coming the other direction, and be prepared for some awkward maneuvering. That said, there were 4-door sedans that made it up. Just go slow. Once at the trailhead there is ample parking and a slew of spots to pitch a tent quickly before you head off to climb Adams. However, the parking lot can and does fill quickly on weekends in late spring and early summer.  Two composting toilets are present and well-maintained. Be sure to get your climbing permit from either the Trout Lake or Randle range stations.

This whole area I'd an amazing part of the Mt. Margaret backcountry.  Camping is by permit in designated sites reservable through recreation.gov. Day hiking opportunities are abundant, however access to water is scarce, especially in late summer when the snow has mostly melted out. Bring good sun protection,  as much of this area is exposed with little to no tree cover. Easily some of the most picturesque and enchanting landscapes in Washington.  Be on the lookout for elk, mountain goats, and black bears. Wildflower season is usually around mid June through July. Abundant berries like trails and are usually ripe by mid July to August.

The trail up to Lake Serene is forested for about the first mile and a half, and gentle. About half a mile after reaching the side trail to Bridal Veil Falls, which is well worth the trip (short but steep), the trail will begin a series of switchbacks that will continue until the you reach Lake Serene. These are rocky and wet in the spring and autumn.  Trekking poles recommended on the way down. Lake Serene lives up to its name, though in spring you can often hear the roar of distant avalanches.  Abundant mushrooms in 5he spring and fall in this area.

This Federally maintained area is a superb stop along US 101 if you're making your way down the coast. Vast numbers of migratory birds are present in the summer, as well as hundreds, if not thousands of seals. There are excellent tidal pools that are accessible via trail. Grey whales can be observed migrating from this point as well. The old Yaquina Head Lighthouse is worth a stop in itself. This area is covered by the America The Beautiful Pass if you have one.

This short, well-maintained trail through old growth to the picturesque Marymere Falls is well-worth a quick stop. For the more adventurous,  this trail also offers access to Mt Storm King, with panoramic views of Lake Crescent,  as well as access to the deep backcountry of Olympic National Park.  The trail to the falls is an easy one, while the branch leading up Storm King is strenuous,  and has some exposure beyond the end of the maintained trail.

This entire area is underappreciated, being in the shadow of the Columbia Gorge to the south, Mt St Helen's to the west, and Rainier to the north. Offering fantastic camping lakes, alpine climbs, and forest trails, the Mt Adams recreation area has something for everyone. Ranger stations in Randall and Trout Lake can offer plenty of excellent advise for enjoying this area. If you plan on climbing Mt. Adams you'll need to swing by and get a permit.

Small but fantastic state park near Olympia on far south end of Puget Sound. Mudflats at low tide offer an astonishing variety of sealife, including a variety of crabs, and razor clams. There are excellent second growth forests with easy hiking trails just off the sandy beach. Sometimes whales are visible from the beach area. The park would be an excellent place for a family picnic on a nice day. Well worth the price of a discovery pass.

Well maintained trailhead at the end of NF-11, offering dispersed camping along the road as well as pit toilets at the trailhead. Trail splits after a mile to the east bank Baker Lake Trail. Great old growth forest, excellent lake and river views. In autumn this is one of the best places to see fall colors in Washington.  Easy grades on the lake and river trails make this excellent for people of all ages.

This trail is an excellent, easily accessible trail for most individuals to explore a temperate rainforest. It is flush with informative placards, travels through diverse forest environments,  and is interconnected to a series of trails for those that would like to explore further. Be sure to drive all the way around the lake for some amazing scenery once you finish this trail.

Deer Park is a gem of a local in the Olympics. The Grand Ridge trail that departs from the ranger station offers a fantastic route to Maiden Head Oeak, and Elk Mountain beyond it, with humbling views of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, Mount Olympus, Hurricane Ridge, and a host of other peaks all the way through to Obstruction Point at the other end.

Fantastic beach on Puget Sound. Lots of parkibg, plays grounds, bird ponds, and fire pits are just some of the features. Dogs are allowed, and the park offers clean restrooms.  This is one of the best spots in Seattle to catch a sunset at. There are limited covered BBQ pavilions as well. As the weather improves, be sure to grab a firepit early!

This is a decent hike but be prepared for a conga line. Parking lot will fill up early on an ok day, so be prepared to hoof it in to the trail head from further down the road. When hang gliders are active here be sure to keep a lookout as they land in a field you must cross to start the hike. Otherwise this has some excellent views of Rainier.

Excellent facilities. Lots of parking as well as established campsites. Two pit toilets at either end. The road up is in excellent condition. There is a climbing registrar at the trail head. Don't expect quiet here. People will be coming and going at all hours. Still an excellent place to catch a rest before heading up the mountain.

This North Seattle park offers a kid play area with water fountains in the summer, a baseball diamond and sports field, as well as wooded trails and an excellent off leash dog park. Additional parking and restrooms are available off the 3rd Avenue entrance.

Kerry Park is a great place to get that postcard picture of Seattle with Rainier in the distance. It is always busy on nice days, especially around sunset. If you plan on setting up a tripod for pictures, arrive an hour or so before sunset to get a spot.

ONP best NP! Seriously,  though, this place is gorgeous, be it along the coast or high up in the Olympics.  There is abundant wildlife everywhere, as well. If you were only going to visit one National Park in the PNW, this is the one to visit.
A great day hike!  Be sure to explore around the lake. Come early for parking, as this is very popular.

We didn't have much time, unfortunately. After stopping at the visitor center and the main river overlooks we drove to Cucumber falls parking lot. It was on a Wednesday but the parking lot was full, so we parked on Middle Ridge Rd and walked from there to Cucumber Falls, after that we took the Great Gorge trail to Meadow Run. We saw river rapids and wildflowers and boaters on the way there. The natural slide at Meadow Run is really long and there were many young people having fun in this area. It was a great summer time experience and we felt like we have seen enough of the park in this short time. FYI the parking lots at Cucumber falls and Meadow run have no bathrooms so if you need one you need to go to the visitor center

The parking lot is relatively small, can fit about 10 cars, there's another parking lot, even smaller. This is a good thing because this park can never get over crowded. The scenic Vista on the yellow trail is okay. Not a big deal if you miss it. We picked up a trail with blue/purple/gray color from the main parking lot which goes along the stream. After you pass the second waterfall that is listed on the map go a little further down the stream, and that's where the second bridge was located. That was my favorite part. Then we got back mostly on the red trail. Hiked almost 8 miles but that includes the yellow.

I recommend going to visit the side views to the right after you get up the steps, also the Mill Creek Quarry Vista on the Standing Stone Trail which is a little over 1.5 miles from the Ledge Quary Vista. Just follow the orange blazes. The view is outstanding. However, we went all the way to Shorb's summit and weren't impressed, it was just a pile of rocks. There were also people who were scrambling on the rocks by the Ledge Quary and we did the same, but didn't think it's worth the effort

There was a storm in the forecast and we wanted to see as much as possible, so we drove around the whole thing and stopped at the most important points, the two lighthouses, Perry Monument, house boats, there is one area in the very beginning of the loop called the Feather which is like a walking pier but it's a form of public art. We loved it!! I wanted to walk the Gull point trail but the park ranger at the visitor center told us that it's under water. Bummer!

The skywalk is great and not scary at all because of the high railing.
We also did the trail on the bottom that goes inbetween to the ruins of the bridge and you can go all the way to the other side and see the twisted rails. Make sure you wear long pants though because there's some bushwacking involved.
The visitor center is great too. I got a PA State parks passport book from the gift shop and now looking forward to getting more stamps in it!

We parked in the Kildoo parking lot and had to go down steps to get to the Mill, Spillway and covered bridge, from there we hiked a loop to the Eckert Bridge and back, on both sides of the Slippery rock river. Even did a little jaunt on the Breakneck trail. The tree roots, rocks, moss and river rapids were beautiful. After this we drove to Hell's hollow trailhead and visited this part of the park as well

If you are planning to walk/hike you may want to print out the map they have online. Very pretty little park, the trails are well marked and easy to follow. Good facilities - plenty of parking, restrooms, bridges, boardwalks, picnic pavilions, benches, boat docks, fishing piers, accommodations for the disabled etc.

We visited in mid-July and Adam Falls had almost no water in it. The trail was nice though because of the rocks. We also hiked the Flat Rock trail which has the ruins of the old building and the water slide as well. Wish there was information about the ruins in the park map or on the trail

I walk there very often,  beautiful in all seasons! I wanted to add that in the winter they have the pictures from the photo contest in the Nature center.  I love that exhibit.  And this winter you were able to vote for your favorite picture in each category.

There was a small parking lot and Porta potties. A few people were having picnics and taking pictures. Beautiful views of the city. There was a building with an observation deck but unfortunately it was closed, I suppose because of the coronavirus

Lovely state Park,  we had just a couple hours and did the Double Run trail and so glad we picked that one!  It was beautiful. You can drive to the Canyon Vista on an unpaved road. The Loyalsock creek is very scenic too

The whole walk a little less than a mile long in a lollipop shape. The path is covered with gravel. You can see the Swatara creek, some graffiti, wildflowers and butterflies. In April it's full of Virginia bluebells

Large parking lot, nice bathrooms, gift store and Overlooks, we hiked the short Overlook Trail. Unfortunately the Turkey path trail was closed. There's also a Lookout tower but we didn't have time to go there.

There is a 5 mile loop hike around the lake with several small hills which is an excellent training hike.  The swimming pool is great too. And the lake is good for boat sports. It's beautiful in all seasons
Loved this park with the blue quartzite stone,  occasional streams with waterfalls coming from the sides of the main trail,  the two big statues,  beautiful bridges and the hermit's cave
Went with a group of friends from Harrisburg. Visited Dingmans and Raymondskill falls too while we were there. Hiked all trails at Bushkill, there was one confusing part on the map.
Light traffic on the hiking trails but super busy beach. If you are doing the Saw Mill run trail in the summer months, please be mindful there's a section covered in poison ivy
The new butterfly garden is lovely and shaped like a butterfly too! Went on the nature trail that goes down to the Conoduguinet creek and that was a nice detour.
We printed out the Self-guided walking tour brochure provided by the Cumberland County historical society and followed the markers.  It was so much fun!
We did the boundary trail.  It was well marked but we ran into this flooded area. Wish there were some boardwalks to help us navigate the marsh better.
You won't be able to find parking on the weekend so I recommend going during the week.  It's a beautiful place with trails on both sides of the stream.
The wood fire pizza is really good, we were very happy with the service as well. They had warm spiced wine which hit the spot on this cold day.
The Boulder field was fairly easy to walk on and the Shades of death trail is beautiful. We also went to Hawk Falls and did the Orchard Trail.
The Creek trail is really nice and also the end of the Janie trail. Most of the trails are covered by gravel so it doesn't get too muddy
It was pretty cool - seeing the pagoda from there and after that we drove to the pagoda and saw the witches hat from there

Really cool, interesting cars as well as photos, films, paintings and other art displays. Ask about the annual Art Car Parade and see video footage from past parades. Visit regularly as the exhibits change frequently to view the most spectacular cars imaginable. THIS IS A NON PROFIT ORGANIZATION SO PLEASE SHOW SUPPORT and its free but please don't touch these one of a kind masterpieces.

See it all and do it all here. It will take a while day to cover all of this resort from the water park to the Aquarium pyramid to Rainforest and more. The Colonel Paddle boat will take you for a nice cruise on the bay as well. See seals, sharks, monkey's,  birds, penguins and much more. Visit the Lone Star Flight museum next door before leaving for WW2 vintage planes as well.

Great place to spend a day, evening, weekend or even week. Hotel on site and other lodging within walking distance. Excellent choices for dining in area to fit all budgets, amusement park for kids of all ages and multiple bar choices on pier as well. See Kemah Boardwalk after the NASA space center and Kemah Boardwalk tour  with Allstar Transportation and Limousine in Houston.

This was such a cool adventure to go on with my dog but keep your dog on leash and close as there are many surprises on the trail. We saw Armadillo, rabbits, turtles, bull frogs and came within feet of large snakes that wont bother you even though deadly. Stay ON the trail, observe, photograph and keep going.

This was awesome! Saw the infamous "Old Sparky" and lots of other cool stuff as well as items confiscated from notorious outlaws Bonnie and Clyde. With the admission only being $5 it's well worth the stop considering it's right on Interstate 45 Service Road so take a road break and stop by.

Really cool neighborhood park! Doesn't look like much from the street but there are trails that go around back with ponds, walking paths, tables for cook outs and viewing nature. Doesn't get overcrowded so its the PERFECT PLACE TO HOLD A PARTY OR REUNION.

Very interesting attraction with many exhibits that change so you should visit at least once per year. Visit on a tour with personal guide from Allstar Transportation Limousine & Tours and do city tour before going. Pickup from your hotel.

A must see attraction when visiting the island. Don't settle for just an exterior view. You must enter to experience the magnificence of this historical home once occupied by one of Galvestons most prominent families.

I always enjoy this tour with some of it on land and some in the water. Good way to get and overview of the islands most popular attractions before deciding what you want to do. Get on in front of the Pleasure Pier.

Coolest park I've seen. There's musical instruments built into the park for you to play. Great place to plan family party as there is much room for kids to roam yet still be seen. Also has a football field there too

Loved it! Very interesting and one of those MUST SEE type places. Took lots of unbelievable photos but won't show all so go by and spend $10. Which was worth it. It's not spooky, not scary just very interesting.
Great experience,  knowledgeable guide. This was Houston's original airport. There's also an annual raffle for a FREE plane. Visit and purchase your tickets for next give sway. Good luck!
A must see attraction when visiting Galveston. Formerly Greshams Castle and a 1900 storm survivor. Filled will lavish furnishings and exotic stone, Mohagany staircases, stained windows.
Phenomenal experience as this is a location we often bring visitors and it is mind blowing each time. Board and explore the only Battleship used in both World War 1 and World War II.
A 5 star park between Museum and Medical Center District with endless activity options from museums, art, zoo, paddle boating and train rides to shows at Miller outdoor theater.
A must-see attraction when visiting Houston. Book a tour with Allstar Transportation limousine and touring service for transport from Houston and get guided tour through NASA.
Fantastic display of artifacts with a great gift shop on location as well. A catered BALL ROOM is also available for rent to hold events, parties or family reunions.
An awesome attraction near the Strand on Galveston island. See it and more on the Galveston Island Tour#4 with Allstar Transportation Limousine and Tours
Great park and my favorite in Clear Lake. Stop by after Nasa Space center visit or take good and family for day trip. Fishing piers and boat ramp 24hrs
This was really cool park with huge, duck filled lake, diverse visitors, friendly environment, good parking, nice views, police patrolled
One of Houston's many fantastic parks located on Buffalo Bayou. Walk up the spiralled path and read some of Houston's history as you go.
Must see Houston attraction where Sam Houston and his army massacred General Santa Anna's army to gain independence from Mexico.
This is one of nd favorite parks in the Hotel District.  Nice restaurant snack bar inside. Excellent place to take your kids.
Highly recommended!  Haven't learned so much in 1 day since college and had so much fun in the process. Thanks!
A must see attraction when visiting Houston and if you're a resident and haven't been here yet "shame on you".

This is an excellent location in north-central pennsylvania, on route 120, about 3 hours north of harrisburg, in clinton county, about an hour north of state college. you pass over a large bridge (west branch susquehanna) and you actually go into the town of hyner. there are many park signs all around so you wont get lost. it is located next to hyner run state park. you have to go up this windy road, that has to be about 5 miles long from the mail road. its is paved, but there arent any markings and its very hard to see around turns. there was once a near-accident from someone speeding down the mountain.

this has an excellent view of the whole valley for miles around, you can see mountains everywhere, and the bridge and town you just drove through are recognizable. it is one of the best views or scenic vistas in pennsylvania, even though the park is only 6 acres large.

its is a great place to go and watch the leaves change colors and just sit down and have a picnic. there are a number of informational monuments and small gazebos that have maps and history and such. there is a wooden ramp that leads straight down the mountain that is used by hanggliders. this is a very popular sport for leaf-peepers and just people who love outdoors.

i *really* *really* *highly* suggest this place, if you check out my pictures its the 3rd or 4th one. it could be the coolest one ever, there is a stone overlook that was constructed decades ago. the park itself is small, i'd say under 10 acres, but has one of the best views for miles around!

"Time flies when you're having fun" This was a pretty fun museum, with all sorts of information about clocks, watches, the history of keeping time. It had all sorts of information from the earliest time pieces (sundials, water clocks, the Antikythera Mechanism) incense clocks, water clocks, to modern wrist watches, atomic clocks, and how they tell time in space.

It literally has all you could ever want to know about Horology (the science of keeping time) Did you know the ancient Babylonians came up with the 60 second minute, and 60 minute hour? Pretty neat. Prior to the contiguous USA adopting the four standard time zones (eastern, central, mountain and pacific) in 1883 there were some 21 separate time recognized across the country.

The exhibits were pretty nice, there were literally hundreds of time keeping devices there. It took us about 45 minutes to cruise through the museum, we didnt spend much time in the gift shop, though we did pick up a free poster. Fall Hours are Tues-Sat 10a-5p, Sunday Noon-4p, closed Mondays, Admission is currently 8.00 for adults, 7.00 for seniors, 4.00 for children. AAA& Military discount.

After looking at the website and asking other people for info I decided to go on a trip to williamsport. Looked on Yelp and then google maps to get basic info, then check the county tourism website for specific info. as it turns out the Lycoming County Historical Society & Taber Museum are in the same building. Admission was 5.00/pp or 4.00 with AAA discount.

It was a large building with different exhibits that explained all about life in the area, from prehistory to modern times. There was info from native american times, the revolutionary war, civil war, lumber era and modern times. There were literally hundreds if not thousands of artifacts and objects from the past.

It was a self guided tour that was fairly interesting (to me.) We spent about an hour or so there, checking everything out, reading plaques, looking at paintings (both local and national) and taking pictures. There were several other families visiting the same day.

There is also a very large train section in the downstairs part. Im not much or a train guy, but it was pretty neat. Children would certainly have a great time there.

Leonard Harrison State Park, is located about 10 miles west of Wellsboro, Pa, near the northern border with New York State. it is about 3 hours north of harrisburg. this is the pennsylvania grand canyon. it is a sight to behold if you love nature or the outdoors. the park has a wonderful overlook and several hiking and biking paths as well as hunting areas. you should check it out. has the "overlook trail" where you go out its not too too bad. you need a decent pair of shoes. then there is the "Turkey path" a formidable hiking experience, and probably the most difficult i've been on in my life. they say it's 1 mile down and 6 miles back up. it is about from the top of the canyon to the bottom where the river is, in zig-zaggy trails. there are some observation platforms and a waterfall at the bottom. it links up with the rail trails at the bottom of the canyon.

there's also in-season hunting, fishing, rustic camping and a great big tower that gives you a great view of the valley. Rail Trails link this area to Jersey Shore, PA 62 miles to the south.

This is a great park in northeast Pennsylvania, near the intersecion of I-81 and I-80, about 15 miles from Hazelton, Pa. It has miles of hiking and biking trails, a lake, camping and fishing.

The thing that sets this apart is the huge boulder field there. It is a National Natural Monument. It can be reached by driving up a 6 mile dirt road that's marked from the main street. It is one of only two left in North America. It is basically about 5 football lengths long and about 2 wide of nothing but boulders on top of boulders on top of more boulders. they range in size from a small pebble, to about 6 x 3 feet across.

It is one of the coolest things I've ran across when traveling across our great state. I just ran from one side to the other last time. they make this strange crunchy noise when you step on them. They just ask that you dont take any with you or deface any of the ones there.

Memorial Lake state park is a pretty cool park that off the Annville / Indiantown gap Exit of I-81 North. It has fishing, boating and hiking. It is a decent place to rent a boat (canoe, kayak, paddleboat, rowboat) and just go out and relax on the lake. It does have a hiking / jogging path all around it, which is one of the few I've ever totally completed. It consists of 230 acres, which is surrounded by Fort Indian Gap military Reservation, near the base of Blue Mountain. It was built to honor servicemen who served in WWI and WWII, hence the name.

Its great for family events, there are always people there having fun and relaxing. Cookouts, pavilions, you name it. There's a modest concession stand and also a small playground for children. Accessible by three different roads.

Stopped here once for the afternoon. Turned out to be a very fun afternoon. Moon Dancer Winery is a very large mansion / chateau on several acres overlooking the beautiful Susquehanna River, just outside of Wrightsville PA.

There's lots of local artwork, paintings, photographs and jewelry (as well as logo tasting glasses) for sale throughout the building. They have samples for most of their wines that are sold there (18-32 a bottle), at a small bar inside. There's live music every weekend (2-5pm), and they have special weekend Festivals (20.00 per person) where food + wine are available for sale.

Available for private parties, bridal showers, weddings, etc. Ample parking available, Hours: Wed, Thur, Fri noon-5pm, Sat & Sunday 11am-6pm
likes: Facilities & Services: Wine samples, Live music, Special festivals, Private event hosting

reviews_attraction.text:
This railroad connected Hollidaysburg with Johnstown back in the day. now it's just a museum that is currently open 7 days a week. There is a Museum and has the Lemon House, some railroad tracks, a hiking trail and a Bridge. It explains how the trains were taken up the mountain and what safety precautions prevented them from falling back down. You can go through the house which dates from the 1800's and check out how the people lived and what they wore, etc.

There was an entrance fee of 4 dollars per person, plenty of parking and the rangers there were very friendly. It was soemthing neat to check out because we were in the area, but other than that it was actually pretty boring. and I like trains and historical places.

Richard M. Nixon County Park is one of the best park / nature centers we have been to. Huge diorama of nature. 180+ acres of land, complete with several ponds and miles of hiking trails.

The nature center itself has a huge collection of stuffed quail, turkey, bison, elk, beats, deer, antelope, etc. The story is that a famous hunter in the York County area donated his collection that had been gathered from multiple international hunting trips prior to his death.

There is a welcome center, small library, bird viewing arae, bathrooms and 2 floors of exhibits. There's a really nice bird and butterfly exhibit. Large dinosaur mural is a hit with the kids.

Be sure to visit Perrydell once you are finished here.

This ia cool little state park next to Altoona. The coolest thing they have there is an old Church that has a large little brown bat colony that's home to about 20,000 bats in the summer. They have educational programs and tours in the summer, but nothing cool in the winter.  Also they have a set of old Kilns that you can hike back to and check out. that's how they made steel a long time ago, they'd superheat these giant furnaces with charcoal and wood and it'd get hot enough to melt it. They are like 100 years old and still in pretty good condition.

Also if you look carefully around this place you can find some Amish going down the road in their buggies.

The national apple museum was a pleasant visit. it was staffed by two elderly people in their 60's and 70's,  got the sense that they were volunteers. They have all kinds of history, photos and equipment that tells the life of apples, farms, original settlers, geography and ecology of the surrounding area. this is a 1 hour tour, in a nearly century old barn. The tour was okay, we didnt get to finish the entire thing because the museum was closing. admission was 2.00 per person, 1.75 for seniors. We were told after the tour we'd get a free glass of apple juice.... though i didnt see any. Knouse and Motts & Mussellman have area operations.

Cowan's Gap is a picturesque state park nestled in the Blue mountains in Franklin county. It has a lake that is open for swimming, fishing, ice fishing and ice skating all year long. It really really is beautiful, and not that far from my home, Harrisburg Pa. It doesnt have anything that's SUPER special compared to the other parks, it has a concession stand and a canoe rental place... but it's beautiful to look at in the fall. Its over 1080 acres, and has a great trail all around it. it took a little while to walk, but still worth it. There are cabins and tents available for overnight camping.

This park is literally surrounded by mountains on three sides. it has a wonderful lake that has a little area to swim in, there is a small food stall that's open mostly in the summer and spring. it's closed on mondays. You just get off the i-81 exit for rt 233, Newville and Kings Gap. turn right and it's about 10 miles up the road. It has some really cool trails, you can walk to the top of the mountain in about 15 minutes and take some great pictures. has over 270 acres of woodland and a 2 acre lake.

Great spot to picnic in the mountains. There a round  green tin carousel pavilion that protects the tables. Small play area and a stream nearby are nice to play in with the kids.

While not much to look at, this is the oldest state park in Pennsylvania, having neen under the Commonwealths ownership for 113 years. Originally a furnace, then a picnicing spot and now a state park. Small parking lot sits just across route 233. Restrooms are available.

Adams-Ricci has courts for the following: Tennis, pickleball, volleyball, horseshoe, bocce, soccer, baseball & t-ball. There's a nice concession stand, ample shade, plenty of benches and three playgrounds. As of 2019 the playground at the intersection of Penn and Magaro has been completely renovated. There are smaller ones deeper in the park.

Several shaded pavilions are open as well. This park is very Kid and Pet friendly.

Nice little park with amazing views of the river! Techincally you are viewing the Lake Aldred area of the Susquehanna River. Ample shading & picnic tables abound. Consider this spot if you want to get away from the hustle & bustle and traffic of the surrounding area. There is both a beginners trail and a much more advanced trail to consider. Parking is available, but it can fill up pretty quick!

GPS DD: 39.84545, -76.34405

Great for kids aged 2 - 10, they can let their imagination run wild. Several rooms to play: a factory, dressup land, a grocery store, a farm, face painting area, post office & jobsite truck play area. They have a per day admission of $9.50/pp or annual membership of $99.00 per family. Free parking.

There's a nice waterfall trail at this county park. Sweet Arrow Waterfall might only be 15' or so high, but it is a good view, and easily accessible.

Sweet Arrow Lake also has a decent trail system, a nice pavillion, fishing access and a small playground.

Worth a visit.

We walked about 3 miles. As Daily in County's newest park, it is about 400 acres. There's some decent flat trails, at least three break stations, which are Adirondack Chairs. The entrance rid right across the street from 3B's Ice Cream in Halifax.

this is a really great place to take the kids. there two small playgrounds, a basketball court, a large pavilion, rest rooms and ample parking. plenty of shade. both playgrounds are newer (2018+) and well maintained.

Great place for ansocially distant hike. Small lake with frogs, salamanders and fish. Love this place. Its a conservation area, so ot will not bw developed in the futire. Worth a stop of youre in the area.
Our kids love playing here.... great nature path, as well as baseball fields, basketball court and decent pavilion & kids playground. Worth a visit and the cost is absolutely free!
Nice open area to walk around. Soccer fields, playgrounds, walking path, access to the creek as well. Ample parking. They host an annual Apple Festival there as well.
really fun spot for kids. they have a large wooden playground as well as swings, pavilion s, picnic tables and nice views of Swatara Creek.
Small park with a playground, basketball court, pavilions and restrooms. Great views, and a solid spot to have a picnic.

We visited Clark Park on spring weekend afternoon and were there with families, dog lovers and solo folks enjoying the activity. The park spans 2 streets with a busy road in-between. There's a section with tables, park benches, sculptures and paved walkways. There was a flea market and some picnics going on when we were there. The other part of the park is called a dog park, but it is a big grassy rolling area where dogs run off leash, with no enclosure. Off to the side was a playground and basketball court. We admired the ornate shed (see photo), wondering if that was a program space in normal times. The park is close to Woodlands Cemetery in West Philly. Free street parking is possible but you have to hunt and we didn't see any trash cans or restrooms on site.

We visited on a Sunday with our dog, hiking from the Pine Road entrance to Verree Road and back. The Park was very crowded, with groups hanging out by the Pennypack Creek, fishing, and strolling. We started out on the paved trail that runs parallel to the creek. This trail was overrun with bicyclists speeding by. Instead, take the unpaved path on the other side of the creek, entering at Verree Road. This path was shady, and less congested with foot traffic. There are no trash cans, and the 1 restroom we saw was locked. HIghlights are Thoreau's Hut, the creek and the park grounds. Across from Pine Road is Fox Chase Farm, an educational working farm open to the public. You can walk the trail and see cows.

Well-maintained nature preserve in Wayne open to all, with lots of short trail choices. Several trails run along a creek or uphill to walk through forested areas. It is a carry in/carry out park which welcomes leashed dogs. Highlights are the Monkey Rocks, the Veterans memorial and crossing some wooden bridges over the creeks. The park is supported by community volunteers who welcome donations. There is free parking in the school lot by the park entrance, when school is out. Visit their website and print out or snap a photo of their color map. If not, no worries, since the trails are clearly marked and labelled. There are a few benches along the trails but no restrooms or water station.

This neighborhood youth recreation center has a baseball/soccer field, playground, outdoor pool and fills a full city block.The outdoor basketball court was recently renovated, and is open daily to everyone. It's a popular dog-walking destination especially in late afternoons and weekends. If you enjoy outdoor art, come to admire 3 large-scale murals celebrating sports, history and the arts. There's a 60-foot mural by Joshua Mays with 40 portraits honoring African-American contributions to baseball. The mural wraps around the Ryan Howard Youth Baseball training center. Mark Stockton's mural of Marian Anderson alone is worth a trip. There are trash cans but no public parking.

First discovered this Philly hidden gem by borrowing a free visitor pass from my public library. Great fall color tour location, but there's so much to enjoy year-round for all ages. There's a treehouse, a living sculpture perfect for hide & seek, toy trains running, and a scarecrow contest in the fall. On our last visit, we made it up to the Zen garden and down to the sauna-like fernery . We stumbled upon a "sculpture garden" with frogs and nymphs half-buried in the grasses. If you have more time, there's a footpath that overlooks the Wissahickon Creek. Note that dogs are not allowed and food options are limited outside of summer peak hours.
likes: Diverse attractions (treehouse, living sculpture, toy trains)
Unique features (Zen garden, fernery, sculpture garden)

reviews_attraction.text: We've been Art Museum members for a few years and it's always an adventure visiting. These photos are from a Highlights tour we did with a relative who had never visited before. The immersive rooms from different centuries are a great place to start. We usually end with the impressionist painting wing with the Van Gogh sunflowers and Monet waterliliies bridge. The best advice is to see the museum over 2 days to avoid overload: the general admission ticket is for 2 days. It includes the Rodin Museum and the other Art Museum building which has more contemporary, temporary exhibits. Looking forward to the opening of the new wing in May 2021.

Photogenic afternoon hiking destination overlooking the Schuylkill River in Fairmount Park. Park at the free WaterWorks lot. At a leisurely pace, you can stroll along the river up to East Falls Bridge and back within the 2 hour parking limit (about 4.5 miles round-trip). The steel truss bridge is a classic beauty. It was built in 1895 with intricate detailing on the railings. From the bridge, you can see back to Laurel Hill Cemetery and watch the river boat action. Saw my first outrigger boats. The river walk and pedestrian bridge are dog-friendly. East Falls restaurants had outdoor seating and several welcomed bikers. We will be back.

Enjoyed a late afternoon walk along the Tacony Creek trail from the entrance by the Juniata Golf Course up to the historic marker for Whitaker Mill. Look for a trail map by the entrance which marks highlights like the Fisher Bridge, built before 1800. Passed by a bunch of graffitied rocks before we discovered gorgeous bird murals on an underpass. There are paved and dirt trails with few benches, no trash cans or restrooms. Right before the Mill marker, look for the overgrown baseball field batting cages. The park is dog-friendly with street parking for visitors.

You can walk, run, bike this part of the Schuylkill River Trail up to the University Avenue Bridge. Highlights include a skate park and a new walkout fishing pier. There is a paved flat trail, with river and city views. There are some benches and trash cans along the way. The start of the Cresent Trail section is popular for fishing. You can find free street parking in the Grays Ferry neighborhood if you want to start the trail from here. We discovered that the Innovation Center ( where we planned to park) is closed to visitors/parking on the weekend.

Starr Garden features a playground, basketball court, a youth recreation center, and a large grassy field used mainly for youth and neighborhood soccer games. It's a cool shady spot in the summer, thanks to the large trees that ring the park. Twice a year, we join other Love your Park volunteers to rake leaves and help spruce it up. There's an afterschool arts program that has created colorful crocheted stars and a ballerina that grace the chain link fences. Starr Garden is friendly for on-leash dogs.

Historic park on the Delaware River that marks where William Penn made his treaty with Native Americans in 1682 of "unbroken faith". Great views and there's a new  paved extension of the river trail leading from the park to the new casino. Like most Philly sites, it was a mutli-use spot, with an abandoned factory and smokestacks beyond the treed park area. Parking is limited on the streets nearby. We took our dog for a stroll here and he enjoyed greeting all the other dogs touring the park too.

Set into the mountains on 89 acres overlooking Uniontown. Built in 1953, it was one of Wright's last houses, and reflects his later Usonian style.
The house is so well-ventilated it needs no air conditioning. Unlike other Wright homes, this has never had structural or leaking problems, thanks to a steel frame. Outdoor photography only allowed, and you must book a guided tour to visit. We enjoyed strolling through the sculpture garden, which includes a section from the Berlin Wall.

One of our favorite walks any time of year. I recommend heading left from the Water Works and stroll past the Art Museum. There is a riverside trail with a historic tribute to early businesses and indigenous peoples. There is a free parking lot with 2-hour parking, if you're lucky. If it's full, you can find free parking up the road at Fairmount Park. This walk is dog-friendly, but there is a flight of stone stairs to head down and the trail ends by the bridge with a turnaround.

Our family visited Memorial Day weekend. The memorial honors the 648 service men and women killed during the Vietnam War. There is a separate memorial in Vietnamese thanking the soliders for their service. The beautifully landscaped installation is open 24/7 with some seating and adjacent to the Korean War Memorial. They are collecting donations (almost near their goal) to build a POW/MIA memorial here. Commemorative services are usually held here on Veterans and Memorial Days.

Nicely maintained park with a bocce court near the Italian Market. Friendly community gathering spot to watch World Cup soccer and enjoy neighborhood celebrations year-round. It's dog friendly and family friendly with a coffee shop, church and community garden nearby. This is a carry in/out park. They organize seasonal family activities, like the milkjug lantern craft during the winter, and community photo exhibit in the spring.

Peaceful, well-maintained little park bookmarked with David Guin's Summer murals from his Mural Arts Seasons Series. There are benches, trash cans and all-weather metal picnic tables. The Friends of this Park take great care of the plantings, and they welcome dog walkers. It is next to the Fleisher Art school. We've walked by wedding ceremonies, outdoor art classes and other happy celebrations here.

Free access to pier for catch and release fishing, picnicking or for panoramic views of the Delaware River. Year-round you can scan from Ben Franklin Bridge out left to the Walt Whitman Bridge on the right.
It's steps from the Walmart/Home Depot shopping center on Columbus Blvd. Or do the 1 mile trail hike from Washington Pier.  Walk a little farther to see the feral cats that locals care for.

Bartram's Garden is a treat to visit across 4 seasons. During our last visit in late winter, we walked the newish Bartram's Garden trail along the river, and explored the boathouse. By Bartram's house, our keen-scenting dog led us to a stone cider press that Bartram built. There's a sign explaining Bartram sold cider to visits who would paddle up in their botas from the  Schuylkill River.

Photogenic hike on unpaved trails along the Rocky Run creek that meandered through woods, abandoned railroad tracks and a meadow. It is a carry in/out park that is dog friendly with limited adjacent parking. Multiple wildlife sightings of frogs, spiders and fish. For the more adventurous, walk the train track planks where you look through the planks at the river far below.

Moving, immersive tribute to the 600+ service men and women from greater Philadelphia who were killed, missing or POW from the Korean War. Names of all laser engraved on stone pillars plus commemorative brick walkway. This outdoor memorial is open 24/7 near Penns Landing and the other Memorial installations. Look for the bronze statue The Final Farewell created 2007.

It was the perfect rainy-day outing for kids of all ages. We adults enjoyed the lego movies, the interactive ride, and Lego Philadelphia. We came with 2 young children and they would happily have stayed all day. Thanks for offering the discounts to make it affordable for our large group. Great that parking is free and you're in the Plymouth Meeting Mall.

We visited the Zoo's first Luminature celebration over the Christmas holiday. We will be back in the spring and next year! The multimedia light and music show was spectacular. Allow at least 2 hours to experience the performers, the polar bear video show and to stroll the grounds. There is paid zoo parking which we recommend that you reserve in advance.

I discovered the Athenaeum during COVID and have attended several of their enlightening online evening presentations such as Philadelphia Builds. I was amazed to find that these talks are free. The building is located near Independence Hall and I hope to visit them in person in the near future.

Stoneleigh House and grounds are free for the public to explore and enjoy  daily thanks to Natural Lands Trust's preservation efforts. In the past year of their guardianship, volunteers have done an amazing job with plantings and maintenance. There is parking onsite, but no dogs are allowed.

One of my top-10 spots to visit and revisit in Philly. Everyone should see Isaiah's wonderland on a sunny day and then come back, as we did, for a Twilight Garden party visit. Then, come back again to do the special basement tour, where most of these photos were taken.

We drove 3.5 hours to get here, and it was worth every minute. Do the tour. We have a 2 and 4 year old, and they were both entranced, as was I.  There are a lot of fun animals to see in the drive through area, as well as the peeing zoo. This includes being to feed giraffes and buffalo and deer, as well as hanging out with hundreds of colorful budgie birds who happily land on you
